nodes.statement: A bemphbipartite factor graph is a graph G=(V,F,E) whose vertex set Vcup F is partitioned into bemphvariables V and bemphclauses F, with undirected edges E joining variables to clauses. We generically denote variables u,v,w, clauses a,b,c, and edges e. For each edge e, we write a(e) for the incident clause and v(e) for the incident variable. Each e comes with a bemphsign SPINL_e, indicating whether the inclusion of variable v(e) in clause a(e) is positive (SPINL_e=SPIN+) or negative (SPINL_e=SPIN-). We allow for multi-edges, so G might have two edges e,e' joining a to v (possibly with SPINL_eneSPINL_e')). If there is a unique edge e joining clause a to variable v, we will sometimes denote it as e=(av)=(va), and write SPINL_eequivSPINL_av. For any vertex xin Vcup F, we write partial x for its neighboring vertices. Similarly we write delta x for the edges incident to x. For each clause ain F we regard partial a and delta a as bemphordered tuples. For each edge ein E we write j(e) to indicate the position of e in delta a(e), so j(e)in[k]. \label{d:vfe}
A \bemph{bipartite factor graph} is a graph $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$ whose vertex set $V\cup F$ is partitioned into \bemph{variables} $V$ and \bemph{clauses} $F$,
with undirected edges $E$ joining variables to clauses.
We generically denote variables $u,v,w$, clauses $a,b,c$, and edges $e$. For each edge $e$, we write $a(e)$ for the incident clause and $v(e)$ for the incident variable. Each $e$ comes with a \bemph{sign} $\SPIN{L}_e$, indicating whether the inclusion of variable $v(e)$ in clause $a(e)$ is positive ($\SPIN{L}_e=\SPIN{+}$) or negative ($\SPIN{L}_e=\SPIN{-}$). We allow for multi-edges, so $\mathscr{G}$ might have two edges $e,e'$ joining $a$ to $v$ (possibly with $\SPIN{L}_e\ne\SPIN{L}_{e'})$). If there is a unique edge $e$ joining clause $a$ to variable $v$, we will sometimes denote it as $e=(av)=(va)$, and write $\SPIN{L}_e\equiv\SPIN{L}_{av}$. For any vertex $x\in V\cup F$, we write $\partial x$ for its neighboring vertices. Similarly we write $\delta x$ for the edges incident to $x$. For each clause $a\in F$ we regard $\partial a$ and $\delta a$ as \bemph{ordered tuples}. For each edge $e\in E$ we write $j(e)$ to indicate the position of $e$ in $\delta a(e)$, so $j(e)\in[k]$. For each variable $v\in V$ we partition its neighbors and incident edges according to edge sign:
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
	\begin{alignat}{2}
	\nonumber
	\delta v(\SPIN{+})
		&\equiv\set{e\in\delta v
			: \SPIN{L}_e=\SPIN{+}}\,,\quad
	& \partial v(\SPIN{+})
		&\equiv\set{a(e) : e\in\delta v(\SPIN{+})}\,,\\
	\delta v(\SPIN{-})
		&\equiv\set{e\in\delta v
			: \SPIN{L}_e=\SPIN{-}}\,,\quad
	&\partial v(\SPIN{-}) 
		&\equiv\set{a(e) : e\in\delta v(\SPIN{-})}\,.
	\label{e:var.signed.half.edges}
	\end{alignat}}
(In scenarios with multi-edges, the sets
$\partial v(\SPIN{+})$ and $\partial v(\SPIN{-})$ can intersect, and are not in one-to-one correspondence with the sets $\delta v(\SPIN{\textpm})$. For this reason, we always work with $\delta v(\SPIN{\textpm})$ to avoid ambiguity, except in cases where multi-edges are expressly prohibited.) 
We will also refer to $\mathscr{G}$ as a \bemph{\textsc{sat} problem instance}. Furthermore we call $\mathscr{G}$ a \bemph{$\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ problem instance} if each clause $a\in F$ has width $|\delta a|=k$.

nodes.statement: If G=(V,F,E) is a bipartite factor graph as in Definition~, it defines a mapping G : setSPIN+,SPIN-^Vto set0,1 as follows: for any bemphvariable assignment vecxinsetSPIN+,SPIN-^V, \[ G(vecx) equivprod_ain F bigg\1 - prod_eindelta a frac1-SPINL_e x_v(e)2bigg\\,. \] The instance G is called bemphsatisfiable if and only if its set \[textupfootnotesize SOL(G) equivG^-1(1) equivbigg\smashvecxinsetSPIN+,SPIN-^V :G(smashvecx)=1bigg\ subseteqsetSPIN+,SPIN-^V\] of bemphsatisfying assignments is nonempty.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:formal.dfn.sat}
If $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$ is a bipartite factor graph as in Definition~\ref{d:vfe}, it defines a mapping
$\mathscr{G} : \set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}^V\to \set{0,1}$
as follows:
for any \bemph{variable assignment}
$\vec{x}\in\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}^V$,
	\[
	\mathscr{G}(\vec{x}) 
	\equiv\prod_{a\in F}
		\bigg\{1 - \prod_{e\in\delta a}
			\frac{1-\SPIN{L}_e x_{v(e)}}{2}\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The instance $\mathscr{G}$ is called \bemph{satisfiable} if and only if its set
	\[\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize SOL}}(\mathscr{G})
	\equiv\mathscr{G}^{-1}(1)
	\equiv\bigg\{\smash{\vec{x}}\in\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}^V
		:\mathscr{G}(\smash{\vec{x}})=1\bigg\}
	\subseteq\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}^V\]
of \bemph{satisfying assignments} is nonempty.

nodes.name: random $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$
nodes.statement: To generate an instance of the bemphrandom textupk-textscsat model at clause density alpha, start with n labelled variables V = [n] equiv set1,ldots,n, as well as M labelled clauses F = [M]equivset1,ldots,M, where M is sampled from the textupPois(nalpha) distribution. Independently for each clause ain F, sample its k-tuple of variables partial a uniformly at random from V^k=[n]^k, then sample the k-tuple of signs (SPINL_e)_eindelta a uniformly at random from setSPIN+,SPIN-^k. This defines a family of probability measures PequivP^n,alpha over textupk-textscsat instances, indexed by n and parametrized by the expected clause density alpha. Writing P_n,m for the measure P conditioned on M=m, we can decompose P equiv P^n,alpha = sum_mge0 textuppois_nalpha(m)P_n,m\,, textuppois_lambda(m) equiv frace^-lambdalambda^mm!\,. Note that the conditional measure P_n,m does not depend on alpha.

nodes.statement: A textscsat problem instance can be equivalently viewed as a hypergraph, with vertices and hyperedges corresponding to variables and clauses respectively. Each hyperedge should be viewed as an ordered tuple (v_1,ldots,v_k) of variables, with corresponding signs (SPINL_1,ldots,SPINL_k). A textupk-textscsat instance thus corresponds to a k-uniform hypergraph. If G=(V,F,E) is the bipartite factor graph representation of a textscsat instance, we assign length 1/2 to all its edges, so that graph distances in G will be consistent with the standard graph distances in the hypergraph representation. For any vertex x in G we will write partial_s x for the set of vertices at distance s from x. We will write N(x)equiv partial_1(x). If v is a variable then N(v) is the set of variables sharing a clause with v, and we often refer to these as the ``neighboring variables of v.''

nodes.statement: Place a graph structure on the set textupfootnotesize SOL(G)equivG^-1(1) of satisfying assignments by putting an edge between any pair of assignments at Hamming distance one, and define a bemphcluster of solutions to be a (maximal) connected component of the graph G^-1(1). As has been explained in the literature (see e.g.\ ), frozen configurations encode clusters in the sense that there is a natural mapping textupcoarsen: G^-1(1) longrightarrow bigg\ textupfrozen configurations on G bigg\\,. If G has no multi-edges, then each cluster Csubseteq G^-1(1) maps to a single frozen configuration textupcoarsen(C). To define the map, given a configuration smashvecxinsetSPIN+,SPIN-,SPINf^V that does not violate any clauses (in the sense of Definition~), let us say that a variable vin V is bemphblocked with respect to smashvecx if there is some eindelta v such that SPINL_e'x_v(e') = SPIN- SPINL_e x_v(e) for all e'indelta a(e)setminus e (cf.\ Definition~). Define textupco(smashvecx) = vecy where \[ y_v=left\hspace-3pt cl x_v & textupif v is blocked with respect to smashvecx;\\ SPINf & textupotherwise. right. \] The map of is defined by iterating textupco until the configuration stabilizes, i.e., textupcoarsenequivtextupco^infty. Note that termination happens in finite time, since if textupco(smashvecx)nesmashvecx then textupco(smashvecx) has strictly more SPINf variables than smashvecx. If G has no multi-edges, then the value of textupco(smashvecx) at any variable v is a function of the neighboring values x_u, uin N(v). Consequently, if smashvecx and smashvecx' differ in a single coordinate, then textupco(smashvecx)=textupco(smashvecx'). Iterating this gives textupcoarsen(smashvecx)=textupcoarsen(smashvecx') as long as smashvecx,smashvecx' lie in the same cluster. This shows that the map takes each cluster C to a single frozen configuration.

nodes.statement: Warning configurations are in bijective correspondence with frozen configurations of G. If vecSPINw is a valid warning configuration of G, we can obtain a valid frozen configuration smashvecx of G simply by taking \[ x_v = dotWbigg( SPINL_e hatSPINw_e : eindelta vbigg) \] for all vin V. Conversely, if smashvecx is a valid frozen configuration of G, we can obtain a valid warning configuration vecSPINw of G by to the following procedure: [(i)] item If eindelta v with x_v=SPINf, then we must have SPINw_e=(SPINf,SPINf). item If eindelta v with x_vinsetSPIN+,SPIN- and SPINL_e x_v=SPIN-, then we must have SPINw_e=(SPIN-,SPINf). item If eindelta v with x_vinsetSPIN+,SPIN- and SPINL_e x_v=SPIN+, then \[ hatSPINw_e =left\rl SPIN+ & textupif SPINw_e'=(SPIN-,SPINf) for all e'indelta a(e)setminus e\\ SPINf & textupotherwise. right. \] item The above determines of hatSPINw_e for all e. We can then determine dotSPINw_e for all e by applying the textscwp rules . We leave the reader to verify that these mappings are inverses of one another.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{r:bij.wp.frozen} Warning configurations are in bijective correspondence with frozen configurations of $\mathscr{G}$. If $\vec{\SPIN{w}}$ is a valid warning configuration of $\mathscr{G}$, we can obtain a valid frozen configuration $\smash{\vec{x}}$ of $\mathscr{G}$ simply by taking
	\[
	x_v = \dot{W}\bigg( \SPIN{L}_e \hat{\SPIN{w}}_e : e\in\delta v\bigg)
	\]
for all $v\in V$. Conversely, if $\smash{\vec{x}}$ is a valid frozen configuration of $\mathscr{G}$, we can obtain a valid warning configuration $\vec{\SPIN{w}}$ of $\mathscr{G}$ by to the following procedure:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $e\in\delta v$ with
$x_v=\SPIN{f}$, then we must have $\SPIN{w}_e=(\SPIN{f},\SPIN{f})$.

\item If $e\in\delta v$ with $x_v\in\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}$ 
and $\SPIN{L}_e x_v=\SPIN{-}$, then we must have $\SPIN{w}_e=(\SPIN{-},\SPIN{f})$.

\item If $e\in\delta v$ with $x_v\in\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}$ 
and $\SPIN{L}_e x_v=\SPIN{+}$, then
	\[
	\hat{\SPIN{w}}_e
	=\left\{\begin{array}{rl}
	\SPIN{+} & \textup{if 
		$\SPIN{w}_{e'}=(\SPIN{-},\SPIN{f})$
		for all $e'\in\delta a(e)\setminus e$}\\
	\SPIN{f} & \textup{otherwise.}
	\end{array}\right.
	\]

\item The above determines of $\hat{\SPIN{w}}_e$ for all $e$. We can then determine $\dot{\SPIN{w}}_e$ for all $e$ by applying the \textsc{wp} rules \eqref{e:dot.WP}.
\end{enumerate}
We leave the reader to verify that these mappings are inverses of one another.

\label{r:bij.color.frozen}
Colorings are in bijective correspondence 
with frozen configurations of $\mathscr{G}$. To see this,
let $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ denote the colors
on the incident edges of variable $v$, 
recall the notation \eqref{e:var.signed.half.edges}, and define
	\begin{equation}\label{e:EVAL.of.color}
	x_v = \textup{\textsf{eval}}_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\equiv\left\{\hspace{-5pt}\begin{array}{rll}
	\SPIN{+} & \text{if
		$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v(\SPIN{-})}$
		is all $\SSPIN{y}$, and
		$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v(\SPIN{+})}$
		is all $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{b}}$
		with at least one $\SSPIN{r}$}
		\\
	\SPIN{-} & \text{if $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v(\SPIN{+})}$
		is all $\SSPIN{y}$, and
		$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v(\SPIN{-})}$
		is all $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{b}}$
		with at least one $\SSPIN{r}$}
		\\
	\SPIN{f} & \text{if 
		$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ is all $\SSPIN{g}$}
		\\
	\varnothing & \text{otherwise.}
	\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
If $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$ is a valid coloring of $\mathscr{G}$, then taking $x_v=\textup{\textsf{eval}}_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})$ for all $v\in V$ defines a valid frozen configuration $\smash{\vec{x}}$ of $\mathscr{G}$. By Remark~\ref{r:bij.wp.frozen}, $\smash{\vec{x}}$ corresponds to a unique warning configuration $\vec{\SPIN{w}}$. We leave the reader to verify that $\textup{\textsf{proj}}$ maps $\vec{\SPIN{w}}$ back to the starting $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$, which completes the correspondence.

\label{r:single.copy.pair}
We will sometimes refer to the color model above as the \bemph{single-copy} color model, to distinguish it from the \bemph{pair} color model which
appears in the second moment: the latter is supported on pairs $(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^1,\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^2)$ with each $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^j$ a valid coloring of the same graph $\mathscr{G}$. If we extend $\varphi_v,\hat{\varphi}_a$ to pair inputs by setting
	\begin{align*}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^1_{\delta v},
		\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^2_{\delta v})
	&\equiv
	\prod_{j=1,2}\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^j_{\delta v})\,,\\
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^1_{\delta a},
		\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^2_{\delta a})
	&\equiv
	\prod_{j=1,2}\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^j_{\delta a})\,,
	\end{align*}

\label{d:simple.types} In a graph $\mathscr{G}$, the \bemph{simple type} $t_e$ of a clause-variable edge $e\equiv(av)\equiv(va)\in E$ is the isomorphism class of $(B_R(v),e)$, the $R$-neighborhood around $v$ rooted at edge $e$.\footnote{The edge-rooted graphs $(T_i,e_i)$, $i=1,2$, are isomorphic if there is a bijective graph homomorphism $\iota : T_1 \to T_2$ which maps $e_1$ to $e_2$, preserves all edge labels $\SPIN{L}_{av}\in\set{\SPIN{+},\SPIN{-}}$ and indices $j(v;a)\in[k]$, and preserves all variable marks $\bm{l}(v)
\in\set{1,\ldots, \exp(\lceil 4^k R\rceil) }$.} We write $j(t_e)\equiv j(v;a)$ to indicate the position of the edge in the clause. The \bemph{simple type} of a vertex $x \in V \cup F$ is the multi-set of simple types of all incident edges, $\set{t_e : e\in\delta x}$. Note that this has a different meaning depending on whether $x$ is a clause or a variable:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $x\in F$ is a clause, then its simple type --- which we hereafter denote $L_x$ --- is a multi-set with no repeated elements, since each edge $e\in\delta x$ has a distinct index $j(t_e)\in[k]$. Thus $L_x$ is equivalently represented as the ordered $k$-tuple $(L_x(1),\ldots,L_x(k))$ where $L_x(j)$ is the type of the $j$-th edge in $\delta x$.

\item If $x\in V$ is a variable, then
its simple type --- which we hereafter denote $T_x$ --- may have repeated elements. It is equivalently represented as the isomorphism class of $B_R(v)$ regarded as a graph rooted at $v$.
\end{enumerate}
We say that an edge $e$ is \bemph{acyclic} if its simple type $t_e$ is acyclic. We say that $e$ is \bemph{proper} if it is acyclic, and moreover no two variables $u\ne w$ in $t_e$ receive the same mark $\bm{l}_R(u)=\bm{l}_R(w)$. A vertex will be termed \bemph{acyclic} (resp.\ \bemph{proper}) if all its incident edges are acyclic (resp.\ proper). If $v\in V$ is a proper variable, then its simple type $T_v$ has no repeated elements.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:directed.trees}
If $T$ is any bipartite factor tree and $e=(av)$ is any edge in $T$:
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item We let $T_{va}$ be the connected component of $T\setminus a$ that contains $v$. We regard $T_{va}$ as being rooted at $v$, where $v$ has parent edge $e$
that points to the deleted clause $a$. We call $T_{va}$ a \bemph{variable-to-clause tree}.
\item Similarly we let $T_{av}$ be the connected component of $T\setminus v$ that contains $a$. 
We regard $T_{av}$ as being rooted at $a$, where $a$ has parent edge $e$
that points to the deleted clause $v$. We call $T_{av}$ a \bemph{clause-to-variable tree}.
\end{enumerate}
We will refer to both $T_{va}$ and $T_{av}$ as \bemph{directed trees}. Note that trees of this kind have already appeared previously, in the discussions of \S\ref{ss:wp.recursions}.

where $\zeta$ is the absolute constant from Definition~\ref{d:error.notation.edge}. Finally we will take $\zeta=\zeta_*/4$ where $\zeta_*$ is the absolute constant from an \textit{a~priori} estimate, Proposition~\ref{p:apriori}.} Recall \eqref{e:radii} that $R'= 10^2 r$. 
Recall \eqref{e:not.j.nice} that 
$D^{*,\mathfrak{i}}$ denotes the set of variables that are acyclic but not $\mathfrak{i}$-nice, for $\mathfrak{i}\in\set{0,1}$.
Let $D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}} \equiv B_{\kappa_*}(D^{*,\mathfrak{i}})$ be the union of $B_{\kappa_*}(v)$ over all $v\in D^{*,\mathfrak{i}}$. The set of \bemph{$\mathfrak{i}$-defective} variables is defined as
	\[\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}
	\equiv\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}(\mathscr{G})
	\equiv
	\bigg\{ v :
	v\in \textup{\textsf{BSP}}\Big( D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}
		\cap B_{R'/2}(v); 
		B_{R'/2}(v)\Big)\bigg\}\,.
	\]
We use \bemph{0-defective} and \bemph{defective} interchangeably; note $\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^0(\mathscr{G})\subseteq\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^1(\mathscr{G})$. Whether a variable is $\mathfrak{i}$-defective can be determined from its $R'$-neighborhood. We say that a clause $a$ is \bemph{$\mathfrak{i}$-defective} if all its incident variables are $\mathfrak{i}$-defective. A $\mathfrak{i}$-\bemph{defect} of $\mathscr{G}$ is a (maximal) connected component of $\mathfrak{i}$-defective variables and clauses. Note that each $\mathfrak{i}$-defect has at its boundary a buffer of nice variables of depth at least $\kappa_*$.

nodes.name: orderly
nodes.statement: For iinset0,1, we say that an acyclic variable v is i-bemphorderly if along any path emanating from v of length at most R', at most (delta_*)^3 fraction of variables along the path are i-defective. In particular, a path leaving v of length less than (delta_*)^-3 cannot contain any i-defective variable: that is to say, an i-bemphorderly variable cannot lie within distance (delta_*)^-3 of any defect. Since being i-defective is a property of a variable's R'-neighborhood, being i-orderly is a property of a variable's 2R'-neighborhood.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:orderly}
For $\mathfrak{i}\in\set{0,1}$, we say that an acyclic variable $v$ is $\mathfrak{i}$-\bemph{orderly} if along any path emanating from $v$ of length at most $R'$, at most $(\delta_*)^3$ fraction of variables along the path are $\mathfrak{i}$-defective. In particular, a path leaving $v$ of length less than $(\delta_*)^{-3}$ cannot contain any $\mathfrak{i}$-defective variable: that is to say, an $\mathfrak{i}$-\bemph{orderly} variable cannot lie within distance $(\delta_*)^{-3}$ of any defect. Since being $\mathfrak{i}$-defective is a property of a variable's $R'$-neighborhood, being $\mathfrak{i}$-orderly is a property of a variable's $2R'$-neighborhood.

nodes.statement: The bemphtotal type bmt equiv bmt_e of an edge e in textupprG is defined to be its compound type if it belongs to a compound enclosure, and its simple total type otherwise. The bemphtotal type of a variable or clause in textupprG is the multi-set of incident edge total types --- since improper variables were removed during processing, the multi-sets are now simply sets. We hereafter use bmT to denote variable total types, and bmL to denote clause total types. For an edge e=(av) of type bmt we write j(bmt)equiv j(v;a) for the position of the variable within the clause. We write bmtinbmL to indicate compatibility of types in the sense that bmL(j(bmt)) = bmt.

nodes.statement: The processed graph G=textupprG' is a subgraph of the original graph G', and therefore carries less information in general. For the rest of this paper, whenever we refer to the processed graph G, we assume that each vertex and each edge of G carries the information of its total type. In particular, each variable in G does carry the information concerning its simple type (Definition~), even if part of its original R-neighborhood is deleted during processing. However, G does not carry the information of the entire original graph G', so we still do allow for the possibility that textupprG'=textupprG'' for G'neG''. We let textupCM(D) denote the set of all graphs G consistent with a given neighborhood sequence D (where G is interpreted as we have just described). In particular, |textupCM(D)| = prod_bmt (n_bmt)! \,. The notation textupCM stands for configuration model. A uniformly random element of textupCM(D) can be sampled by a generalization of the standard configuration model for graphs with given degree sequence --- this type of construction goes back to , and we refer to for a survey. Generalized configuration models were analyzed in detail in , and the sampling procedure can be described as follows. Start with a collection of isolated vertices --- n variables V together with m clauses F --- labelled with total types according to D. Each vertex is then equipped with the appropriate number of ``half-edges,'' all labelled with edge total types. The total number of half-edges incident to each vertex corresponds to its degree in the processed graph G. Let delta V denote the variable-incident half-edges, and delta F the clause-incident half-edges. Then take a uniformly random matching between delta V and delta F that bemphrespects edge total types. (A full edge consists of one variable-incident half-edge matched together with one clause-incident half-edge.) This procedure generates a uniformly random element of textupCM(D). This discussion is most relevant to the statement of Proposition~ below.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem~\ref{t:main}
nodes.statement: Propositions~~and~ together show that for random textupk-textscsat with kge k_0, the textup1-textscrsb free energy Phi(alpha) is well-defined, with a unique root alpha_star in the interval . It follows from Proposition~ that alpha_star upper bounds the satisfiability regime, so it remains to show the lower bound. To this end, let alpha<alpha_star (still within the regime ), so that Phi(alpha)>0. We divide the rest of the argument into two parts: bemphStep 1. Lower bound on separable colorings. Analogously to , decompose \[(bmZ_textupsep)^2=sum_z (bmZ_textupsep)^2[z]\,.\] Let (bmZ_textupsep)^2[I] denote the sum of (bmZ_textupsep)^2[z] over zin Isubseteq[0,1]. By the separability condition (Definition~), \[(bmZ_textupsep)^2Big[[0,1]setminus I_0Big] le e^o(n) bmZ_textupsep le e^o(n) bmZ\] almost surely. Recall the definition of L_textupgirth from . Proposition~ gives the bound \[L_textupgirthBigg( E_DBig[(bmZ_textupsep)^2[I_0]Big] leE_DBig[bmZ^2[I_0]Big] le CBig(E_DbmZBig)^2 Bigg) = 1-o_n(1)\] for C=C(k,R). Combining the above bounds gives L_textupgirthBigg( E_DBig((bmZ_textupsep)^2Big) le C Big(E_DbmZBig)^2 + e^o(n)\,E_DbmZ Bigg) = 1-o_n(1)\,. nodes.statement: Note that Propositions -- (stated in S, proved in Section~) are not directly referenced in the above proof of Theorem~. Instead, they are used indirectly via the other propositions. In particular, for the first moment (Proposition~), the uniformity result (Proposition~) provides a simple combinatorial formula for E_DbmZ. We then need the result that only o_R(1) fraction of the variables are removed (Proposition~) to relate the combinatorial formula to the textup1-textscrsb free energy . The second moment (Proposition~) similarly relies on Proposition~ for the combinatorial formula, but additionally requires the result that each type occurs linearly many times (Proposition~) to estimate the combinatorial formula up to a constant multiplicative error.

It suffices to verify that
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{\nu}_v(\sigma_{av}=\sigma)
	&\cong
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma_{av})
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}}
	\Ind{\sigma_{av}=\sigma}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{b \in \partial v\setminus a}
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{bv}(\sigma_{bv})\\
	&\cong{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma_{av})
	\bigg\{
	\Big(\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{va}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}]\Big)(\sigma_{av})
	\bigg\}
	={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma_{av})
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{va}(\sigma_{av})
	\cong {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)\,,
	\label{e:marginal.of.nu.BP}
	\end{align}
where $\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}$ is the belief propagation mapping for the color model (the unweighted version of \eqref{e:bp}),
and the last two identities follow from the fact that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}$, ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{va}$, and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{av}$ are all based on the \bemph{same} tree, namely,
the $r$-neighborhood of $v$ in $\mathscr{G}$
(see also Remark~\ref{r:first.rmk.coherence}).

\label{d:bethe.laws.of.color.messages}
Let $\mu$ be the measure given by Proposition~\ref{p:fp}, and let $\smash{\vec{\eta}}$ be an array of i.i.d.\ samples from $\mu$. Let $\smash{\vec{d}} \equiv (d^\SPIN{+},d^\SPIN{-})$ be two independent samples from the $\textup{\textsf{Pois}}(\alpha k/2)$ distribution. Define $\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}\equiv\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}(\vec d,\vec\eta)$ as in \eqref{e:Pi.PM}, and define
(cf.\ \eqref{e:intro.dist.recurs})
	\[
	\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{+})
	= \frac{(1-\Pi^\SPIN{+})\Pi^\SPIN{-}}
		{\Pi^\SPIN{+}+\Pi^\SPIN{-}-\Pi^\SPIN{+}\Pi^\SPIN{-}},\quad
	\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{-})
	= \frac{(1-\Pi^\SPIN{-})\Pi^\SPIN{+}}
		{\Pi^\SPIN{+}+\Pi^\SPIN{-}-\Pi^\SPIN{+}\Pi^\SPIN{-}},\quad
	\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{f})
	= \frac{\Pi^\SPIN{+}\Pi^\SPIN{-}}
		{\Pi^\SPIN{+}+\Pi^\SPIN{-}-\Pi^\SPIN{+}\Pi^\SPIN{-}}\,,
	\]
so that $\bm{\eta}$ is a (random) probability measure over $\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}$. Now let $\bm{\eta}_j$ be i.i.d.\ copies of $\bm{\eta}$, and define (cf.\ \eqref{e:first.defn.of.bhu})
	\begin{equation}\label{e:second.defn.of.bhu}
	\bm{\hat{u}}
	\equiv 
	\Big(\bm{\hat{u}}(\SPIN{+}),\bm{\hat{u}}(\SPIN{f})\Big)
		= 
		\bigg(
		\prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \bm{\eta}_j(\SPIN{-}),
		1-\prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \bm{\eta}_j(\SPIN{-})
		\bigg)\,.\end{equation}
We substitute the random measures $\bm{\eta}$ and $\bm{\hat{u}}$
into \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta}
to define random messages for the color model:
	\begin{align}
	\label{e:color.recursions.eta.again}
	\dot{q}(\bm{\eta})
	&=(\dot{q}(\SSPIN{r}),
		\dot{q}(\SSPIN{y}),
		\dot{q}(\SSPIN{g}),\dot{q}(\SSPIN{b}))
	=\frac{( \bm{\eta}(\SPIN{+})+\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{f}),
		\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{-}),
		\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{f}),
		\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{+})
		 )}
		{ 2-\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{-}) }\,,\\
	\hat{q}[(\bm{\eta}_j)_{j\ge1}]
		&=(\hat{q}(\SSPIN{r}),
			\hat{q}(\SSPIN{y})=\hat{q}(\SSPIN{g})=\hat{q}(\SSPIN{b}))
		= \frac{(\bm{\hat{u}}(\SPIN{+}),
		\bm{\hat{u}}(\SPIN{f}))}
			{3-2\bm{\hat{u}}(\SPIN{+})}\,.
	\nonumber
	\end{align}
Let $\mu^\textup{col}$ denote the law of $\dot{q}$,
and let $\hat{\mu}^\textup{col}$
denote the law of $\hat{q}$.

\label{d:Phi.col}
Given a sequence of probability measures $\vec{\dot{q}}=(\dot{q}_1,\ldots,\dot{q}_k)$ on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$,
we define a probability measure on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$ by
(cf. \eqref{e:clause.tuple.measure.weighted} and \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star})
	\[
	\Big(\hat{\nu}[\vec{\dot{q}}]\Big)
		(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)
	\equiv 
	\frac{\hat{\varphi}_a(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)}
	{\bm{\hat{z}}[\vec{\dot{q}}]}
	\prod_{i=1}^k
	\dot{q}_i(\sigma_i)\,,
	\]
with $\hat{\varphi}_a$ given by \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring}.
Similarly, given integers $\smash{\vec{d}} \equiv (d^\SPIN{+},d^\SPIN{-})$
with $d=d^\SPIN{+} + d^\SPIN{-}$,
and an array $\vec{\hat{q}}
\equiv ((\hat{q}^\SPIN{+})_i,(\hat{q}^\SPIN{-})_i)_i$
of probability measures
on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$,
we define a probability measure on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^d$ by
(cf.\ \eqref{e:clause.tuple.measure.weighted} and \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star})
	\[\Big(
	\dot{\nu}[\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{\hat{q}}]\Big)(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)
	\equiv \frac{\varphi_v(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)}
		{\bm{\dot{z}}[\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{\hat{q}}]}
	\Bigg(
	\prod_{i=1}^{d^\SPIN{+}}
	(\hat{q}^\SPIN{+})_i(\sigma_i)
	\Bigg)
	\Bigg(
	\prod_{i=d^\SPIN{+}+1}^d
	(\hat{q}^\SPIN{-})_i(\sigma_i)
	\Bigg)\,,
	\]
with $\varphi_v$ given by \eqref{e:color.model.variable.factor} for a variable in which the first $d^\SPIN{+}$ incident edges have the $\SPIN{+}$ sign, and the remaining $d^\SPIN{-}$ incident edges have the $\SPIN{-}$ sign. Finally, given two measures $\dot{q}$ and $\hat{q}$ on $
\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$, define (cf.\ \eqref{e:edge.marginal.q.times.q}
and \eqref{e:defn.canonical.edge.marginal})
	\[
	\Big(\bar{\nu}[\dot{q},\hat{q}]\Big)
	(\sigma)
	\equiv \frac{\dot{q}(\sigma)\hat{q}(\sigma)}
		{\bar{z}[\dot{q},\hat{q}]}\,.
	\]
Abbreviate $\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}$ for the law of $\smash{\vec{d}}$,
and recall 
$\mu^\textup{col}$
and $\hat{\mu}^\textup{col}$
from Definition~\ref{d:bethe.laws.of.color.messages}.
Define
	\begin{align*}
	H^{\textup{col},\textup{v}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv\int
	\mathcal{H}\Big(\dot{\nu}[\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{\hat{q}}]\Big)
	\,d\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}(\smash{\vec{d}})
	\,d(\hat{\mu}^\textup{col})^\otimes(\vec{\hat{q}})\,,\\
	H^{\textup{col},\textup{cl}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv
	\int\mathcal{H}\Big(\hat{\nu}[\vec{\dot{q}}]\Big)
	\,d(\mu^\textup{col})^\otimes(\vec{\dot{q}})\,,\\
	H^{\textup{col},\textup{e}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv
	\int\int\mathcal{H}\Big(\bar{\nu}[\dot{q},\hat{q}]\Big)
	\,d\mu^\textup{col}(\dot{q})
	\,d\hat{\mu}^\textup{col}(\hat{q})\,.
	\end{align*}
(The dependence on $\alpha$ is through the law of $\smash{\vec{d}}$ as well as the measures $\mu^\textup{col}$
and $\hat{\mu}^\textup{col}$.) The \bemph{Bethe free energy of the color model} is given by (cf.\ \eqref{e:rate.function.given.gen.degseq})
	\begin{equation}\label{e:phi.col.entropic.formula}
	\Phi^\textup{col}(\alpha)
	\equiv
	H^{\textup{col},\textup{v}}(\alpha)
	+ \alpha \bigg\{
	H^{\textup{col},\textup{cl}}(\alpha)
	- k\,
		H^{\textup{col},\textup{e}}(\alpha)
		\bigg\}\,.
	\end{equation}
An equivalent (and more commonly seen) expression is given by defining
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	\Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{v}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv\int
	\ln\bm{\dot{z}}[\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{\hat{q}}]
	\,d\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}(\smash{\vec{d}})
	\,d(\hat{\mu}^\textup{col})^\otimes(\vec{\hat{q}})\,,\\
	\nonumber
	\Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{cl}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv
	\int \ln\bm{\hat{z}}[\vec{\dot{q}}]
	\,d(\mu^\textup{col})^\otimes(\vec{\dot{q}})\,,\\
	\Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{e}}(\alpha)
	&\equiv
	\int\int \ln\bar{z}[\dot{q},\hat{q}]
	\,d\mu^\textup{col}(\dot{q})
	\,d\hat{\mu}^\textup{col}(\hat{q})\,.
	\label{e:simplified.phi.col.terms}
	\end{align}
It is straightforward to check that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:simplified.phi.col}
	\Phi^\textup{col}(\alpha)
	= \Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{v}}(\alpha)
	+ \alpha \bigg\{
	\Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{cl}}(\alpha)
	- k\,\Phi^{\textup{col},\textup{e}}(\alpha)
		\bigg\}\,.
	\end{equation}
We will show in \S\ref{ss:judicious.first.mmt}
(Lemma~\ref{l:phi.equals.phi.col}) that 
$\Phi^\textup{col}(\alpha)$
is exactly the same as the $\textup{1-\textsc{rsb}}$ free energy

nodes.statement: As bmZ is defined to count only judicious configurations, in order for the contribution bmZ^2(omega) to be non-zero, omega must satisfy two properties. First, the single-copy marginals of omega must agree with the measure _starhspace-1ptomega defined in the statement of Corollary~: that is to say, for both i=1,2, we must have _starhspace-1ptomega_bmL,j(sigma^i) = (omega_bmL,j)^j(sigma^i) equiv sum_tauinsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb^2 Indtau^i=sigma^i omega_bmL,j(tau) for all bmL,j. Secondly, omega must arise as the marginal of a valid vertex measure nu=(dotnu,hatnu). We say that omega is bemphjudicious if it satisfies both these properties. (The second property is important mainly for computing the dimension of the space of feasible omega, as we will see in the proof of Lemma~ below.)

nodes.name: judicious measures on trees

Let partial_circ U be a designated nonempty subset of leaf variables. We use delta U to denote the edges incident to partial_circ U. \label{d:constrained.opt.compound.enclosure}
Let $U$ be a finite bipartite factor tree,
with all vertices and edges labelled by (mutually compatible) \bemph{compound} total types, such that all the leaves of $U$ are variables.
Let $\partial_\circ U$ be a designated nonempty subset of leaf variables. We use $\delta U$ to denote the edges incident to $\partial_\circ U$. Define the simplex of probability measures
	\[
	\bm{\Delta}(U)
	\equiv \left\{
	\hspace{-3pt}\begin{array}{c}
	\textup{probability measures $\nu$
		over pair}\\
	\textup{colorings 
		$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\equiv(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^1,\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^2)$
		of $U$}
	\end{array}\hspace{-3pt}\right\}\,.
	\]
We say that $\nu\in\bm{\Delta}(U)$ is \bemph{judicious}
if all of its edge marginals match the canonical marginals of Definition~\ref{d:canonical}: that is, for all edges $e$ in $U$ and for both $j=1,2$, 
we have
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma^j)
	=(\nu_e)^j(\sigma^j)
	\equiv \nu((\sigma_e)^j=\sigma^j)
	\equiv \sum_\tau
		\Ind{\tau^j=\sigma^j}
		\nu(\tau_e=\tau)
	\]
for all $\sigma^j\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. Note that, since all the edges in $U$ are assumed to be of compound type, this is equivalent to saying that all the edge marginals $\nu_e$ satisfy the condition \eqref{e:margin.judicious} from Definition~\ref{d:judicious.pair}. Let
$\omega$ denote a tuple $(\omega_e)_e$ 
where 
$\omega_e$ is a judicious probability measure on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$ for each edge $e$ in $U$. We then let
	\[
	\bm{J}(U ; \omega_{\delta U})
	\equiv
	\left\{
	\hspace{-3pt}\begin{array}{c}
	\nu\in\bm{\Delta}(U):
	\textup{$\nu$ is judicious,}\\
	\textup{and
	$\nu_e=\omega_e$ for all $e\in\delta U$}
	\end{array}\hspace{-3pt}
	\right\}\,,
	\]
where $\nu_e$ denotes the marginal of $\nu$ on edge $e$. We also let
	\[\bm{\Delta}(U;\omega_U)
	\equiv
	\bigg\{\nu\in\bm{\Delta}(U) : \nu_e=\omega_e
		\textup{ for all }e\in E_U\bigg\}\,,
	\]
and note that
$\bm{\Delta}(U;\omega_U)
\subseteq \bm{J}(U ; \omega_{\delta U})
\subseteq \bm{\Delta}(U)$
for any judicious $\omega$.

We also abbreviate omega_Uequiv(omega_textupin,omega_delta U) and omega_textupbdequiv(omega_delta U,omega_textupout). Assume the neighborhood profile D of G is bounded away from zero in the sense of . Then, using the notation of Definition~, we have &max_acuteomega Bigg\ bmPsi_D,2(acuteomega) -bmPsi_D,2(omega) : textupomega and acuteomega are judicious, acuteomega_textupbd=omega_textupbd Bigg\\\ &=c_textupin Bigg( max_nu Bigg\ H(nu) : nu in bmJ(U,omega_delta U)Bigg\ - max_nu Bigg\ H(nu) : nu in bmDelta(U;omega_U)Bigg\ Bigg)\,, where c_textupin depends only on D and on U, and is lower bounded by c_1. To be concrete, consider the compound case from Proposition~\ref{p:update.compound}. Roughly speaking, the approach will be to find a weight $\Lambda(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})$ (where $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$ is a pair coloring of the enclosure $U$)
which is ``Lagrangian'' in the sense that $\langle\ln\Lambda,\nu\rangle$ is constant over $\nu\in\bm{J}(U;\omega_{\delta U})$, and which turns the constrained maximization problem into an unconstrained one:
	\[
	\nu
	=\textup{arg\,max}\Bigg\{
	\mathcal{H}(\nu) : \nu\in\bm{J}(U;\omega_{\delta U})
	\Bigg\}
	=\textup{arg\,max}
	\Bigg\{
	\mathcal{H}(\nu) + \langle\ln\Lambda,\nu\rangle
	: \nu\in\bm{\Delta}(U)
	\Bigg\}\,.
	\]
By calculus, the solution is given simply by $\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})\cong\Lambda(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})$, the $\Lambda$-weighted Gibbs measure on $U$. Thus, if $q$ denotes the \textsc{bp} messages for the $\Lambda$-weighted model, we can easily read off edge marginals of $\nu$ from the usual formula $\nu_e\cong \dot{q}_e\hat{q}_e$. The basic strategy of the proof of \eqref{e:contraction.simplified} is to show that
\bemph{in the pair coloring model, the the \textsc{bp} recursion contracts towards the product message ${}_{*}q\equiv {}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q\otimes{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q$, provided we start close enough to ${}_{*}q$.} As a consequence, if the boundary condition $\omega_{\delta U}$ is close to product, we will be able to construct weights $\Lambda$ that are close to ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda\otimes{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda$ (for ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda$ from Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights}). Then, for $e$ in the interior of $U$, the messages $\dot{q}_e$ and $\hat{q}_e$ will be closer to product than the messages on $\delta U$, so the discrepandy between $\omega_e\cong{}_{*}\dot{q}_e{}_{*}\hat{q}_e$ and ${}_{*}\omega_e$ will be closer than the discrepancies on $\delta U$. This gives the rough idea of the proof of \eqref{e:contraction.simplified}, and we leave the details to Sections~\ref{s:contract}--\ref{s:merge}.

The purpose of this remark is to emphasize that the canonical marginal ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ can in general be supported a strict subset of $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. In fact, although $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ always contains the \SPIN{green} spin, $(\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e)\setminus\SSPIN{g}$ can be any subset of $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{b}}$. 
For example, suppose in a $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ instance $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$ that a clause $a\in F$ has among its neighbors two leaf variables $u\ne v$. Then both $u$ and $v$ must always be \SPIN{free}, so
	\[
	\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}=\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}=\set{\SSPIN{g}}\,.
	\]
The clause $a$ can never be forcing, so for any other variable $w\in\partial a\setminus\set{u,v}$ we must have
$\SSPIN{r}\notin\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{aw}$. However, such $w$ can be forced by other clauses $b\in\partial w\setminus a$ --- indeed, $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{aw}$ contains $\set{\SSPIN{b}}$ if and only if $w$ may be forced by some $b\in\partial w(\SPIN{+}\SPIN{L}_{aw})\setminus a$; and it contains $\set{\SSPIN{y}}$ if and only if $w$ may be forced by some $b\in\partial w(\SPIN{-}\SPIN{L}_{aw})$. Therefore, in this scenario, $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{aw}\setminus\SSPIN{g}$ can be any subset of $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{b}}$. Similarly, on edges $e\in E$ where forcing can occur (meaning $\SSPIN{r}\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$), it is easy to construct examples to see that $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e\setminus\set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{r}}$ can be 
 any subset of $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{b}}$.

\label{l:coher.feasibility}
For a clause $a\in F$, a tuple $\pi=(\pi_e)_{e\in\delta a}$
is weakly coherent if and only if there exists a probability measure $\nu_{\delta a}$ over valid colorings of $\delta a$ with edge marginals $\pi$: that is,
	\[\pi_e(\sigma)
	= \sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}}
	\Ind{\sigma_e=\sigma}
	\nu_{\delta a}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})\]
for all $e\in\delta a$ and all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that a valid coloring of $\delta a$ is a tuple $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\equiv \smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^{\delta a}$ for which $\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})=1$, as defined by \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring} with the grouping $\SSPIN{c}=\set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. If $|\delta a|=k$, then a valid coloring $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$ falls in one of two cases: (i) it has exactly one $\SSPIN{r}$ entry with the remaining entries $\SSPIN{y}$; or (ii) all entries are in $\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$ and at least two entries are $\SSPIN{c}$. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, let
$(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)$ be the associated marginal probabilities of $\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}$ on each coordinate $i \in \set{1,\ldots,k}$, so for instance
	\[
	R_i \equiv \nu(\sigma_i=\SSPIN{r})
		= \sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k}
		\Ind{\sigma_i=\SSPIN{r}}
		\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})\,.
	\]
Thus, for each $i\in[k]\equiv\set{1,\ldots,k}$, the quantities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. This lemma is purely a claim about the feasible polytope of edge marginals coming from probability measures over valid colorings: the assertion is that for any $k\ge3$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item \label{i:polytope.linconds} The tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ satisfies the following constraints: for each $i\in[k]$, the quantities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Moreover, with $R\equiv R_1+\ldots+R_k$, we have $Y_i\ge R-R_i$ for each $i$. Lastly, writing $C_i \equiv G_i + B_i$, and $C\equiv C_1+\ldots+C_k$, we have $C \ge 2(1-R)$.
\item \label{i:polytope.probcond} The marginals $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ can be realized by a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$.
\end{enumerate} 
Let us first verify the straightforward direction, that
\eqref{i:polytope.probcond} implies \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, then for each coordinate $i$ it is clear that the marginal probabilities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Next, since the color $\SSPIN{r}$ can only occur together with $k-1$ entries $\SSPIN{y}$, we have
$R_i = \nu(\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i})$ for each $i\in[k]$. This implies 
	\[
	Y_i
	\ge \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i}
		\nu(\SSPIN{y}^{j-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-j})
	= \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i} R_j = R-R_i\,.
	\]
On the other hand, since any valid $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$ with no $\SSPIN{r}$ entry must be in $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k$ with at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ entries, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:total.mass.cyan.weak.ineq.proof}
	\sum_{i=1}^k C_i
	=
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in \set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\sum_{i=1}^k \Ind{\sigma_i=\SSPIN{c}}
	\ge 2
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in \set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	= 2(1-R)\,.
	\end{equation}
This proves that \eqref{i:polytope.probcond} implies \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}.

In the converse direction, given $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ satisfying the conditions of \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}, we now describe one particular construction of a measure $\nu$ on valid colorings that realizes these marginals.\footnote{The total number of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$ is $3^k-k-1$, so $\nu$ ranges over a $(3^k-k-2)$-dimensional simplex. On the other hand, since $R_i+Y_i+G_i+B_i=1$ for all $i$, the tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ is restricted to an affine space of dimension $3k$. Thus, simply by comparing dimensions, we would expect that any generic feasible tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ can be realized by an uncountable (and convex) family of measures $\nu$.} First, it is clear that we must set $\nu(\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i})=R_i$ for each $i\in[k]$. This step assigns $R$ of the probability mass of $\nu$, where the conditions in \eqref{i:polytope.linconds} ensure that $0\le R \le R_i + Y_i \le 1$. If $R=1$ then we are done, so assume otherwise, meaning there is a positive amount $1-R$ of mass left over that remains to be assigned. On each $i$ let $y_i$ denote the marginal weight of $\SSPIN{y}$ left over after the first step:
	\[
	y_i = Y_i - \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i} R_j
	= Y_i + R_i - R\,,
	\]
which is nonnegative by \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. The total mass left over on each edge $i$ is $C_i+y_i=1-R$. Let $\bm{C}_1,\ldots,\bm{C}_k$ be consecutive intervals of length $C_i$,
	\[\bm{C}_i=\bigg[ \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} C_j,
		\sum_{j=1}^i C_j \bigg)\,.\]
These intervals give a partition of $[0,C)$, which in turn is a subset of $[0,k(1-R))$. Let $J\equiv[0,1-R)$, and let $p$ be the mapping from $\mathbb{R}$ to $J$ which sends each real number to its representative modulo $(1-R)\mathbb{Z}$ in $J$. Let $J_{i,\SSPIN{c}}$ be the image of $\bm{C}_i$ under $p$ (i.e., the consecutive intervals get ``wrapped around''), and note that the restriction of $p$ to $\bm{C}_i$ is one-to-one since $|\bm{C}_i|=C_i\le 1-R$. Let $J_{i,\SSPIN{g}}$ be any subset of $J_{i,\SSPIN{c}}$ with Lebesgue measure $G_i$, and let $J_{i,\SSPIN{b}} \equiv J_{i,\SSPIN{c}} \setminus J_{i,\SSPIN{g}}$. Let $J_{i,\SSPIN{y}}\equiv J\setminus J_{i,\SSPIN{c}}$. For $t\in J$ let $\sigma_i(t)$ be the unique element $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$ such that $t\in J_{i,\sigma}$. Let $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)\equiv(\sigma_i(t))_{i\in[k]}$. For $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, let
	\[
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\equiv
	\textup{Leb}\bigg(
	\Big\{t\in J : \smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t) = \smash{\vec{\sigma}} \Big\}
	\bigg)
	= \textup{Leb}
	\bigg( \bigcap_{i=1}^k J_{i,\sigma_i}
	\bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\textup{Leb}$ denotes Lebesgue measure. This completes the definition of $\nu$. It is immediate from the construction that $\nu$ has marginals $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$, and all configurations in its support are of form $\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i}$, or lie in $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$. It remains to check that all colorings of the latter case are valid, which is to say that $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)$ has at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ entries for every $t\in J$. By definition, $\sigma_i(t)=\SSPIN{c}$ if and only if $t\in J_{i,\SSPIN{c}} = p(\bm{C}_i)$, which occurs if and only if $t + \ell(1-R) \in \bm{C}_i$ for some integer $\ell$. It follows that the number of $\SSPIN{c}$ entries in $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)$ is
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}
	\mathbf{1}\bigg\{t + \ell(1-R) \in \bm{C}_i \bigg\}
	= \sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}
	\mathbf{1}\bigg\{
	t + \ell(1-R) \in [0,C) \bigg\}\ge2\,,
	\]
where the last inequality holds for all $t\in J\equiv [0,1-R)$ using the final condition $C\ge2(1-R)$ from \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. This shows that $\nu$ is supported on valid colorings, thereby concluding our proof that \eqref{i:polytope.linconds} implies \eqref{i:polytope.probcond}.\end{proof}

Recall that a valid coloring of $\delta a$ is a tuple $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\equiv \smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^{\delta a}$ for which $\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})=1$, as defined by \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring} with the grouping $\SSPIN{c}=\set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. If $|\delta a|=k$, then a valid coloring $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$ falls in one of two cases: (i) it has exactly one $\SSPIN{r}$ entry with the remaining entries $\SSPIN{y}$; or (ii) all entries are in $\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$ and at least two entries are $\SSPIN{c}$. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, let
$(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)$ be the associated marginal probabilities of $\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}$ on each coordinate $i \in \set{1,\ldots,k}$, so for instance
	\[
	R_i \equiv \nu(\sigma_i=\SSPIN{r})
		= \sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k}
		\Ind{\sigma_i=\SSPIN{r}}
		\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})\,.
	\]
Thus, for each $i\in[k]\equiv\set{1,\ldots,k}$, the quantities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. This lemma is purely a claim about the feasible polytope of edge marginals coming from probability measures over valid colorings: the assertion is that for any $k\ge3$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item \label{i:polytope.linconds} The tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ satisfies the following constraints: for each $i\in[k]$, the quantities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Moreover, with $R\equiv R_1+\ldots+R_k$, we have $Y_i\ge R-R_i$ for each $i$. Lastly, writing $C_i \equiv G_i + B_i$, and $C\equiv C_1+\ldots+C_k$, we have $C \ge 2(1-R)$.
\item \label{i:polytope.probcond} The marginals $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ can be realized by a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$.
\end{enumerate} 
Let us first verify the straightforward direction, that
\eqref{i:polytope.probcond} implies \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. If $\nu$ is a probability measure on valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, then for each coordinate $i$ it is clear that the marginal probabilities $R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Next, since the color $\SSPIN{r}$ can only occur together with $k-1$ entries $\SSPIN{y}$, we have
$R_i = \nu(\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i})$ for each $i\in[k]$. This implies 
	\[
	Y_i
	\ge \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i}
		\nu(\SSPIN{y}^{j-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-j})
	= \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i} R_j = R-R_i\,.
	\]
On the other hand, since any valid $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$ with no $\SSPIN{r}$ entry must be in $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k$ with at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ entries, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:total.mass.cyan.weak.ineq.proof}
	\sum_{i=1}^k C_i
	=
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in \set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\sum_{i=1}^k \Ind{\sigma_i=\SSPIN{c}}
	\ge 2
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in \set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^k}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	= 2(1-R)\,.
	\end{equation}
This proves that \eqref{i:polytope.probcond} implies \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}.

In the converse direction, given $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ satisfying the conditions of \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}, we now describe one particular construction of a measure $\nu$ on valid colorings that realizes these marginals.\footnote{The total number of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$ is $3^k-k-1$, so $\nu$ ranges over a $(3^k-k-2)$-dimensional simplex. On the other hand, since $R_i+Y_i+G_i+B_i=1$ for all $i$, the tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ is restricted to an affine space of dimension $3k$. Thus, simply by comparing dimensions, we would expect that any generic feasible tuple $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$ can be realized by an uncountable (and convex) family of measures $\nu$.} First, it is clear that we must set $\nu(\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i})=R_i$ for each $i\in[k]$. This step assigns $R$ of the probability mass of $\nu$, where the conditions in \eqref{i:polytope.linconds} ensure that $0\le R \le R_i + Y_i \le 1$. If $R=1$ then we are done, so assume otherwise, meaning there is a positive amount $1-R$ of mass left over that remains to be assigned. On each $i$ let $y_i$ denote the marginal weight of $\SSPIN{y}$ left over after the first step:
	\[
	y_i = Y_i - \sum_{j\in[k]\setminus i} R_j
	= Y_i + R_i - R\,,
	\]
which is nonnegative by \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. The total mass left over on each edge $i$ is $C_i+y_i=1-R$. Let $\bm{C}_1,\ldots,\bm{C}_k$ be consecutive intervals of length $C_i$,
	\[\bm{C}_i=\bigg[ \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} C_j,
		\sum_{j=1}^i C_j \bigg)\,.\]
These intervals give a partition of $[0,C)$, which in turn is a subset of $[0,k(1-R))$. Let $J\equiv[0,1-R)$, and let $p$ be the mapping from $\mathbb{R}$ to $J$ which sends each real number to its representative modulo $(1-R)\mathbb{Z}$ in $J$. Let $J_{i,\SSPIN{c}}$ be the image of $\bm{C}_i$ under $p$ (i.e., the consecutive intervals get ``wrapped around''), and note that the restriction of $p$ to $\bm{C}_i$ is one-to-one since $|\bm{C}_i|=C_i\le 1-R$. Let $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)\equiv(\sigma_i(t))_{i\in[k]}$. For $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}\in\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$, let
	\[
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\equiv
	\textup{Leb}\bigg(
	\Big\{t\in J : \smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t) = \smash{\vec{\sigma}} \Big\}
	\bigg)
	= \textup{Leb}
	\bigg( \bigcap_{i=1}^k J_{i,\sigma_i}
	\bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\textup{Leb}$ denotes Lebesgue measure. This completes the definition of $\nu$. It is immediate from the construction that $\nu$ has marginals $(R_i,Y_i,G_i,B_i)_{1\le i\le k}$, and all configurations in its support are of form $\SSPIN{y}^{i-1}\SSPIN{r}\SSPIN{y}^{k-i}$, or lie in $\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^k$. It remains to check that all colorings of the latter case are valid, which is to say that $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)$ has at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ entries for every $t\in J$. By definition, $\sigma_i(t)=\SSPIN{c}$ if and only if $t\in J_{i,\SSPIN{c}} = p(\bm{C}_i)$, which occurs if and only if $t + \ell(1-R) \in \bm{C}_i$ for some integer $\ell$. It follows that the number of $\SSPIN{c}$ entries in $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}(t)$ is
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}
	\mathbf{1}\bigg\{t + \ell(1-R) \in \bm{C}_i \bigg\}
	= \sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}
	\mathbf{1}\bigg\{
	t + \ell(1-R) \in [0,C) \bigg\}\ge2\,,
	\]
where the last inequality holds for all $t\in J\equiv [0,1-R)$ using the final condition $C\ge2(1-R)$ from \eqref{i:polytope.linconds}. This shows that $\nu$ is supported on valid colorings, thereby concluding our proof that \eqref{i:polytope.linconds} implies \eqref{i:polytope.probcond}.

\label{l:clause.based.marginals.cohere} For an acyclic clause $a\in F$, the clause-based marginals ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi=({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e)_{e\in\delta a}$ are strictly coherent for all $r\ge2$.

\begin{proof}
Recall from Remark~\ref{r:first.rmk.coherence}
that the probability measure
	\[
	\nu_{\delta a}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	=\frac1{\bm{\hat{z}}_a}
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in\delta a}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}(\sigma_e)
	\]
has marginals ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. It therefore follows immediately from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} that ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ is weakly coherent. Recall from \eqref{e:defn.canonical.edge.marginal} that ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)$ is proportional ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_e(\sigma){}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \hat{q}_e(\sigma)$. It follows from the correspondence \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta} that 
${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{g})$ and ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \hat{q}_e(\SSPIN{g})$ are positive for all $r\ge2$,
so ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{g})$ is positive on any edge $e$.
Now suppose ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{y})$ is positive: this implies that 
${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{y})$ and ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \hat{q}_e(\SSPIN{y})$ must both be positive, therefore
	\[
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{y})
	-\sum_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})
	\ge
	\nu_{\delta a}\bigg(
	\textup{$\sigma_e=\SSPIN{y}$, and 
	$\sigma_{e'}=\SSPIN{g}$ for all 
	$e'\in\delta a\setminus e$}
	\bigg)
	= \frac1{\bm{\hat{z}}_a}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{y})
	\prod_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{g})>0\,,
	\]
which shows that ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ satisfies \eqref{e:cohere.y.for.r} with strict inequality whenever ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{y})$.
Next, recalling the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility},
we see that
\eqref{e:total.mass.cyan.weak.ineq.proof}
holds with equality if and only if $\nu_{\delta a}$
gives zero mass to configurations $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$ with more than two $\SSPIN{c}$ entries. This does not happen in the current situation, since
	\[
	\nu_{\delta a}(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{g}
		\textup{ for all }e\in\delta a)
	= \frac1{\bm{\hat{z}}_a}
	\prod_{e\in\delta a}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt} \dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{g})>0\,.
	\]
This proves that ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ always satisfies
\eqref{e:cohere.enough.cyan} with strict inequality. The claim follows.
\end{proof}

\label{l:clause.strict.coherence}
For a clause $a\in F$, if the tuple $\pi\equiv (\pi_e)_{e\in\delta a}$ is strictly coherent,
then there exists a measure $\bar{\nu}_{\delta a}$ with edge marginals $\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta a$, and 
$\textup{supp}\bar{\nu}_{\delta a}=\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$ where
	\[\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}
	\equiv\bigg\{
	\textup{valid colorings }\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}
	\,\bigg|\, \sigma_e\in\textup{supp}\pi_e
	\textup{ for all }e\in\delta a
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]

\begin{proof} It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} that there is a probability measure $\nu_{\delta a}$ with edge marginals $\pi\equiv(\pi_e)_{e\in\delta a}$, which of course implies $\textup{supp} \nu_{\delta a}\subseteq\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$. If $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$ is a singleton then we must have $\textup{supp} \nu_{\delta a}\subseteq\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$, in which case the assertion follows immediately by taking $\bar{\nu}_{\delta a}=\nu_{\delta a}$. We thus assume for the remainder of the proof that $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$ has at least two elements.

Now let $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$ denote the space of \emph{all} edge marginals $\pi\equiv (\pi_e)_{e\in\delta a}$ which can arise from probability measures over $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} that $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$ is characterized by the conditions \eqref{e:cohere.y.for.r} and \eqref{e:cohere.enough.cyan}, together with the constraints imposed by the supports of the $\pi_e$. To describe this more explicitly, let
	\[
	R(\pi)
	\equiv\sum_{e\in\delta a}\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})\,,\quad
	C(\pi)
	\equiv\sum_{e\in\delta a}\pi_e(\SSPIN{c})\,.
	\]
We then divide the scenarios into three cases, according to the number of edges $e\in\delta a$ with $\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})>0$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $|\set{e\in\delta a : \pi_e(\SSPIN{r})>0}|\ge2$, then we must have $\pi_e(\SSPIN{y})>0$ for all $e\in\delta a$, and
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}
	\equiv\left\{
	\pi
	\,\left|\,
	\begin{array}{l}
	\pi_e(\SSPIN{y}) \ge R(\pi) - \pi_e(\SSPIN{r})
	\textup{ for all } e\in\delta a\,, \\
	C(\pi) \ge 2[1-R(\pi)]\,,\\
	\textup{supp}\pi_e\subseteq\textup{supp}\pi_e
	\textup{ for all } e\in\delta a
	\end{array}\right.
	\right\}\,.
	\]

\item If there is a unique edge $e'\in\delta a$ with $\pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})>0$, then
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}
	\equiv\left\{
	\pi
	\,\left|\,
	\begin{array}{l} 
	\pi_e(\SSPIN{y}) \ge R(\pi)= \pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})
	\textup{ for all }
	e\in\delta a \setminus \set{e'} \,, \\
	C(\pi) \ge 2[1-R(\pi)]
		=2[1-\pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})]
		\,,\\
	\textup{supp}\pi_e\subseteq\textup{supp}\pi_e
	\textup{ for all } e\in\delta a
	\end{array}\right.
	\right\}\,.
	\]

\item If $|\set{e\in\delta a : \pi_e(\SSPIN{r})>0}|=0$, then
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}
	\equiv\left\{
	\pi
	\,\left|\,
	\begin{array}{l}
	C(\pi) \ge 2[1-R(\pi)] = 2\,,\\
	\textup{supp}\pi_e\subseteq\textup{supp}\pi_e
	\textup{ for all } e\in\delta a
	\end{array}\right.
	\right\}\,.
	\]
\end{enumerate}
In all cases, the definition of strict coherence ensures that $\pi\in\textup{ri}\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$, the relative interior of $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$. Now let $u_{\delta a}$ be the uniform measure on $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$, and let $\pi^\textup{unif}$ be the marginals resulting from $u_{\delta a}$. Since $\pi^\textup{unif}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$ and $\pi\in\textup{ri}\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}$, it must hold for sufficiently small $\epsilon$ that
	\[
	\pi^\epsilon\equiv
	\frac{\pi-\epsilon\pi^\textup{unif}}{1-\epsilon}
	\in \textup{\textsf{\footnotesize MARG}}_{\delta a}\,.
	\]
By Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} there is a probability measure $\nu^\epsilon$ on $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$ with edge marginals $\pi^\epsilon$. Then $\bar{\nu}_{\delta a}
\equiv (1-\epsilon)\nu^\epsilon + \epsilon u_{\delta a}$
is fully supported on $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta a}$, with edge marginals
	\[
	(1-\epsilon)\pi^\epsilon + \epsilon \pi^\textup{unif}
	=(1-\epsilon)
	\frac{\pi-\epsilon\pi^\textup{unif}}{1-\epsilon}
	 + \epsilon \pi^\textup{unif}
	= \pi\,.
	\]
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement: In the setting of Corollary~ we have d_1(D)=bms(D)-wp(D). Recall from that d_1(D) counts the dimension of the space setnu:nusim_starhspace-1ptomega. Recall from Definition~ that nuequiv(dotnu,hatnu) is the empirical measure of vertex colorings. Since _starhspace-1ptomega is fixed, we can treat each vertex type separately: if d_1(bmT) is the dimension of the space of variable empirical measures dotnu_bmT that are consistent with _starhspace-1ptomega, and d_1(bmL) is the dimension of the space of clause empirical measures hatnu_bmL that are consistent with _starhspace-1ptomega, then d_1(D)=sum_bmLd_1(bmL)+sum_bmT d_1(bmT)\,. For any given clause type bmL, let A' be the matrix from , which we showed to be of full rank in the proof of Corollary~. The space of hatnu_bmL that are consistent with _starhspace-1ptomega is an affine shift of the kernel of A' (intersected with the simplex of probability measures). It follows that \[ d_1(bmL) =dimker A' =s_bmL - textuprk A' =s_bmL -1 - sum_j (s_bmL(j)-1)\,. \] To make the analogous calculation for a variable type bmT, we argue in a few steps: [a.] item First we need the analogue of the (strict) coherence condition for a collection of empirical measures around a variable v (rather than around a clause, as in Definition~). We shall say that (pi_e)_eindelta v is bemphweakly coherent if there exists a probability measure mu on setSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf such that \[bigg(pi_e(SSPINp),pi_e(SSPINy),pi_e(SSPINg)bigg) = bigg(mu(SPIN+SPINL_e),mu(SPIN-SPINL_e),mu(SPINf)bigg)\] for all eindelta v, and for both SPINLinsetSPIN-,SPIN+ we have sum_eindelta v(SPINL) pi_e(SSPINr) ge mu(SPINL)\,. We say that (pi_e)_eindelta v is bemphstrictly coherent if mu(SPINf) is strictly positive and holds with strict inequality for both SPINLinsetSPIN-,SPIN+. By a very similar argument as in Lemma~, the canonical measures (_starhspace-1ptpi_e)_eindelta v are strictly coherent. item By a similar argument as in Lemma~, if (pi_e)_eindelta v is weakly coherent then there exists a measure dotnu on variable colorings smashvecsigma_delta v with edge marginals pi_e for all eindelta v. Indeed, clearly, dotnu should give weight mu(SPINf) to the all-SPINgreen coloring. For SPINLinsetSPIN-,SPIN+, the measure dotnu must give weight mu(SPINL) to the colorings that are SPINpurple on all of delta v(SPIN+SPINL) and SPINyellow on all of delta v(SPIN-SPINL). \label{l:dimension.count}
In the setting of Corollary~\ref{c:first.moment.exponent} we have $d_1(\mathscr{D})=\bm{s}(\mathscr{D})-\wp(\mathscr{D})$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall from
\eqref{e:dim.nu.given.omega}
that $d_1(\mathscr{D})$ counts the dimension of the space $\set{\nu:\nu\sim{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega}$.
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:pi.omega.nu.notation} that $\nu\equiv(\dot{\nu},\hat{\nu})$ is the empirical measure of vertex colorings.
Since ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$ is fixed, we can treat each vertex type separately:
if $d_1(\bm{T})$ is the dimension of the space of variable empirical measures $\dot{\nu}_{\bm{T}}$ that are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$,
and $d_1(\bm{L})$ is the dimension of the space of clause empirical measures $\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ that are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$, then
	\begin{equation}\label{e:dimension.one.decompose.into.types}
	d_1(\mathscr{D})=\sum_{\bm{L}}d_1(\bm{L})+\sum_{\bm{T}} d_1(\bm{T})\,.\end{equation}
For any given clause type $\bm{L}$, let $A'$ be the matrix from \eqref{e:matrix.A.prime.clause}, which we showed to be of full rank
in the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}.
The space of $\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ that are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$ is an affine shift of the kernel of $A'$ (intersected with the simplex of probability measures). It follows that
	\[
	d_1(\bm{L})
	=\dim\ker A'
	=s_{\bm{L}} - \textup{rk} A'
	=s_{\bm{L}} -1 - \sum_j (s_{\bm{L}(j)}-1)\,.
	\]
To make the analogous calculation for a variable type $\bm{T}$, we argue in a few steps:
\begin{enumerate}[a.]
\item First we need the analogue of the (strict) coherence condition for a collection of empirical measures around a variable $v$
 (rather than around a clause, as in Definition~\ref{d:coherence}). We shall say that $(\pi_e)_{e\in\delta v}$ is \bemph{weakly coherent} if there exists a probability measure $\mu$ on $\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}$ such that
	\[\bigg(\pi_e(\SSPIN{p}),\pi_e(\SSPIN{y}),\pi_e(\SSPIN{g})\bigg)
	= \bigg(\mu(\SPIN{+}\SPIN{L}_e),\mu(\SPIN{-}\SPIN{L}_e),\mu(\SPIN{f})\bigg)\]
for all $e\in\delta v$, and for both $\SPIN{L}\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+}}$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:variable.coherence.red}
	\sum_{e\in\delta v(\SPIN{L})} \pi_e(\SSPIN{r}) \ge \mu(\SPIN{L})\,.
	\end{equation}
We say that $(\pi_e)_{e\in\delta v}$ is \bemph{strictly coherent} if $\mu(\SPIN{f})$ is strictly positive and \eqref{e:variable.coherence.red}
holds with strict inequality for both $\SPIN{L}\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+}}$. By a very similar argument as in Lemma~\ref{l:clause.based.marginals.cohere}, the canonical measures $({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e)_{e\in\delta v}$ are strictly coherent. 

\item By a similar argument as in Lemma~\ref{l:clause.strict.coherence}, if $(\pi_e)_{e\in\delta v}$ is weakly coherent then there exists a measure $\dot{\nu}$ on variable colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ with edge marginals $\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta v$. Indeed, clearly, $\dot{\nu}$ should give weight $\mu(\SPIN{f})$ to the all-\SPIN{green} coloring. For $\SPIN{L}\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+}}$, the measure $\dot{\nu}$ must give weight $\mu(\SPIN{L})$ to the colorings that are \SPIN{purple} on all of $\delta v(\SPIN{+}\SPIN{L})$ and \SPIN{yellow} on all of $\delta v(\SPIN{-}\SPIN{L})$. The only non-trivial step is to separate \SPIN{purple} into \SPIN{red} and \SPIN{blue}, and this can be done by repeating the ``wrapping around consecutive intervals'' construction from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility}.

\item Similarly as in Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}, we define a matrix (the variable analogue of \eqref{e:matrix.A.prime.clause})
	\begin{equation}\label{e:matrix.B.prime.variable}
	B' = \begin{pmatrix} B \\ \mathbf{1}^\textup{\textsf{t}}\end{pmatrix}
	\end{equation}
which encodes the edge marginal constraints. The columns of the matrix are indexed by the valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ around the variable. 
For each frozen spin $\SPIN{L}\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+}}$ that the variable can take, the matrix $B$ also has a row which is the indicator on the colorings that are \SPIN{purple} on $\delta v(\SPIN{+}\SPIN{L})$. 
For each edge $e\in\delta v$ where both colors $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{b}}$ can appear, the matrix $B$ has a row
with entries $\Ind{\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r}}$. Since $({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e)_{e\in\delta v}$ is strictly coherent, we can repeat the argument of 
Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange} to show that $B'$ is a full rank matrix.
\end{enumerate}
For each edge type $\bm{t}\in\bm{T}$, let $r_{\bm{t}}=\Ind{\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{b}}\subseteq\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{\bm{t}}}$. It follows that
	\[
	d_1(\bm{T})
	= \dim\ker B'
	=s_{\bm{T}}-\textup{rk} B'
	=s_{\bm{T}}-1-x_{\bm{T}}-\sum_{\bm{t}\in\bm{T}} r_{\bm{t}}\,,
	\]
where we recall from the discussion around \eqref{e:wp.of.R} that $x_{\bm{T}}\in\set{0,1,2}$ counts the number of frozen spins that can appear on a variable of type $\bm{T}$. Substituting into \eqref{e:dimension.one.decompose.into.types} gives an expression for $d_1(\mathscr{D})$. Combining with our earlier calculation 
\eqref{e:stirling.correction.number} of $\bm{s}(\mathscr{D})$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	\bm{s}(\mathscr{D})
	-d_1(\mathscr{D})
	&=\bm{s}(\mathscr{D})
	\equiv\sum_{\bm{L}} \sum_j (s_{\bm{L}(j)}-1)
	-\sum_{\bm{T}}\bigg(
	-x_{\bm{T}}+\sum_{\bm{t}\in\bm{T}} (s_{\bm{t}}-1-r_{\bm{t}})
	\bigg)
	\\
	&=\sum_{\bm{L}} \sum_j (s_{\bm{L}(j)}-1)
	-\sum_{\bm{T}} x_{\bm{T}}\bigg(
		|\set{\bm{t} : \bm{t} \in\bm{T}}|-1
		\bigg)\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last equality uses that for all $\bm{t}\in\bm{T}$ we have
$s_{\bm{t}}=|\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{\bm{t}}|=1+x_{\bm{T}}+r_{\bm{t}}$.
This matches the expression for $\wp(\mathscr{D})$ from \eqref{e:wp.of.R}, and concludes the proof.
\end{proof}

Let $A''$ be the matrix whose rows are given by the pairwise tensor products $u\otimes w$ of rows $u,w$ from $A'$, \bemph{except} if $u$ and $w$ come from distinct blocks $A[j]\ne A[k]$. Since $A'$ is of full rank (as was shown in the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}), so is $A''$. It follows that

nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma~ we have j_2(D)=bms_2(D)- d_2(D)- 2wp(D). Recall that j_2(D) counts the dimension of the space of judicious pair empirical measures omega around the product measure _*omega. Given a pair empirical measure omega (which we assume throughout this proof to be close to _*omega), let pi_bmt be the average of the entries omega_bmL,j such that bmL(j)=bmt: pi_bmt =sum_bmL pi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt) omega_bmL,j where pi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt) is as in . If omega is judicious, then pi_bmt must also be judicious. In order for omega to be feasible, for each bmT there must exist a measure mu_bmT on setSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf^2 which is consistent with pi_bmt for every bmtinbmT. The measure mu_bmT must also be judicious, in the sense that its single-copy marginals are consistent with _starhspace-1ptpi_bmt for bmtinbmT. Recall that x_bmTinset0,1,2 counts the number of frozen spins that can appear at a variable of type bmT. Let \[ C' = C \\ 1^textupt inR^(1+x_bmT)times(1+x_bmT)\,, \] where for each frozen spin that can appear at bmT, the matrix C contains a row which is the indicator of that spin. Then the matrix \[ C'' = Cotimes 1^textupt\\ 1^textuptotimes C\\ 1^textuptotimes 1^textupt inR^ (2x_bmT+1) times (1+x_bmT)^2 \] encodes the judicious constraints on mu_bmT in the pair model. It follows that \[ d_2(mu_bmT) equivdimbigg\ mu_bmT :textupmu_bmT is judiciousbigg\ =dimker C'' =(1+x_bmT)^2 -bigg( 2x_bmT+1bigg) =(x_bmT)^2\,. \] Now note that for each bmtinbmT, the choice of mu_bmT already fixes pi_bmt as a measure on setSSPINp,SSPINy,SSPINg^2. It remains to separate SPINpurple into SPINred and SPINblue in such a way that the resulting pi_bmt has single-copy marginals _starhspace-1ptpi_bmt: d_2(pi_bmt\,|\,mu_bmT) &equivdimbigg\ pi_bmt :textuppi_bmt is judicious and consistent with mu_bmT bigg\\\ &= dimbigg\ pi_bmt :textuppi_bmt is judicious bigg\ -dimbigg\ mu_bmT :textupmu_bmT is judiciousbigg\ =( s_bmt-1)^2 -(x_bmT)^2\,. In order for omega to be consistent with pi_bmt, it must satisfy the linear constraints . Note that some of these are redundant with the judicious constraints on the individual measures omega_bmL,j. Altogether d_2( (omega_bmL,j)_bmL(j)=bmt \,|\,pi_bmt) &equivdimbigg\ (omega_bmL,j)_bmL(j)=bmt: textupomega is judicious and consistent with pi_bmtbigg\\\ &=sum_bmL,j : bmL(j)=t ( s_bmL(j)-1)^2 - (s_bmt-1)^2 Combining these calculations gives j_2(D) &= sum_bmTBigg( d_2(mu_bmT) +sum_bmtinbmT bigg[ d_2(pi_bmt\,|\,mu_bmT) +d_2( (omega_bmL,j)_bmL(j)=bmt \,|\,pi_bmt) bigg]Bigg)\\ &= -sum_bmT (x_bmT)^2 bigg(|setbmt:bmtinbmT|-1bigg) +sum_bmL,j (s_bmL(j)-1)^2\,. Now recall that bms_2(D) is given in , and d_2(D) was calculated in Lemma~. Thus, if we abbreviate wp_2(D)equiv bms_2(D)-d_2(D)-j_2(D), then we obtain \[ wp_2(D) = sum_bmTBigg( (x_bmT)^2 |setbmt:bmtinbmT| + 2x_bmT+(2x_bmT+3)r_bmT -sum_bmtinbmT Big[ (s_bmt)^2-1Big] Bigg) +2sum_bmL,j (s_bmL(j)-1)\,. \] For bmtinbmT, we can expand s_bmt=1 +x_bmt + r_bmt, so \[ sum_bmtinbmT bigg( (s_bmt)^2-1bigg) =sum_bmtinbmT bigg( (x_bmT)^2 + 2x_bmT +2x_bmTr_bmt + 3r_bmtbigg) =bigg((x_bmT)^2 + 2x_bmTbigg) |setbmt:bmtinbmT| +(2x_bmT+3)r_bmT\,, \] where we recall that r_bmT is the sum of r_bmt over all bmtinbmT. Substituting into the previous calculation gives \[ wp_2(D) = -2 sum_bmT x_bmT (|setbmt:bmtinbmT|-1) +2sum_bmL,j (s_bmL(j)-1)\,, \] which is exactly twice the value of wp(D) from . This proves the claim.
