\label{c:cohere.weights} Let $U'$ be any finite bipartite tree, and suppose $U\subseteq U'$ is a tree containing at least one clause, whose leaves are all variables. For each edge $e=(av)$ in $U'$, let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ be the canonical marginal on $e$ based on $B_r(v)$, the $r$-neighborhood of $v$ relative to $U'$. If all clauses in $U$ are strictly coherent, then there is a set of edge weights $\gamma_e : \set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}\to[0,\infty)$ (for $e$ in $U$, and with the convention $\gamma_e(\SSPIN{g})\equiv1$), such that in the Gibbs measure on valid colorings of $U$
where the edges are weighted by $\gamma$ and the boundary variables are weighted by ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}$, 
all edge marginals agree with the canonical ones ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. (The Gibbs measure is explicitly given by \eqref{e:gamma.weighted.gibbs} below.)

\begin{proof} Let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$ be the canonical messages (based on $r$-neighborhoods) on the edges of $U$, as in Definition~\ref{d:canonical}. For each variable $v$ of $U$, let $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$ be the set of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ such that $\sigma_e\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta v$. Now recall the discussion around \eqref{e:var.tuple.measure.weighted}: the probability measure
	\begin{equation}\label{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var}
	\nu_{\delta v}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	= \frac1{\bm{\dot{z}}_v}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\end{equation}
is supported on valid colorings of $\delta v$, and has edge marginals on $\delta v$ that are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Moreover, it is clear from the above expression that if $e\in\delta v$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)>0$, then we must have ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)>0$. Consequently, for any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$, we have $\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})=1$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)>0$ for all $e\in\delta a$, which means that \eqref{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var} is positive. That is to say, the measure $\nu_{\delta v}$ defined by \eqref{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var} has support exactly equal to $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$.

We next make a simple observation: for any edge $e$ of $U$ and any vertex $x$ incident to $e$, we have $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ if and only if there exists
$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$ which has value $\sigma$ on edge $e$. The ``if'' direction is obvious.
For the ``only if'' direction, recall that we have constructed $\nu_{\delta x}$ with marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ (this follows from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} if $x$ is a clause, and from the above discussion if $x$ is a variable). Since ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ is the marginal of $\nu_{\delta x}$, if $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ then the measure $\nu_{\delta x}$ must give positive weight to some $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}$ which has value $\sigma$ on edge $e$. Then $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in \textup{supp} \nu_{\delta x}\subseteq\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$, as desired.

Now define $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U$ to be the set of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_U$ of $U$ such that $\sigma_e\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all edges $e$ of $U$. This is simply because $U$ is a tree, so we can construct an element of $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U$ as follows: start from any vertex $x$ of $U$, and choose $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$. For each vertex $y\in\partial x$, by the preceding observation, the set $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta y}$ must contain an element $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$ which agrees with $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$ on the edge $e=(xy)$. Choose this $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$, and proceed in the same way to color the edges incident to the neighbors of $y$, and so on until all of $U$ is colored. This shows $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U\ne\varnothing$.

Now recall from \eqref{e:defn.canonical.edge.marginal} that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)$ is proportional to ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)$. In particular, if $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, then ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)$ must be positive, in which case we can define
	\[
	\gamma_e(\sigma)
	\equiv \frac{w_e(\sigma)}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{g})\,.
	\]
for $w_e$ as given by Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}. 
 Recall that $\SSPIN{g}\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$
and we took the convention
$w_e(\SSPIN{g})\equiv1$, so now
$\gamma_e(\SSPIN{g})\equiv1$ also. For $\sigma\notin\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ we simply define $\gamma_e(\sigma)=0$. We write $U=(V,F,E)$. Write $\mathcal{L} U$ for all the leaves of $U$, which were assumed to be variables. For each $u\in\mathcal{L} U$ let $a(u)$ denote the unique clause in $U$ that neighbors $u$. The Gibbs measure described in the statement of this lemma can be expressed as 
	\begin{equation}\label{e:gamma.weighted.gibbs}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_U)
	\cong
	\prod_{v\in V\setminus\mathcal{L} U}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{a\in F}
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in E}
	\gamma_e(\sigma_e)
	\prod_{u\in\mathcal{L} U}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{u a(u)}(\sigma_{u a(u)})
	\,,
	\end{equation}
where $\cong$ denotes the normalization constant, which is positive since $\textup{supp}\gamma_e=\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e\supseteq\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, and $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U\ne\varnothing$. We claim that this measure $\nu$ has marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ on the edges of $U$. To this end, note that the canonical messages ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$ solve the belief progagation equations for $\nu_U$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $u\in\mathcal{L} U$, then we regard $u$ as being weighted only by ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{ua(u)}$, so then the \textsc{bp} message from $u$ to $a(u)$ will be ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{ua(u)}$
simply by the standard conventions of \textsc{bp} at the leaves of trees. 
\item If $v$ is an internal variable of $U$, then we regard $v$ as being unweighted, and the equation
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{va}(\sigma)=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{va}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}]$ is satisfied 
for all $a\in\partial v$ by definition of ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$ (cf.\ Remark~\ref{r:first.rmk.coherence}). 
\item Finally, if $a$ is a clause of $U$, then we regard $a$ as being weighted by the product of $\gamma_e$ over $e\in\delta a$. Consider
	\begin{equation}\label{e:putative.nu.delta.a}
	\nu_{\delta a}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\cong
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in \delta a}
	\bigg\{
	\gamma_e(\sigma_e)
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\bigg\}
	\cong \hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in \delta a}
	w_e(\sigma_e)\,.\end{equation}
(We are not yet claiming that $\nu_{\delta a}$ is the marginal of $\nu$.) By the result of Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}, the measure $\nu_{\delta a}$ has marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, so
for all $e=(av)\in\delta a$ we have
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \cong
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}}
	\Ind{\sigma_e=\sigma}
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e'\in \delta a}
	\bigg\{
	\gamma_{e'}(\sigma_{e'})
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\sigma_{e'})
	\bigg\}
	\cong

Let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$ be the canonical messages (based on $r$-neighborhoods) on the edges of $U$, as in Definition~\ref{d:canonical}. For each variable $v$ of $U$, let $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$ be the set of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$ such that $\sigma_e\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta v$. Now recall the discussion around \eqref{e:var.tuple.measure.weighted}: the probability measure
	\begin{equation}\label{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var}
	\nu_{\delta v}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	= \frac1{\bm{\dot{z}}_v}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\end{equation}
is supported on valid colorings of $\delta v$, and has edge marginals on $\delta v$ that are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Moreover, it is clear from the above expression that if $e\in\delta v$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)>0$, then we must have ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)>0$. Consequently, for any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$, we have $\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})=1$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)>0$ for all $e\in\delta a$, which means that \eqref{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var} is positive. That is to say, the measure $\nu_{\delta v}$ defined by \eqref{e:within.proof.max.entropy.var} has support exactly equal to $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta v}$.

We next make a simple observation: for any edge $e$ of $U$ and any vertex $x$ incident to $e$, we have $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ if and only if there exists
$\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$ which has value $\sigma$ on edge $e$. The ``if'' direction is obvious.
For the ``only if'' direction, recall that we have constructed $\nu_{\delta x}$ with marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ (this follows from Lemma~\ref{l:coher.feasibility} if $x$ is a clause, and from the above discussion if $x$ is a variable). Since ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ is the marginal of $\nu_{\delta x}$, if $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ then the measure $\nu_{\delta x}$ must give positive weight to some $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}$ which has value $\sigma$ on edge $e$. Then $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in \textup{supp} \nu_{\delta x}\subseteq\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$, as desired.

Now define $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U$ to be the set of valid colorings $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_U$ of $U$ such that $\sigma_e\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all edges $e$ of $U$. This is simply because $U$ is a tree, so we can construct an element of $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U$ as follows: start from any vertex $x$ of $U$, and choose $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta x}\in\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta x}$. For each vertex $y\in\partial x$, by the preceding observation, the set $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_{\delta y}$ must contain an element $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$ which agrees with $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$ on the edge $e=(xy)$. Choose this $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta y}$, and proceed in the same way to color the edges incident to the neighbors of $y$, and so on until all of $U$ is colored. This shows $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U\ne\varnothing$.

Now recall from \eqref{e:defn.canonical.edge.marginal} that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)$ is proportional to ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)$. In particular, if $\sigma\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, then ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)$ must be positive, in which case we can define
	\[
	\gamma_e(\sigma)
	\equiv \frac{w_e(\sigma)}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{g})\,.
	\]
for $w_e$ as given by Corollary~\ref{c:clause.strict.coherence.lagrange}. 
 Recall that $\SSPIN{g}\in\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$
and we took the convention
$w_e(\SSPIN{g})\equiv1$, so now
$\gamma_e(\SSPIN{g})\equiv1$ also. For $\sigma\notin\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ we simply define $\gamma_e(\sigma)=0$. We write $U=(V,F,E)$. Write $\mathcal{L} U$ for all the leaves of $U$, which were assumed to be variables. For each $u\in\mathcal{L} U$ let $a(u)$ denote the unique clause in $U$ that neighbors $u$. The Gibbs measure described in the statement of this lemma can be expressed as 
	\begin{equation}\label{e:gamma.weighted.gibbs}
	\nu(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_U)
	\cong
	\prod_{v\in V\setminus\mathcal{L} U}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{a\in F}
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in E}
	\gamma_e(\sigma_e)
	\prod_{u\in\mathcal{L} U}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{u a(u)}(\sigma_{u a(u)})
	\,,
	\end{equation}
where $\cong$ denotes the normalization constant, which is positive since $\textup{supp}\gamma_e=\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, $\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e\supseteq\textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$, and $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize COLS}}_U\ne\varnothing$. \begin{enumerate}[(i)]

simply by the standard conventions of \textsc{bp} at the leaves of trees. 
\item If $v$ is an internal variable of $U$, then we regard $v$ as being unweighted, and the equation
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{va}(\sigma)=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{va}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}]$ is satisfied 
for all $a\in\partial v$ by definition of ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$ (cf.\ Remark~\ref{r:first.rmk.coherence}). 
\item Finally, if $a$ is a clause of $U$, then we regard $a$ as being weighted by the product of $\gamma_e$ over $e\in\delta a$. Consider
	\begin{equation}\label{e:putative.nu.delta.a}
	\nu_{\delta a}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\cong
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in \delta a}
	\bigg\{
	\gamma_e(\sigma_e)
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\bigg\}
	\cong \hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in \delta a}
	w_e(\sigma_e)\,.\end{equation}

for all $e=(av)\in\delta a$ we have
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \cong
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}}
	\Ind{\sigma_e=\sigma}
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e'\in \delta a}
	\bigg\{
	\gamma_{e'}(\sigma_{e'})
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\sigma_{e'})
	\bigg\}
	\cong
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)
	\cdot \textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{av}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q};\gamma](\sigma)\,.
	\]
On the other hand we know ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)\cong{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)$, so it must be that
$\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{av}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q};\gamma](\sigma)={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma)$.
\end{enumerate}
This proves our claim that $({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q})$ solves
the belief propagation equations for $\nu$. It follows from this that the marginal of $\nu$ on each $\delta a$ is indeed correctly described by \eqref{e:putative.nu.delta.a}, which in turn implies that the edge marginals are consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$.

\label{c:clause.bp.weights}
In the setting of Corollary~\ref{c:cohere.weights}, 
there is a system ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$ of positive variable weights
	\[
	\Lambda_v = \begin{pmatrix}
	\lambda_v \equiv (\lambda_v(\SPIN{+})=1, \lambda_v(\SPIN{-}),\lambda_v(\SPIN{f}))\\
	\lambda_e \equiv \lambda_e(\SSPIN{r})
	\end{pmatrix}
	\]
such that the ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$-weighted Gibbs measure on valid colorings of $U$ has all edge marginals agreeing with the canonical edge marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$.
(However, since the weights were shifted from clauses to variables, the associated \textsc{bp} messages will no longer be ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$.)

\begin{proof} 
The Gibbs measure \eqref{e:gamma.weighted.gibbs}
is equivalent to the Gibbs measure in which all variables are unweighted;
all internal edges $e$ of $U$ are weighted by $\tilde{\gamma}_e=\gamma_e$; and all leaf edges $e$ of $U$ are weighted by
	\[\tilde{\gamma}_e(\sigma)
	= \frac{\gamma_e(\sigma) {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)}
		{\sum_\tau
		\gamma_e(\tau) {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\tau)}\,.
	\]
To define ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$, we redistribute the weights as follows. For each internal variable $v$ of $U$,
we let $x_v\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}$ denote the frozen spin corresponding corresponding to $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}$, and put the weight
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\equiv
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_v(x_v)
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e(\sigma_e)\,,
	\]
where ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_v$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e$ are defined by 
\eqref{e:redistribute.weights}. For each leaf variable $v\in\mathcal{L} U$, the set $\delta v$ consists of a single edge $e$, and in this case we will simply take the weight
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_v(\sigma_e)
	\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e(\sigma_e)
	\equiv\tilde{\gamma}_e(\sigma_e)\,.
	\]
For the redistributed weights,
the \textsc{bp} messages on all edges $e$ of $U$ are given by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:redistributed.bp.messages}
	{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\cong {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\gamma_e(\sigma_e)\,,\quad
	{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)
	\cong \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)}
		{\gamma_e(\sigma_e)}\,.
	\end{equation}
Thus the messages for the redistributed weights
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$ also satisfy the familiar identity
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma_e)
\cong {}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e){}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma_e)$.
Moreover, if $e$ is a leaf edge then
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e=\tilde{\gamma}_e={}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e$.
\end{proof}

nodes.name: Galton--Watson measure, ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$
nodes.statement: We define the bemphbipartite Poisson Galton--Watson tree to be the random bipartite factor tree T which is generated as follows: starting from a root variable v_textuptextscrt, each variable independently generates textupPois(alpha k) child clauses, and each clause generates k-1 child variables. Each edge is labelled with a literal SPINL which takes values SPIN+ or SPIN- with equal probability, independently over all the edges. We write textupPGW for the law of this tree.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:uPGW} We define the \bemph{bipartite Poisson Galton--Watson tree} 
to be the random bipartite factor tree $\mathscr{T}$ which is generated as follows: starting from a root variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, each variable independently generates $\textup{\textsf{Pois}}(\alpha k)$ child clauses, and each clause generates $k-1$ child variables. Each edge is labelled with a literal $\SPIN{L}$ which takes values $\SPIN{+}$ or $\SPIN{-}$ with equal probability, independently over all the edges. We write ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ for the law of this tree.

Each edge is labelled with a literal SPINL which takes values SPIN+ or SPIN- with equal probability, independently over all the edges. We write textupPGW for the law of this tree.

nodes.statement: The measure textupPGW is the ``local weak limit'' of the random textupk-textscsat graph in the following formal sense: if G_n=(V_n,F_n,E_n) denotes an instance of random textupk-textscsat at clause density alpha on n variables, and I_n is a uniformly random element of V_nequiv[n], then it holds for any finite r that \[ lim_ntoinfty Pbigg(B_r(I_n;G_n)cong Tbigg) = textupPGW^alphabigg( B_r(v_textuptextscrt;T) cong T bigg) \] for every T. In the above, B_r(I_n;G_n) is the r-neighborhood of I_n in G_n, viewed as a graph rooted at I_n. Likewise B_r(v_textuptextscrt;T) is the r-neighborhood of v_textuptextscrt in T, viewed as a graph rooted at v_textuptextscrt. Finally T is any graph with a root o, and cong denotes isomorphism of rooted graphs. The measure textupPGW is bemphunimodular (cf.\ and ): intbigg[sum_u f(T,v_textuptextscrt,u)bigg] dtextupPGW(T) =intbigg[sum_u f(T,u,v_textuptextscrt)bigg] dtextupPGW(T) where the sum goes over all variables u in T, and f is any nonnegative Borel function on the space G_starstar of bi-rooted graphs.footnoteA bi-rooted graph is a graph rooted at an ordered pair of vertices. For a detailed account and careful discussion of topological considerations (in particular, what it means to be a Borel function on the space G_starstar), we refer to . To see why should hold, note that changing the order of summation gives Esum_uin partial I_n f(G_n,I_n ,u) =frac1|V_n| sum_vin V_nbigg[ sum_uin N(v) f(G_n , v,u )bigg] =Esum_uin partial I_n f(G_n,u,I_n )\,. In the limit ntoinfty, the left-hand side of converges to the left-hand side of , while the right-hand side of converges to the right-hand side of .
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{r:unimodular}
The measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ is the ``local weak limit'' of the random $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ graph in the following formal sense: if $\mathscr{G}_n=(V_n,F_n,E_n)$ denotes an instance of random $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ at clause density $\alpha$ on $n$ variables,
and $I_n$ is a uniformly random element of $V_n\equiv[n]$,
then it holds for any finite $r$ that
	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{P}\bigg(B_r(I_n;\mathscr{G}_n)\cong T\bigg)
	= {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}^\alpha\bigg( B_r(v_\textup{\textsc{rt}};\mathscr{T}) \cong T \bigg)
	\]
for every $T$. In the above, $B_r(I_n;\mathscr{G}_n)$ is the $r$-neighborhood of $I_n$ in $\mathscr{G}_n$, viewed as a graph rooted at $I_n$. Likewise $B_r(v_\textup{\textsc{rt}};\mathscr{T})$
is the $r$-neighborhood of $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ in $\mathscr{T}$,
viewed as a graph rooted at $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$. Finally $T$ is any graph with a root $o$, and $\cong$ denotes isomorphism of rooted graphs. The measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ is \bemph{unimodular} (cf.\ \cite{MR1336708} and \cite[Defn.~2.1]{MR2354165}):
	\begin{equation}\label{e:unimodular}
	\int\bigg[\sum_u
	f(\mathscr{T},v_\textup{\textsc{rt}},u)\bigg]
	d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(\mathscr{T})
	=\int\bigg[\sum_u
	f(\mathscr{T},u,v_\textup{\textsc{rt}})\bigg]
	d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(\mathscr{T})
	\end{equation}
where the sum goes over all variables $u$ in $\mathscr{T}$, and $f$ is any nonnegative Borel function on the space $\mathcal{G}_{\star\star}$ of bi-rooted graphs.\footnote{A bi-rooted graph is a graph rooted at an ordered pair of vertices. For a detailed account and careful discussion of topological considerations (in particular, what it means to be a Borel function on the space $\mathcal{G}_{\star\star}$), we refer to \cite{MR2354165}.} To see why \eqref{e:unimodular} should hold, note that changing the order of summation gives
	\begin{equation}\label{e:unim.n}
	\mathbb{E}\sum_{u\in \partial I_n} f(\mathscr{G}_n,I_n ,u)
	=\frac1{|V_n|}
	\sum_{v\in V_n}\bigg[
	\sum_{u\in N(v)}
	f(\mathscr{G}_n , v,u )\bigg]
	=\mathbb{E}\sum_{u\in \partial I_n} f(\mathscr{G}_n,u,I_n )\,.
	\end{equation}
In the limit $n\to\infty$, the left-hand side of \eqref{e:unim.n} converges to the left-hand side of
\eqref{e:unimodular}, while the right-hand side of 
\eqref{e:unim.n} converges to the right-hand side of
\eqref{e:unimodular}.

nodes.name: Galton--Watson based on fixed tree, ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$
nodes.statement: Let T be any fixed tree rooted at a variable v_textuptextscrt, such that all clauses in T have at most k-1 children. At every variable v of T (including v=v_textuptextscrt), attach an independent subtree T_vsimtextupPGW (by identifying v with the root of T_v). At every clause a of T, if a has k-1-j children, attach j independent samples of textupfootnotesize PGW as subtrees to a. Let textupPGW(T) be the law of the resulting tree. Similarly, if T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt is a fixed variable-to-clause tree where every clause has at most k-1 children, we can perform the same procedure as above to obtain a random variable-to-clause tree, whose law we denote textupfootnotesize PGW(T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt). Likewise, if T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt is any fixed clause-to-variable tree where every clause has at most k-1 children, we use widehattextupfootnotesize PGW(T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt) to denote the law of the random clause-to-variable tree based on T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:PGW.based.on.T}
Let $T$ be any fixed tree rooted at a variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$,
such that all clauses in $T$ have at most $k-1$ children.
At every variable $v$ of $T$ (including $v=v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$), attach an independent subtree $\mathscr{T}_v\sim{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ (by identifying $v$ with the root of $\mathscr{T}_v$). At every clause $a$ of $T$, if $a$ has $k-1-j$ children, attach $j$ independent samples of ${\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}$ as subtrees to $a$. Let ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$ be the law of the resulting tree.

Similarly, if $T_{v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$ is a fixed variable-to-clause tree where every clause has at most $k-1$ children, we can perform the same procedure as above to obtain a random variable-to-clause tree, whose law we denote ${\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}(T_{v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}})$. Likewise, if $T_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$ is any fixed clause-to-variable tree where every clause has at most $k-1$ children, we use $\widehat{{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}}(T_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}})$ to denote the law of the random clause-to-variable tree based on $T_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$.

At every clause a of T, if a has k-1-j children, attach j independent samples of textupfootnotesize PGW as subtrees to a. Let textupPGW(T) be the law of the resulting tree. Similarly, if T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt is a fixed variable-to-clause tree where every clause has at most k-1 children, we can perform the same procedure as above to obtain a random variable-to-clause tree, whose law we denote textupfootnotesize PGW(T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt). Likewise, if T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt is any fixed clause-to-variable tree where every clause has at most k-1 children, we use widehattextupfootnotesize PGW(T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt) to denote the law of the random clause-to-variable tree based on T_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt.

nodes.name:
Galton--Watson with random deletions,
${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Let textupPGW_epsilon be the law of the random tree generated as follows: starting from a root variable v_textuptextscrt, each variable independently generates textupPois(alpha k) clauses, and each clause independently generates either k-1 child variables (with probability 1-epsilon) or k-2 child variables (with probability epsilon). When epsilon=0, the measure textupPGW_epsilon coincides with the measure textupPGW of Definition~. The measure textupPGW_epsilon is also unimodular, because it can also be obtained via a local weak limit: let hatepsilon and hatalpha be defined by \[ epsilon = frac(k-1)hatepsilonk-hatepsilon\,, hatalpha = fracalpha1-hatepsilon/k \] Start with n isolated variables and nhatalpha isolated clauses. For each of the first 1-hatepsilon fraction of the clauses, put k edges to randomly chosen variables. For the last hatepsilon fraction of the clauses, put k-1 edges to randomly chosen variables. The total number of edges in the resulting random graph is \[ nhatalpha bigg((1-hatepsilon)k +hatepsilon(k-1)bigg) = nalpha k\,. \] In the limit ntoinfty, this random graph converges locally weakly to the textupPGW_epsilon measure, justifying our claims that textupPGW_epsilon is unimodular. Define likewise textupfootnotesize PGW_epsilon and widehattextupfootnotesize PGW_epsilon to be the obvious generalizations of the measures textupfootnotesize PGW and widehattextupfootnotesize PGW from Definitions~~and~. We hereafter write textupcl_epsilon for the probability measure which puts weight 1-epsilon on k, and weight epsilon on k-1.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:PGW.with.clauses.one.less}
Let ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ be the law of the random tree generated as follows: starting from a root variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, each variable independently generates $\textup{\textsf{Pois}}(\alpha k)$ clauses, and each clause independently generates either $k-1$ child variables (with probability $1-\epsilon$)
or $k-2$ child variables (with probability $\epsilon$). When $\epsilon=0$, the measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ coincides with the measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ of Definition~\ref{d:uPGW}. The measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ is also unimodular, because it can also be obtained via a local weak limit: let $\hat{\epsilon}$ and $\hat{\alpha}$ be defined by
	\[
	\epsilon = \frac{(k-1)\hat{\epsilon}}{k-\hat{\epsilon}}\,,\quad
	\hat{\alpha} = \frac{\alpha}{1-\hat{\epsilon}/k}
	\]
Start with $n$ isolated variables and $n\hat{\alpha}$ isolated clauses. For each of the first $1-\hat{\epsilon}$ fraction of the clauses, put $k$ edges to randomly chosen variables. For the last $\hat{\epsilon}$ fraction of the clauses, put $k-1$ edges to randomly chosen variables. The total number of edges in the resulting random graph is
	\[
	n\hat{\alpha} \bigg((1-\hat{\epsilon})k
	+\hat{\epsilon}(k-1)\bigg)
	= n\alpha k\,.
	\]
In the limit $n\to\infty$, this random graph converges locally weakly to the ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ measure, justifying our claims that ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ is unimodular. Define likewise ${\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}_\epsilon$ and $\widehat{{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}}_\epsilon$ to be the obvious generalizations of the measures ${\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}$ and $\widehat{{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}}$ from Definitions~\ref{d:vtoc.PGW}~and~\ref{d:ctov.PGW}. 
We hereafter write $\textup{\textsf{cl}}_\epsilon$ for the probability measure which puts weight $1-\epsilon$ on $k$, and weight $\epsilon$ on $k-1$.

\label{d:full.dist.recurs}
Let $\mathcal{R}_\epsilon$ denote the composition $\smash{\dot{\mathcal{R}}} \circ \smash{\hat{\mathcal{R}}}_\epsilon$: this gives a mapping from $\mathscr{P}$ to $\mathcal{P}$, which captures how randomness is passed through one full update (clause updates follows by variable update) of variable-to-clause messages. We can explicitly describe $\mathcal{R}_\epsilon$ as follows: given $\mu\in\mathscr{P}$, let $\smash{\vec{\eta}}$ be
an array of i.i.d.\ samples from $\mu$, as in \eqref{e:defn.array.ueta}. Independently, let $\smash{\vec{d}}\sim\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}$, and let $\vec{K}\equiv(K_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a sequence of i.i.d.\ samples from $\textup{\textsf{cl}}_\epsilon$ (as in Definition~\ref{d:PGW.with.clauses.one.less}). 
From this, define the random variables
	\[\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}
	\equiv \Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}(\smash{\vec{d}},\smash{\vec{\eta}})
	\equiv \prod_{i=1}^{d^\SPIN{\textpm}}
			\bigg(
			1 - \prod_{j=1}^{K_i-1} \eta^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij}
			\bigg)
	=\prod_{i=1}^{d^\SPIN{\textpm}}
			\bigg(
			1 - \hat{u}^\SPIN{\textpm}_i
			\bigg)
	\,.\]
Substitute these $\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}$ into \eqref{e:eta.in.terms.of.signed.Pis}
to define $\bm{\eta}=\bm{\eta}(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}})$. Then the law of $\bm{\eta}(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}})$ is $\mathcal{R}_\epsilon\mu\in\mathcal{P}$. As in \eqref{e:intro.dist.recurs} we let
	\[R(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}}) 
	\equiv \Big[\bm{\eta}(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}})
	\Big](\SPIN{-})\,.\]
As we noted in \S\ref{ss:intro.onersb.threshold},
since all the $\eta$'s must lie in $[0,1)$,
we must have $\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}\in(0,1]$ and therefore $R(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}})\in[0,1)$. We finally define $\bm{R}_\epsilon\mu\in\mathscr{P}$ to be the law of $R(\smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}})$, so $\bm{R}_\epsilon$ gives a mapping from $\mathscr{P}$ to itself.\footnote{The formal characterization of $\bm{R}_\epsilon$ is that for any measurable $B\subseteq [0,1)$,
	\[(\bm{R}_\epsilon\mu)( \eta \in B )= 
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{d}}}
	\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}(\vec d) 
	\int \Bigg[
	\int\Ind{R( \smash{\vec{d}},\vec{K},\smash{\vec{\eta}} )\in B}
	\, d\mu^{\otimes}(\smash{\vec{\eta}})\Bigg]
	\, d(\textup{\textsf{cl}}_\epsilon)^\otimes(\vec{K})
	\,,\]
where we abbreviate $\mu^{\otimes}$ for the law of the array $\smash{\vec{\eta}}$ of i.i.d.\ samples from $\mu$, and similarly we abbreviate $(\textup{\textsf{cl}}_\epsilon)^\otimes$
for the law of the sequence $\vec{K}$ of i.i.d.\ samples from $\textup{\textsf{cl}}_\epsilon$.} We denote $\mathcal{R}\equiv\mathcal{R}_\epsilon$ and $\bm{R}\equiv\bm{R}_\epsilon$ for the $\epsilon=0$ case.

Sample smashvecd=(d^SPIN+,d^SPIN-) from textuppo_SPINtextpm and smashveceta from (mu^ell)^otimesinfty, so that eta^ell+1=R(smashvecd,smashveceta) has law mu^ell+1. We then expand ln fraceta^ell+11-eta^ell+1 =ln frac Pi^SPIN+(1-Pi^SPIN-) Pi^SPIN- =ln(1-Pi^SPIN-) +lnfrac1Pi^SPIN- -lnfrac1Pi^SPIN+\,. Conditional on smashvecd we can decompose Sigma^SPINtextpmequivln(1/Pi^SPINtextpm) as a sum of i.i.d.\ terms: Sigma^SPINtextpm equivln frac1Pi^SPINtextpm = sum_i=1^d^SPINtextpm bigg\-ln bigg( 1 - prod_j=1^k-1 eta^SPINtextpm_ij bigg)bigg\ equiv sum_i=1^d^SPINtextpm X_i^SPINtextpm ge0\,, where the X_i^SPINtextpm are equidistributed as the random variable X of Lemma~. The remainder of the proof is divided into a few steps. bemphStep 1. Concentration bounds for Sigma^SPINtextpm. Consider Sigma^SPIN+, and define the truncated random variables \[Y_iequiv X^SPIN+_i 1bigg\ X^SPIN+_i le bigg(frac2^1/102bigg)^k-1 bigg\\,, Yequiv X 1bigg\ X le bigg(frac2^1/102bigg)^k-1 bigg\\,.\] Next define the events \[ textupfootnotesize BIG equivbigg\ max_ile alpha k X^SPIN+_i ge bigg(frac2^1/102bigg)^k-1 bigg\\,, textupfootnotesize DEG equiv bigg\bigg| d^SPIN+-fracalpha k2bigg| ge k^2 2^5k/8bigg\\,. \] On the complement of the event textupfootnotesize DEGcuptextupfootnotesize BIG, it follows using Lemma~ that bigg|sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ X^SPIN+_i - fracalpha k2E X bigg| &=bigg|sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ Y_i - fracalpha k2E X bigg| le bigg| sum_i=1^alpha k/2 Y_i - fracalpha k2E Y bigg| +frack^2 2^5k/82^9k/10 + alpha k E(X-Y) \\ &lebigg| sum_i=1^alpha k/2 Y_i - fracalpha k2E Y bigg| +frack^2 2^5k/82^9k/10 + fracalpha kexp\Omega(k2^k/4)\ le bigg| sum_i=1^alpha k/2 Y_i - fracalpha k2E Y bigg| + frac1k^5 2^k/4\,. Consequently, for t ge 1/(k2^k/4), we obtain by a union bound that \[ Pbigg( bigg| sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ X^SPIN+_i - fracalpha k2E X bigg|ge tbigg) leP(textupfootnotesize BIGcuptextupfootnotesize DEG)+ Pbigg( bigg| sum_i=1^alpha k/2 Y_i - fracalpha k2E Y bigg|ge fract2bigg)\,. \] By Lemma~ and a trivial union bound over 1le ile alpha k, we have \[P(textupfootnotesize BIG) le fracalpha k exp\Omega(k2^k/4)\ le frac1exp\Omega(k2^k/4)\\,.\] In the Poisson Chernoff bound , for small u we have f(u)asymp u^2, so P(textupfootnotesize DEG)leexp\-Omega(k^3 2^k/4)\. Finally, by the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality, it holds for all tge0 that Pbigg( bigg|sum_i=1^alpha k/2 (Y_i-E Y_i)bigg| ge tbigg) le fracO(1)exp\Omega(t^2 2^4k/5/k)\\,. We now rewrite the decomposition~ as ln fraceta^ell+11-eta^ell+1 = lnbigg(1-frac1exp Sigma^SPIN-bigg) +Sigma^SPIN--Sigma^SPIN+ le |Sigma^SPIN--Sigma^SPIN+| le bigg|Sigma^SPIN+-fracalpha k2E Xbigg| +bigg|Sigma^SPIN--fracalpha k2E Xbigg| \,. We can then apply the preceding bound~ to obtain that for all k/2^11k/40 le s le 1, \[ mu^ell+1bigg( ln fraceta^ell+11-eta^ell+1 ge s bigg) le Pbigg( |Sigma^SPIN--Sigma^SPIN+| ge s bigg) le 2Pbigg( bigg|Sigma^SPIN--fracalpha k2E Xbigg| ge fracs2 bigg) le frac1exp\ Omega( s k 2^k/4) \\,. \] This implies the desired upper bound for 2^-k/4 le s le 1. bemphStep 3. On the event textupfootnotesize DEG^s we have &bigg|sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ Y_i -fracalpha k2E Xbigg| le bigg|sum_i=1^alpha k/2 (Y_i-E Y_i)bigg| +bigg|sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ Y_i - sum_i=1^alpha k/2 Y_i bigg| + fracalpha k2E(X-Y)\\ & le bigg|sum_i=1^alpha k/2 (Y_i-E Y_i)bigg| + s 2^k/4 bigg( frac2^1/102 bigg)^k-1 + frac1exp\Omega(k2^k/4)\ le bigg|sum_i=1^alpha k/2 (Y_i-E Y_i)bigg| + fracs2^k/2 \,, where we used Lemma~ to bound E(X-Y), and the last bound holds for all sge1. Together they imply, with preccurlyeq denoting stochastic domination, that sum_i=1^d^SPIN+ (X^SPIN+_i-Y_i) preccurlyeq sum_i=1^d^SPIN+I_i(1+Z_i) where I_i are i.i.d.\ textupBer(e^-theta) indicators, and the Z_i are i.i.d.\ theta^-1textupExp random variables (where textupExp denotes a standard exponential random variable), with theta=ck2^k/4 for some absolute constant c>0. Given any tree T rooted at a variable v_textuptextscrt, we say that Q is a bemphc-modification of T if Q can be obtained from T by [--] item deleting at most one subtree T(u) for uin N(v_textuptextscrt), and item changing at most c subtrees T(u) for uinpartial_2v_textuptextscrt. The new subtrees Q(u), for uinpartial_2v_textuptextscrt, can be arbitrary. We then say that an acyclic variable v is bemphc-robust if every c-modification of B_r(v) is nice. Note that being c-robust is stronger than being 1-nice.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:J.robust}
If $U$ is any rooted tree and $x$ is any vertex in $U$, we let $U(x)$ denote the subtree of $U$ that lies below $x$. Given any tree $\mathscr{T}$ rooted at a variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, we say that $\mathscr{Q}$ is a \bemph{$\mathfrak{c}$-modification} of $\mathscr{T}$ if $\mathscr{Q}$ can be obtained from $\mathscr{T}$ by
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item deleting at most one subtree $\mathscr{T}(u)$ for $u\in N(v_\textup{\textsc{rt}})$, and 
\item changing at most $\mathfrak{c}$ subtrees $\mathscr{T}(u)$ for $u\in\partial_2v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.
\end{enumerate}
The new subtrees $\mathscr{Q}(u)$, for $u\in\partial_2v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, can be arbitrary. We then say that an acyclic variable $v$ is \bemph{$\mathfrak{c}$-robust} if every $\mathfrak{c}$-modification of $B_r(v)$ is nice. Note that being $\mathfrak{c}$-robust is stronger than being $1$-nice.

We allow T=varnothing, in which case P=textupfootnotesize PGW(varnothing)=textupfootnotesize PGW. If TequivT_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt is sampled from P, then \[PBigg( maxBigg\ sum_xinsetSPIN+,SPIN-,SPINf Big| 2^kIndx=SPINf bmeta'(x)-frac12Big| \,Bigg|\,hspace-3pt c textupbmeta' =F_ell(Q_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt), for Q_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt \\ textupa c-perturbation of T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt hspace-3pt Bigg\ ge frac12^k/4 Bigg) le frac1exp(Omega(k2^k/4)) \] for all ellge0. Throughout this proof we will abbreviate Tequiv T_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt, TequivT_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt, and QequivQ_v_textuptextscrta_textuptextscrt. From the definitions (see, in particular, the discussion below ), the measure bmetaequivF_ell(T) only depends on the tree up to depth ell below v_textuptextscrt. For 0le ellle1, any c-perturbation has bmeta'=bmeta, so there is nothing more to prove. We therefore assume ellge2 for the rest of the proof. We next describe a procedure to generate a sample of bmeta. In the fixed tree T, we partition the first layer of clauses (at depth 1/2 below v_textuptextscrt) according to the signs on the edges from these clauses to v_textuptextscrt: \[ (partial^SPIN+ T,partial^SPIN- T) equiv bigg( T cap partial v_textuptextscrt(SPIN+a_textuptextscrt)\,, T cap partial v_textuptextscrt(SPIN-a_textuptextscrt)bigg)\,. \] Let d^SPINtextpm(T)equiv|partial^SPINtextpm T|; these are both upper bounded by c. (If T=varnothing we define d^SPINtextpm(T)equiv0.) For 1le ile d^SPIN+(T), the i-th clause in partial^SPIN+ T has c^SPIN+(i) child variables in T. Let T(SPIN+,i,j) be the subtree of T descended from the j-th child variable of the i-th clause in partial^SPIN+(T). Define similarly c^SPIN-(i) and T(SPIN-,i,j). Now define bmeta by the following steps: [(i)] item Sample an array of independent random trees T^SPINtextpm_ijsimtextupfootnotesize PGW(T(SPINtextpm,i,j)), and define the corresponding messages \[ eta^SPINtextpm_ij(T)equiv Big[ F_ell-1(T^SPINtextpm_ij) Big](SPIN-)\,, \] for 1le ile d^SPINtextpm(T) and 1le jle c^SPINtextpm(i). item Let smashveceta be an array (as in ) of i.i.d.\ samples from mu^ell-1= bmR^ell-1mu^0, where mu^0=delta_1/2 as before. Let \[ u^SPIN+_i(T) equiv prod_j=1^c^SPIN+(i) eta^SPIN+_ij(T) prod_j=c^SPIN+(i)+1^k-1 eta^SPIN+_ij\,, u^SPIN+_i equiv prod_j=1^k-1 eta^SPIN+_ij\,. \] Define similarly u^SPIN-_i(T) and u^SPIN-_i. item Let smashvecdequiv(d^SPIN+,d^SPIN-) be an independent sample from textuppo_SPINtextpm, and define Pi^SPIN+(T) equivprod_i=1^d^SPIN+(T) bigg(1-u^SPIN+_i(T)bigg)\,, Pi^SPIN+ equivprod_i=d^SPIN+(T)+1^d^SPIN+(T)+d^SPIN+ bigg(1-u^SPIN+_ibigg)\,, Pi^*SPIN+ equiv Pi^SPIN+(T)Pi^SPIN+\,. Define similarly Pi^SPIN-(T), Pi^SPIN-, and Pi^*SPIN-=Pi^SPIN-(T)Pi^SPIN-. item Substitute the Pi^*SPINtextpm into to define bmeta: \[ bigg( bmeta(SPIN+),bmeta(SPIN-),bmeta(SPINf) bigg) = bigg(fracPi^*SPIN-(1-Pi^*SPIN+) Pi^*SPIN+ + Pi^*SPIN- - Pi^*SPIN+ Pi^*SPIN- , fracPi^*SPIN+(1-Pi^*SPIN-) Pi^*SPIN+ + Pi^*SPIN- - Pi^*SPIN+ Pi^*SPIN- , fracPi^*SPIN+Pi^*SPIN- Pi^*SPIN+ + Pi^*SPIN- - Pi^*SPIN+ Pi^*SPIN- bigg)\,. \] The bmeta that results from this construction can be regarded as a sample of F_ell(T) for Tsimtextupfootnotesize PGW(T), although we did not explicitly generate all of T. Moreover, if bmeta'=F_ell(Q) where Q is any c-perturbation of T, then bmeta' can also be obtained from the above procedure by modifying at most c of the messages from depth one. For convenience we will let vectheta denote the messages that are actually used in the definition of bmeta, so \[ theta^SPIN+_ij equivleft\ cl eta^SPIN+_ij(T) &textupif 1le ile d^SPIN+(T) textup and 1le jle c^SPIN+(i);\\ eta^SPIN+_ij &textupotherwise, right. \] and similarly theta^SPIN-_ij. To bound the different between bmeta and bmeta', we first assume a fixed set of affected indices: without loss of generality, let vecvartheta denote a new set of messages such that \[ bigg\ (i,j):vartheta^SPINtextpm_ijnetheta^SPINtextpm_ij bigg\ subseteq bigg\ (i,j): 1le ile 2c, 1le jle 2c bigg\\,. \] Returning to , let Sigma^SPINtextpm(T)equiv-ln Pi^SPINtextpm(T), Sigma^SPINtextpmequiv-ln Pi^SPINtextpm, and Sigma^*SPINtextpmequiv -lnPi^*SPINtextpm. Let Xi^SPINtextpm(T), Xi^SPINtextpm, and Xi^*SPINtextpm be defined analogously as the Sigma quantities, but with vecvartheta in place of vectheta. It is then straightforward to check that |Xi^*SPIN+ -Sigma^SPIN+| &le sum_i=1^d^SPIN+(T) -lnbigg( 1-prod_j=1^k-1 vartheta^SPIN+_ijbigg) +sum_i=d^SPIN+(T)+1^2c bigg| ln bigg( 1-prod_j=1^k-1 vartheta^SPIN+_ijbigg) -lnbigg( 1-prod_j=1^k-1 theta^SPIN+_ij bigg)bigg|\\ &lesum_i=1^2cbigg[underbrace -lnbigg( 1-prod_j=2c+1^k-1 theta^SPIN+_ij bigg)_Delta^SPIN+(i)bigg] equiv sum_i=1^2c Delta^SPIN+(i)\,. By the same argument as for the estimate~ from the proof of Lemma~, we have \[ Pbigg( |Xi^*SPIN+-Sigma^SPIN+| gebigg(frac2^1/202bigg)^k bigg) le 2ccdot Pbigg( |Delta^SPIN+(i)| gebigg(frac2^1/212bigg)^k bigg) le frac1exp\Omega(k2^k/4)\\,, \] and the same bound applies for |Xi^*SPIN--Sigma^SPIN-|. Now recall the bound~ from the proof of Lemma~, which says that the Sigma^SPINtextpm are well concentrated around kln2. In particular, it holds with probability at least 1-exp(-Omega(k2^k/4)) that |Sigma^SPINtextpm-kln2| le k/2^11k/40 and |Xi^*SPINtextpm-Sigma^SPINtextpm| le (2^1/20/2)^k, in which case bmeta'(SPINtextpm) &= fracexp(Xi^*SPINtextpm)-1 exp(Xi^*SPINtextpm)+exp(Xi^*SPINtextpm)-1 = frac1 + O(k/2^11k/40)2\,,\\ bmeta'(SPINf) &=frac1 exp(Xi^*SPINtextpm)+exp(Xi^*SPINtextpm)-1 =frac1 + O(k/2^11k/40)2^k+1\,. Thus, given a fixed choice of at most c perturbed indices, it holds with probability at least 1-exp(-Omega(k2^k/4)) that any resulting message bmeta' satisfies the above estimates, regardless of how those c indices are perturbed. To conclude, we note that by the event textupfootnotesize DEG^+equiv\ \ d^SPIN+,d^SPIN- \ ge 4^k/k \ has probability upper bounded by exp(-Omega(4^k)). On the complement of textupfootnotesize DEG^+, the number of distinct choices for the c perturbed indices is exp(O(k)), so we can take a union bound over all choices to obtain the result.

Throughout this proof we will abbreviate $T\equiv T_{v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$, $\mathscr{T}\equiv\mathscr{T}_{v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$, and $\mathscr{Q}\equiv\mathscr{Q}_{v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$. From the definitions (see, in particular, the discussion below \eqref{e:def.FF.of.tree}), the measure $\bm{\eta}\equiv\mathbf{F}_\ell(\mathscr{T})$ only depends on the tree up to depth $\ell$ below $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$. For $0\le \ell\le1$, any $\mathfrak{c}$-perturbation has $\bm{\eta}'=\bm{\eta}$, so there is nothing more to prove. We therefore assume $\ell\ge2$ for the rest of the proof.

We next describe a procedure to generate a sample of $\bm{\eta}$. In the fixed tree $T$, we partition the first layer of clauses (at depth $1/2$ below $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$) according to the signs on the edges from these clauses to $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$:
	\[
	(\partial^\SPIN{+} T,\partial^\SPIN{-} T)
	\equiv
	\bigg( T \cap \partial v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}(\SPIN{+}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}})\,,
	T \cap \partial v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}(\SPIN{-}a_\textup{\textsc{rt}})\bigg)\,.
	\]
Let $d^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)\equiv|\partial^\SPIN{\textpm} T|$; these are both upper bounded by $\mathfrak{c}$. (If $T=\varnothing$ we define $d^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)\equiv0$.) For $1\le i\le d^\SPIN{+}(T)$, the $i$-th clause in $\partial^\SPIN{+} T$ has $\mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{+}(i)$ child variables in $T$. Let $T(\SPIN{+},i,j)$ be the subtree of $T$ descended from the $j$-th child variable of the $i$-th clause in $\partial^\SPIN{+}(T)$. Define similarly $\mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{-}(i)$ and $T(\SPIN{-},i,j)$. Now define $\bm{\eta}$ by the following steps:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Sample an array of independent random trees
$\mathscr{T}^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij}\sim{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}(T(\SPIN{\textpm},i,j))$,
and define the corresponding messages
	\[
	\eta^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij}(T)\equiv
	\Big[
	\mathbf{F}_{\ell-1}(\mathscr{T}^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij})
	\Big](\SPIN{-})\,,
	\]
for $1\le i\le d^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)$ and $1\le j\le \mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{\textpm}(i)$.

\item Let $\smash{\vec{\eta}}$ be an array (as in \eqref{e:defn.array.ueta}) of i.i.d.\ samples from $\mu^{\ell-1}=
\bm{R}^{\ell-1}\mu^0$, where $\mu^0=\delta_{1/2}$ as before. Let
	\[
	u^\SPIN{+}_i(T)
	\equiv \prod_{j=1}^{\mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{+}(i)} 
	\eta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}(T)
	\prod_{j=\mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{+}(i)+1}^{k-1}
	\eta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}\,,\quad
	u^\SPIN{+}_i
	\equiv \prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \eta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}\,.
	\]
Define similarly $u^\SPIN{-}_i(T)$ and $u^\SPIN{-}_i$.

\item Let $\smash{\vec{d}}\equiv(d^\SPIN{+},d^\SPIN{-})$ be an independent sample from $\textup{\textsf{po}}_{\SPIN{\textpm}}$, and define
	\begin{equation}\label{e:Pi.with.embedded.T}
	\Pi^\SPIN{+}(T)
	\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{d^\SPIN{+}(T)}
	\bigg(1-u^\SPIN{+}_i(T)\bigg)\,,\quad
	\Pi^\SPIN{+}
	\equiv\prod_{i=d^\SPIN{+}(T)+1}^{d^\SPIN{+}(T)+d^\SPIN{+}}
	\bigg(1-u^\SPIN{+}_i\bigg)\,,\quad
	\Pi^{*\SPIN{+}}
	\equiv
	\Pi^\SPIN{+}(T)\Pi^\SPIN{+}\,.
	\end{equation}
Define similarly $\Pi^\SPIN{-}(T)$, $\Pi^\SPIN{-}$, and $\Pi^{*\SPIN{-}}=\Pi^\SPIN{-}(T)\Pi^\SPIN{-}$.
\item Substitute the $\Pi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}}$ into \eqref{e:eta.in.terms.of.signed.Pis} to define $\bm{\eta}$:
	\[
	\bigg(
	\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{+}),\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{-}),\bm{\eta}(\SPIN{f})
	\bigg)
	=
	\bigg(\frac{\Pi^{*\SPIN{-}}(1-\Pi^{*\SPIN{+}})}
		{ \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} + \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} 
			- \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} },
	\frac{\Pi^{*\SPIN{+}}(1-\Pi^{*\SPIN{-}})}
		{ \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} + \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} 
			- \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} },
	\frac{\Pi^{*\SPIN{+}}\Pi^{*\SPIN{-}}}
		{ \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} + \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} 
			- \Pi^{*\SPIN{+}} \Pi^{*\SPIN{-}} }
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
\end{enumerate}
The $\bm{\eta}$ that results from this construction can be regarded as a sample of $\mathbf{F}_\ell(\mathscr{T})$ for $\mathscr{T}\sim{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}(T)$, although we did not explicitly generate all of $\mathscr{T}$. Moreover, if $\bm{\eta}'=\mathbf{F}_\ell(\mathscr{Q})$ where $\mathscr{Q}$ is any $\mathfrak{c}$-perturbation of $\mathscr{T}$, then $\bm{\eta}'$ can also be obtained from the above procedure by modifying at most $\mathfrak{c}$ of the messages from depth one.

For convenience we will let $\vec{\theta}$ denote the messages that are actually used in the definition of $\bm{\eta}$, so
	\[
	\theta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}
	\equiv\left\{
	\begin{array}{cl}
	\eta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}(T)
	&\textup{if }1\le i\le d^\SPIN{+}(T)
	\textup{ and }1\le j\le \mathfrak{c}^\SPIN{+}(i);\\
		\eta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}
	&\textup{otherwise,}
	\end{array}
	\right.
	\]
and similarly $\theta^\SPIN{-}_{ij}$. To bound the different between $\bm{\eta}$ and $\bm{\eta}'$,
we first assume a \emph{fixed} set of affected indices: without loss of generality, let $\vec{\vartheta}$ denote a new set of messages such that
	\[
	\bigg\{
	(i,j):\vartheta^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij}\ne\theta^\SPIN{\textpm}_{ij}
	\bigg\}
	\subseteq
	\bigg\{
	(i,j):
	1\le i\le 2\mathfrak{c},
	1\le j\le 2\mathfrak{c}
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Returning to \eqref{e:Pi.with.embedded.T},
let $\Sigma^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)\equiv-\ln \Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)$,
$\Sigma^\SPIN{\textpm}\equiv-\ln \Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}$,
and $\Sigma^{*\SPIN{\textpm}}\equiv -\ln\Pi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}}$.
Let $\Xi^\SPIN{\textpm}(T)$, $\Xi^\SPIN{\textpm}$, and $\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}}$
be defined analogously as the $\Sigma$ quantities,
but with $\vec{\vartheta}$ in place of $\vec{\theta}$. 
It is then straightforward to check that
	\begin{align*}
	|\Xi^{*\SPIN{+}}
		-\Sigma^\SPIN{+}|
	&\le
	\sum_{i=1}^{d^\SPIN{+}(T)}
	-\ln\bigg( 1-\prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \vartheta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}\bigg)
	+\sum_{i=d^\SPIN{+}(T)+1}^{2\mathfrak{c}}
	\bigg| \ln \bigg( 1-\prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \vartheta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}\bigg)
		-\ln\bigg( 1-\prod_{j=1}^{k-1} \theta^\SPIN{+}_{ij}
		\bigg)\bigg|\\
	&\le\sum_{i=1}^{2\mathfrak{c}}\bigg[\underbrace{
	-\ln\bigg( 1-\prod_{j=2\mathfrak{c}+1}^{k-1} \theta^\SPIN{+}_{ij} \bigg)}_{\Delta^\SPIN{+}(i)}\bigg]
	\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{2\mathfrak{c}} \Delta^\SPIN{+}(i)\,.
	\end{align*}
By the same argument as for the estimate~\eqref{e:X.upper.tail.small} from the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:X.tail.bounds}, we have
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\bigg(
	|\Xi^{*\SPIN{+}}-\Sigma^\SPIN{+}|
	\ge\bigg(\frac{2^{1/20}}{2}\bigg)^k
	\bigg)
	\le 2\mathfrak{c}\cdot \mathbb{P}\bigg(
	|\Delta^\SPIN{+}(i)|
	\ge\bigg(\frac{2^{1/21}}{2}\bigg)^k
	\bigg)
	\le \frac1{\exp\{\Omega(k2^{k/4})\}}\,,
	\]
and the same bound applies for $|\Xi^{*\SPIN{-}}-\Sigma^\SPIN{-}|$. Now recall the bound~\eqref{e:simple.bound.on.Sigma} from the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:mu.ell.tail.bounds}, which says that the $\Sigma^\SPIN{\textpm}$ are well concentrated around $k\ln2$. 
In particular, it holds with probability at least 
$1-\exp(-\Omega(k2^{k/4}))$
that $|\Sigma^\SPIN{\textpm}-k\ln2| \le k/2^{11k/40}$
and $|\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}}-\Sigma^\SPIN{\textpm}| \le (2^{1/20}/2)^k$,
in which case
	\begin{align*}
	\bm{\eta}'(\SPIN{\textpm})
	&= \frac{\exp(\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}})-1}
		{\exp(\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}})+\exp(\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}})-1}
	= \frac{1 + O(k/2^{11k/40})}2\,,\\
	\bm{\eta}'(\SPIN{f})
	&=\frac1
		{\exp(\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}})+\exp(\Xi^{*\SPIN{\textpm}})-1}
	=\frac{1 + O(k/2^{11k/40})}{2^{k+1}}\,.
	\end{align*}
Thus, given a \emph{fixed} choice of at most $\mathfrak{c}$ perturbed indices, it holds with probability at least $1-\exp(-\Omega(k2^{k/4}))$ that any resulting message $\bm{\eta}'$ satisfies the above estimates, regardless of how those $\mathfrak{c}$ indices are perturbed. To conclude, we note that by \eqref{e:poisson.chernoff.bound} the event $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize DEG}}^+\equiv\{ \{ d^\SPIN{+},d^\SPIN{-} \} \ge 4^k/k \}$ has probability upper bounded by $\exp(-\Omega(4^k))$. On the complement of $\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize DEG}}^+$, the number of distinct choices for the $\mathfrak{c}$ perturbed indices is $\exp(O(k))$,
so we can take a union bound over all choices to obtain the result.

\label{c:pth.moment.of.eta}
Let $\mu$ be any probability measure over $\eta\in[0,1)$ that satisfies condition~\eqref{i:mu.ell.upper.tail.bound} from Lemma~\ref{l:mu.ell.tail.bounds}. If $p=2^{k\delta}$ for any $1/100 \le \delta \le 1/9$, then we have the $p$-th moment bound
	\[
	\int \eta^p \,d\mu(\eta)
	\le \frac1{2^p}\bigg[
	1 + \frac{k}{2^{k(1/4-2\delta)}}\bigg]\,.
	\]

\begin{proof} 
Write $\delta'\equiv 1/4-\delta$. We can decompose
	\[
	E(p) \equiv
	\int \eta^p \,d\mu(\eta)
	\le
	\frac1{2^p}
	\bigg(
	1+\frac{\ln k}{2^{k\delta'}}
	\bigg)^p
	+ \bigg(\frac23\bigg)^p
	\mu\bigg( \eta \ge 
	\frac12 \bigg(1+\frac{\ln k}{2^{k\delta'}}\bigg)
	\bigg)
	+\mu\bigg( \eta \ge \frac23\bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\delta'>\delta$, so $(p\ln k)/2^{k\delta'}$ is small. Combining with \eqref{i:mu.ell.upper.tail.bound} gives
	\[
	E(p)
	\le
	\frac1{2^p}
	\bigg\{ 1 +\frac{O(p\ln k)}{2^{k\delta'}}\bigg\}
	+\frac{(2/3)^p}
		{\exp(\Omega( 2^{k/4} 2^{-k\delta'}\ln k ))}
	+\frac1{\exp(\Omega(2^{k/4}))}\,.
	\]
Substituting $p=2^{k\delta}$ and $\delta'=1/4-\delta$ into the above gives
	\[E(p)
	\le\frac1{2^p}\bigg[
	1 + \frac{O(\ln k)}{2^{k(1/4-2\delta)}}
	+\frac{\exp\{2^{k\delta}\ln(4/3)\}}
		{\exp(\Omega( 2^{k\delta}\ln k)
			)}
	+\frac{\exp\{ 2^{k\delta}\ln2 \}}{\exp(\Omega(2^{k/4}))}
	\bigg]
	\le \frac1{2^p}\bigg[
	1 + \frac{O(\ln k)}{2^{k(1/4-2\delta)}}\bigg]\,,
	\]
which concludes the proof.
\end{proof}

The quantity of interest can be written as
$\mathbb{E}[D^p /e^{\gamma D}]$ for
	\[
	\gamma
	\equiv \frac{p}{2^{k-1}}\bigg[
	1-\frac{k^3}{2^{k/4}}
	\bigg]\,.
	\]
We can check by differentiation
that $d^p / e^{\gamma d}$ is
decreasing with respect to $d$ for all
	\[
	d > \frac{p}{\gamma}
	= 2^{k-1} \bigg/ \bigg[
	1-\frac{k^3}{2^{k/4}}
	\bigg]\,.\]
For all $\alpha$ in the regime
\eqref{e:alpha.regime}, the mean 
$\mathbb{E} D=\alpha k/2$ is much larger than $p/\gamma$.
As in \eqref{e:alpha.regime} let $\alpha_\textup{ubd}\equiv 2^k\ln2$.
Then
	\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \frac{D^p}{\exp(\gamma D)}
	; D \ge \frac{k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}
	\bigg]
	&\le 
	\bigg(\frac{k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}\bigg)^p
	\exp\bigg\{-\frac{\gamma k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}\bigg\}\\
	&= \bigg(
	\frac{k 2^k \ln2}{2}
	\exp\bigg\{ -k\ln2
		\bigg[1-\frac{k^3}{2^{k/4}}\bigg] \bigg\}
	\bigg)^p
	\le O(1) \bigg(
		\frac{k\ln2}{2}\bigg)^p\,.
	\end{align*}
On the other hand, we can use the Poisson moment-generating function to bound
	\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \frac{D^p}{\exp(\gamma D)}
	; D \le \frac{k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}
	\bigg]
	&\le
	\bigg(\frac{k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}\bigg)^p
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[\frac1{ \exp(\gamma D)}\bigg]\\
	&=\bigg(\frac{k\alpha_\textup{ubd}}{2}\bigg)^p
	\exp\bigg\{- \frac{\alpha k}{2}
		\bigg(1-\frac1{e^\gamma}\bigg)\bigg\}
	\le 
	O(1) \bigg( \frac{k\ln2}{2}\bigg)^p\,.
	\end{align*}
Combining the bounds gives the claim.

\label{l:wk.rademacher.bound}
Let $Z,Z_i$ be i.i.d.\ random variables
with symmetric distribution
(meaning that $Z$ is equidistributed as $-Z$).
Then, for any positive integer $d$ and positive even integer $p$,
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\bigg( \sum_{i=1}^d Z_i\bigg)^p
	\le O(1) \bigg( \frac{dp}{e}\bigg)^{p/2}
	\mathbb{E}(|Z|^p)\,.
	\]


\begin{proof}
Writing $\vec{i}\equiv(i_1,\ldots,i_p)$ for elements of $[d]^p$, we expand
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\bigg( \sum_{i=1}^d Z_i\bigg)^p
	= \sum_{\vec{i}\in[d]^p}
	\mathbb{E}[ Z_{i_1} \cdots Z_{i_p}]\,.
	\]
On the right-hand side, $\mathbb{E}[ Z_{i_1} \cdots Z_{i_p}]$ is zero unless every index appears an even number of times. The number of choices for $\vec{i}$ for which this holds is upper bounded by $d^{p/2}(p-1)!!$, where
$(p-1)!!$ is the number of matchings on $p$ elements. By Stirling's formula,
	\[
	d^{p/2}(p-1)!!
	=\frac{d^{p/2} p!}{2^{p/2} (p/2)!}
	\le O(1) \bigg( \frac{dp}{e}\bigg)^{p/2}\,.
	\]
By Jensen's inequality, for any $\vec{i}$ we have
$\mathbb{E}[ Z_{i_1} \cdots Z_{i_p}] \le \mathbb{E}(|Z|^p)$. Combining these bounds gives the claim.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement: Take the random sequence (bmeta^ell)_ellge0 as in or , with epsilon=0. Then, as noted in the discussion around , the marginal law of each eta^ell is precisely mu^ell equiv bmR^ellmu^0, the same as the mu^ell appearing in the statement of this proposition. It follows from Lemma~ that for p=2lceil 2^k/10 rceil we have \[ sum_ellge0 Ebigg[ Big|eta^ell+1-eta^ellBig|^pbigg]^1/p le 2sum_ellge0 EBigg[ bigg|fraceta^ell+1-eta^ell eta^ell+1+eta^ellbigg|^p Bigg]^1/p < infty\,. \] Thus (eta^ell)_ellge0 is a Cauchy sequence in L^p, hence it must converge in L^p to a limiting random variable eta as elltoinfty. It follows that mu^ell converges weakly to a limiting probability measure mu as elltoinfty. Since mu^ell = bmRmu^ell-1 and the mapping bmR is continuous with respect to the weak topology on the space of distributions, we conclude mu = bmRmu.

\label{l:support.of.pi.measures}
Let $\mathscr{T}_{va}$ be any variable-to-clause tree in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:directed.trees}. Similarly as in 
\eqref{e:coupling.of.all.eta.ell} or \eqref{e:coupling.eta.with.eps.param}, let
	\[
	(\bm{\eta}^\ell)_{\ell\ge0}
	\equiv \bigg(\mathbf{F}_\ell(
	\mathscr{T}_{va} )\bigg)_{\ell\ge0}\,.
	\]
It holds for any $\mathscr{T}_{va}$ and any $\ell\ge0$ that if
$\bm{\eta}^\ell(\SPIN{+})=0$ then $\bm{\eta}^{\ell+1}(\SPIN{+})=0$ also;
likewise if $\bm{\eta}^\ell(\SPIN{-})=0$ then $\bm{\eta}^{\ell+1}(\SPIN{-})=0$ also.
Moreover $\bm{\eta}^\ell(\SPIN{f})\in(0,1]$ for all $\ell\ge1$. As a consequence we always have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:compare.support.of.pis}
	\set{\SSPIN{g}}\subseteq \textup{supp}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi\subseteq\textup{supp}{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi\,,\end{equation}
for all $r\ge2$,
for ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ and ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ as in
Definition~\ref{d:canonical}.


\begin{proof}Thanks to the symmetry between $\SPIN{+}$ and $\SPIN{-}$, it suffices to prove the first assertion for the quantities $\eta^\ell \equiv \bm{\eta}^\ell(\SPIN{-})$. That is to say, we shall argue that if
$\eta^\ell=0$ then $\eta^{\ell+1}=0$ also, for all $\ell\ge0$. Note that $\eta^0=1/2\ne0$ by assumption, so the statement holds trivially for $\ell=0$. Suppose inductively that it holds up to $\ell-1$; we then compare $\eta^\ell$ with $\eta^{\ell+1}$. Similarly as in Definitions~\ref{d:distributional.clause.recursion}--\ref{d:full.dist.recurs}
and the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:stability}, we can express
	\[
	\eta^{\ell+1} = \frac{\Pi^\SPIN{+}(1-\Pi^\SPIN{-})}
		{\Pi^\SPIN{+} + \Pi^\SPIN{-} - \Pi^\SPIN{+} \Pi^\SPIN{-} }\,,\quad
	\Pi^\SPIN{\textpm}\equiv \prod_{b\in\partial v(\SPIN{\textpm} a)} \bigg(
		1 - \prod_{u\in\partial b\setminus v} \eta^\ell(\mathscr{T}_{ub})
		\bigg)
	\]
and similarly
	\[
	\eta^\ell = \frac{\pi^\SPIN{+}(1-\pi^\SPIN{-})}
		{\pi^\SPIN{+} + \pi^\SPIN{-} - \pi^\SPIN{+} \pi^\SPIN{-} }\,,\quad

\label{l:root.is.stable.EPSILON}
For the measure ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ of Definition~\ref{d:PGW.with.clauses.one.less},
we have
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon\Big(
		\textup{$v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ not stable}\Big)
	\le \frac1{\exp(2^{k/12} R)}\,,
	\]
where ``stable'' means $0$-stable in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:j.stable}. This bound holds for all $0\le\epsilon\le1$.


\begin{proof}
For any tree $\mathscr{T}$ and any edge $(au)$ of $\mathscr{T}$,
we can consider the variable-to-clause
 tree $\mathscr{T}_{ua}\subseteq\mathscr{T}$, and define (cf.\ \eqref{e:coupling.of.all.eta.ell}~and~\eqref{e:coupling.eta.with.eps.param})
the measures $\bm{\eta}^\ell_{ua}\equiv \mathbf{F}_\ell(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$.
We define two functions on variable-to-clause trees,
	\begin{align*}
	f^\SPIN{+}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})
	&\equiv
	\mathbf{1}\Bigg\{
	\max\bigg\{
	\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+}),
	\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})
	\bigg\} \ge 
	1-\frac1{k^r}\Bigg\}\,,\\
	g^\SPIN{+}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})
	&\equiv \mathbf{1} \Bigg\{\Bigg|
		\frac{\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})
			-\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})}
		{\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})+
		\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})}\Bigg|
	\ge \frac1{2^{kr/8}}
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\end{align*}
and likewise 
$f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$
and $g^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$.
If $u$ and $w$ are neighboring variables on $\mathscr{T}$,
we let $a(uw)\equiv a(wu)$ denote the unique clause that they share. For the rest of the proof, we let $\mathscr{T}$ be a sample from ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$, rooted at $v\equiv v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.
Since ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ is unimodular, we can apply \eqref{e:unimodular} to evaluate
	\begin{equation}\label{e:unimodular.applied}
	\int\bigg[ \sum_{u\in N(v)}
	f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})
	=\int \bigg[\sum_{u\in N(v)}
	f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{u a(uv)})\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})\,.
	\end{equation}
Note that, given $B_1(v)$,
the $f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})$ are not conditionally independent over $u\in N(v)$,
but the $f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{u a(uv)})$ are.
The above is therefore upper bounded by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}
	k^2\alpha
	\int f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\,d{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\le
	\frac{k^2\alpha}{\exp(\Omega(r 2^{k/4} ))}\,,\end{equation}
where the last bound is
by the upper tail bound \eqref{i:mu.ell.upper.tail.bound} from Lemma~\ref{l:mu.ell.tail.bounds}.
By symmetry, 
the bound \eqref{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}
also holds with $f^\SPIN{+}$
in place of $f^\SPIN{-}$.
With $g^\SPIN{-}$ in place of $f^\SPIN{-}$, the identity \eqref{e:unimodular.applied} also holds, and conditional independence gives the upper bound
	\[
	k^2\alpha
	\int g^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\,d{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\le
	k^2\alpha
	\,\mathbb{P}_\epsilon\Bigg(
	 \Bigg|\frac{\eta^r-\eta^{r-1}}
		{\eta^r+\eta^{r-1}}\Bigg|
	\ge \frac1{2^{kr/8}}
	\Bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\mathbb{P}_\epsilon$ is the measure from Lemma~\ref{l:stability}. From the bound of 
Lemma~\ref{l:stability}, the last expression is
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.pgw.bound}
	\le
	k^2\alpha(2^{kr/8})^p
	\mathbb{E}_\epsilon\Bigg[\Bigg(
	 \Bigg|\frac{\eta^r-\eta^{r-1}}
		{\eta^r+\eta^{r-1}}\Bigg|^p\Bigg]
	\le
	\frac{k^2\alpha 2^{kpr/8} }{2^{kpr/7}}
	\le
	\frac{4^k}{2^{kpr/56}}
	\le \frac1{\exp(k r 2^{k/11} )}\,.
	\end{equation}
Let $A=f^\SPIN{+}+f^\SPIN{-}+g^\SPIN{+}+g^\SPIN{-}$, and define
the ($B_r(v;\mathscr{T})$-measurable) event
	\[
	\bm{E}\equiv
	\bigcap_{a\in\partial v}
	\bigg\{A(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0
	\textup{ for all }u\in\partial a
	\bigg\}\,.\]
We then find by Markov's inequality together with \eqref{e:unimodular.applied}, \eqref{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}, and \eqref{e:stability.pgw.bound} that
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\bm{E}^c)
	\le
	\int\bigg[\sum_{u\in\partial v}\bigg\{
	\frac{A(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})}{k-2}
	+A(\mathscr{T}_{u a(u v)})\bigg\}\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})
	\le \frac1{\exp(r 2^{k/11})}\,.
	\]
We will prove that the root $v$ is stable on event $\bm{E}$. 

Recall from Definition~\ref{d:j.stable} that $v$ is stable if all its incident edges $e\in\delta v$ are both message-stable and marginal-stable (Definition~\ref{d:stable}). It is clear that $\bm{E}$ implies that every edge incident to $v$ satisfies the message-stability condition \eqref{e:message.stability}. (The first part of \eqref{e:message.stability} holds because $\bm{E}$ implies $f^\SPIN{\textpm}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0$ for all $a\in \partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$. The second part of \eqref{e:message.stability} holds because $\bm{E}$ implies $g^\SPIN{\textpm}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0$ for all $a\in \partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$.) Therefore it remains only to check the marginal-stability conditions \eqref{e:stable.yellow}--\eqref{e:stable.positivity}.

For the rest of the proof, for all $a\in\partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$, we will denote
$H_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{-})$,
$h_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{-})$,
$P_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})$, and
$p_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})$.
For $a\in\partial v$ we also let
	\[
	\hat{u}_{av}
	\equiv \prod_{u\in\partial a\setminus v} h_{ua}\,.
	\]
With this notation, and using the correspondence
\eqref{e:color.recursions.eta},
we have for all $a\in\partial v$ that
	\[
	\bigg({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{r}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{y}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{b}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{c})
	\bigg)
	= \bigg(
		\frac{(1-H_{va})\hat{u}_{av}}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{H_{va}(1-\hat{u}_{av})}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{
		P_{va}(1-\hat{u}_{av})}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{
		(1-H_{va})(1-\hat{u}_{av})
		}{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}}
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
We can obtain ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}$ from the same expressions, only $h_{va}$ and $p_{va}$ in place of $H_{va}$ and $P_{va}$ (keeping $\hat{u}_{av}$ the same). By Lemma~\ref{l:support.of.pi.measures},
if $h_{va}=0$ then $H_{va}=0$,
and if $p_{va}=0$ then $P_{va}=0$.
On the event $\bm{E}$, if $(H,h,\hat{u})=(H_{va},h_{va},\hat{u}_{av})$ for any $a\in\partial v$, then either 
$h=H=0$, or $h>0$ and
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{H}{h}-1\bigg|= \frac{|H-h|}{h}
	\le 2\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|
		\bigg/
		\Bigg( 1-\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|\Bigg)
	\le \frac{O(1)}{2^{kr/8}}
	&\le \frac{1}{2^{kr/9} k^{10}} \,,\\
	\frac{|(1-\hat{u} H)-(1-\hat{u} h)|}
		{1-\hat{u}h}
	\le
	\frac{|H-h|}{1-h}
	\le k^r|H-h|
	\le 2 k^r
	\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|
	\le \frac{2 k^r}{2^{kr/8}}
	&\le \frac{1}{2^{kr/9} k^{10}} \,.
	\end{align*}
The analogous bounds hold with $(P,p)=(P_{va},p_{va})$ in place of $(H,h)$. It follows that for all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{b}}$, we have either ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)=0$,
or ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)>0$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{e:yrc.diff.div.y}
	\bigg|\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)-{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)}
		{{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)}\bigg|
	\le \frac1{2^{kr/9}}
	\end{equation}
For $\sigma=\SSPIN{c}$,
we know that 
${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{c})\ge {}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{g})$ is always positive, and the estimate \eqref{e:yrc.diff.div.y} holds on all of $\bm{E}$. This implies the last stability condition~\eqref{e:stable.positivity}.
It remains to verify the other three conditions
\eqref{e:stable.yellow},
\eqref{e:stable.cyan}, and \eqref{e:stable.red}.
This essentially amounts to a quantitative version of the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:clause.based.marginals.cohere}.
Using \eqref{e:clause.tuple.measure.weighted}
and the correspondence \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta}, we have
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	= \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\bigg[1-\prod_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} h_{wa}
	-\sum_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} (1-h_{wa})
		\prod_{z\in\partial a \setminus \set{u,w}} h_{za}
	\bigg]\,,
	\]
where $\hat{z}_a$ is the clause normalization, given explicitly by
	\[
	\hat{z}_a
	= 1-\prod_{w\in\partial a} h_{wa} \le 1\,.
	\]
If $w,z$ are any two distinct variables in $\partial a\setminus u$, on the event $\bm{E}$ we have the crude lower bound
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	\ge \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a} 
		(1-h_{wa})(1-h_{za})
	\ge \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a k^{2r}}\,.
	\]
Similarly, if $u,w,z$ are any three distinct variables in $\partial a$, then 
 on the event $\bm{E}$ we have 
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_a({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	\ge\frac1{\hat{z}_a}
	(1-\eta_{ua})
	(1-\eta_{wa})
	(1-\eta_{za})
	\ge \frac1{\hat{z}_a k^{3r}}
	\ge \frac1{k^{3r}}\,.
	\]
On the other hand, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:yellow.vs.coher.edge}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{y})
	=\frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\bigg[1-\prod_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} h_{wa}\bigg]
	\le\frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\le k^{2r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
Similarly, for all $w\in\partial a\setminus u$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:red.vs.coher.edge}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{aw}(\SSPIN{r})
	=\frac{(1-h_{wa})}{\hat{z}_a}
	\prod_{z\in\partial a\setminus w} h_{za}
	\le \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\le k^{2r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
For all $u\in\partial a$, we have trivially
	\begin{equation}\label{e:coher.a.is.large}
	\bigg\{
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{c})+{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{r})
	\bigg\}
	\le 1 \le k^{3r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_a({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
The bounds \eqref{e:stable.yellow},
\eqref{e:stable.cyan}, and \eqref{e:stable.red}
follow by combining
 \eqref{e:yrc.diff.div.y} with
\eqref{e:yellow.vs.coher.edge}, \eqref{e:red.vs.coher.edge}, \eqref{e:coher.a.is.large}.
\end{proof}

For any tree $\mathscr{T}$ and any edge $(au)$ of $\mathscr{T}$,
we can consider the variable-to-clause
 tree $\mathscr{T}_{ua}\subseteq\mathscr{T}$, and define (cf.\ \eqref{e:coupling.of.all.eta.ell}~and~\eqref{e:coupling.eta.with.eps.param})
the measures $\bm{\eta}^\ell_{ua}\equiv \mathbf{F}_\ell(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$.
We define two functions on variable-to-clause trees,
	\begin{align*}
	f^\SPIN{+}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})
	&\equiv
	\mathbf{1}\Bigg\{
	\max\bigg\{
	\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+}),
	\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})
	\bigg\} \ge 
	1-\frac1{k^r}\Bigg\}\,,\\
	g^\SPIN{+}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})
	&\equiv \mathbf{1} \Bigg\{\Bigg|
		\frac{\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})
			-\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})}
		{\bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})+
		\bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})}\Bigg|
	\ge \frac1{2^{kr/8}}
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\end{align*}
and likewise 
$f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$
and $g^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})$.
If $u$ and $w$ are neighboring variables on $\mathscr{T}$,
we let $a(uw)\equiv a(wu)$ denote the unique clause that they share. For the rest of the proof, we let $\mathscr{T}$ be a sample from ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$, rooted at $v\equiv v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.
Since ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon$ is unimodular, we can apply \eqref{e:unimodular} to evaluate
	\begin{equation}\label{e:unimodular.applied}
	\int\bigg[ \sum_{u\in N(v)}
	f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})
	=\int \bigg[\sum_{u\in N(v)}
	f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{u a(uv)})\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})\,.
	\end{equation}
Note that, given $B_1(v)$,
the $f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})$ are not conditionally independent over $u\in N(v)$,
but the $f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{u a(uv)})$ are.
The above is therefore upper bounded by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}
	k^2\alpha
	\int f^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\,d{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\le
	\frac{k^2\alpha}{\exp(\Omega(r 2^{k/4} ))}\,,\end{equation}
where the last bound is
by the upper tail bound \eqref{i:mu.ell.upper.tail.bound} from Lemma~\ref{l:mu.ell.tail.bounds}.
By symmetry, 
the bound \eqref{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}
also holds with $f^\SPIN{+}$
in place of $f^\SPIN{-}$.
With $g^\SPIN{-}$ in place of $f^\SPIN{-}$, the identity \eqref{e:unimodular.applied} also holds, and conditional independence gives the upper bound
	\[
	k^2\alpha
	\int g^\SPIN{-}(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\,d{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T}_{va})
	\le
	k^2\alpha
	\,\mathbb{P}_\epsilon\Bigg(
	 \Bigg|\frac{\eta^r-\eta^{r-1}}
		{\eta^r+\eta^{r-1}}\Bigg|
	\ge \frac1{2^{kr/8}}
	\Bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\mathbb{P}_\epsilon$ is the measure from Lemma~\ref{l:stability}. From the bound of 
Lemma~\ref{l:stability}, the last expression is
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.pgw.bound}
	\le
	k^2\alpha(2^{kr/8})^p
	\mathbb{E}_\epsilon\Bigg[\Bigg(
	 \Bigg|\frac{\eta^r-\eta^{r-1}}
		{\eta^r+\eta^{r-1}}\Bigg|^p\Bigg]
	\le
	\frac{k^2\alpha 2^{kpr/8} }{2^{kpr/7}}
	\le
	\frac{4^k}{2^{kpr/56}}
	\le \frac1{\exp(k r 2^{k/11} )}\,.
	\end{equation}
Let $A=f^\SPIN{+}+f^\SPIN{-}+g^\SPIN{+}+g^\SPIN{-}$, and define
the ($B_r(v;\mathscr{T})$-measurable) event
	\[
	\bm{E}\equiv
	\bigcap_{a\in\partial v}
	\bigg\{A(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0
	\textup{ for all }u\in\partial a
	\bigg\}\,.\]
We then find by Markov's inequality together with \eqref{e:unimodular.applied}, \eqref{e:not.too.forcing.pgw.bound}, and \eqref{e:stability.pgw.bound} that
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\bm{E}^c)
	\le
	\int\bigg[\sum_{u\in\partial v}\bigg\{
	\frac{A(\mathscr{T}_{v a(v u)})}{k-2}
	+A(\mathscr{T}_{u a(u v)})\bigg\}\bigg]
	\,d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\epsilon(\mathscr{T})
	\le \frac1{\exp(r 2^{k/11})}\,.
	\]
We will prove that the root $v$ is stable on event $\bm{E}$. 

Recall from Definition~\ref{d:j.stable} that $v$ is stable if all its incident edges $e\in\delta v$ are both message-stable and marginal-stable (Definition~\ref{d:stable}). It is clear that $\bm{E}$ implies that every edge incident to $v$ satisfies the message-stability condition \eqref{e:message.stability}. (The first part of \eqref{e:message.stability} holds because $\bm{E}$ implies $f^\SPIN{\textpm}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0$ for all $a\in \partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$. The second part of \eqref{e:message.stability} holds because $\bm{E}$ implies $g^\SPIN{\textpm}(\mathscr{T}_{ua})=0$ for all $a\in \partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$.) Therefore it remains only to check the marginal-stability conditions \eqref{e:stable.yellow}--\eqref{e:stable.positivity}.

For the rest of the proof, for all $a\in\partial v$ and $u\in\partial a$, we will denote
$H_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{-})$,
$h_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{-})$,
$P_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^r_{ua}(\SPIN{+})$, and
$p_{ua}\equiv \bm{\eta}^{r-1}_{ua}(\SPIN{+})$.
For $a\in\partial v$ we also let
	\[
	\hat{u}_{av}
	\equiv \prod_{u\in\partial a\setminus v} h_{ua}\,.
	\]
With this notation, and using the correspondence
\eqref{e:color.recursions.eta},
we have for all $a\in\partial v$ that
	\[
	\bigg({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{r}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{y}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{b}),
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{c})
	\bigg)
	= \bigg(
		\frac{(1-H_{va})\hat{u}_{av}}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{H_{va}(1-\hat{u}_{av})}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{
		P_{va}(1-\hat{u}_{av})}
		{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}},
		\frac{
		(1-H_{va})(1-\hat{u}_{av})
		}{1-\hat{u}_{av} H_{va}}
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
We can obtain ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}$ from the same expressions, only $h_{va}$ and $p_{va}$ in place of $H_{va}$ and $P_{va}$ (keeping $\hat{u}_{av}$ the same). By Lemma~\ref{l:support.of.pi.measures},
if $h_{va}=0$ then $H_{va}=0$,
and if $p_{va}=0$ then $P_{va}=0$.
On the event $\bm{E}$, if $(H,h,\hat{u})=(H_{va},h_{va},\hat{u}_{av})$ for any $a\in\partial v$, then either 
$h=H=0$, or $h>0$ and
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{H}{h}-1\bigg|= \frac{|H-h|}{h}
	\le 2\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|
		\bigg/
		\Bigg( 1-\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|\Bigg)
	\le \frac{O(1)}{2^{kr/8}}
	&\le \frac{1}{2^{kr/9} k^{10}} \,,\\
	\frac{|(1-\hat{u} H)-(1-\hat{u} h)|}
		{1-\hat{u}h}
	\le
	\frac{|H-h|}{1-h}
	\le k^r|H-h|
	\le 2 k^r
	\bigg|\frac{H-h}{H+h}\bigg|
	\le \frac{2 k^r}{2^{kr/8}}
	&\le \frac{1}{2^{kr/9} k^{10}} \,.
	\end{align*}
The analogous bounds hold with $(P,p)=(P_{va},p_{va})$ in place of $(H,h)$. It follows that for all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{b}}$, we have either ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)=0$,
or ${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)>0$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{e:yrc.diff.div.y}
	\bigg|\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)-{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)}
		{{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\sigma)}\bigg|
	\le \frac1{2^{kr/9}}
	\end{equation}
For $\sigma=\SSPIN{c}$,
we know that 
${}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{c})\ge {}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{av}(\SSPIN{g})$ is always positive, and the estimate \eqref{e:yrc.diff.div.y} holds on all of $\bm{E}$. This implies the last stability condition~\eqref{e:stable.positivity}.
It remains to verify the other three conditions
\eqref{e:stable.yellow},
\eqref{e:stable.cyan}, and \eqref{e:stable.red}.
This essentially amounts to a quantitative version of the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:clause.based.marginals.cohere}.
Using \eqref{e:clause.tuple.measure.weighted}
and the correspondence \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta}, we have
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	= \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\bigg[1-\prod_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} h_{wa}
	-\sum_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} (1-h_{wa})
		\prod_{z\in\partial a \setminus \set{u,w}} h_{za}
	\bigg]\,,
	\]
where $\hat{z}_a$ is the clause normalization, given explicitly by
	\[
	\hat{z}_a
	= 1-\prod_{w\in\partial a} h_{wa} \le 1\,.
	\]
If $w,z$ are any two distinct variables in $\partial a\setminus u$, on the event $\bm{E}$ we have the crude lower bound
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	\ge \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a} 
		(1-h_{wa})(1-h_{za})
	\ge \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a k^{2r}}\,.
	\]
Similarly, if $u,w,z$ are any three distinct variables in $\partial a$, then 
 on the event $\bm{E}$ we have 
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{coher}}_a({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)
	\ge\frac1{\hat{z}_a}
	(1-\eta_{ua})
	(1-\eta_{wa})
	(1-\eta_{za})
	\ge \frac1{\hat{z}_a k^{3r}}
	\ge \frac1{k^{3r}}\,.
	\]
On the other hand, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:yellow.vs.coher.edge}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{y})
	=\frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\bigg[1-\prod_{w\in\partial a\setminus u} h_{wa}\bigg]
	\le\frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\le k^{2r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
Similarly, for all $w\in\partial a\setminus u$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:red.vs.coher.edge}
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{aw}(\SSPIN{r})
	=\frac{(1-h_{wa})}{\hat{z}_a}
	\prod_{z\in\partial a\setminus w} h_{za}
	\le \frac{h_{ua}}{\hat{z}_a}
	\le k^{2r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_{au}({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
For all $u\in\partial a$, we have trivially
	\begin{equation}\label{e:coher.a.is.large}
	\bigg\{
	{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{c})+{}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{au}(\SSPIN{r})
	\bigg\}
	\le 1 \le k^{3r} \textup{\textsf{coher}}_a({}_{\scalebox{0.4}{$\square$}}\hspace{-1pt}\pi)\,.
	\end{equation}
The bounds \eqref{e:stable.yellow},
\eqref{e:stable.cyan}, and \eqref{e:stable.red}
follow by combining
 \eqref{e:yrc.diff.div.y} with
\eqref{e:yellow.vs.coher.edge}, \eqref{e:red.vs.coher.edge}, \eqref{e:coher.a.is.large}.
