nodes.statement: We will deduce the bound from Theorem~ by taking a particular choice of zeta,m which is suggested by the survey propagation heuristic. Let muinP be the fixed point given by Proposition~. Let bmmu=Rmu for RequivR_0 as given by Definition~. Now fix beta>0, and let Big(rho_SPIN+,rho_SPIN-,rho_SPINfBig) equiv Big(beta,-beta,0Big)\,. Let eta be defined as the law of rho_y where yinsetSPIN+,SPIN-,SPINf is distributed according to bmeta, and bmeta is distributed according to bmmu: formally, for any Borel set BsubseteqR (where it suffices to consider Bsubseteqsetbeta,-beta,0), \[ eta(B) = int bmeta(y) 1Big\rho_yin BBig\ \,dbmmu(bmeta)\,. \] Thus etainM_1 is an bmeta-measurable random measure supported on setrho_SPIN+,rho_SPIN-,rho_SPINf=setbeta,-beta,0subseteqR. Let zeta denote the law of eta, so zetainM_2 and the randomness in zeta is the randomness of bmeta. For xinsetSPIN-,SPIN+ and smashvecy_ainsetSPIN+,SPIN-,SPINf^k-1, let \[ bmu_a(x|smashvecy_a) equiv sum_smashvecx insetSPINtextpm^k fracIndx_k=x exp(betatheta_a(smashvecx)) prod_j=1^k-1 r(x_j | y_a,j)\,, r(x|y) equiv fracexp\rho_y x\2chrho_y\,.\] Note it follows from the definition that \[ r(SPIN+|SPIN+) =r(SPIN-|SPIN-) = frace^beta2chbeta = 1-r(SPIN-|SPIN+) = 1-r(SPIN+|SPIN-)\,. \] It follows by combining with the definition of theta_a that bmu_aBig( SPIN-SPINL_a,k \,Big|\, (SPIN-SPINL_a,j)_1le jle k-1 Big) &= frac1e^beta prod_j=1^k-1 r( SPIN-SPINL_a,j|SPIN-SPINL_a,j ) + bigg\ 1- prod_j=1^k-1 r( SPIN-SPINL_a,j|SPIN-SPINL_a,j ) bigg\ \\ &=frac1e^beta bigg( frace^beta2chbetabigg)^k-1 +bigg\ 1- bigg( frace^beta2chbetabigg)^k-1 bigg\ le frac1e^beta/2\,, where the last bound holds assuming k is large enough and betage k. Thus, with P' denoting the law of vecrho conditioned on d,vectheta,veceta, for xinsetSPINtextpm we have \[ P'bigg( underbraceprod_a=1^d bmu_a(x) > frac1e^beta/2_textupevent F_xbigg) le Pi^x equivprod_a : SPINL_a,k=x bigg( 1-prod_j=1^k-1 bmeta_a,j ( SPIN-SPINL_a,j ) bigg)\,. \] Since F_x can be decided by looking only at the clauses partial v(x), we have P'( F_SPIN+ cup F_SPIN- ) le 1 - (1-Pi^SPIN+)(1-Pi^SPIN-), so \[E'bigg[ Big( sum_xinsetSPINtextpm prod_a=1^d bmu_a(x) Big)^m bigg] le 2^m P'Big(F_SPIN+ cup F_SPIN-Big) + bigg( frac2e^beta/2bigg)^m le 2^m bigg( Pi^SPIN++Pi^SPIN- -Pi^SPIN+Pi^SPIN- + frac1e^mbeta/2 bigg)\,.\] Similar considerations give \[ E'Big[ (bmu_a)^m Big] ge frac12^m P'bigg(bmu_agefrac12bigg) ge frac12^mbigg( 1 - prod_j=1^k eta_a,j (SPIN-SPINL_a,j)bigg)\,. \] Combining the above bounds gives \[ m Phi_textup1-textscrsb(beta,zeta,m) le m 4^k + Eln fracPi^SPIN++Pi^SPIN- -Pi^SPIN+Pi^SPIN- + e^-mbeta/2 [1-prod_j=1^k-1 eta_j]^(k-1)alpha . \] Taking m=1/beta^1/2, the right-hand side converges to the function Phi(alpha) from in the limit betatoinfty. Now assume alpha>alpha_star, so that Phi(alpha)<0 (of course, this uses Proposition~). Then, for sufficiently large beta, we will have F_n(beta) le Phi_textup1-textscrsbbigg(beta,zeta,frac1beta^1/2bigg) le 4^k + fracbeta^1/2 Phi(alpha)2 le fracbeta^1/2 Phi(alpha)4 < 0. To conclude, recall that the log-partition function ln Z_n(beta) is well concentrated about its expected value nF_n(beta) (take the Doob martingale of ln Z_n(beta) with respect to the textupk-textscsat clause-revealing filtration, and apply the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality). Thus implies that with high probability ln Z_n(beta) is negative, i.e., the textscsat instance is unsatisfiable.

\label{l:clause.tuple.measure.corrected} Let $\omega$ be as specified by Definition~\ref{d:judicious}. If $\bm{L}$ is a stable clause type
(Definition~\ref{d:stable}), then there exists a measure $\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$
which is consistent with $\omega$ and satisfies,
for all $r\ge (\ln k)^2$,
	\[\mathcal{H}(\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}) \ge \mathcal{H}({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}) - 
\frac1{k^{r/2}}\]


\begin{proof} Throughout this proof we fix a clause $a$ of type $\bm{L}$, and suppress these from the notation when possible. The idea is to start from the explicit measure $\hat{\nu}_\star\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ of \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star} --- which 
has incorrect edge marginals as commented above ---
and make small iterative adjustments to achieve the required edge marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Indeed, for all $e\in\delta a$, by the message-stability condition \eqref{e:message.stability} on $e$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:conseq.of.message.stab}
	\frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\sigma)}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}
	=\Bigg(\frac{\tilde{q}_e(\sigma)}
		{\displaystyle \sum_\tau
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\tau) \tilde{q}_e(\tau)}\Bigg)
	\Bigg/\Bigg(
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)}{\displaystyle \sum_\tau
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\tau) {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\tau)}\Bigg)
	= 1 + \frac{O(1)}{k^r}
	\end{equation}
for all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. This shows that the edge marginals of $\hat{\nu}_\star$ are only slightly off from the canonical ones ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 1. Correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} We first reweight $\hat{\nu}_\star$ to produce a measure $\hat{\nu}_0$ which has the correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins. To this end, let $\SPIN{CY}$ denote the event that $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$ has no $\SPIN{red}$ spins. It follows by using \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring} and \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star} that for any $e'\ne e''$ in $\delta a$,
	\[
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	= 1-\sum_{e\in\delta a}\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	\ge
	\hat{\nu}_\star\Big(\sigma_{e'}=\SSPIN{c}=\sigma_{e'}\Big)
	= \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c}){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}
		{\bm{\hat{z}}_\star}
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus\set{e',e''}}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{f}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,,
	\]
where $\bm{\hat{z}}_\star$ is the normalizing constant in \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star}. It is given by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:normalizing.constant.cancel}
	\bm{\hat{z}}_\star
	=\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})
	-\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{y})
	+ \overbrace{\bigg[ \sum_{e\in\delta a} 
		\Big({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{r})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c})\Big)
		\prod_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{y})\bigg]}^\textup{zero}
	\le\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})
	\,,
	\end{equation}
where the term in square brackets vanishes by
the correspondence \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta}.
It also follows from \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta},
in combination with the message-stability condition
\eqref{e:message.stability},
that 
	\[
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	=1- {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\eta_e(\SPIN{-}) \ge \frac1{2^r}\,.
	\]
Combining these bounds gives, assuming $r\ge (\ln k)^2$,
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	\ge
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\cdot
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\ge \frac1{4^r}\,.
	\end{equation}
On the other hand, for any measure $\hat{\nu}$ that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta a$, we must have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.error.on.CY}
	\frac{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}-1
	= \frac1{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg(\sum_{e\in\delta a}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	 - \sum_{e\in\delta a}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\SSPIN{r})\bigg)
	= O\bigg(\frac{4^r}{k^r}\bigg)\,,
	\end{equation}
where the last inequality follows by combining \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab} with \eqref{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}.
It follows by using \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab} and \eqref{e:stability.error.on.CY} that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:red.reweight.gamma.estimate}
	\gamma_e
	\equiv\bigg(
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}\bigg)
	\bigg/\bigg(\frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})}
		{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}\bigg)
	= 1 + O\bigg(\frac{4^r}{k^r}\bigg)\,,
	\end{equation}
for all $e\in\delta a$, where $\hat{\nu}$ again stands for any measure that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Then define
	\[\hat{\nu}_0(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\equiv \frac1{\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in\partial a}
	(\gamma_e)^{\Ind{\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r}}}\,,\]
where $\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ$ is the normalization constant that makes $\hat{\nu}_0$ a probability measure. We then calculate
	\[\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ
	=\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	+\sum_{e\in\delta a}
		\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})\gamma_e
	= \frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}\]
(using the definition of $\gamma$ with some simple algebra). It follows that
	\[
	\hat{\nu}_0(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	= \frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r}) \gamma_e}
		{\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ}
	= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})\,,
	\]
for all $e\in\delta a$,
so $\hat{\nu}_0$ has the correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins, as desired.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 2. Estimates for measure conditional on no $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} Note that the above reweighting does not change the measure conditional on $\SPIN{CY}$, that is to say, $\hat{\mu}_0(\cdot)\equiv\hat{\nu}_0( \cdot \,|\, \SPIN{CY})$ is the same as $\hat{\nu}_\star( \cdot \,|\, \SPIN{CY})$. It remains to correct the edge marginals conditional on $\SPIN{CY}$.
If $\hat{\nu}$ is any measure that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, we must have for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$ that
	\[\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)\equiv
	\hat{\nu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	=\frac1{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)
	-\Ind{\sigma=\SSPIN{y}} 
	\sum_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})
	\bigg)
	\le \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}
	\]
It follows using \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab},
\eqref{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}, and \eqref{e:stability.error.on.CY} that, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$,
	\begin{equation}\label{e:error.cond.on.CY}
	\hat{\mu}_0\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
		-\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
	=
	\hat{\nu}_\star\Big(
		\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	-\hat{\nu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	= O\bigg( \frac{4^r}{k^r}\cdot \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}
		{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg)
	= O\bigg( \frac{16^r}{k^r}
	\bigg)\,.
	\end{equation}
Now, with respect to a given coloring $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$, let us say that an edge $e\in\delta a$ is $\SSPIN{w}\equiv\SPIN{white}$ if at least two of the other edges in the clause are $\SPIN{cyan}$: that is, if
	\[\bigg|
	\Big\{
	e'\in\delta a\setminus e:\sigma_{e'}
	\in \set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}\Big\}\bigg|\ge2\,.\]	
Again recalling \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring}, the interpretation of $e$ being $\SPIN{white}$ is that $\sigma_e$ can be freely flipped between $\SSPIN{c}$ and $\SSPIN{y}$ without invalidating the coloring around $a$.
For each $e\in\delta a$, we can choose any $e'\ne e''$ in $\delta a\setminus e$ and lower bound
	\[
	W_e(\sigma)
	\equiv
	\frac{\mu_0( \sigma_e=\sigma;\textup{$e$
	is $\SPIN{white}$} )}
	{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) / 
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	} \ge
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c}){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}
	{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \bm{\hat{z}}_\star }
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus\set{e,e',e''}} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_f(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,.\]
By a similar calculation as in \eqref{e:normalizing.constant.cancel}, we have
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \bm{\hat{z}}_\star
	\le
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma) 
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus e} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_f(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,.
	\]
It follows that, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$
and any choice of three distinct edges $e,e',e''\in\delta a$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:enough.white.to.shift}
	W_e(\sigma)
	\ge 
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\cdot\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\ge\frac1{4^r}\,.\end{equation}
Recalling the definition of $W_e(\sigma)$ above,
\eqref{e:enough.white.to.shift}
says that 
$\mu_0( \sigma_e=\sigma;\textup{$e$
	is $\SPIN{white}$})$ is large relative to \eqref{e:error.cond.on.CY}.\smallskip
	
\noindent\bemph{Step 3. Correct marginals given no $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} We can now define a sequence of measures $\hat{\mu}_0,\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{|\delta a|}$ where $\hat{\mu}_0$ is as defined above, and $\hat{\mu}_j$ will be consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ on the first $j$ edges in $\delta a$.
Given $\hat{\mu}_0$, we look at the first edge and define $\hat{\mu}_1$ to satisfying the following constraints:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item \label{i.not.white.no.shift} For any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1}$ that contains only one $\SSPIN{c}$ spin, $\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
=\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})$;
\item \label{i.white.keep.cyan.plus.yellow.const}
For any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1}$ that contains at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ spins, $\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	+\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{y},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	=\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	+\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{y},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})$; 
\item \label{i.white.shift.cyan.and.yellow}
The appropriate amount of mass is shifted between $\set{\sigma_1=\SSPIN{c}}$ and $\set{\sigma_1=\SSPIN{y}}$:
	\[
	\hat{\mu}_1\Big(\sigma_{e_1}=\sigma; \textup{$e_1$
		is $\SPIN{white}$}\Big)
	=\hat{\mu}_0\Big(\sigma_{e_1}=\sigma; \textup{$e_1$
		is $\SPIN{white}$}\Big)
		+\bigg\{\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
		-\hat{\mu}_0\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)\bigg\}\,.
	\]
\end{enumerate}
Constraints \eqref{i.not.white.no.shift} and \eqref{i.white.keep.cyan.plus.yellow.const} ensure that the marginals on the other edges are not affected. Finally, constraint~\eqref{i.white.shift.cyan.and.yellow} ensures that $\hat{\mu}_1$ will have marginals consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ on the first edge in $\delta a$, and it is feasible thanks to the estimates \eqref{e:error.cond.on.CY}~and~\eqref{e:enough.white.to.shift} from above. 
We can repeat the procedure with the remaining edges in $\delta a$ to arrive at $\hat{\mu}_{|\delta a|}\equiv\hat{\mu}$. From the construction and from \eqref{e:error.cond.on.CY} we have the very crude bound
	\begin{equation}\label{e:tvdistance.on.CY}
	\Big|\hat{\mu}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	-\hat{\mu}_0(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})\Big|
	\le
	\sum_{e\in\delta a}
	\bigg|\hat{\mu}_0\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
		-\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)\bigg|
	\le O\bigg( \frac{16^rk}{k^r}\bigg)\,,
	\end{equation}
for all $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}\in\SPIN{CY}$.
 We then finally define a measure on all valid colorings of $\delta a$ by
	\[
	\hat{\nu}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\equiv \hat{\nu}_0\Big(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a} ;
		\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}\notin \SPIN{CY}\Big)
	+\hat{\nu}_0(\SPIN{CY}) \hat{\mu}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})\,.\]
By construction, $\hat{\nu}$ is consistent with the marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, and satisfies
	\[\Big|
	\hat{\nu}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	-\hat{\nu}_\star(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})\Big|
	\le
	O\bigg( \frac{16^rk}{k^r}\bigg)
	\]
for all $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$, by combining \eqref{e:tvdistance.on.CY} with our earlier estimate \eqref{e:red.reweight.gamma.estimate} on the weights $\gamma_e$. This gives
	\[
	\mathcal{H}(\hat{\nu}) \ge \mathcal{H}(\hat{\nu}_\star) - \frac1{k^{r/2}}\,,
	\]
concluding the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

Throughout this proof we fix a clause $a$ of type $\bm{L}$, and suppress these from the notation when possible. The idea is to start from the explicit measure $\hat{\nu}_\star\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ of \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star} --- which 
has incorrect edge marginals as commented above ---
and make small iterative adjustments to achieve the required edge marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Indeed, for all $e\in\delta a$, by the message-stability condition \eqref{e:message.stability} on $e$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:conseq.of.message.stab}
	\frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\sigma)}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}
	=\Bigg(\frac{\tilde{q}_e(\sigma)}
		{\displaystyle \sum_\tau
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\tau) \tilde{q}_e(\tau)}\Bigg)
	\Bigg/\Bigg(
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)}{\displaystyle \sum_\tau
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\tau) {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\tau)}\Bigg)
	= 1 + \frac{O(1)}{k^r}
	\end{equation}
for all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$. This shows that the edge marginals of $\hat{\nu}_\star$ are only slightly off from the canonical ones ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 1. Correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} We first reweight $\hat{\nu}_\star$ to produce a measure $\hat{\nu}_0$ which has the correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins. To this end, let $\SPIN{CY}$ denote the event that $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$ has no $\SPIN{red}$ spins. It follows by using \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring} and \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star} that for any $e'\ne e''$ in $\delta a$,
	\[
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	= 1-\sum_{e\in\delta a}\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	\ge
	\hat{\nu}_\star\Big(\sigma_{e'}=\SSPIN{c}=\sigma_{e'}\Big)
	= \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c}){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}
		{\bm{\hat{z}}_\star}
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus\set{e',e''}}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{f}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,,
	\]
where $\bm{\hat{z}}_\star$ is the normalizing constant in \eqref{e:opt.clause.tuple.measure.star}. It is given by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:normalizing.constant.cancel}
	\bm{\hat{z}}_\star
	=\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})
	-\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{y})
	+ \overbrace{\bigg[ \sum_{e\in\delta a} 
		\Big({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{r})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c})\Big)
		\prod_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{y})\bigg]}^\textup{zero}
	\le\prod_{e\in\delta a} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})
	\,,
	\end{equation}
where the term in square brackets vanishes by
the correspondence \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta}.
It also follows from \eqref{e:color.recursions.eta},
in combination with the message-stability condition
\eqref{e:message.stability},
that 
	\[
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	=1- {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\eta_e(\SPIN{-}) \ge \frac1{2^r}\,.
	\]
Combining these bounds gives, assuming $r\ge (\ln k)^2$,
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	\ge
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\cdot
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\ge \frac1{4^r}\,.
	\end{equation}
On the other hand, for any measure $\hat{\nu}$ that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e$ for all $e\in\delta a$, we must have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:stability.error.on.CY}
	\frac{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}-1
	= \frac1{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg(\sum_{e\in\delta a}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	 - \sum_{e\in\delta a}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\SSPIN{r})\bigg)
	= O\bigg(\frac{4^r}{k^r}\bigg)\,,
	\end{equation}
where the last inequality follows by combining \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab} with \eqref{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}.
It follows by using \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab} and \eqref{e:stability.error.on.CY} that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:red.reweight.gamma.estimate}
	\gamma_e
	\equiv\bigg(
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}\bigg)
	\bigg/\bigg(\frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})}
		{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}\bigg)
	= 1 + O\bigg(\frac{4^r}{k^r}\bigg)\,,
	\end{equation}
for all $e\in\delta a$, where $\hat{\nu}$ again stands for any measure that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. Then define
	\[\hat{\nu}_0(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\equiv \frac1{\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ}
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in\partial a}
	(\gamma_e)^{\Ind{\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r}}}\,,\]
where $\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ$ is the normalization constant that makes $\hat{\nu}_0$ a probability measure. We then calculate
	\[\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ
	=\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	+\sum_{e\in\delta a}
		\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})\gamma_e
	= \frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}\]
(using the definition of $\gamma$ with some simple algebra). It follows that
	\[
	\hat{\nu}_0(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r})
	= \frac{\hat{\nu}_\star(\sigma_e=\SSPIN{r}) \gamma_e}
		{\bm{\hat{z}}_\circ}
	= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\SSPIN{r})\,,
	\]
for all $e\in\delta a$,
so $\hat{\nu}_0$ has the correct marginal proportions of $\SPIN{red}$ spins, as desired.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 2. Estimates for measure conditional on no $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} Note that the above reweighting does not change the measure conditional on $\SPIN{CY}$, that is to say, $\hat{\mu}_0(\cdot)\equiv\hat{\nu}_0( \cdot \,|\, \SPIN{CY})$ is the same as $\hat{\nu}_\star( \cdot \,|\, \SPIN{CY})$. It remains to correct the edge marginals conditional on $\SPIN{CY}$.
If $\hat{\nu}$ is any measure that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, we must have for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$ that
	\[\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)\equiv
	\hat{\nu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	=\frac1{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)
	-\Ind{\sigma=\SSPIN{y}} 
	\sum_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{e'}(\SSPIN{r})
	\bigg)
	\le \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}{\hat{\nu}(\SPIN{CY})}
	\]
It follows using \eqref{e:conseq.of.message.stab},
\eqref{e:stability.lbd.no.red.spins}, and \eqref{e:stability.error.on.CY} that, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$,
	\begin{equation}\label{e:error.cond.on.CY}
	\hat{\mu}_0\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
		-\hat{\mu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\Big)
	=
	\hat{\nu}_\star\Big(
		\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	-\hat{\nu}\Big(\sigma_e=\sigma\,\Big|\,\SPIN{CY}\Big)
	= O\bigg( \frac{4^r}{k^r}\cdot \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma)}
		{\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})}
	\bigg)
	= O\bigg( \frac{16^r}{k^r}
	\bigg)\,.
	\end{equation}
Now, with respect to a given coloring $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}$, let us say that an edge $e\in\delta a$ is $\SSPIN{w}\equiv\SPIN{white}$ if at least two of the other edges in the clause are $\SPIN{cyan}$: that is, if
	\[\bigg|
	\Big\{
	e'\in\delta a\setminus e:\sigma_{e'}
	\in \set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}\Big\}\bigg|\ge2\,.\]	
Again recalling \eqref{e:indicator.of.valid.clause.coloring}, the interpretation of $e$ being $\SPIN{white}$ is that $\sigma_e$ can be freely flipped between $\SSPIN{c}$ and $\SSPIN{y}$ without invalidating the coloring around $a$.
For each $e\in\delta a$, we can choose any $e'\ne e''$ in $\delta a\setminus e$ and lower bound
	\[
	W_e(\sigma)
	\equiv
	\frac{\mu_0( \sigma_e=\sigma;\textup{$e$
	is $\SPIN{white}$} )}
	{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) / 
	\hat{\nu}_\star(\SPIN{CY})
	} \ge
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma)
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c}){}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}
	{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \bm{\hat{z}}_\star }
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus\set{e,e',e''}} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_f(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,.\]
By a similar calculation as in \eqref{e:normalizing.constant.cancel}, we have
	\[
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma) \bm{\hat{z}}_\star
	\le
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma) 
	\prod_{f\in\delta a \setminus e} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_f(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})\,.
	\]
It follows that, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y}}$
and any choice of three distinct edges $e,e',e''\in\delta a$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:enough.white.to.shift}
	W_e(\sigma)
	\ge 
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\cdot\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{c},\SSPIN{y})}
	\ge\frac1{4^r}\,.\end{equation}
Recalling the definition of $W_e(\sigma)$ above,
\eqref{e:enough.white.to.shift}
says that 
$\mu_0( \sigma_e=\sigma;\textup{$e$
	is $\SPIN{white}$})$ is large relative to \eqref{e:error.cond.on.CY}.\smallskip
	
\noindent\bemph{Step 3. Correct marginals given no $\SPIN{red}$ spins.} We can now define a sequence of measures $\hat{\mu}_0,\ldots,\hat{\mu}_{|\delta a|}$ where $\hat{\mu}_0$ is as defined above, and $\hat{\mu}_j$ will be consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ on the first $j$ edges in $\delta a$.
Given $\hat{\mu}_0$, we look at the first edge and define $\hat{\mu}_1$ to satisfying the following constraints:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item \label{i.not.white.no.shift} For any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1}$ that contains only one $\SSPIN{c}$ spin, $\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
=\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})$;
\item \label{i.white.keep.cyan.plus.yellow.const}
For any $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1}$ that contains at least two $\SSPIN{c}$ spins, $\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	+\hat{\mu}_1(\SSPIN{y},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	=\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{c},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})
	+\hat{\mu}_0(\SSPIN{y},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{-1})$; 
\item \label{i.white.shift.cyan.and.yellow}
The appropriate amount of mass is shifted between $\set{\sigma_1=\SSPIN{c}}$ and $\set{\sigma_1=\SSPIN{y}}$:
	\[

	\[\Big|

	\mathcal{H}(\hat{\nu}) \ge \mathcal{H}(\hat{\nu}_\star) - \frac1{k^{r/2}}\,,
	\]
concluding the proof of the lemma.

\label{l:BSP.in.tree.bounded.expansion}
Let $\mathscr{T}$ be any bipartite factor tree in which all clauses have degree at most $k$. Then
	\[
	|A| 
	\ge \frac{|\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(A;\mathscr{T})|}{2k}
	\]
for any finite subset $A$ of variables in $\mathscr{T}$.

\begin{proof} Let $A_0\equiv A$, and for $t\ge1$ we let $A_t$ be the union of $A_{t-1}$ with all variables $u\in\mathscr{T}$ with $|N(u)\cap A_{t-1}|\ge2$. Thus $A=A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq \ldots$, and
(as in \eqref{eq-bootstrap-percolation}) we define
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(A;\mathscr{T})
	=\bigcup_{t\ge0} A_t\,.
	\]
For all $t\ge0$, let $G_t\equiv (A_t,F_t,E_t)$ be the subgraph of $\mathscr{T}$ induced by $A_t$ --- that is, $F_t$ is the set of all clauses in $\mathscr{T}$ having at least two incident variables in $A_t$, and $E_t$ is the set of all edges in $\mathscr{T}$ between $A_t$ and $F_t$. As long as $t$ is finite, $G_t$ is a finite subgraph of $\mathscr{T}$.
If we denote the (maximal) connected components of $G_t$
by $G_{t,i}\equiv (A_{t,i},F_{t,i},E_{t,i})$
for $1\le i\le i(t)$, and let $A_i\equiv A \cap G_{t,i}$, then we must have $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(A_i; G_{t,i})=A_{t,i}$. If we can show for all $i$ that $|A_{t,i}|\le 2k|A_i|$, then summing over $i$ gives
 	\[
	|A_t|
	=\sum_{i=1}^{i(t)} |A_{t,i}|
	\le 2k\sum_{i=1}^{i(t)} |A_i|
	= 2k|A|\,.
	\]
If the bound holds for all $t$, then the conclusion of the lemma follows. Since each $G_{t,i}$ is a finite tree, we conclude that it suffices to show the following special case of the lemma: for any finite bipartite factor tree $\mathscr{T}=(V,F,E)$ in which all clauses have width at most $k$, if $A\subseteq V$ such that $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(A;\mathscr{T})=V$, then we must have $|V| \le 2k|A|$.

To show the last assertion, for all $v\in V$ let $\tau(v)\equiv \min\set{j\ge0: v\in A_j}$. For each edge $e=(av)\in E$, let
	\[
	m(av)
	\equiv\min\bigg\{ 2,
	\Big|\Big\{ u\in\partial a:
		\tau(u)<\tau(v) \Big\}\Big|
	\bigg\}\in\set{0,1,2}\,.
	\]
Since $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(A;\mathscr{T})=V$, the definition of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}$ implies that each variable $v\in V$ must have
	\[\sum_{a\in\partial v} m(av)\ge2\,.\]
On the other hand, for each clause $a\in F$, if we reorder the variables in $\partial a$ as $(v_1,\ldots,v_{|\partial a|})$ such that $\tau(v_i)$ is nondecreasing in $i$, then we must have 
$m(av_1)=0$ and $m(av_2)\in\set{0,1}$, so
	\[
	\sum_{v\in\partial a}m(av) 
	\le 0 + 1 + (|\partial a|-2)2 = 2|\partial a|-3\,.
	\]
Combining these inequalities gives
	\[
	2|V\setminus A|
	\le
	\sum_{v\in V} \sum_{a\in\partial v} m(av)
	= \sum_{a\in F} \sum_{v\in\partial a} m(av)
	\le \sum_{a\in F}\Big(2|\partial a|-3\Big)
	=2|E|-3|F|\,.
	\]
Since $\mathscr{T}=(V,F,E)$ is by assumption a finite tree where all clauses have degree at most $k$, we must have
	\[
	|V|-1 = |E|-|F|
	=\sum_{a\in F}\bigg(|\partial a|-1\bigg)
	\le (k-1) |F|\,.
	\]
Substituting into the previous gives
	\[
	2|V\setminus A|
	\le 2\Big(|V|-|1|\Big)-|F|
	\le \bigg(2-\frac1{k-1}\bigg)
		\Big(|V|-1\Big)\,.
	\]
Rearranging gives
	\[
	|A| \ge 1 + \frac{|V|-1}{2(k-1)}
	\ge \frac{|V|}{2k}\,,
	\]
which proves the claim. The lemma follows as discussed above.
\end{proof}

\label{l:larger.tree.intersecting.bsp.init.set}
Let $\mathscr{T}$ be any bipartite factor tree in which all clauses have degree at most $k$.
For any $\mathfrak{c}\ge2$ and $\ell\ge1$,
and any $T\in\bm{\Lambda}_{\mathfrak{c},\ell}(\mathscr{T})$,
there is a tree $T'\in\bm{\Lambda}_{\mathfrak{c}',\ell'}(\mathscr{T})$, with $\mathfrak{c}'=\mathfrak{c}+2$ and $\ell\le \ell'\le \ell(\mathfrak{c}')^{R'}$, such that
	\[
	|D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}\cap V_{T'}|
	\ge
	\frac1{2k}
	\bigg(
	|\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_T|
	+|V_{T'}\setminus V_T|
	\bigg)
	\]
for $\mathfrak{i}\in\set{0,1}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall Definition~\ref{d:j.defective} that $v \in \textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}$ if and only if $v\in\textup{\textsf{BSP}}( D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}\cap B_{R'/2}(v);B_{R'/2}(v))$. Let $\mathscr{T}'\equiv B_{R'/2}(T)$, that is, the union of the $(R'/2)$-neighborhoods of all variables in $T$. Let $A_0\equiv D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}} \cap \mathscr{T}'$,
and for $t\ge1$ let $A_t$ be the union of $A_{t-1}$ with all variables in $\mathscr{T}'$ that have at least two neighbors in $A_{t-1}$. Then let
	\[
	A_\infty
	\equiv \bigcup_{t\ge0} A_t
	= \textup{\textsf{BSP}}( D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}} \cap \mathscr{T}'; \mathscr{T}').
	\]
Let $G_t$ be the subgraph of $\mathscr{T}'$ induced by $A_t$. We will construct a sequence 
of trees $T_s\equiv(V_s,E_s,F_s)\subseteq G_\infty$ (terminating at $T'$), as follows.
Let $T_0\equiv T$.
For all variables $u\in A_\infty$, let $\tau(u)\equiv \min\set{t\ge0: u\in A_t}$. For $s\ge0$, let
	\[
	U(T_s)
	\equiv
	\bigg\{
	u\in V_s \,\bigg|
	\begin{array}{c} 
	1\le \tau(u)<\infty, 
	\textup{ and $u$ does not have at least}\\
	\textup{two neighboring variables 
	in $T_s$ with smaller $\tau$}
	\end{array}
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
If $U(T_s)=\varnothing$, we terminate the process and set $T_s=T_\infty$. Otherwise, take any $u\in U(T_s)$: it must have at least one neighboring variable $u'$ that does not lie in $T_s$ and has $\tau(u')<\tau(u)$. Among all such $u'$, choose one with minimal $\tau$. Let $T_{s+1}$ be the graph induced by $V_s \cup \set{u'}$. In the resulting $T_\infty\equiv T'$, any vertex that did not belong to $T$ will have degree at most $3$, while any vertex that did belong to $T$ will have its degree in $T'$ at most two larger than its degree in $T$. It follows that 
$T'\in\bm{\Lambda}_{\mathfrak{c}',\ell'}(\mathscr{T})$, with $\mathfrak{c}'=\mathfrak{c}+2$ and $\ell\le \ell'\le \ell(\mathfrak{c}')^{R'}$. It is straightforward to check (e.g.\ by induction) that the above construction implies
	\[(\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_T)
	\cup (V_{T'} \setminus V_T)
	\subseteq
	\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}\cap V_{T'};T')\,.
	\]
Combining with Lemma~\ref{l:BSP.in.tree.bounded.expansion} gives
	\[
	\frac1{2k}
	\bigg(
	|\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_T|
	+|V_{T'}\setminus V_T|
	\bigg)
	\le 
	\frac{\textup{\textsf{BSP}}(D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}\cap V_{T'}; T')}{2k}
	\le|D^{\kappa_*,\mathfrak{i}}\cap V_{T'}|\,,
	\]
as claimed.\end{proof}

\label{l:radon.derivative.pgwT}
Let $T$ be any fixed variable-rooted tree of maximum degree $\mathfrak{c}$,
where $\mathfrak{c}$ is an absolute constant.
Then the Radon--Nikodyn derivative between the measures ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$ and ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ satisfies the second moment bound 
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[\bigg( \frac{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)}{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}}
		\bigg)^2\bigg] \le 2\,,
	\]
where $\mathbb{E}$ denotes expectation under ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$.
(The bound holds for $k\ge k_0$ where $k_0$ depends only on $\mathfrak{c}$.)

\begin{proof}
According to the original definitions, in a random tree $\mathscr{T}\sim{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$
or $\mathscr{T}\sim{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$, only the root variable is distinguished, while all other variables are unlabelled. For the purposes of this proof, however, we now instead consider both $\mathscr{T}\sim{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ and $\mathscr{T}\sim{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$ as rooted \emph{labelled} trees, where the children of each vertex are ordered uniformly at random. Separately, we also assume that $T$ comes with a fixed labelling of its vertices, so that we may speak of embeddings
$T\hookrightarrow\mathscr{T}$.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 1. Martingale of Radon--Nikodym derivatives.} If ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)\ll{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$, then the labellings discussed above do not affect the value of the Radon--Nikodym derivative, which we hereafter write as
	\[\mathfrak{X} 
	\equiv \frac{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)}{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}}(\mathscr{T})
	\equiv \mathfrak{X}(\mathscr{T};T) \,.\]
To show that ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)\ll{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$ (so that $\mathfrak{X}$ is well-defined), and to obtain the bound on $\mathfrak{X}$ claimed in the statement of the lemma, we shall take the limit of depth $\ell\to\infty$. Let $T_\ell \equiv B_\ell(o;T)$; and let $\mathscr{T}_\ell \equiv B_\ell(v_\textup{\textsc{rt}};\mathscr{T})$ where $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ is the root variable of $\mathscr{T}$. Let $\mathscr{F}_\ell$ be the $\sigma$-field generated by $\mathscr{T}_\ell$. Define the restricted measures
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\equiv{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\Big|_{\mathscr{F}_\ell}\,,\quad
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell(T)
	\equiv {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)\Big|_{\mathscr{F}_\ell}
	= {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell(T_\ell)\,.
	\]
For finite $\ell$ it is clear that ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell(T)\ll {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell$, so we can define the Radon--Nikodym derivative
	\[
	\mathfrak{X}_\ell \equiv
	\frac{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell(T_\ell)}{d{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}_\ell}
	\equiv \mathfrak{X}_\ell(\mathscr{T}_\ell ; T_\ell)\,,
	\]
which is a nonnegative martingale. We will show 
inductively that for all $\ell\ge0$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:rn.induction.hypothesis}
	M(\ell)
	\equiv \max_{T_\ell} \mathbb{E}\bigg[
		\Big(\mathfrak{X}_\ell(\mathscr{T}_\ell;T_\ell) \Big)^2
		\bigg]\le2\,,
	\end{equation}
where the maximum is taken over all depth-$\ell$ trees $T_\ell$ of maximum degree $\mathfrak{c}$. This will imply that the martingale $\mathfrak{X}_\ell$ is bounded in $L^2$,
so that (by the $L^2$ martingale convergence theorem)
it converges almost surely to a finite limit $\mathfrak{X}\equiv\mathfrak{X}_\infty$ satisfying the same $L^2$ bound.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 2. $L^2$ bound on martingale.}

If $\ell\epsilon=0$ the bound is vacuous, so we assume without loss that $\ell\epsilon\ge1$.
Suppose $\mathscr{T}$ contains a path $P$ of $\ell$ variables emanating from $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, such that $S_0\equiv \cancel{O}^\mathfrak{i}\cap V_P$ has size $|S_0|\ge\ell\epsilon$. For any $u\in S_0$
there is a path $\gamma(u)\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ that emanates from $u$, along which more than $(\delta_*)^3$ fraction of the variables are $\mathfrak{i}$-defective. We will define a sequence $S_0\supseteq S_1 \supseteq \ldots$ as follows:
as long as $S_{s-1}\ne\varnothing$, take
	\[
	u_s
	\in\textup{arg\,max}\bigg\{ |\gamma(u)| : u\in S_{s-1}\bigg\}\,,
	\quad
	S_s
	\equiv S_{s-1} \,\bigg\backslash \,
		B_{2|\gamma(u_s)|+1}(u_s)\,.
	\]
Eventually this terminates at $S_{s_{\max}}=\varnothing$, and the resulting sequence of paths $\gamma(u_s)$ will be mutually disjoint. Since $S_0$ was a subset of the path $P$, we have
	\[
	\Big|S_{s-1}\setminus S_s\Big|
	\le \Big|V_P \cap B_{2|\gamma(u_s)|+1}(u_s)\Big|
	\le 4|V_{\gamma(u_s)}|\,.
	\]
Let $U$ be the union of the paths $\gamma(u_s)$: then
	\[
	|V_U|
	=\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} |V_{\gamma(u_s)}|
	\ge
	\frac14\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} 
	\bigg( |S_{s-1}|-|S_s|\bigg)
	= \frac{|S_0|}{4}
	\ge \frac{\ell\epsilon}{4}\,.
	\]
Let $T = P \cup U$. Then $T\in\bm{\Lambda}_{3,\ell'}(\mathscr{T})$ for some $\ell'\ge\ell$, and $| \textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}\cap V_T|\ge | \textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}\cap V_U|\ge |V_U|(\delta_*)^3$. Note that since $|V_U|\ge\ell\epsilon/4$
and also $|V_T|\le |V_P|+|V_U|$, we have
	\[
	|V_U|
	\ge \frac{\ell\epsilon}{8}
		+\frac{|V_T|-|V_P|}{2}
	= \frac{\ell\epsilon}{8}
		+\frac{|V_T|-|V_P|}{2}
	= \frac{\ell\epsilon}{8}
		+\frac{\ell'-\ell}{2}\,.
	\]
It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\left(
	\hspace{-4pt}
	\begin{array}{c}
	\text{$\mathscr{T}$ contains a path 
	$P$ of $\ell$ variables,}\\
	\text{emanating from $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$,
	with $|\cancel{O}^\mathfrak{i}\cap V_P|\ge\ell\epsilon$}
	\end{array}
	\hspace{-4pt}
	\right)\\
	&\le
	\sum_{\ell'\ge\ell}
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\Bigg(
	\textup{some $T\in\bm{\Lambda}_{3,\ell'}(\mathscr{T})$
	has
	$|\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i}\cap V_T|\ge
	\bigg[
	 \frac{\ell\epsilon}{8}
		+\frac{\ell'-\ell}{2}
	\bigg](\delta_*)^3 $}
	\Bigg)\,.
	\end{align*}
It follows from Proposition~\ref{p:sparse.subtree.with.many.defects} that the last expression is upper bounded by
	\[
	\sum_{\ell'\ge\ell}
	\frac{\exp(k^2[\ell + (\ell'-\ell)] )}
	{ \exp( 
		(\delta_*)^32^{k/4}
		[\ell\epsilon/8
		+ (\ell'-\ell)/2] /k^2 ) }
	\le 
	\frac{O(1) \exp(k^2\ell)}
	{ \exp( (\delta_*)^3
	2^{k/4} \ell\epsilon /(8k^2) ) }\,,
	\]

Let $S_0\equiv \cancel{S}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_P$. For each $u\in S_0$, by definition there exists $g(u)$ such that 
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align}
	\nonumber
	&1\le d(u,g(u)) \le R'\,,\\
	&1\le d(u,g(u)) < \textup{rad}^\mathfrak{i}(g(u))
		\le \chi^\mathfrak{i}(g(u)) \le 2R'\,.
	\label{e:chi.at.least.two}
	\end{align}}
We will first build a tree $T'$,
with $P\subseteq T' \subseteq\mathscr{T}$,
by combining $P$ with paths between $u$ and $g(u)$ for a subset of $u$ from $S_0$, as follows.
We will keep track of 
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	\cancel{S}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_P
	&=S_0 \supseteq S_1 
	\supseteq\ldots \supseteq S_{s_{\max}}=\varnothing\,,\\
	P
	&=T_0\subseteq T_1 \subseteq \ldots \subseteq
	T_{s_{\max}} = T'\,.
	\end{align*}}
As long as $S_{s-1}\ne\varnothing$, we can choose $u_s$ from $S_{s-1}$ such that $g(u_s)$ achieves
	\[
	\chi^\mathfrak{i}(g(u_s))
	= \chi_s
	\equiv\max\bigg\{
	\chi^\mathfrak{i}(g(u))
	: u\in S_{s-1}
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Let $P_s$ be the path joining $u_s$ to $g(u_s)$; it has length $|P_s|= d(u_s,g(u_s)) \le \textup{rad}^\mathfrak{i}(g(u_s))-1 \le \chi_s-1$. Let
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	T_s &\equiv T_{s-1} \cup P_s\,,\\
	S_s &\equiv S_{s-1} \setminus 
	B_{4(\chi_s-1)}(g(u_s))\,.
	\end{align*}}
Then the paths $P_s$ will be mutually disjoint: indeed, for any $s<t$, by definition the variable $u_t$ must lie outside the ball $B_{4(\chi_s-1)}(g(u_s))$,
so the distance between $g(u_s)$ and $u_t$ 
must be at least $4(\chi_s-1)+1$.
Since $g(u_s)\in P_s$
and $u_t\in P_t$, we conclude that the minimum distance between $P_s$ and $P_t$ must satisfy
	\[
	d(P_s,P_t)
	\ge d(g(u_s),u_t)
		-|P_s|-|P_t|
	\ge
	\bigg(4(\chi_s-1)+1\bigg)
	- (\chi_s-1)-(\chi_t-1)
	\ge 2\chi_s-1\,,
	\]
where the last step uses that $\chi_s\ge\chi_t$. We then continue the procedure until we reach $S_{s_{\max}}=\varnothing$, at which point we define $T'\equiv T_{s_{\max}}$. Note
	\begin{equation}\label{e:candidate.thick.tree}
	|V_{T'}|
	\le \ell + \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} d(u_s,g(u_s))
	\le \ell + \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}}
		(\chi_s-1)\,.
	\end{equation}
The intersection between $B_{4(\chi_s-1)}(g(u_s))$ with (any) path $P$ can contain at most $8(\chi_s-1)+1 \le 9(\chi_s-1)$ variables, where the last inequality holds since $\chi_s\ge2$ from \eqref{e:chi.at.least.two}. Therefore $|S_s| \ge |S_{s-1}|-9(\chi_s-1)$, which implies
	\begin{equation}\label{e:large.sum.chi}
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} (\chi_s -1)
	\ge 
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} \frac{|S_{s-1}|-|S_s|}{9}
	= \frac{|S_0|}{9} \ge \frac{\ell\epsilon}{9}\,.
	\end{equation}
Recall \eqref{e:def.chi.JJ} that $\chi^\mathfrak{i}(v)=\max\set{ \gamma^\mathfrak{i}(v),\bar{\gamma}(v)}$, so one of the following must hold:
	\begin{align}
	\label{e:i.case.tree.with.many.defects}
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} 
	\Big(\gamma^\mathfrak{i}( g(u_s)) -1\Big)
	&\ge \frac12 \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}}
	\Big(\chi^\mathfrak{i}( g(u_s)) -1\Big)\,,\\
	\label{e:ii.case.thick.tree}
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} 
	\Big(\bar{\gamma}( g(u_s)) -1\Big)
	&\ge \frac12 \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}}
	\Big(\chi^\mathfrak{i}( g(u_s)) -1\Big)
	\end{align}
We consider separately the two cases:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item[\eqref{i:case.thick}] If \eqref{e:ii.case.thick.tree} occurs, then we let $T=T'$. Combining with
\eqref{e:candidate.thick.tree}
and \eqref{e:large.sum.chi} gives
	\[
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} \Big(\bar{\gamma}(g(u_s)) -1 \Big)
	\ge
	\frac12\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} (\chi_s-1)
	\ge
	\frac14\bigg[
	 (\ell'-\ell)
	+ \frac{\ell\epsilon}{9}
	\bigg]
	\,.
	\]
Therefore the tree $T=T'$ is $\epsilon'$-thick
for $\epsilon'$ as defined in the statement of the lemma.

\item[\eqref{i:case.defect}] If \eqref{e:i.case.tree.with.many.defects} occurs,
then for each $s$ we can find a path $Q_s$ emanating from $g(u_s)$ with $\gamma^\mathfrak{i}(g(u_s))$ variables,
of which at least $(\delta_*)^3$ fraction are $\mathfrak{i}$-defective. Let $T$ be the union of $T'$ with all the paths $Q_s$, for $1\le s\le s_{\max}$. The $Q_s$ are mutually disjoint. Recalling \eqref{e:candidate.thick.tree}, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:size.bound.replacing.thick.tree.eqn}
	\ell'=|V_T|\le
	\ell + \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} (\chi_s-1)
	+ \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} \Big(\gamma^\mathfrak{i}(g(u_s)) -1\Big)
	\le 
	\ell +2 \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} (\chi_s-1)\,.\end{equation}
Combining 
\eqref{e:large.sum.chi},
\eqref{e:i.case.tree.with.many.defects},
and \eqref{e:size.bound.replacing.thick.tree.eqn}
 gives
	\begin{align*}
	|\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i} \cap V_T|
	&\ge \sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}}
	|\textup{\textsf{DEF}}^\mathfrak{i} \cap Q_s|
	\ge (\delta_*)^3
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} \gamma^\mathfrak{i}(g(u_s))
	\ge \frac{(\delta_*)^3}{2}
	\sum_{s=1}^{s_{\max}} (\chi_s-1)\\
	&\ge
	\frac{(\delta_*)^3}{4}
	\bigg[\frac{\ell'-\ell}{2}
	+\frac{\ell\epsilon}{9}
	\bigg]\,.
	\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
Combining the two cases gives the claim.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary~\ref{c:fair}
nodes.statement: Recall from Definition~ that an acyclic variable is termed i-fair if (i) it is i-stable; (ii) its 5R'-neighborhood contains no more than exp\k^2(5R')\ variables; and (iii) every length-R' path emanating from it contains at least one i-perfect variable, where i-perfect means both i-orderly and i-self-contained. For condition (i), it follows from Proposition~ that \[ textupPGWBig(v_textuptextscrt not i-stableBig) le frac1exp(2^k/20R)\,. \] For condition (ii), it follows from Lemma~ and Markov's inequality that \[ textupPGWbigg( |B_5R'(v_textuptextscrt)| ge exp\k^2(5R')\ bigg) lefrac e exp \ exp\k^2(5R') \ / (alpha k^2)^5R'\ le frac1exp(exp(kR))\,. \] For condition (iii), it follows by combining Propositions~~and~ that \[ textupPGWleft( c T contains a path P of R' variables,\\ emanating from v_textuptextscrt, with V_PsubseteqcancelS^icupcancelO^i right) le fracO(1) exp(k^2 R') exp( Omega( 2^kdelta_*/3 R')) \,. \] Combining these bounds gives the result.

Recall from Definition~\ref{d:perfect.fair} that an acyclic variable is termed $\mathfrak{i}$-fair if (i) it is $\mathfrak{i}$-stable; (ii) its $5R'$-neighborhood contains no more than $\exp\{k^2(5R')\}$ variables; and (iii) every length-$R'$ path emanating from it contains at least one $\mathfrak{i}$-perfect variable, where $\mathfrak{i}$-perfect means both $\mathfrak{i}$-orderly and $\mathfrak{i}$-self-contained. For condition (i), it follows from Proposition~\ref{p:one.stable} that
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\Big(\text{$v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ not $\mathfrak{i}$-stable}\Big)
	\le \frac1{\exp(2^{k/20}R)}\,.
	\]
For condition (ii), it follows from Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.bound.PGW}
and Markov's inequality that
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\bigg(
	|B_{5R'}(v_\textup{\textsc{rt}})| \ge \exp\{k^2(5R')\}
	\bigg)
	\le\frac{ e }
	{	\exp \{ \exp\{k^2(5R') \}
	 / (\alpha k^2)^{5R'}\}}
	\le \frac1{\exp(\exp(kR))}\,.
	\]
For condition (iii), it follows by combining Propositions~\ref{p:path.intersect.not.selfcont}~and~\ref{p:path.intersect.not.orderly} that
	\[
	{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\left(
	\begin{array}{c}
	\text{$\mathscr{T}$ contains a path $P$ 
	of $R'$ variables,}\\
	\text{emanating from $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$,
	with $V_P\subseteq\cancel{S}^\mathfrak{i}\cup\cancel{O}^\mathfrak{i}$}
	\end{array}
	\right)
	\le 
	\frac{O(1) \exp(k^2 R')}
	{ \exp( \Omega( 2^{k\delta_*/3} R')) }\,.
	\]
Combining these bounds gives the result.

nodes.statement: Recall from Definition~ that an acyclic variable v is termed i-excellent if its neighborhood T=B_10R'(v) satisfies condition~, which we repeat here for convenience: \[ p_textupex,i(T)equiv textupPGWleft( left.c B_20R'(u) contains any\\ variable which is not i-fair \, right| \, B_10R'(u) cong T right) le frac1exp\k^3 R' \\,. \] By Markov's inequality and iterated expectations, p &equiv textupPGWBig(v_textuptextscrt not i-excellentBig) le int fracp_textupex,i( B_10R'(v_textuptextscrt;T) ) 1/exp\k^3 R' \ \,dtextupPGW(T)\\ &=exp\k^3 R' \ \,textupPGWbigg( textupB_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T) contains any variable which is not i-fair bigg)\,. By another application of Markov's inequality, together with the unimodularity property , we find p &leexp\k^3 R' \ int sum_uin B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T) 1bigg\textupu is not i-fairbigg\ \,dtextupPGW(T)\\ &=exp\k^3 R' \ int |B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| 1 Big\textupv_textuptextscrt not i-fairBig\ \,dtextupPGW(T) le p_textupsmall + p_textuplarge \,, where p_textupsmall is the contribution from the event |B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| le exp\k^2R\, and p_textuplarge is the contribution from the complementary event. It follows from Corollary~ that \[ p_textupsmall =exp\ k^3 R'+ k^2 R\ textupPGWBig(textupv_textuptextscrt not i-fairBig) le frac1exp( 2^kdelta_*/3R/k^2) \,. \] The contribution from the complementary event is fracp_textuplargeexp\k^3 R'\ &= int |B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| 1 bigg\ |B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| ge exp\k^2R\ bigg\\,dtextupPGW(T)\\ &le exp\k^2R\ textupPGWbigg(|B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| ge exp\k^2R\bigg) +int_exp\k^2R\^infty textupPGWbigg(|B_20R'(v_textuptextscrt;T)| ge sbigg)\,ds\,. It follows from Lemma~ that this is very small: p_textuplarge le 1/exp(exp(kR)), which is negligible compared with the bound on p_textupsmall. Combining these gives the claimed bound (it is easy to show, using Markov's inequality, that the probability for v_textuptextscrt to be improper is negligible).

nodes.statement: Let T=(V,F,E) be a finite bipartite factor tree in which all clauses have degree k. Assume that T has diameter Lge 8R. If A is a subset of V such that textupBSP'(A;T)=T, then there is a 1/(80R)-corrupted subtree TsubseteqT of diameter L and maximum degree at most four. Since textupdiamT = L, it must contain some path P of length L. Let v_textuptextscrt denote one of the endpoints of this path. From now on we regard T as being rooted at v_textuptextscrt. bemphStep 1. Simplified bootstrap percolation of marked blocks. We now define a much simpler bootstrap percolation process, which we will show (in subsequent steps) to dominate textupBSP'(A;T) in an appropriate sense. For integers jge0, let T[j] denote the subgraph of T induced by variables whose distance to the root v_textuptextscrt lies between 4Rj and 4R(j+1); we then consider each connected component of T[j] as a ``block.'' Note that the blocks themselves have a tree-like (i.e., hierarchical) structure: if U is a block rooted at depth 4R(j+1), then its root is a leaf of a block U' rooted at depth 4Rj, and we say that U is a ``child block'' of U'. Let B be the tree structure of blocks. Let A_0 be the set of all blocks that intersect A. For tge1 we will say that a block belongs to A_t if either it belongs to A_t-1, or has at least two child blocks in A_t-1. Iterate this to define the set of all ``marked'' blocks, \[textupmark(A_0;B) equivbigcup_tge0A_t\,.\] Note that this ``marking'' is also a bootstrap-percolation-type process, but is much simpler than textupBSP'. bemphStep 2. A general property of textupBSP'(A;T). We next state and prove a useful property of the textupBSP'(A;T) process: if S is any subset of V which does not intersect A, then in the first round of textupBSP'(A;T) in which any variable is deleted from S, it must be the case that some variable on its internal boundary \[partial^textupint S equivbigg\ uin S : textupuin B_1(w;T) for some win Vsetminus S bigg\\] is also deleted. To see that this property holds, say the first deletion from S occurs at round t+1. This means that after round t, the subgraph remaining in the textupBSP'(A;T) process is T_t=(V_t,F_t,E_t)subseteqT with V_tsupseteq S (i.e., no variable has yet been deleted from S). The subgraph remaining after the next round t+1 is T_t+1=(V_t+1,F_t+1,E_t+1)subseteqT_t where V_tsetminus V_t+1 intersects S. By the definition of textupBSP', \[T_t+1 = T_t \,biggbackslash \, B_R(A_t;T_t)\] where A_-1=A and A_t=textupAct(T_t) for tge1. Now suppose for contradiction that V_tsetminus V_t+1 does not intersect partial^textupint S. For any variable v, its neighborhood B_R(v;T_t) is a connected subgraph of T_t (hence also of T). As a result it must be that for all vin A_t, the neighborhood B_R(v;T_t) is either disjoint from S, or contained in Ssetminus partial^textupintS. Since V_tsetminus V_t+1 intersects S, there must be at least one vin A_t with B_R(v;T_t)subseteq Ssetminus partial^textupint S. Since S does not intersect A, it must be that tge0 and vin A_t=textupAct(T_t). By definition of textupAct(T_t), this means that some clause a in B_R(v;T_t) must have degree less than k. Since all clauses in T were assumed to be of degree k, this means that in T there was a variable uin partial a which was deleted by the end of round t. However u must also belong to S, contradicting the hypothesis that no deletion occurred from S by the end of round t. This proves the claim. bemphStep 3. Comparison of marking and textupBSP'. We now argue that the marking process ``dominates'' textupBSP'(A;T) in the following sense. Let us say that a block U is a ``tall block'' if it has depth at least 2R; otherwise we call U a ``shallow block.'' We claim that any tall block must be marked. Suppose for contradiction that this is not the case, then let U be any block of maximal depth among all the unmarked tall blocks. This means that all the child blocks of U must be marked, or be shallow blocks. Since U itself is unmarked, the definition of the marking process implies that at most one child block of U can be marked. If such a block exists we will denote it U'. We let W denote any child block of U which is unmarked; this means that W must be a shallow block. We now argue that throughout the textupBSP'(A;T) process, W has no influence on U. To see this, apply the claim from Step 2 with S=W. Since W is a shallow block, it follows that at the first round during textupBSP'(A;T) in which any variable is removed from the upper half of W, the root of W must also be removed. After this, any variables remaining in W will be disconnected from U. \label{l:marked.blocks.corrupt.tree}Let $\mathscr{T}=(V,F,E)$ be a finite bipartite factor tree in which all clauses have degree $k$. Assume that $\mathscr{T}$ has diameter $L\ge 8R$. If $A$ is a subset of $V$ such that $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})=\mathscr{T}$, then there is a $1/(80R)$-corrupted subtree $T\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ of diameter $L$ and maximum degree at most four.

\begin{proof} Since $\textup{diam}\mathscr{T} = L$, it must contain some path $P$ of length $L$. Let $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ denote one of the endpoints of this path. From now on we regard $\mathscr{T}$ as being rooted at $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.

\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 1. Simplified bootstrap percolation of marked blocks.} We now define a much simpler bootstrap percolation process, which we will show (in subsequent steps) to dominate $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ in an appropriate sense. For integers $j\ge0$, let $\mathscr{T}[j]$ denote the subgraph of $\mathscr{T}$ induced by variables whose distance to the root $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ lies between $4Rj$ and $4R(j+1)$; we then consider each connected component of $\mathscr{T}[j]$ as a ``block.'' Note that the blocks themselves have a tree-like (i.e., hierarchical) structure: if $U$ is a block rooted at depth $4R(j+1)$, then its root is a leaf of a block $U'$ rooted at depth $4Rj$, and we say that $U$ is a ``child block'' of $U'$. Let $\mathfrak{B}$ be the tree structure of blocks. Let $\mathcal{A}_0$ be the set of all blocks that intersect $A$. For $t\ge1$ we will say that a block belongs to $\mathcal{A}_t$ if either it belongs to $\mathcal{A}_{t-1}$, or has at least two child blocks in $\mathcal{A}_{t-1}$. Iterate this to define the set of all ``marked'' blocks,
	\[\textup{\textsf{mark}}(\mathcal{A}_0;\mathfrak{B})
	\equiv\bigcup_{t\ge0}\mathcal{A}_t\,.\]
Note that this ``marking'' is also a bootstrap-percolation-type process, but is much simpler than $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'$.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 2. A general property of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$.} We next state and prove a useful property of the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process: if $S$ is any subset of $V$ which does not intersect $A$, then in the first round of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ in which \emph{any} variable is deleted from $S$, it must be the case that some variable on its internal boundary
	\[\partial^\textup{int} S
	\equiv\bigg\{
	u\in S : \textup{$u\in B_1(w;\mathscr{T})$
		for some $w\in V\setminus S$}
	\bigg\}\]
is also deleted. To see that this property holds, say the first deletion from $S$ occurs at round $t+1$. This means that after round $t$, the subgraph remaining in the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process is $\mathscr{T}_t=(V_t,F_t,E_t)\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ with $V_t\supseteq S$ (i.e., no variable has yet been deleted from $S$). The subgraph remaining after the next round $t+1$ is $\mathscr{T}_{t+1}=(V_{t+1},F_{t+1},E_{t+1})\subseteq\mathscr{T}_t$ where $V_t\setminus V_{t+1}$ intersects $S$. 
By the definition of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'$,
	\[\mathscr{T}_{t+1} = \mathscr{T}_t
	\,\bigg\backslash \, 
	B_R(A_t;\mathscr{T}_t)\]
where $A_{-1}=A$ and $A_t=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{T}_t)$ for $t\ge1$. Now suppose for contradiction that $V_t\setminus V_{t+1}$ does not intersect $\partial^\textup{int} S$. For any variable $v$, its neighborhood $B_R(v;\mathscr{T}_t)$ is a connected subgraph of $\mathscr{T}_t$ (hence also of $\mathscr{T}$). As a result it must be that for all $v\in A_t$, the neighborhood $B_R(v;\mathscr{T}_t)$ is either disjoint from $S$, or contained in $S\setminus \partial^\textup{int}S$. Since $V_t\setminus V_{t+1}$ intersects $S$, there must be at least one $v\in A_t$ with $B_R(v;\mathscr{T}_t)\subseteq S\setminus \partial^\textup{int} S$. Since $S$ does not intersect $A$, it must be that $t\ge0$ and $v\in A_t=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{T}_t)$. By definition of $\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{T}_t)$,
this means that some clause $a$ in $B_R(v;\mathscr{T}_t)$ must have degree less than $k$. Since all clauses in $\mathscr{T}$ were assumed to be of degree $k$, this means that in $\mathscr{T}$ there was a variable $u\in \partial a$ which was deleted by the end of round $t$. However $u$ must also belong to $S$, contradicting the hypothesis that no deletion occurred from $S$ by the end of round $t$. This proves the claim.\medskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 3. Comparison of marking and $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'$.} We now argue that the marking process ``dominates'' $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ in the following sense. Let us say that a block $U$ is a ``tall block'' if it has depth at least $2R$; otherwise we call $U$ a ``shallow block.'' We claim that any tall block must be marked. Suppose for contradiction that this is not the case, then let $U$ be any block of maximal depth among all the unmarked tall blocks. This means that all the child blocks of $U$ must be marked, or be shallow blocks. Since $U$ itself is unmarked, the definition of the marking process implies that at most one child block of $U$ can be marked. If such a block exists we will denote it $U'$. We let $W$ denote any child block of $U$ which is unmarked; this means that $W$ must be a shallow block.

We now argue that throughout the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process, $W$ has no influence on $U$. To see this, apply the claim from Step 2 with $S=W$. Since $W$ is a shallow block, it follows that at the first round during $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ in which any variable is removed from the upper half of $W$, the root of $W$ must also be removed. After this, any variables remaining in $W$ will be disconnected from $U$. Thus, throughout $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$, there is no time at which any variable $u\in U$ has in its $(3R/10)$-neighborhood a clause $a$ of degree less than $k$ that lies in $W$. This shows that $W$ has no influence on the evolution of $U$ under $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$.

Let $\rho$ denote the root of $U$, and let $\rho'$ denote the root of $U'$ (if it exists). Let $\tau$ be the first time during $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ that any variable is deleted from $U$; note that $\tau$ must be finite by the assumption that $U$ is a tall block. Let $\tau_\rho$ be the time that $\rho$ is deleted, and let $\tau_{\rho'}$ be the time that $\rho'$ is deleted. It follows from the preceding discussion that $\tau=\min\set{\tau_\rho,\tau_{\rho'}}$. Let us suppose first $\tau=\tau_\rho<\tau_{\rho'}$. At time $\tau$, the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process deletes a connected component $U_\rho$ containing $\rho$. The definition of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'$ implies that variables in $U_\rho$ can lie at depth at most $13R/10$ below $\rho$, and hence at distance at least $27R/10$ from $\rho'$. As a result, no other variables will be removed from $U$ until time $\tau_{\rho'}$, when the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process deletes a connected component $U_{\rho'}$ containing $\rho'$. Variables in $U_{\rho'}$ can lie at distance at most $13R/10$ from $ \rho'$, hence at distance at least $7R/10$ from $U_\rho$. No other variables will be removed from $U$ after time $\tau_{\rho'}$. In particular, this contradicts the assumption that $U$ is a tall block and $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})=\mathscr{T}$. Very similar arguments give the desired contradiction in the cases $\tau=\tau_{\rho'}<\tau_\rho$ and $\tau=\tau_{\rho'}=\tau_\rho$. This proves our claim that any tall block must also be marked.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 4. Extraction of sparse subtree.} Now recall that the tree $\mathscr{T}$ is rooted at a variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, from which there emanates a path $P$
of length $L\ge 8R$. 
Let $\ell\equiv \ell/(8R)$ and note that $\lfloor L/(4R)\rfloor \ge L/(4R)-1 \ge \ell$. It follows that there is a path of blocks $\mathfrak{P}=(U_1,\ldots,U_\ell)$, where $U_1$ is rooted at $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ and $U_i$ is a child block of $U_{i-1}$ for each $2\le i\le \ell$. By the claim proved in the previous step, each $U_i$ must be a marked block: that is, each $U_i$ either intersects $A$ or has at least two marked child blocks. It follows from the definition of the marking process that the path $\mathfrak{P}$ can be covered by a disjoint union
	\[\mathfrak{T}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^s\mathfrak{T}_j\]
where each $\mathfrak{T}_j$ is a nonempty full binary tree of marked blocks, rooted at a block $U_{i(j)}\in\mathfrak{P}$, such that the leaves $\mathfrak{L}_j$ of $\mathfrak{T}_j$ are all blocks intersecting $A$.\footnote{We will explain the $\mathfrak{T}_j$ by an example. The root of $\mathfrak{T}_1$ is always $U_1$, so $i(1)=1$. Suppose that $U_1$ does not intersect $A$, in which case it must have two marked child blocks, say $U_2$ and $\tilde{U}_2$. Suppose that these do intersect $A$. Then $\mathfrak{T}_1$ consists of $U_1$, $U_2$, and $\tilde{U}_2$. We then take $\mathfrak{T}_2$ to be rooted at $U_3$, so in this case $i(2)=3$. Suppose $U_3$ also intersects $A$; then $\mathfrak{T}_2$ consists only of $U_3$. We take $\mathfrak{T}_3$ to be rooted at $U_4$, and so on.}
Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be the tree of blocks given by the union of $\mathfrak{T}_1,\ldots,\mathfrak{T}_s$; it has maximum degree at most four. We then construct a subtree $T\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[a.]
\item For $1\le j\le s$ let $B_j\subseteq A$ be defined by taking one variable from $U\cap A$ for each $U\in\mathfrak{L}_j$.

\item For $1\le j\le s$ let $T_j\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ be defined by taking the union of all paths between $B_j$ and the root of $U_{i(j)}$.

\item For $1\le j\le s-1$, let $Q_j$ be the union of $T_j$ with a path joining the roots of $U_{i(j+1)-1}$ and $U_{i(j+1)}$. Let $Q_s$ be the union of $T_s$ with a path joining the root of $U_\ell$ with a variable of maximal depth in $U_\ell$. (The precise definition of $Q_s$ is not so important; we choose this one as it will guarantee $\textup{diam} T = L$.)

\item Let $T\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ be the union of $Q_1,\ldots,Q_s$. Let $B'$ be the (disjoint) union of $B_1,\ldots,B_s$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus $T$ is a subtree of $\mathscr{T}$ that includes the root $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ and has maximum degree at most four. We now argue that $T$ is $1/(80R)$-corrupted. The intersection of $T_j$ with any block $U$ is given by a union of at most two paths, so contains at most $8R$ variables. This implies
	\[
	|V_{T_j}|
	\le \sum_{U\in\mathfrak{T}_j}
		|V_{T_j}\cap U|
	\le 8R |\mathfrak{T}_j|
	\]
where $|\mathfrak{T}_j|$ denotes the number of blocks in $\mathfrak{T}_j$. We then have 
$|V_{Q_j}|\le |V_{T_j}|+4R
\le 8R (|\mathfrak{T}_j|+1)$, so

	|V_T|

Let $\tau_\rho$ be the time that $\rho$ is deleted, and let $\tau_{\rho'}$ be the time that $\rho'$ is deleted. It follows from the preceding discussion that $\tau=\min\set{\tau_\rho,\tau_{\rho'}}$. Let us suppose first $\tau=\tau_\rho<\tau_{\rho'}$. At time $\tau$, the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process deletes a connected component $U_\rho$ containing $\rho$. The definition of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'$ implies that variables in $U_\rho$ can lie at depth at most $13R/10$ below $\rho$, and hence at distance at least $27R/10$ from $\rho'$. As a result, no other variables will be removed from $U$ until time $\tau_{\rho'}$, when the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})$ process deletes a connected component $U_{\rho'}$ containing $\rho'$. Variables in $U_{\rho'}$ can lie at distance at most $13R/10$ from $ \rho'$, hence at distance at least $7R/10$ from $U_\rho$. No other variables will be removed from $U$ after time $\tau_{\rho'}$. In particular, this contradicts the assumption that $U$ is a tall block and $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{T})=\mathscr{T}$. Very similar arguments give the desired contradiction in the cases $\tau=\tau_{\rho'}<\tau_\rho$ and $\tau=\tau_{\rho'}=\tau_\rho$. This proves our claim that any tall block must also be marked.\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 4. Extraction of sparse subtree.} Now recall that the tree $\mathscr{T}$ is rooted at a variable $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, from which there emanates a path $P$
of length $L\ge 8R$. 
Let $\ell\equiv \ell/(8R)$ and note that $\lfloor L/(4R)\rfloor \ge L/(4R)-1 \ge \ell$. It follows that there is a path of blocks $\mathfrak{P}=(U_1,\ldots,U_\ell)$, where $U_1$ is rooted at $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ and $U_i$ is a child block of $U_{i-1}$ for each $2\le i\le \ell$. By the claim proved in the previous step, each $U_i$ must be a marked block: that is, each $U_i$ either intersects $A$ or has at least two marked child blocks. It follows from the definition of the marking process that the path $\mathfrak{P}$ can be covered by a disjoint union
	\[\mathfrak{T}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^s\mathfrak{T}_j\]
where each $\mathfrak{T}_j$ is a nonempty full binary tree of marked blocks, rooted at a block $U_{i(j)}\in\mathfrak{P}$, such that the leaves $\mathfrak{L}_j$ of $\mathfrak{T}_j$ are all blocks intersecting $A$.\footnote{We will explain the $\mathfrak{T}_j$ by an example. The root of $\mathfrak{T}_1$ is always $U_1$, so $i(1)=1$. Suppose that $U_1$ does not intersect $A$, in which case it must have two marked child blocks, say $U_2$ and $\tilde{U}_2$. Suppose that these do intersect $A$. Then $\mathfrak{T}_1$ consists of $U_1$, $U_2$, and $\tilde{U}_2$. We then take $\mathfrak{T}_2$ to be rooted at $U_3$, so in this case $i(2)=3$. Suppose $U_3$ also intersects $A$; then $\mathfrak{T}_2$ consists only of $U_3$. We take $\mathfrak{T}_3$ to be rooted at $U_4$, and so on.}
Let $\mathfrak{T}$ be the tree of blocks given by the union of $\mathfrak{T}_1,\ldots,\mathfrak{T}_s$; it has maximum degree at most four. We then construct a subtree $T\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[a.]
\item For $1\le j\le s$ let $B_j\subseteq A$ be defined by taking one variable from $U\cap A$ for each $U\in\mathfrak{L}_j$.

\item For $1\le j\le s$ let $T_j\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ be defined by taking the union of all paths between $B_j$ and the root of $U_{i(j)}$.

\item For $1\le j\le s-1$, let $Q_j$ be the union of $T_j$ with a path joining the roots of $U_{i(j+1)-1}$ and $U_{i(j+1)}$. Let $Q_s$ be the union of $T_s$ with a path joining the root of $U_\ell$ with a variable of maximal depth in $U_\ell$. (The precise definition of $Q_s$ is not so important; we choose this one as it will guarantee $\textup{diam} T = L$.)

\item Let $T\subseteq\mathscr{T}$ be the union of $Q_1,\ldots,Q_s$. Let $B'$ be the (disjoint) union of $B_1,\ldots,B_s$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus $T$ is a subtree of $\mathscr{T}$ that includes the root $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ and has maximum degree at most four. We now argue that $T$ is $1/(80R)$-corrupted. The intersection of $T_j$ with any block $U$ is given by a union of at most two paths, so contains at most $8R$ variables. This implies
	\[
	|V_{T_j}|
	\le \sum_{U\in\mathfrak{T}_j}
		|V_{T_j}\cap U|
	\le 8R |\mathfrak{T}_j|
	\]
where $|\mathfrak{T}_j|$ denotes the number of blocks in $\mathfrak{T}_j$. We then have 
$|V_{Q_j}|\le |V_{T_j}|+4R
\le 8R (|\mathfrak{T}_j|+1)$, so
	\begin{equation}\label{e:corrupt.paths.ubd}
	|V_T|
	\le \sum_{j=1}^s |V_{Q_j}|
	\le 8R \sum_{j=1}^s \Big(|\mathfrak{T}_j|+1\Big)\,.
	\end{equation}
On the other hand, in any nonempty full binary tree, the number of leaf nodes is exactly one plus the number of internal nodes, so
	\begin{equation}\label{e:corrupt.leaves.lbd}
	|V_T\cap A|
	\ge |B'|
	= \sum_{j=1}^s|B_j|
	\ge\sum_{j=1}^s|\mathfrak{L}_j|
	= \sum_{j=1}^s \frac{|\mathfrak{T}_j|+1}2\,.
	\end{equation}
Since $\mathfrak{T}$ has maximum degree at most four,
we can extract $B\subseteq B'$ with $|B| \ge |B'|/5 $ such that variables in $B$ lie at pairwise distance greater than $2R$. Combining with 
\eqref{e:corrupt.paths.ubd}~and~\eqref{e:corrupt.leaves.lbd} gives
	\[
	\frac{|B|}{|V_T|}
	\ge
	\frac{|B'|}{5|V_T|}
	\ge \frac1{80R}\,,
	\]
so $T$ is $1/(80R)$-corrupted as claimed. (Note in this case that the condition that $T\cup B_R(B;\mathscr{T})$ be acyclic is trivially satisfied, since $\mathscr{T}$ is a tree.)

nodes.statement: Let G=(V,F,E) be any bipartite factor graph (finite or infinite), and let A be a finite subset of V. Recall from Definition~ that the removal process textupBSP'(A;G) goes from G_t to G_t+1 (for tge-1) by removing the R-neighborhoods of all the variables in A_t, where A_-1 is the initial set A, and A_t is defined inductively using as textupAct(G_t). We now define the process textupBSP''(A;G) which is equivalent to textupBSP'(A;G) except that it removes one R-neighborhood at a time. That is to say, for each tge-1, we arbitrarily order the variables in A_t as \[ bigg(v_t,i : 1le i le |A_t|bigg)\,, \] and then remove first B_R(v_t,1;G_t), then B_R(v_t,2;G_t), and so on. We say that v_t,i is visited at the i-th step of this process (even if it may have been deleted at an earlier step). Thus textupBSP'' reaches the graph G_t+1 in \[sum_s=-1^t|A_s|\] steps. The point of textupBSP'' is that each step cannot increase the maximum component diameter (of the removed subgraph) by too much: if the maximum component diameter before a textupBSP'' step is ell, the maximum component diameter after the textupBSP'' step is at most 2(ell+R+1). We let textupBSP^s denote the textupBSP'' process stopped after s steps.

Recall from Definition~\ref{d:proc} that the removal process $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ goes from $\mathscr{G}_t$ to $\mathscr{G}_{t+1}$ (for $t\ge-1$) by removing the $R$-neighborhoods of all the variables in $A_t$, where $A_{-1}$ is the initial set $A$, and $A_t$ is defined inductively using \eqref{e:bspprime.activated.set} as $\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_t)$. We now define the process $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''(A;\mathscr{G})$ which is equivalent to $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ except that it removes one $R$-neighborhood at a time. That is to say, for each $t\ge-1$, we arbitrarily order the variables in $A_t$ as
	\[
	\bigg(v_{t,i} : 1\le i \le |A_t|\bigg)\,,
	\]
and then remove first 
$B_R(v_{t,1};\mathscr{G}_t)$,
then $B_R(v_{t,2};\mathscr{G}_t)$,
and so on. We say that $v_{t,i}$ is \textbf{visited} at the $i$-th step of this process (even if it may have been deleted at an earlier step). Thus $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''$ reaches the graph $\mathscr{G}_{t+1}$ in
	\[\sum_{s=-1}^t|A_s|\]
steps. The point of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''$ is that each step cannot increase the maximum component diameter (of the removed subgraph) by too much: if the maximum component diameter before a $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''$ step is $\ell$, the maximum component diameter after the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''$ step is at most $2(\ell+R+1)$. We let $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s$ denote the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}''$ process stopped after $s$ steps.

\label{l:bspprime.within}
Let $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$ be any bipartite graph (finite or infinite) in which all clauses have degree $k$. Let $A$ be a finite subset of $V$. If for some finite $s$ we have $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})=\mathscr{H}$,
then $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A_{\mathscr{H}};\mathscr{H})=\mathscr{H}$ where $A_{\mathscr{H}}$ denotes the restriction of $A$ to $\mathscr{H}$.

\begin{proof} First we note that $A_{\mathscr{H}}$ is a strict subset of $A$ if and only if $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s$ stops before the initial round of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ is finished, i.e., if and only if $s<|A_{-1}|$. In this case the result is straightforward: let $U_{-1}\subseteq A_{-1}$ denote the first $s$ variables in $A_{-1}$, so $\mathscr{H}=\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})= B_R(U_{-1};\mathscr{G})$. This implies $U_{-1}\subseteq A_{\mathscr{H}}$
and $B_R(U_{-1};\mathscr{G})=B_R(U_{-1};\mathscr{H})$. From this we obtain the chain of relations
	\[
	\mathscr{H}\supseteq
	\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A_{\mathscr{H}};\mathscr{H})
	\supseteq B_R(A_{\mathscr{H}};\mathscr{H})
	\supseteq B_R(U_{-1};\mathscr{H})
	= B_R(U_{-1};\mathscr{G}) = \mathscr{H}\,,
	\]
and so we have $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A_{\mathscr{H}};\mathscr{H})=\mathscr{H}$ as desired. We therefore assume from now on that $s\ge|A_{-1}|$. This means that $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ completes the initial round of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$, producing $\mathscr{G}_0 = \mathscr{G}\setminus B_R(A;\mathscr{G})$.
It also means that $A_{\mathscr{H}}=A$, and $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})$ completes its initial round to produce $\mathscr{H}_0 = \mathscr{H}\setminus B_R(A;\mathscr{H}) = \mathscr{H}\setminus B_R(A;\mathscr{G})$. We hereafter index this initial round as the ``zeroth round.''

We now suppose inductively, for $i\ge0$, the following hypothesis: provided that $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ fully completes
the first $i$ rounds
 of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ (again, $i$ starts from zero), the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $A_t=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_t)=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_t)$ for all $t\le i-1$; and
\item The subgraph $\mathscr{R}_i$ removed from $\mathscr{G}$ within the first $i$ rounds of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$
agrees with the subgraph removed from $\mathscr{H}$
 within the first $i$ rounds of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})$, i.e.,
 	\begin{equation}\label{e:same.R.i}
	\mathscr{R}_i
	\equiv\bigcup_{t=-1}^{i-1}
		B_R(A_t;\mathscr{G}_t)
	=\bigcup_{t=-1}^{i-1}B_R(A_t;\mathscr{H}_t)\,.
	\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} 
The base case $i=0$ follows from the preceding argument.
Let $\mathscr{G}_i$ be the graph remaining after the first $i$ rounds of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$, and let $\mathscr{H}_i$ be the graph remaining after the first $i$ rounds of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})$. By induction, $\mathscr{G}_i=\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{R}_i$
and $\mathscr{H}_i=\mathscr{H}\setminus\mathscr{R}_i = \mathscr{G}_i \cap \mathscr{H}$.
We will say that a subgraph is ``lacking'' if it contains at least two clauses of degree $k-1$, or at least one clause of degree $\le k-2$. Then, recalling \eqref{e:bspprime.activated.set}, 
for the next round we must consider
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_i)
	&=\bigg\{\textup{variables $v$ in $\mathscr{G}_i$
	such that $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$ is lacking}\bigg\}\,,\\
	\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)
	&=\bigg\{\textup{variables $v$ in $\mathscr{H}_i$
	such that $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ is lacking}
	\bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
The inductive hypothesis implies $\mathscr{H}_i\subseteq\mathscr{G}_i$,
so $B_R(v;\mathscr{H}_i)\subseteq B_R(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$ for any variable $v$. On the other hand, let $U_i$ be the vertices in $\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_i)$
that are visited by $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$
(for ``visited'' in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:slowed.bspprime}). If $v\in U_i$ then
the $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ process removes
 $B_R(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$, which means it lies inside $\mathscr{H}$. This implies
$B_R(v;\mathscr{G}_i)\subseteq
\mathscr{G}_i \cap \mathscr{H}=\mathscr{H}_i$, where the last equality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves that
	$B_R(v;\mathscr{G}_i)=B_R(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$
for all $v\in U_i$,
hence also $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)=B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$
for all $v\in U_i$. Moreover, all variables in $U_i$ are removed, so $U_i$ must be contained in $\mathscr{G}_i\cap\mathscr{H}=\mathscr{H}_i$
(using the inductive hypothesis again). It follows from this that
	\[
	U_i
	= \bigg\{v\in U_i : 
	\textup{$B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$ is lacking}\bigg\}
	\subseteq \bigg\{v\in \mathscr{H}_i : 
	\textup{$B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ is lacking}\bigg\}
	=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)\,.\]
Conversely, suppose $v\in\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)$, so $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ is lacking: either there are two clauses $a_1,a_2 \in B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ of degree $k-1$, or there is a single clause $a\in B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ of degree $\le k-2$. We have by induction $\mathscr{H}_i\subseteq\mathscr{G}_i$, therefore $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)\subseteq B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$ which means these clauses are also present in $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$. All clauses have degree $k$ in $\mathscr{G}$ (and hence also in $\mathscr{H}$), so if a clause $a\in B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$
has degree $k-j$ relative to $\mathscr{H}_i$, there must be $j$ edges joining that clause to variables in $\mathscr{R}_i$. It then follows from the inductive hypothesis \eqref{e:same.R.i}
that the clause has degree $\le k-j$ in $\mathscr{G}_i$. This implies that $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{G}_i)$ must also be lacking,
so $\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)\subseteq\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_i)$. If the $(i+1)$-st round is completed, then we obtain $A_i=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{G}_i) = U_i = \textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)$. Since we proved above that $B_R(v;\mathscr{G}_i)=B_R(v;\mathscr{H}_i)$ for all $v\in U_i = A_i$, we conclude
$\mathscr{R}_{i+1}= \mathscr{R}_i \cup B_R(A_i;\mathscr{G}_i)=B_R(A_i;\mathscr{H}_i)$.
This verifies the inductive hypothesis.

If $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ completes exactly the first $i$ rounds of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ (and no more), then the above induction implies $\mathscr{H}=\mathscr{R}_i=\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})$, as desired. It remains finally to consider the case that $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ completes the first $i$ rounds, and does not complete the $(i+1)$-st round. In this case, $\mathscr{H}=\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G}) = \mathscr{R}_i \cup B_R(U_i;\mathscr{G}_i)$. The above argument also gives
$U_i\subseteq \textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i)$. Altogether we obtain the chain of relations
	\[
	\mathscr{H}\supseteq \textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})
	\supseteq\mathscr{R}_i \cup B_R(\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H}_i);\mathscr{H}_i)
	\supseteq\mathscr{R}_i \cup B_R( U_i ;\mathscr{H}_i)
	=\mathscr{H}\,.
	\]
This gives $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{H})=\mathscr{H}$ in the case where $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}^s(A;\mathscr{G})$ stops partway through some round of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$,
and concludes the proof of the lemma.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement: Instead of textupBSP'(A;G), we follow the slowed removal process textupBSP''(A;G) (Definition~) where we remove one R-neighborhood at a time. Recall that if the maximum component diameter before a textupBSP'' step is ell, then the maximum component diameter after the textupBSP'' step is at most 2(ell+R+1). Let t_star be the first time that textupBSP''(A;G) creates any component HsubseteqB of diameter at least 5L.
