\label{c:excellent.under.uPGW.T}
Let $T$ be any fixed variable-rooted tree of maximum degree $\mathfrak{c}$,
where $\mathfrak{c}$ is an absolute constant.
Then
	\[
	\Big[{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)\Big]\bigg(
	\textup{$v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ is improper or not $\mathfrak{i}$-excellent}
	\bigg)
	\le \frac1{\exp( 2^{k\delta_*/4} R / k )}\]
for $\mathfrak{i}\in\set{0,1}$ and $k\ge k_0$, where $k_0$ is an absolute constant depending only on $\delta_*$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.

\begin{proof}
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:radon.derivative.pgwT},
let $\mathfrak{X}$ denote the Radon--Nikodym derivative 
of ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)$ with respect to ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$.
Let $\mathbb{E}$ denote expectation with respect to ${\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}$.
For any event $E$ we can trivially bound
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \mathbf{1}_E \mathfrak{X} ; \mathfrak{X} \le \frac1{{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}}\bigg]
	\le {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{1/3}\,.
	\]
On the other hand we can use Lemma~\ref{l:radon.derivative.pgwT}
together with Markov's inequality to bound
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \mathfrak{X} ; \mathfrak{X} > \frac1{{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}}\bigg]^2
	\le \mathbb{E}\Big[\mathfrak{X}^2\Big]
			{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}\bigg(\mathfrak{X} \ge \frac1{{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}}\bigg)
	\le 2 (\mathbb{E}\mathfrak{X}) \, {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}
	= 2 \, {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}\,.
	\]
Combining the bounds gives
	\[\Big[{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(T)\Big](E)
	=\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbf{1}_E\mathfrak{X}\Big]
	\le \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \mathbf{1}_E \mathfrak{X} ; \mathfrak{X} \le \frac1{{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}}\bigg]
		+\mathbb{E}\bigg[ \mathfrak{X} ; \mathfrak{X} > \frac1{{\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{2/3}}\bigg]
	\le 3 \, {\textup{\textbf{PGW}}}(E)^{1/3}\,.
	\]
The result then follows by combining with Corollary~\ref{c:excellent}.
\end{proof}

For vin V we let Y_v be the indicator that v lies within distance 10R of a variable that is removed during processing, i.e., \[ Y_v=1bigg\ vin B_10RBig(textupBSP'(A;G);GBig) bigg\ \] where A is the set of all variables that are improper or not 1-good in G (Definition~). Let \[ barY_v =1bigg\ c textupv lies within distance 10R of a connected component of\\ textuptextupBSP'(A;G) having diameter at most L_textupBSP'equiv (ln n)/2^kdelta_*/5 bigg\ le Y_v\,. \] We first argue that, with high probability, Y_v=barY_v for all vin V. Indeed, Proposition~ implies that if textupBSP'(A;G) has a connected component of diameter more than L_textupBSP', then either (i) there is a connected subgraph B'subseteqG with textupdiam B' le 11 L_textupBSP'/5 that contains more than one cycle, or (ii) there is a 1/(80R)-corrupted subtree T'subseteqG that has maximum degree at most four and textupdiam T ge L_textupBSP'/5. Thus Pbigg( hspace-3ptc Y_vne barY_v\\ textup for any vin V hspace-3ptbigg) &le sum_vin V bigg\ Pbigg(hspace-3ptc textupB_11L_textupBSP'/5(v) contains\\ textupmore than one cycle hspace-3ptbigg) +Pbigg(hspace-3ptc textupsome TinbmLambda_4, L_textupBSP'/5 (G, v)\\ textupis 1/(80R)-corrupt hspace-3ptbigg) bigg\\\ &stackrelodotle n bigg\ bigg( fracexp(5 L_textupBSP' k^2)nbigg)^2 + frac1exp\ 2^kdelta_*/4 L_textupBSP'/ k^2 \ bigg\ =o_n(1)\,, where the bound marked odot follows from Lemma~ together with very crude bounds on the chance to see more than one cycle in a neighborhood of v of radius 5L_textupBSP'. This proves that Y=barY with high probability where \[ Yequivsum_vin V Y_v\,, barYequiv sum_vin V barY_v\,. \] We now turn to estimating barY. Let B'(ell) be the union of all connected components of textupBSP'(A;G) of diameter ell that contain more than one cycle; and let T'(ell) be the union of all subtrees of textupBSP'(A;G) of diameter at least ell that are 1/(80R)-corrupted. Let A'(ell)equiv B'(ell) cup T'(ell/5). Proposition~ implies that if barY_v=1, then either v lies within distance 2010R from A, or v lies within distance ell+10R from A'(ell) for some 2000Rleell le L_textupBSP'. Therefore EbarY le E Big|B_2010R(A)Big| +sum_ell= 2000R^L_textupBSP' E Big|B_ell+10R(A'(ell))Big|\,. Let gamma=exp(-2^kdelta_*/4 R / (2k)), and note that Corollary~ together with Markov's inequality gives \[ PBig(|A|ge ngammaBig) le fracE Angamma = fracP(vin A)gamma le fracexp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / (2k)) exp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / k) = gamma\,. \] Combining with Lemma~ gives, for L=2010R and gamma=exp(-2^kdelta_*/4 R / (2k)), nonumber E Big|B_2010R(A)Big| &le ngamma exp(k^2 L) +nPBig( |A| ge n gammaBig) +n Pbigg( hspace-3ptc textupthere exists Ssubseteq V with |S|=ngamma\\ textupand |B_L(S)|ge ngamma exp(k^2 L) hspace-3pt bigg) \\ &le fracn exp(2010k^2 R) exp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / (2k)) + fracn exp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / (2k)) + fracnexp(n e^kL gamma) le fracn exp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / (3k)) \,. Combining with Lemma~ gives nonumber EBig| B_ell+10R(A'(ell))Big| &le ngamma_ell exp(k^2(ell+10R)) +nPBig(|A'(ell)| ge ngamma_ellBig) +nPbigg( hspace-3ptc textupthere exists Ssubseteq V with |S|=ngamma_ell and\\ textup|B_ell+10R(S)|ge ngamma_ell exp(k^2(ell+10R)) hspace-3pt bigg) \\ &le fracn exp(k^2(ell+10R))exp(2^kdelta_*/4ell/ k^2) + fracnexp(2^kdelta_*/4ell/ k^2) + fracnexp(n e^k(ell+10R) gamma_ell) le fracnexp(2^kdelta_*/4ell/ k^3)\,, for all ellge2000R. Substituting and into gives \[ E barY le fracnexp(2^kdelta_*/4 R / k^4)\,. \] Next note that under P_n,m, for any une v the radius-(L_textupBSP'+10R) neighborhoods of u and v intersect with chance o_n(1), and so are nearly independent of one another. nodes.name: feasible types
nodes.statement: A clause total type bmLequiv(L_0,L_infty) is termed bemphfeasible if there exists some bipartite factor graph H, with girth larger than 8R, such that P_n',n'alpha'(H)>0 for some n',alpha', and some clause a_starintextupprH has total type bmL. Thus L_0 and L_infty are both trees, which we regard as being rooted at a_star.

nodes.name: tree based on feasible type
nodes.statement: Given a feasible clause total type bmL, we now construct a corresponding tree T(bmL) as follows. Among all pairs (H,a_star) for which the conditions of Definition~ hold, fix one such that H has minimal size. Let T_star be the (4R)-neighborhood of a_star in H, which we regard as a tree rooted at a_star. We regard L_0,L_infty as subtrees of T_star, and make the following definitions: [a.] item Let V_1 denote the set of variables of L_0setminus L_infty which neighbor some clause in L_infty. For each vin V_1, let T_star(v,ell) be the subtree of T_star induced by all the descendants of v that lie within distance ell of v. Let Y_textupout(v) be the variables in T_star(v) that lie at depth exactly R below v --- we will argue in the proof of Corollary~ below that Y_textupout(v) is nonempty for all vin V_1. We take a union over V_1 to define T_star,textupout equivbigcup_vin V_1 T_star(v,2R)\,, N_textupoutequivbigcup_vin V_1 T_star(v,R-1)\,, Y_textupoutequivbigcup_vin V_1 Y_textupout(v)\,. For each yin Y_textupout, let Z_textupout(y) be the variables that lie at depth exactly R below y. If Z_textupout(y) is nonempty, then we fix an arbitrary win Z_textupout(v), and modify w by redefining bml(w) to be the same as bml(v) where v is the ancestor of y in V_1. We let T_textupout denote the resulting modification of T_star,textupout (the two graphs can differ only in the markings bml at the last level). item Now let T_starstar be the component of T_starsetminusT_textupout that contains the root clause a_star. Let W denote the variables at the boundary of L_infty. From the definition of the processing algorithm, each variable left in textupprH is 1-good, which means (Definition~) that any length-(2R/5) path emanating from the variable must contain at least one variable that is 1-excellent. This in turn means we can find a set X of 1-excellent variables that lie below W, at distance at most 2R/5 from W, such that X forms a cutset in T_starstar that encloses L_infty. Let Y be the variables in T_starstar that lie at depth exactly R/10 below X. Let T_textupin be the subtree of T_starstar enclosed by Y. Let T(bmL) be the subtree of T_star induced by the union of T_textupin and T_textupout.

For any clause ain F, we let bmE_aequivbmE_a(bmL) be the event that T'equiv B_4R(a;G) is a tree, and there is an embedding phi:T(bmL)hookrightarrowT' that maps a_starmapsto a, and satisfies the following: [(i)] item For any variable vin phi(T(bmL))subseteqT', either all or none of its child variables (with respect to T') lie in phi(T(bmL)). item For any variable vin V_1, the subtree of v in T(bmL) agrees with the depth-2R subtree of phi(v) in T'. If bmE_a occurs, let X' be the cutset of variables in T' lying at distance exactly R/10 below phi(Y). Let Z be the cutset of variables in T' lying at distance exactly R below phi(Y). Let U be the subgraph of T' that lies sandwiched between phi(X) and X' (inclusive). Let N be the subgraph of T' that lies sandwiched between phi(Y) and Z, including phi(Y) but not including Z. We then let bmK_aequivbmK_a(bmL) be the event that GinbmE_a, and every variable in Ncup Z survives in textupprG'.

nodes.statement: Suppose that bmL is a feasible clause type in the sense of Definition~. Suppose G has girth greater than 8R and belongs to the event bmG_a cap bmK_a, and let G' be as defined by . Let A,A' be the variables that are improper or not 1-good with respect to G,G' respectively. Then Asubseteq A' subseteq G'setminusN and A'setminus A= phi(N_textupout) cap A'. Throughout the proof we fix H as in Definition~, and let T(bmL) be the tree given by Definition~. Let A_H denote the set of all variables that are improper or not 1-good with respect to H. Then, with N_textupout as defined by , we first observe that A_H cap Big( T_textupin cup N_textupout Big) = varnothing --- this is because the R-neighborhood of each variable in A_H is removed in the first step of processing on H, but T_textupin is assumed to survive in textupprH. We now turn to the comparison of A and A'. To begin, recall that one way for a variable to be improper is that its R-neighborhood contains a cycle --- however, by the girth assumption, this never happens in G or G'. It remains to consider all the ways for an acyclic variable to belong to A or A': [bullet] item Let A(R) denote the variables vin A for which B_R(v;G) contains a repeat marking --- i.e., two variables une w with the same marking bml(u)=bml(w). Define similarly A'(R)subseteq A', and note A'(R)subseteq A(R) since the R-neighborhood of any variable relative to G' is a subgraph of its R-neighborhood relative to G. Let \[G''equiv G'\,Bigbackslash\, Big( N cupphi(N_textupout)Big)\,,\] that is to say, G'' is the subgraph of G induced by variables lying at distance at least R from phi(T_textupin). If variable v lies in G'', then B_R(v;G)=B_R(v;G'), and so \[ A(R) cap G'' = A'(R) cap G''\,. \] If v lies in GsetminusG'', we distinguish two cases: [circ] item If vinphi(T_textupin)cupN, property~ implies that v must be proper in G, so vnotin A(R). item If vinphi(N_textupout), it follows from that v'equivphi^-1(v) must be proper with respect to H, so B_R(v';H) has no repeat marking. We claim that the same holds for B_R(v;G). Indeed, suppose for contradiction that in B_R(v;G) there are two variables une w with bml(u)=bml(w). [--] item If both u,w lie in phi(T_textupout), then we have two variables phi^-1(u)nephi^-1(w) inside B_R(v';H) with the same marking, contradicting the above observation. item If both u,w lie in phi(T_textupin)cupN, then it must be possible to join them by a path inside phi(T_textupin)cupN of length at most 2R-1. It follows that u,win B_R(barv;G) for barvinphi(T_textupin)cupN, which contradicts property~. item If uinphi(T_textupout) while winphi(T_textupin)cupN, we must have bml(u)nebml(w) by property~. The above shows that A(R) cannot intersect GsetminusG''. Since A'(R)subseteq A(R), we obtain that A'(R) also cannot intersect GsetminusG''. Combining with the earlier observation gives A(R)=A'(R)subseteq G''\,. item Let A(1),A'(1) denote the variables that fail to be 1-good with respect to G,G' respectively. Recall that any variable in G or G' is acyclic, so whether it is 1-good depends only on its (2R/5)-neighborhood. If v lies in G at distance at least 2R/5 from phi(T_textupin), then it has the same (2R/5)-neighborhood in both G and G', so vin A(1) if and only if vin A'(1). For v lying at distance less than 2R/5 from phi(T_textupin), we distinguish three cases: [circ] item First suppose that v lies either in phi(N_textupout), or in the part of phi(T_textupin) above phi(X). Then it follows from that v'equivphi^-1(v) must be 1-good (hence 1-fair) in H. Since being 1-fair is a property of the (R/10)-neighborhood, and B_R/10(v;G)cong B_R/10(v';H), we see that v is 1-fair in G. Now consider a path gamma of length 2R/5 emanating from v: [--] item Suppose gamma never intersects phi(X). Since v'=phi^-1(v) is 1-good in H, the path phi^-1(gamma) must contain a variable u'=phi^-1(u) which is 1-excellent in H. Since being 1-excellent is a property of the (R/10)-neighborhood, and B_R/10(u;G)cong B_R/10(u';H), we see that uingamma is 1-excellent in G. item Otherwise, gamma contains a variable uinphi(X). From the construction (Definition~), the variable u'=phi^-1(u) is 1-excellent in H. By the same reasoning as in the last case, u must then be 1-excellent in G. This proves that v is 1-good in G, i.e., vnotin A(1). item Next suppose v lies in U (i.e., between phi(X) and X', inclusive). Then v is 1-fair in G simply by property~. A path of length 2R/5 emanating from v must contain a variable u from either phi(X) or X'. If uinphi(X), then it is 1-excellent in G as argued above. If uin X', then it is 1-excellent in G by property~. Thus, vnotin A(1). item It remains to consider the case that v lies in NsetminusU. For any variable in G at distance at least R/10 from phi(T_textupin), the (R/10)-neighborhoods in G,G' are the same, so that variable is 1-fair in G if and only if it is 1-fair in G'; the same applies to the 1-excellent property. In particular, this tells us that vinNsetminusU is 1-fair in G if and only if it is 1-fair in G'. If a path of length 2R/5 emanates from v and never intersects X', then it must stay at least distance R/10 away from phi(T_textupin), so the path contains a 1-excellent variable of G if and only if it contains a 1-excellent variable of G'. Otherwise, the path contains a variable from X' which is 1-excellent in both G and G' by property~. This proves that A(1) cap (NsetminusU) = A'(1) cap (NsetminusU). It follows from the above that A(1)subseteq A'(1) and A(1) cap phi(N_textupout) = varnothing\,. Now note that A' is by definition a subset of G', and on the event bmK_a it must not intersect N. Thus, on the event bmK_a, we have A(1)subseteq A'(1)subseteqG'setminusN. We also noted that variables at distance at least 2R/5 from phi(T_textupin) belong in A(1) if and only if they belong in A'(1), so in particular A(1)capG''=A'(1)capG''. It follows that \[A'(1)setminus A(1) subseteq(G'setminusN) Bigbackslash G'' =phi(N_textupout)\,.\] We already saw in (without appealing to bmK_a) that A(R)=A'(R)subseteqG''. Combining with finishes the proof of the lemma, since A=A(R)cup A(1) and A'=A'(R)cup A'(1).

\label{l:event.implies.A.Aprime.comparison} Suppose that $\bm{L}$ is a feasible clause type in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:feasible.clause.type}. Suppose $\mathscr{G}$ has girth greater than $8R$ and belongs to the event $\bm{G}_a \cap \bm{K}_a$, and let $\mathscr{G}'$ be as defined by \eqref{e:Gprime.cavity}. Let $A,A'$ be the variables that are improper or not $1$-good with respect to $\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}'$ respectively. Then $A\subseteq A' \subseteq \mathscr{G}'\setminus\mathscr{N}$
and $A'\setminus A= \phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out}) \cap A'$.

\begin{proof}Throughout the proof we fix $\mathscr{H}$ as in Definition~\ref{d:feasible.clause.type}, and let $\mathscr{T}(\bm{L})$ be the tree given by Definition~\ref{d:tree.based.on.feasible.type}. Let $A_{\mathscr{H}}$ denote the set of all variables that are improper or not $1$-good with respect to $\mathscr{H}$. Then, with $\mathscr{N}_\textup{out}$ as defined by \eqref{e:defn.Tout}, we first observe that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:obs.A.HH}
	A_{\mathscr{H}} \cap \Big( \mathscr{T}_\textup{in} \cup \mathscr{N}_\textup{out} \Big) = \varnothing
	\end{equation}
--- this is because the $R$-neighborhood of each variable in $A_{\mathscr{H}}$ is removed in the first step of processing on $\mathscr{H}$, but $\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}$ is assumed to survive in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{H}$.

We now turn to the comparison of $A$ and $A'$. To begin, recall that one way for a variable to be improper is that its $R$-neighborhood contains a cycle --- however, by the girth assumption, this never happens in $\mathscr{G}$ or $\mathscr{G}'$. It remains to consider all the ways for an acyclic variable to belong to $A$ or $A'$:
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\item Let $A(R)$ denote the variables $v\in A$ for which $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ contains a repeat marking --- i.e., two variables $u\ne w$ with the same marking $\bm{l}(u)=\bm{l}(w)$. Define similarly $A'(R)\subseteq A'$, and note $A'(R)\subseteq A(R)$ since the $R$-neighborhood of any variable relative to $\mathscr{G}'$ is a subgraph of its $R$-neighborhood relative to $\mathscr{G}$. Let 
	\[\mathscr{G}''\equiv \mathscr{G}'\,\Big\backslash\,
		\Big( \mathscr{N} \cup\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})\Big)\,,\]
that is to say, $\mathscr{G}''$ is the subgraph of $\mathscr{G}$ induced by variables lying at distance at least $R$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$. If variable $v$ lies in $\mathscr{G}''$, then $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})=B_R(v;\mathscr{G}')$, and so
	\[
	A(R) \cap \mathscr{G}'' = A'(R) \cap \mathscr{G}''\,.
	\]
If $v$ lies in $\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{G}''$, we distinguish two cases:
\begin{enumerate}[$\circ$]
\item If $v\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$,
property~\eqref{i:Tin.and.P.are.proper} implies that $v$ must be proper in $\mathscr{G}$, so $v\notin A(R)$. 

\item If $v\in\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})$, it follows from \eqref{e:obs.A.HH} that
$v'\equiv\phi^{-1}(v)$ must be proper with respect to $\mathscr{H}$, so $B_R(v';\mathscr{H})$ has no repeat marking. We claim that the same holds for $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$. Indeed, suppose for contradiction that
in $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ there are two variables $u\ne w$ with $\bm{l}(u)=\bm{l}(w)$.
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item If both $u,w$ lie in $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{out})$, then we have two variables
$\phi^{-1}(u)\ne\phi^{-1}(w)$ inside $B_R(v';\mathscr{H})$ with the same marking, contradicting the above observation.
\item If both $u,w$ lie in $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$,
then it must be possible to join them by a path
\emph{inside} $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$ of length at most $2R-1$.
It follows that $u,w\in B_R(\bar{v};\mathscr{G})$ for $\bar{v}\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$,
which contradicts property~\eqref{i:Tin.and.P.are.proper}.
\item If $u\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{out})$ while $w\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$, we must have $\bm{l}(u)\ne\bm{l}(w)$ by property~\eqref{i:Tin.Tout.diff.labels}. 
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
The above shows that $A(R)$ cannot intersect $\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{G}''$.
Since $A'(R)\subseteq A(R)$, we obtain that $A'(R)$
also cannot intersect $\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{G}''$. 
Combining with the earlier observation gives
	\begin{equation}\label{e:matching.A.R.sets}
	A(R)=A'(R)\subseteq \mathscr{G}''\,.
	\end{equation}

\item Let $A(1),A'(1)$ denote the variables that fail to be $1$-good with respect to $\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}'$ respectively. Recall that any variable in $\mathscr{G}$ or $\mathscr{G}'$ is acyclic, so whether it is $1$-good depends only on its 
 $(2R/5)$-neighborhood. If $v$ lies in $\mathscr{G}$ at distance at least $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, then it has the same $(2R/5)$-neighborhood in both $\mathscr{G}$ and $\mathscr{G}'$, so $v\in A(1)$ if and only if $v\in A'(1)$. For $v$ lying at distance less than $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, we distinguish three cases:
\begin{enumerate}[$\circ$]
\item First suppose that $v$ lies either in $\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})$, or in the part of $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$ above $\phi(X)$. Then it follows from \eqref{e:obs.A.HH} that $v'\equiv\phi^{-1}(v)$ must be $1$-good (hence $1$-fair) in $\mathscr{H}$. Since being $1$-fair is a property of the $(R/10)$-neighborhood, and $B_{R/10}(v;\mathscr{G})\cong B_{R/10}(v';\mathscr{H})$, we see that $v$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$. Now consider a path $\gamma$ of length $2R/5$ emanating from $v$:
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item Suppose $\gamma$ never intersects $\phi(X)$. Since $v'=\phi^{-1}(v)$ is $1$-good in $\mathscr{H}$, the path $\phi^{-1}(\gamma)$ must contain a variable $u'=\phi^{-1}(u)$ which is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{H}$. Since being $1$-excellent is a property of the $(R/10)$-neighborhood, and $B_{R/10}(u;\mathscr{G})\cong B_{R/10}(u';\mathscr{H})$, we see that $u\in\gamma$ is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$.

\item Otherwise, $\gamma$ contains a variable $u\in\phi(X)$.
From the construction (Definition~\ref{d:tree.based.on.feasible.type}),
the variable $u'=\phi^{-1}(u)$ is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{H}$. By the same reasoning as in the last case, $u$ must then be $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$.
\end{enumerate}
This proves that $v$ is $1$-good in $\mathscr{G}$, i.e., $v\notin A(1)$.

\item Next suppose $v$ lies in $\mathscr{U}$ (i.e., between $\phi(X)$ and $X'$, inclusive). Then $v$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ simply by property~\eqref{i:U.is.fair}. A path of length $2R/5$ emanating from $v$ must contain a variable $u$ from either $\phi(X)$ or $X'$.
If $u\in\phi(X)$, then it is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$ as argued above. If $u\in X'$, then it is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$ by property~\eqref{i:Xprime.is.excellent}. Thus, $v\notin A(1)$.

\item It remains to consider the case that $v$ lies in $\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}$.
For any variable in $\mathscr{G}$ at distance at least $R/10$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$,
the $(R/10)$-neighborhoods in $\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}'$ are the same,
so that variable is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}'$;
the same applies to the $1$-excellent property.
In particular, this tells us that $v\in\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}'$. If a path of length $2R/5$ emanates from $v$ and never intersects $X'$, then it must stay at least distance $R/10$ away from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, so the path contains a $1$-excellent variable of $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it contains a $1$-excellent variable of $\mathscr{G}'$. Otherwise, the path contains a variable from $X'$ which is $1$-excellent in both $\mathscr{G}$ and $\mathscr{G}'$ by property~\eqref{i:Xprime.is.excellent}. This proves that
	$A(1) \cap (\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}) = A'(1) \cap (\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U})$.
\end{enumerate}
It follows from the above that $A(1)\subseteq A'(1)$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{e:compare.A.one.sets}
	A(1) \cap \phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out}) = \varnothing\,.
	\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Now note that $A'$ is by definition a subset of $\mathscr{G}'$, and on the event $\bm{K}_a$ it must not intersect $\mathscr{N}$. Thus, on the event $\bm{K}_a$, we have $A(1)\subseteq A'(1)\subseteq\mathscr{G}'\setminus\mathscr{N}$. We also noted that variables at distance at least $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$ belong in $A(1)$ if and only if they belong in $A'(1)$, so in particular $A(1)\cap\mathscr{G}''=A'(1)\cap\mathscr{G}''$. It follows that
	\[A'(1)\setminus A(1)
	\subseteq(\mathscr{G}'\setminus\mathscr{N})
		\Big\backslash \mathscr{G}''
	=\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})\,.\]
We already saw in \eqref{e:matching.A.R.sets} (without appealing to $\bm{K}_a$) that $A(R)=A'(R)\subseteq\mathscr{G}''$. Combining with \eqref{e:compare.A.one.sets} finishes the proof of the lemma, since $A=A(R)\cup A(1)$ and $A'=A'(R)\cup A'(1)$.
\end{proof}

\item If $u\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{out})$ while $w\in\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})\cup\mathscr{N}$, we must have $\bm{l}(u)\ne\bm{l}(w)$ by property~\eqref{i:Tin.Tout.diff.labels}. 
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
The above shows that $A(R)$ cannot intersect $\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{G}''$.
Since $A'(R)\subseteq A(R)$, we obtain that $A'(R)$
also cannot intersect $\mathscr{G}\setminus\mathscr{G}''$. 
Combining with the earlier observation gives
	\begin{equation}\label{e:matching.A.R.sets}
	A(R)=A'(R)\subseteq \mathscr{G}''\,.
	\end{equation}

\item Let $A(1),A'(1)$ denote the variables that fail to be $1$-good with respect to $\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}'$ respectively. Recall that any variable in $\mathscr{G}$ or $\mathscr{G}'$ is acyclic, so whether it is $1$-good depends only on its 
 $(2R/5)$-neighborhood. If $v$ lies in $\mathscr{G}$ at distance at least $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, then it has the same $(2R/5)$-neighborhood in both $\mathscr{G}$ and $\mathscr{G}'$, so $v\in A(1)$ if and only if $v\in A'(1)$. For $v$ lying at distance less than $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, we distinguish three cases:
\begin{enumerate}[$\circ$]
\item First suppose that $v$ lies either in $\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})$, or in the part of $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$ above $\phi(X)$. Then it follows from \eqref{e:obs.A.HH} that $v'\equiv\phi^{-1}(v)$ must be $1$-good (hence $1$-fair) in $\mathscr{H}$. Since being $1$-fair is a property of the $(R/10)$-neighborhood, and $B_{R/10}(v;\mathscr{G})\cong B_{R/10}(v';\mathscr{H})$, we see that $v$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$. Now consider a path $\gamma$ of length $2R/5$ emanating from $v$:
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item Suppose $\gamma$ never intersects $\phi(X)$. Since $v'=\phi^{-1}(v)$ is $1$-good in $\mathscr{H}$, the path $\phi^{-1}(\gamma)$ must contain a variable $u'=\phi^{-1}(u)$ which is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{H}$. Since being $1$-excellent is a property of the $(R/10)$-neighborhood, and $B_{R/10}(u;\mathscr{G})\cong B_{R/10}(u';\mathscr{H})$, we see that $u\in\gamma$ is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$.

\item Otherwise, $\gamma$ contains a variable $u\in\phi(X)$.
From the construction (Definition~\ref{d:tree.based.on.feasible.type}),
the variable $u'=\phi^{-1}(u)$ is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{H}$. By the same reasoning as in the last case, $u$ must then be $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$.
\end{enumerate}
This proves that $v$ is $1$-good in $\mathscr{G}$, i.e., $v\notin A(1)$.

\item Next suppose $v$ lies in $\mathscr{U}$ (i.e., between $\phi(X)$ and $X'$, inclusive). Then $v$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ simply by property~\eqref{i:U.is.fair}. A path of length $2R/5$ emanating from $v$ must contain a variable $u$ from either $\phi(X)$ or $X'$.
If $u\in\phi(X)$, then it is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$ as argued above. If $u\in X'$, then it is $1$-excellent in $\mathscr{G}$ by property~\eqref{i:Xprime.is.excellent}. Thus, $v\notin A(1)$.

\item It remains to consider the case that $v$ lies in $\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}$.
For any variable in $\mathscr{G}$ at distance at least $R/10$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$,
the $(R/10)$-neighborhoods in $\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}'$ are the same,
so that variable is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}'$;
the same applies to the $1$-excellent property.
In particular, this tells us that $v\in\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}$ is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it is $1$-fair in $\mathscr{G}'$. If a path of length $2R/5$ emanates from $v$ and never intersects $X'$, then it must stay at least distance $R/10$ away from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$, so the path contains a $1$-excellent variable of $\mathscr{G}$ if and only if it contains a $1$-excellent variable of $\mathscr{G}'$. Otherwise, the path contains a variable from $X'$ which is $1$-excellent in both $\mathscr{G}$ and $\mathscr{G}'$ by property~\eqref{i:Xprime.is.excellent}. This proves that
	$A(1) \cap (\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U}) = A'(1) \cap (\mathscr{N}\setminus\mathscr{U})$.
\end{enumerate}
It follows from the above that $A(1)\subseteq A'(1)$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{e:compare.A.one.sets}
	A(1) \cap \phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out}) = \varnothing\,.
	\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Now note that $A'$ is by definition a subset of $\mathscr{G}'$, and on the event $\bm{K}_a$ it must not intersect $\mathscr{N}$. Thus, on the event $\bm{K}_a$, we have $A(1)\subseteq A'(1)\subseteq\mathscr{G}'\setminus\mathscr{N}$. We also noted that variables at distance at least $2R/5$ from $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in})$ belong in $A(1)$ if and only if they belong in $A'(1)$, so in particular $A(1)\cap\mathscr{G}''=A'(1)\cap\mathscr{G}''$. It follows that
	\[A'(1)\setminus A(1)
	\subseteq(\mathscr{G}'\setminus\mathscr{N})
		\Big\backslash \mathscr{G}''
	=\phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})\,.\]
We already saw in \eqref{e:matching.A.R.sets} (without appealing to $\bm{K}_a$) that $A(R)=A'(R)\subseteq\mathscr{G}''$. Combining with \eqref{e:compare.A.one.sets} finishes the proof of the lemma, since $A=A(R)\cup A(1)$ and $A'=A'(R)\cup A'(1)$.

\label{c:event.implies.desired.type} Suppose that $\bm{L}\equiv(L_0,L_\infty)$ is a feasible clause type in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:feasible.clause.type}. If $\mathscr{G}$ has girth greater than $8R$ and belongs to the event $\bm{G}_a \cap \bm{K}_a$, then the clause $a$ has total type $\bm{L}_a=\bm{L}$.

	\begin{equation}\label{e:Yout.intersect.A.nonempty}
	Y_\textup{out}(v) \cap A \ne\varnothing\quad\textup{for all }v\in V_1\,.
	\end{equation}
We separate this into two cases:
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\item If $Z_\textup{out}(y)\ne\varnothing$ for some $y\in Y_\textup{out}(v)$, then recall from Definition~\ref{d:tree.based.on.feasible.type} that we choose some $w\in Z_\textup{out}(y)$ and set $\bm{l}(w)=\bm{l}(y)$, which ensures $y\in A(R)\subseteq A$.

\item Now suppose that we do not have $Z_\textup{out}(y)\ne\varnothing$ for any $y\in Y_\textup{out}(v)$. Let $a'$ be the parent clause of $v$ in $\mathscr{T}(\bm{L})$, so $a'$ lies in $\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}$. Since the preprocessing algorithm on $\mathscr{H}$ removes $v$ but leaves $a'$ behind, it must be that at some stage of the algorithm a removal is triggered by a vertex $u$ which lies at depth exactly $R$ below $v$. (In particular, $u\in Y_\textup{out}(v)$ which proves that $Y_\textup{out}(v)$ must be nonempty.) We now argue that in fact there must be some $u\in Y_\textup{out}(v)\cap A$. If not, then $u$ triggers a removal \emph{after} the initial stage of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$ --- that is to say, at some stage, the $R$-neighborhood of $u$ must contain either one clause of degree $\le k-2$, or two clauses of degree $k-1$. Let $u'$ be the parent variable of $u$: by the assumption that $Z_\textup{out}(v)=\varnothing$, the $R$-neighborhood of $u'$ contains the $R$-neighborhood of $u$, which means that $u'$ should trigger a removal at the same stage of $\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'(A;\mathscr{G})$. 	\[Y_+\equiv\bigg\{ y\in Y_\textup{out} : Z_\textup{out}(y)\ne\varnothing\bigg\}\,.

	&=\bigg\{B_R(A;\mathscr{G}) \Big\backslash \phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})\bigg\}
	\cup\bigg\{
	\bigcup_{v\in \phi(\mathscr{N}_\textup{out})\cap A'}\Big(B_R(v;\mathscr{G}') \Big\backslash

	\cup K'\,,\end{align}

	\begin{equation}\label{e:G.with.K}

	=\bigg\{\Big(\mathscr{G}'' \cup \mathscr{N}\Big)

	\begin{equation}\label{e:coupling.G.Gprime.zero}
	\mathscr{G}(0) \Big\backslash (K\cup K_\varnothing)
	= \Big( \mathscr{G}'(0) \cup \phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)\Big)
		\Big\backslash K'\,.

	\begin{equation}\label{e:coupling.G.Gprime}

	= \Big( \mathscr{G}'(t) \cup \phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)\Big)
		\Big\backslash K'\,.
	\end{equation}

	\[A'(t)\equiv\textup{\textsf{Act}}\Big(\mathscr{G}'(t) \setminus K'\Big)
	\subseteq

If the $\gamma_i$ are both contained in $\mathscr{G}'(t)$, then $v$ must belong to $A'(t)$ as well. Otherwise, by the same argument as above, at least one of the paths must intersect $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)$. On the event $\bm{K}_a$, the clauses $a_i$ cannot be in $\mathscr{N}$, so they must both be $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)$. This contradicts the construction of $\phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)$ which was based on the processed graph $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{H}$.
\end{enumerate}
The above shows that $A(t)=A'(t)\subseteq\mathscr{G}'(t)\setminus\mathscr{N}$,
from which it follows that
	\[B_R\Big(A(t);\mathscr{G}(t)\Big)
	=B_R\Big(A'(t);\mathscr{G}'(t)\Big)\subseteq \mathscr{G}'(t)\,.\]
This implies that \eqref{e:coupling.G.Gprime} holds at the next stage $t+1$. It follows that
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}\Big\backslash (K\cup K_\varnothing)
	= \Big(\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}' \cup \phi(\mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y)\Big)
		\Big\backslash K'\,,
	\]
so that the clause $a$ in graph $\mathscr{G}$ has final type $L_\infty$.

nodes.statement: Let P=P_n,m for |m-nalpha| le n^1/2ln n, and GsimP. Then, for all n large enough, we have \[ PBig(GinbmG_a(bmL) \,Big|\, GinbmE_a(bmL)Big) ge frac78\,. \] for all ain[m] and all clause total types bmL that are feasible in the sense of Definition~. Throughout the proof, bmL is fixed and often suppressed from the notation. Let bmP_a be the event that bmE_a holds, and that G satisfies properties and of Definition~. Then bmE_asubseteqbmP_asubseteqbmK_a, and it is clear that PBig(GinbmP_a \,Big|\,Gin bmE_a Big) ge frac2425\,. This is simply because the markings bml are chosen uniformly at random from a very large set (see ), so if we consider all the variables in Gsetminusphi(T(bmL)) within distance 2R of phi(T(bmL)), it holds with probability at least 9/10 that all their markings are distinct from one another and from the markings on phi(T(bmL)). Next we let bmF_a be the event that bmE_a holds, and that G satisfies property of Definition~. For xinphi(X), let U(x) denote the subtree of U descended from x. Let bmF_a(x) be the event that bmE_a holds, and that every uinU(x) is 1-fair (with respect to G). Then \[ bmF_a = bigcap_xinphi(X) bmF_a(x)\,. \] For xinphi(X), let U_+(x) denote the subtree of UcupN induced by descendants of x that lie within distance 3R/10 of x, so that U(x)subseteqU_+(x)subseteqUcupN. Since bmF_asubseteqbmE_a where bmE_a imposes that B_4R(a;G) is a tree, for any variable in B_(4-1/10)R(a;G) we can determine whether it is 1-fair based on its (R/10)-neighborhood only. It follows that the event bmF_a(x) can be determined from \[ B_R/10(x;G) cup U_+(x)\,. \] An important point is that the above does not see any part of phi(T(bmL)) at distance more than R/10 from x, because phi(T(bmL)) cap bigg\ B_R/10(x;G) cup U_+(x)bigg\ =phi(T(bmL)) cap B_R/10(x;G)\,. Indeed, when we condition on bmE_a, we in fact reveal information about the neighborhood of x in G beyond depth R/10 (simply because phi(T(bmL)) contains vertices at distance more than R/10 from x), but allows us to disregard the additional information. It follows from the 1-excellence condition that PBig(GinbmF_a(x)\,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) ge 1- frac1exp(k^3 R) + o_n(1)\,, where the o_n(1) comes from the discrepancy between the Galton--Watson law and the breadth-first exploration in G. Since all variables in T_textupin must be 1-fair, it follows from property in Definition~ that T_textupin has cardinality at most exp(O(k^2 R)). Therefore we conclude PBig(GinbmF_a\,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) ge frac2425 by taking a union bound of over xinphi(X). Finally, let bmD_a be the event that bmE_a holds, and that G satisfies property of Definition~. For yinphi(Y), let X'(y) denote the subset of variables in X' that lie at depth R/10 below y. Let X''(y) denote the variables in X'(y) that fail to be 1-excellent in G. Again, on the event bmE_a which imposes that B_4R(a;G) is acyclic, for any variable in B_(4-1/10)R(a;G) we can determine whether it is 1-excellent based on its (R/10)-neighborhood only. Consequently, by similar considerations as for , we have nonumber E Big( X'(y)\,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) &= o_n(1) + int bigg|bigg\hspace-3ptcxinT : textupd(v_textuptextscrt,x)=R/10 \\ textupand x is not 1-excellent hspace-3pt bigg\bigg| \,dtextupPGW(T)\\ &= o_n(1) + int 1 bigg\hspace-3ptc textupthe root v_textuptextscrt of T is\\ textupnot 1-excellent hspace-3pt bigg\ Z_R/10(T) \,dtextupPGW(T)\,, where Z_R/10(T) denotes the number of variables at depth R/10 in T, and the last equality is by the unimodularity property . Now recall from Corollary~ that \[textupPGWBig(textupv_textuptextscrt not 1-excellentBig) lefrac1 exp( 2^kdelta_*/4R) \,. \] On the other hand, by a similar argument as in the proof of Lemma~, we can bound \[int Big(Z_R/10(T)Big)^2 \,dtextupPGW(T) le exp(O(kR))\,. \] Combining these and applying Cauchy--Schwarz in gives \[E Big( X'(y)\,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) le frac exp(O(kR)) exp( 2^kdelta_*/4R) \,. \] Since we noted above that T_textupin has cardinality at most exp(O(k^2 R)), it follows by Markov's inequality and a union bound over yinphi(Y) that PBig((bmD_a)^c \,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) lesum_yinphi(Y)EBig( X'(y)\, \,Big|\, GinbmE_aBig) le frac125\,. The lemma follows by combining , , and , since bmG_a= bmP_a cap bmF_a cap bmD_a.

Let $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)\sim\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{n,m}$. Let $\bm{L}$ be any feasible type, in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:feasible.clause.type}. For any fixed $\bm{L}$ we consider the events $\bm{E}_a(\bm{L})$, $\bm{G}_a(\bm{L})$, $\bm{F}_a(\bm{L})$ as in Definition~\ref{d:pos.frac.events}. Let
	\[
	J(\bm{L})\equiv
	\sum_{a\in F} J_a(\bm{L})
	\equiv
	\sum_{a\in F}\mathbf{1}\Big\{ \bm{E}_a(\bm{L})
		\cap \bm{G}_a(\bm{L}) \cap \bm{K}_a(\bm{L})\Big\}\,.
	\]
It follows by combining Lemmas~\ref{l:lbd.Ea}--\ref{l:prob.Ka.given.Ea} that for all feasible $\bm{L}$ we have
	\[
	\mathbb{E} \bm{J}(\bm{L})
	\ge \frac{3nc_0(k,R)}{4}\,.
	\]
We will argue that each $\bm{J}(\bm{L})$ is sufficiently concentrated around its mean, such that 
	\begin{equation}\label{e:pos.frac.sufficient}
	\mathbb{P}\bigg( J(\bm{L}) \ge \frac{n c_0(k,R)}{2}\bigg) = o_n(1)\,.
	\end{equation}
Note that \eqref{e:pos.frac.sufficient} implies the result: as discussed in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:lbd.Ea}, the total number of feasible types $\bm{L}$ is upper bounded by some $C_0(k,R)$, so \eqref{e:pos.frac.sufficient}
(together with the fact that $\mathscr{G}$ has girth greater than $8R$ with probability at least $c_0(k,R)$) implies
	\[\mathbb{P}\bigg( J(\bm{L}) \ge \frac{n c_0(k,R)}{2}
		\textup{ for all feasible }\bm{L}
		\,\bigg|\, \textup{girth}(\mathscr{G})>8R
		\bigg) = o_n(1)\,.
	\]
In light of Corollary~\ref{c:event.implies.desired.type}, this directly implies the result. It therefore remains only to prove the concentration result \eqref{e:pos.frac.sufficient}. Let $\mathscr{T}(\bm{L})$ be the tree based on $\bm{L}$ that is given by Definition~\ref{d:tree.based.on.feasible.type}, and recall from Definition~\ref{d:pos.frac.events} that $\bm{E}_a(\bm{L})$ is the event that there is a certain embedding $\phi_a:\mathscr{T}(\bm{L})\hookrightarrow\mathscr{G}$ mapping $a_\star\mapsto a$, together with some local girth condition. The events $\bm{E}_a(\bm{L})$ and $\bm{G}_a(\bm{L})$ are clearly local --- they do not depend on more than $B_{4R}(a;\mathscr{G})$. By contrast, the event $\bm{K}_a(\bm{L})$ concerns preprocessing on the graph
	\[\mathscr{G}'(a)
	\equiv\mathscr{G}\Big\backslash \phi_a\Big( \mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y\Big)\,,\]
which (\textit{a~priori}) cannot be locally determined. This can be addressed with a similar argument as for Proposition~\ref{p:small.fraction.removed.in.processing}: as we saw in that proof, preprocessing is in fact fairly localized with high probability. In particular, we can define
	\[
	\mathscr{G}^\circ(a)
	\equiv \Big\{ B_{(\ln n)/2^{k\delta_*/6}}
		(a;\mathscr{G})\Big\}
	\Big\backslash \phi_a\Big( \mathscr{T}_\textup{in}\setminus Y\Big)
	\subseteq
	\mathscr{G}'(a)\,.
	\]
Let $A^\circ(a)$ be the variables $u\in\mathscr{G}^\circ(a)$ with
$B_R(u;\mathscr{G}'(a))\subseteq\mathscr{G}^\circ(a)$, that fail to proper or $1$-good with respect to $\mathscr{G}^\circ(a)$, and let
(cf. \eqref{e:equiv.defn.Ka})
	\[
	\overline{\bm{K}}_a(\bm{L})
	=\bm{E}_a(\bm{L})\cap \bigg\{\phi_a(Y)
	\textup{ does not intersect }
	B_R\bigg( 
	\textup{\textsf{BSP}}'\Big( A^\circ(a) ;\mathscr{G}^\circ(a)\Big)
	; \mathscr{G}^\circ(a)\bigg)
	\bigg\}
	\]
Let $\bar{J}(\bm{L})$ be defined as $J(\bm{L})$, but with $\overline{\bm{K}}_a(\bm{L})$ in place of $\bm{K}_a(\bm{L})$. It follows from the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:small.fraction.removed.in.processing} that $J(\bm{L})$ and $\bar{J}(\bm{L})$ agree with high probability, and so
	\[\mathbb{E}\bar{J}(\bm{L})
	=\mathbb{E} J (\bm{L}) - o(n)
	\ge \frac{3n c_0(k,R)}{4} - o(n)\,.
	\]
For any pair of distinct clauses $a\ne b$, their $(\ln n)/2^{k\delta_*/6}$-neighborhoods do not intersect with high probability, and so are roughly independent. It follows that $\bar{J}(\bm{L})$ has variance $o(n^2)$, and so by Chebychev's inequality
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\bigg(\bar{J}(\bm{L}) < \frac{n c_0(k,R)}{2}\bigg)
	\le \mathbb{P}\bigg( \Big |\bar{J}(\bm{L})-\mathbb{E}\bar{J}(\bm{L})\Big| \ge 
		 \frac{n c_0(k,R)}{5}\bigg)
	\le o_n(1)\,.
	\]
Since $\mathbb{P}(J(\bm{L})\ne\bar{J}(\bm{L}))=o_n(1)$, this proves \eqref{e:pos.frac.sufficient}, and the result follows as argued above.

Fix any $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ instance $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$ that can arise under the measure $\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}^{n,\alpha}$. In the processed graph $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$, choose any two edges $e_i=(a_iu_i)$ ($i=1,2$) having the same total type (Definition~\ref{d:cpd.type}). Let $\textup{\textsf{sw}}$ denote the switching operation in which we cut the edges $e_i$, and reconnect the resulting half-edges as $f_1=(a_1u_2)$ and $f_2=(a_2u_1)$. Then the switching and processing operations commute:
	\[\textup{\textsf{pr}}\Big(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}\Big)
	=\textup{\textsf{sw}}\Big(\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}\Big)\,.\]
In particular, this implies that $f_i$ survive in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$.

Membership of a variable in A_-1 (resp.\ S_-1) is a property of its R-neighborhood relative to G (resp.\ textupswG). If B_R(v;G) is the same as B_R(v;textupswG), then v belongs either to both sets A_-1 and S_-1, or to neither. If B_R(v;G) is not the same as B_R(v;textupswG), then it must be that B_R(v;G) contains at least one of the e_i, and so B_R(v;textupswG) contains at least one of the f_i. In both cases C will contain an improper variable that will cause one of the e_i to be removed during processing on G. Altogether this proves that A_-1=S_-1, as claimed.

\label{l:init.set.agree.after.switch}
 In the setting of Proposition~\ref{p:switch.process.commutation},
the initial set (of variables that are improper or not $1$-good)
in $\mathscr{G}$ is the same as in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}$.

\begin{proof} Denote the initial set (of variables that are improper or not $1$-good) as $A_{-1}$ in $\mathscr{G}$, and $S_{-1}$ in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}$. Membership of a variable in $A_{-1}$ (resp.\ $S_{-1}$) is a property of its $R$-neighborhood relative to $\mathscr{G}$ (resp.\ $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}$). If $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ is the same as $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$, then $v$ belongs either to both sets $A_{-1}$ and $S_{-1}$, or to neither. 

If $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ is not the same as $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$, then it must be that $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ contains at least one of the $e_i$, and so $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ contains at least one of the $f_i$. In this situation, we have two observations:
\begin{enumerate}[(I)] 
\item We must have $v\notin A_{-1}$ by the assumption that the $e_i$ survive in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$ --- in particular, this implies that $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ must be proper (acyclic, with no repeated $\bm{l}$ markings). It follows that $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$ must contain exactly one of the $e_i$ while being disjoint from the other --- otherwise, it would contain two variables with the same marking $\bm{l}$, making $v$ improper.
\item Similarly, $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ must contain exactly one of the $f_i$ while being disjoint from the other --- otherwise, there is a path $\gamma_\star\subseteq\mathscr{G}\cap(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ of length at most $2R-1$
that joins the $f_i$ in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}$. In the graph $\mathscr{G}$, either $\gamma_\star$ forms a cycle with one of the $e_i$, or it joins $e_1$ to $e_2$. In both cases $\gamma_\star$ will contain an improper variable that will cause one of the $e_i$ to be removed during processing on $\mathscr{G}$.
\end{enumerate}
Since we only switch two edges $e_i=(a_iu_i)$ of the same type, if $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ is also acyclic then it must be isomorphic to $B_R(v;\mathscr{G})$, so in this case $v\notin S_{-1}$. The last possibility is that $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ contains a cycle $C$. By observation (II), we can suppose without loss that $B_R(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$ contains $f_1$ but not $f_2$. If $f_1$ is disjoint from $C$, then $C$ will also appear in
$B_R(u_i;\mathscr{G})$ for one of the $u_i$. If $f_1$ lies on $C$, then $C\setminus f_1$ is a path in $\mathscr{G}$ joining $e_1$ to $e_2$. In both cases $C$ will contain an improper variable that will cause one of the $e_i$ to be removed during processing on $\mathscr{G}$. Altogether this proves that $A_{-1}=S_{-1}$, as claimed.
\end{proof}

Denote the initial set (of variables that are improper or not $1$-good) as $A_{-1}$ in $\mathscr{G}$, and $S_{-1}$ in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}$. We showed in Lemma~\ref{l:init.set.agree.after.switch} that $A_{-1}=S_{-1}$. Note also that $B_R(A_{-1};\mathscr{G})$ cannot include either of the $e_i$, again by the assumption that the $e_i$ survive in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$. It follows that $B_R(A_{-1};\mathscr{G})=B_R(A_{-1};\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})$, and consequently
	\begin{equation}\label{e:init.step.commutes}
	\textup{\textsf{pr}}_0\Big(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}\Big)
	=\Big(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}\Big) \Big\backslash
		B_R\Big(A_{-1};\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}\Big)
	=\textup{\textsf{sw}} \bigg( \mathscr{G} \Big\backslash
		B_R\Big(A_{-1};\mathscr{G}\Big)\bigg)
	= \textup{\textsf{sw}}\Big(\textup{\textsf{pr}}_0\mathscr{G}\Big)\,,
	\end{equation}
that is to say, switching commutes with the initial preprocessing step.
For $t\ge0$ let us abbreviate
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	A_t &\equiv \textup{\textsf{Act}}(\textup{\textsf{pr}}_t\mathscr{G})\,,\\
	S_t &\equiv \textup{\textsf{Act}}(\textup{\textsf{pr}}_t\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})\,.
	\end{align*}}
If $A_\ell=S_\ell$ for all $0\le \ell<t$, then the same logic that led to \eqref{e:init.step.commutes} gives
	\begin{equation}\label{e:commute.up.to.t}
	\textup{\textsf{pr}}_t\Big(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G}\Big)
	=\textup{\textsf{sw}}\Big(\textup{\textsf{pr}}_t\mathscr{G}\Big)\,.\end{equation}
Thus, let $t$ be the first time that $A_t\ne S_t$; we will argue that this leads to a contradiction. Abbreviate $\mathscr{H}\equiv\textup{\textsf{pr}}_t\mathscr{G}$. \smallskip

\noindent\textbf{Case 1. $A_t\setminus S_t\ne\varnothing$.} 
Recall from the definition \eqref{e:bspprime.activated.set} that
membership of a variable in $A_t$ or $S_t$ is a property of its $(3R/10)$-neighborhood. Consequently, if there is any variable $v\in A_t\setminus S_t$, then $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H})$ must contain at least one of the $e_i$. But the very next step of processing on $\mathscr{G}$ will remove $B_R(v;\mathscr{H})$, contradicting the assumption that both edges $e_i$ survive in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$. This proves that $A_t\subseteq S_t$.\smallskip

\noindent\textbf{Case 2. $S_t\setminus A_t\ne\varnothing$.}
Suppose $v\in S_t\setminus A_t$. From the above definitions and the relation \eqref{e:commute.up.to.t}, we have $A_t=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\mathscr{H})$ and $S_t=\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$. Thus, since $v\in S_t$, it must be that $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$ contains at least one clause of degree $\le k-2$, or two clauses of degree $k-1$. On the other hand, since $v\notin A_t$, the same statement must not hold for $B_{3R/10}(v;\mathscr{H})$. It follows that $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$ must contain at least one of the switched edges $f_i$. In fact, by observation~(II) in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:init.set.agree.after.switch}, it must contain exactly one of the $f_i$, say $f_1$.

\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item If $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$ contains any clause $b_\star$ of degree $\le k-2$, then the path joining $v$ to $b_\star$ must pass through at least one of the $f_i$, so the distance between $b_\star$ and $\set{f_1,f_2}$ in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H}$ is less than $3R/10$. It follows that the distance between $b_\star$ and $\set{e_1,e_2}$ in $\mathscr{H}$ is also less than $3R/10$, which again yields a contradiction since it means that at least one of the $e_i$ will be deleted in the next preprocessing step.

\item It remains to consider the case that $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$ contains two clauses $b_1\ne b_2$, each of degree $k-1$. If $\pi_i$ is the path joining $v$ to $b_i$ in $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$, then at least one of the $\pi_i$, say $\pi_1$, must pass through a switched edge. It follows that the distance between $b_1$ and $\set{f_1,f_2}$ in $\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H}$ is less than $3R/10$; and so the distance between $b_1$ and $\set{e_1,e_2}$ in $\mathscr{H}$ is also less than $3R/10$. We now consider the path $\gamma$ in $B_{3R/10}(v;\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{H})$ that joins $b_1$ to $b_2$, and distinguish two cases:

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $\gamma$ does not pass through either $f_i$, then it is also a path in $\mathscr{H}$. It has length at most $6R/10$ and joins $b_1$ to $b_2$, and we noted above that the distance between $b_1$ and $\set{e_1,e_2}$ in $\mathscr{H}$ is less than $3R/10$. It follows that the next preprocessing step in $\mathscr{G}$ will remove the $R$-neighborhood of some variable on $\gamma$, and thereby also remove one of the $e_i$. This gives a contradiction.


\item Now consider the case that $\gamma$ passes through $f_1$. This situation is shown in Figure~\ref{f:switch.two.edges.in.path}. We label $f_1=(xz)$ and $f_2=(wy)$ where $\set{x,w}$ is the same as either $\set{a_1,a_2}$ or $\set{u_1,u_2}$. Then $e_1=(xy)$ and $e_2=(wz)$.

	\[
	\textup{len}(\rho_1) + \textup{len}(\rho_2) + \frac12
	= \textup{len}(\gamma) \le \frac{6R}{10}
	\]
where we use $\textup{len}$ to denote path length. Recall from Remark~\ref{r:distance} that an edge $e=(av)$ has length $1/2$, so a path joining two neighboring variables has length one. On the left-hand side above, the $1/2$ term accounts for the length of the edge $f_1=(x z)$. In the graph $\mathscr{H}$, the path $\rho_1$ joins $b_1$ to $x$ without passing through $y$. Since we assume that $e_1=(xy)$ survives in $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$, any further processing on $\mathscr{G}$ cannot remove $b_1$ without leaving behind a clause on $\rho_1$ of degree less than $k$ that lies even closer to $x$. It follows that the final graph $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$ contains a path $\bar{\rho}_1\subseteq\rho_1$ joining $x$ to a clause $\bar{b}_1$ of degree less than $k$. Likewise, $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$ must contain a path $\bar{\rho}_2\subseteq\rho_2$ joining $z$ to a clause $\bar{b}_2$ of degree less than $k$. Now note that $x$ and $z$ lie on opposite sides of the bipartite graph (one is a clause while the other is a variable). On the other hand, by the assumption that the $e_i$ have the same total type, there must be an isomorphism
	\[
	\phi : B_R\Big(x;\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}\Big) \to B_R\Big(w;\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}\Big),\quad
	\phi(x)=w,\quad\phi(y)=z\,.
	\]
It follows that $B_R(w;\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G})$ must contain a path $\phi(\bar{\rho}_1)$ that joins $w$ to a clause $\phi(\bar{b}_1)$ of degree less than $k$. Then in the graph $\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}$ we have
	\[
	d\Big(\bar{b}_2,\phi(\bar{\rho}_1);\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G}\Big)
	= \textup{len}(\phi(\bar{\rho}_1)) + \textup{len}(\bar{\rho_2}) + \frac12
	\le \textup{len}(\rho_1) + \textup{len}(\rho_2) + \frac12 \le \frac{6R}{10}\,.
	\]
This contradicts the fact that, by definition, $\textup{\textsf{Act}}(\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G})$ must be empty.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}\smallskip

\noindent \textbf{Conclusion.}
The above argument shows that in fact $A_t=S_t$ for all $t$, so that the same logic leading to \eqref{e:init.step.commutes} and \eqref{e:commute.up.to.t} gives
the desired conclusion, that $\textup{\textsf{pr}}(\textup{\textsf{sw}}\mathscr{G})=\textup{\textsf{sw}}(\textup{\textsf{pr}}\mathscr{G})$.

\label{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit}
In the setting of Corollaries~\ref{c:cohere.weights}~and~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights}, suppose all the edges in $U$ are stable and nice. Then, for every clause $a$ of $U$, the canonical messages
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e$ (for $e\in\delta a$)
satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{l:clause.bp.weights},
with $\delta=1/11$ in \eqref{e:bds.on.red.yellow}
and $\epsilon_e,\dot{\epsilon}_e \le O(1/k^r)$ in \eqref{e:assumed.bp.error.eps}. Consequently,
Lemma~\ref{l:clause.bp.weights} guarantees, for each $a$ in $U$, the existence of edge weights
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Gamma_a=(\gamma_e:e\in\delta a)$ 
satisfying
(cf.\ \eqref{e:resulting.gamma.error.bound}) $|\gamma_e(\sigma)-1|\le 1/k^{r/2}$ for all $\sigma$, and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_e({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Gamma_a)$ for all $e\in\delta a$. As a consequence, the weighted Gibbs measure \eqref{e:gamma.weighted.gibbs} has all edge marginals and messages agreeing with the canonical ones ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi,{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$.
Redistributing the weights as in 
\eqref{e:redistribute.weights}
(and as in 
Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights})
produces a system
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda$ of variable weights such that the ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda$-weighted Gibbs measure again has edge marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. (However, since the weights were shifted from clauses to variables, the \textsc{bp} messages will be given by ${}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$
from \eqref{e:redistributed.bp.messages}
rather than by ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q},{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}$). 

\begin{proof}
We need only to check that the conditions of Lemma~\ref{l:clause.bp.weights} are satisfied.
Indeed, for each edge $e\in U$,
if we take ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e$ and 
use \eqref{e:reweighted.messages.single}
to define 
its reweighted version
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}Q_e$,
then ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}Q_e$ will satisfy the error bound
\eqref{e:bds.on.red.yellow} with $\delta=1/11$,
because the edges in $U$ are assumed to be nice
(Definition~\ref{d:nice}).
Moreover, we will have the error bounds
\eqref{e:assumed.bp.error.eps}
with $\epsilon_e,\dot{\epsilon}_e \le O(1/k^r)$
because the edges in $U$ are assumed to be stable
(Definition~\ref{d:stable}).
The claimed result then follows directly from
Lemma~\ref{l:clause.bp.weights}. 
\end{proof}

nodes.name: sampling from the planted measure
nodes.statement: Recall from Proposition~ that P_D coincides with the uniform measure over textupCM(D), and can be sampled as a configuration model, as discussed in Remark~. It is well known that one can also sample from Q_D by a configuration-model-type procedure, as we now describe. As in Remark~, we fix a set of variables V and a set of clauses F, equipped with incident half-edges delta V and delta F, all labelled with types according to D. Then a graph G corresponds to a matching M of delta V to delta F that respects the edge types. The number of all such matchings is given by . Let bmsigma be any coloring of delta Vsqcupdelta F that gives a valid coloring of delta x for every xin Vsqcup F. We say that a valid coloring bmsigma is bemphjudicious, abbreviated bmsigmainJ, if the empirical measure of bmsigma:delta VtosetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb agrees with the canonical marginal _starhspace-1ptpi, and the empirical measure of bmsigma:delta FtosetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb agrees with _starhspace-1ptomega (up to rounding, cf.\ Definition~). We write Msimbmsigma if the matching M also respects the edge colors specified by bmsigma. Then a pair (G,smashvecsigma) is equivalent to a pair (M,bmsigma) such that Msimbmsigma. Thus we can regard Q_D as the measure over pairs (M,bmsigma) given by \[ Q_D(M,bmsigma) =fracInd bmsigmainJ, Msimbmsigma Z\,, \] where Z is the normalizing constant. The marginal probability of bmsigma under Q_D is given by \[ Q_D(bmsigma) =fracIndbmsigmainJ Zcdot bigg|Big\ M :Msimbmsigma Big\bigg| =fracIndbmsigmainJZ cdot prod_bmt,sigma (n_bmt cdot _starhspace-1ptpi_bmt(sigma))!\,, \] which we emphasize is constant over all judicious bmsigma. This implies \[Q_D(bmsigma) = fracIndbmsigmainJ |J|\,, \] i.e., the marginal law of bmsigma under Q_D is simply uniform over J. It further implies that for any bmsigmainJ, \[ Q_D(M\,|\,bmsigma) = fracIndMsimbmsigma Z/|J| = fracIndMsimbmsigma | setM : M simbmsigma | \,, \] i.e., under Q_D, the law of M conditional on bmsigma is uniform among the matchings compatible with bmsigma. In conclusion, to generate a sample from Q_D, we can first sample a uniformly random coloring bmsigmainJ, then sample a uniformly matching M that satisfies Msimbmsigma.

\label{r:sample.planted.msr}
Recall from Proposition~\ref{p:unif}
that $\mathbb{P}_\mathcal{D}$ coincides with the uniform measure over
$\textup{\textbf{\textsf{CM}}}(\mathcal{D})$, and can be sampled as a configuration model, as discussed in Remark~\ref{r:processed.graph.types.CM}.
It is well known that one can also sample from $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$ by a configuration-model-type procedure, as we now describe.
As in Remark~\ref{r:processed.graph.types.CM},
we fix a set of variables $V$ and a set of clauses $F$, equipped with incident half-edges $\delta V$ and $\delta F$, all labelled with types according to $\mathcal{D}$. Then a graph $\mathscr{G}$ corresponds to a matching $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\delta V$ to $\delta F$ that respects the edge types. The number of all such matchings is given by \eqref{e:size.CM.D}. Let $\bm{\sigma}$ be any coloring of $\delta V\sqcup\delta F$ that gives a valid coloring of $\delta x$ for every $x\in V\sqcup F$. We say that a valid coloring $\bm{\sigma}$ is \bemph{judicious},
abbreviated $\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}$, 
if the empirical measure of $\bm{\sigma}:\delta V\to\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$ agrees with the canonical marginal ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, and the empirical measure of $\bm{\sigma}:\delta F\to\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}$ agrees with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$
(up to rounding, cf.\ Definition~\ref{d:judicious}). We write $\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}$ if the matching $\mathfrak{M}$ also respects the edge colors specified by $\bm{\sigma}$. Then a pair $(\mathscr{G},\smash{\vec{\sigma}})$
is equivalent to a pair $(\mathfrak{M},\bm{\sigma})$
such that $\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}$. Thus we can regard $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$ as the measure over pairs
$(\mathfrak{M},\bm{\sigma})$ given by
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{M},\bm{\sigma})
	=\frac{\Ind{
	\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J},
	 \mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma} }}
		{\mathcal{Z}}\,,
	\]
where $\mathcal{Z}$ is the normalizing constant. 
The marginal probability of $\bm{\sigma}$
under $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$ is given by
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}(\bm{\sigma})
	=\frac{\Ind{\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}}}
	{\mathcal{Z}}\cdot
	\bigg|\Big\{ \mathfrak{M}
	:\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}
		\Big\}\bigg|
	=\frac{\Ind{\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}}}{\mathcal{Z}}
	\cdot
	\prod_{\bm{t},\sigma}
	(n_{\bm{t}} \cdot {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{\bm{t}}(\sigma))!\,,
	\]
which we emphasize is constant over all judicious
$\bm{\sigma}$. This implies
	\[\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}(\bm{\sigma})
	= \frac{\Ind{\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}}}
		{|\mathcal{J}|}\,,
	\]
i.e., the marginal law of $\bm{\sigma}$ under $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$ is simply uniform over $\mathcal{J}$. It further implies that for any $\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}$,
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{M}\,|\,\bm{\sigma})
	= \frac{\Ind{\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}}}
		{\mathcal{Z}/|\mathcal{J}|}
	= \frac{\Ind{\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}}}
	{ | \set{\mathfrak{M}
		: \mathfrak{M} \sim\bm{\sigma} } | }\,,
	\]
i.e., under $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$, the law of $\mathfrak{M}$
conditional on $\bm{\sigma}$ is uniform among the matchings compatible with $\bm{\sigma}$. In conclusion, to generate a sample from $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$, 
we can first sample a uniformly random coloring $\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}$, then sample a uniformly matching $\mathfrak{M}$ that satisfies $\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}$.

Given a coloring $\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}$,
we 
associate the variable empirical measure
$\dot{\nu}$ as in \eqref{e:variable.color.cond.on.type},
and the clause empirical measure
$\hat{\nu}$ as in \eqref{e:clause.color.cond.on.type}.
Abbreviate $\nu\equiv(\dot{\nu},\hat{\nu})\equiv\nu(\bm{\sigma})$. Then, for any $
\nu$ that is consistent with ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega$, we have
	\[
	\bigg|\Big\{\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}
		: \nu(\bm{\sigma}) \Big\}\bigg|
	=\Bigg\{ \prod_{\bm{T}}\binom{n_{\bm{T}}}{n_{\bm{T}}
		\dot{\nu}_{\bm{T}}}\Bigg\}
	\Bigg\{ \prod_{\bm{L}}
		\binom{m_{\bm{L}}}{m_{\bm{L}} \hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}}
	\Bigg\}\,.
	\]
By comparing with \eqref{e:config.model.first.moment.given.omega} and \eqref{e:nu.opt}, we see that if $\bm{\sigma}$ is sampled uniformly at random from $\mathcal{J}$, then its empirical measure $\nu(\bm{\sigma})$ is very close to $\nu^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega]$ with high probability: more precisely, as long as
$\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero in the sense of \eqref{e:pos.frac}
(as guaranteed by Proposition~\ref{p:posfrac} with high probability), then
	\[\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}
	\bigg(\Big\|\nu- \nu^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega]
		\Big\|_\infty
		\ge \frac{\ln n}{n^{1/2}}\bigg)
	\le \exp\bigg\{ - C(k,R) (\ln n)^2\bigg\}\,.\]
We recall that
$\nu^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega]
=(\dot{\nu}^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega],\hat{\nu}^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega])$ 
where $\dot{\nu}=\dot{\nu}^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega]$
is given by Lemma~\ref{l:nu.star.as.optimizer.for.starpi},

is given by a reweighted measure:
if $a$ denotes a clause of type $\bm{L}$, then
	\[

	=
	\hat{\varphi}_a(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a})
	\prod_{e\in\delta a}
	\bigg\{
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma_e)\gamma_e(\sigma_e)
	\bigg\}
	\]
where the weights $\gamma_e$
are given by Corollary~\ref{c:cohere.weights},
since all clauses in the processed graph must be coherent. If all the edges in the clause are nice,
then the weights $\gamma_e$ are estimated by
Lemma~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit}.
We will use this observation in the proofs that follow.

\label{r:defective.clauses} Recall from Definition~\ref{d:j.defective} that if a variable is non-defective, then it has at most one defective variable in its depth-one neighborhood. The clauses $a\in F$ therefore can be divided into three categories:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The clause $a$ neighbors only defective variables, in which case we say that $a$ is a \bemph{defective clause}.
\item The clause $a$ has only one defective variable among its neighbors.
\item The clause $a$ has no defective variables among its neighbors, in which case we say that $a$ is a \bemph{strongly non-defective clause}.
(The strongly non-defective property will be used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:noNonDiverse}.)
\end{enumerate}
In both cases (ii) and (iii) we say that $a$ is a \bemph{non-defective clause}. If $v$ is a non-defective variable, then $\partial v$ contains only non-defective clauses; moreover, at most one clause in $\partial v$ can fail to be strongly non-defective. 
We say that $v$ is \bemph{strongly non-defective} if every clause in $\partial v$ is strongly non-defective.
We say that an edge $e$ is \bemph{strongly non-defective} if and only if $e\in\delta v$ for a strongly non-defective variable $v$. Lastly, we say that an edge $e$ is \bemph{internal} to a defect if it is incident to some internal clause of the defect.

nodes.statement: Given a valid coloring smashvecsigma of G=(V,F,E), we define a subgraph F subseteqG as follows. Let V_F be the variables in V that are incident to only SPINgreen edges under smashvecsigma. Let F_F be the clauses in F that are incident to only SPINgreen or SPINyellow edges under smashvecsigma. Note that, by the rules of the coloring model, each ain F_F must be incident to at least two variables u,vin V_F. Let E_F be the edges between V_F and F_F. We shall call F equiv(V_F, F_F,E_F) the bemphfree subgraph of G induced by smashvecsigma.

\label{l:free.subgraph.no.bicycle}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{p:ext} we have
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}\bigg(
	\Big\{
	(\mathscr{G},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}) :
	\textup{any connected component of
	$\mathfrak{F}$
	contains a bicycle}
	\Big\}
	\bigg)
	= o_n(1)\,,
	\]
with high probability over $\mathcal{D}$.

\begin{proof}
We assume throughout the proof that $\mathcal{D}$ is fixed, such that its unordered version $\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero in the sense of
\eqref{e:pos.frac}
(as guaranteed by
Proposition~\ref{p:posfrac} with high probability). Then, as in Remark~\ref{r:sample.planted.msr},
 we first sample a uniformly random coloring
$\bm{\sigma}\in\mathcal{J}$, followed by a uniformly random matching $\mathfrak{M}$
such that $\mathfrak{M}\sim\bm{\sigma}$.
The resulting pair $(\mathfrak{M},\bm{\sigma})$
is equivalent to a sample
$(\mathscr{G},\smash{\vec{\sigma}})\sim\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$. Let $\nu\equiv(\dot{\nu},\hat{\nu})$ be the empirical measure of $\smash{\vec{\sigma}}$. We can assume that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:appx.nu.by.nustar}
	\Big\|\nu- \nu^\textup{op}[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\omega]
		\Big\|_\infty
		\le \frac{\ln n}{n^{1/2}}\,,
	\end{equation}
since this event holds with high probability under $\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}$ by Remark~\ref{r:planted.measure.empir.msr}.
Moreover, given $\bm{\sigma}$, the random matching $\mathfrak{M}$ can be explored in breadth-first manner, as we analyze next.

Fix an initial variable $v\in V$ of type $\bm{T}$, and suppose under $\bm{\sigma}$ that it is incident to only $\SPIN{green}$ edges. 
Let $\mathfrak{F}(v)$ be the connected component of $\mathfrak{F}$ containing $v$.
Under the randomness of the matching $\mathfrak{M}$, the expected number of variables $w\in\mathfrak{F}(v)$
at unit distance from $v$ is
	\begin{equation}\label{e:free.branching}
	f(\bm{T}) \equiv 
	\sum_{e\in\delta v}
	\sum_{\bm{L}}
	\pi(\bm{L} \,|\, \bm{t}_e)
	\underbrace{
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a}
		\in \set{\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{y}}^{\delta a}}
	\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}
		(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a} \,|\, \sigma_e=\SSPIN{g})
	\sum_{e'\in\delta a\setminus e}
		\Ind{\sigma_{e'}=\SSPIN{g}}
		}_{\textup{denote this $g(\bm{t},\bm{L})$}}\,.
	\end{equation}
In the above $\pi(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t})$ is the chance that an edge $e\in\delta v$ of type $\bm{t}$ is matched with an edge $e'\in\delta a$ such that $\bm{L}_a=\bm{L}$. 
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:vfe} that the type $\bm{t}$ includes the position $j(\bm{t})$ that the edge takes in the clause, so
	\begin{equation}\label{e:conditional.law.of.clause.type}
	\pi(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t})
	= \hat{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L})
	\Bigg/\Bigg(
	\sum_{\bm{L}'}
	\Ind{(\bm{L}')_{j(\bm{t})} = \bm{t}}
	\hat{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}')
	\Bigg)\,.
	\end{equation}
Consider the quantity $g(\bm{t},\bm{L})$ defined by \eqref{e:free.branching}: it is given explicitly by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:nice.free.branching}
	g(\bm{t},\bm{L})
	= 
	\frac{\displaystyle
	\sum_{e'\in\delta a \setminus e}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\SSPIN{g})\gamma_{e'}(\SSPIN{g})
	\prod_{e'' \in \delta a \setminus
		\set{e,e'}}
		\bigg(
		\sum_{\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g}}}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\sigma)\gamma_{e''}(\sigma)
	\bigg)}{\displaystyle
	\prod_{e'' \in \delta a \setminus e}
	\bigg(
	\sum_{\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\sigma)\gamma_{e''}(\sigma)
	\bigg)
	-\prod_{e'' \in \delta a \setminus e}
	\bigg(
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e''}(\SSPIN{y})\gamma_{e''}(\SSPIN{y})
	\bigg)
	}
	\Bigg[ 1 + O\bigg( \frac{\ln n}{n^{1/2}}\bigg)
	\Bigg]\,,
	\end{equation}
where the error estimate comes from \eqref{e:appx.nu.by.nustar}.
If $\bm{L}$ is a nice clause type, then we can use 
Definition~\ref{d:nice} together with
Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit} to bound $g(\bm{t},\bm{L}) \le O(k/4^k)$.



If the variable $v$ is of a non-defective type $\bm{T}$,
(Definition~\ref{d:j.defective}), then
it can only neighbor nice clause types $\bm{L}$, and must have degree $|\delta v| = O(k2^k)$.
Thus we see from
\eqref{e:free.branching}
that $f(\bm{T}) \le O(k^2/2^k)$. If $\bm{T}$ is a
defective type,
then we recall from \eqref{e:every.variable.is.enclosed}
that $v$ must lie in a compound enclosure $U$ of diameter at most $R'$, such that the containment radius $s=\textup{rad}(v)$ is upper bounded by the distance between $v$ and the boundary of $U$. Moreover, by Definition~\ref{d:cpd.type}, the total type $\bm{T}$ encodes the isomorphism class of $U$, the position of $v$ within $U$, and the simple total type of every edge in $U$. It follows that $\bm{T}$ encodes the isomorphism class of $B_s(v)$, and the simple total type of every clause in $B_s(v)$. 
As before, suppose that $v$ is incident under $\bm{\sigma}$ to only $\SPIN{green}$ edges. Then,
under the randomness of the matching $\mathfrak{M}$,
the expected number of variables
in $\mathfrak{F}(v) \cap B_s(v)$ is
	\[
	f(\bm{T})
	\equiv
	\sum_{\ell=1}^s
	\sum_{v_0 a_1 v_1 \cdots a_\ell v_\ell}
	\prod_{j=1}^\ell
	\underbrace{\Bigg(
	\sum_{\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a_j} }
	\hat{\nu}_{a_j}
	\Big(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a_j} \,\Big|\,
		\sigma_{v_{j-1} a_j}=\SSPIN{g} \Big)

	\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta a_j}

$v=v_0 a_1 v_1 \cdots a_\ell v_\ell$ emanating from $v$. If $a_j$ is a nice clause, then we have 
$g(v_{j-1},a_j,v_j) \le O(1/4^k)$
by a similar calculation as for \eqref{e:nice.free.branching}.

$g(v_{j-1},a_j,v_j)\le1$.

that $\mathfrak{B}(v,w)$ counts the number of defective variables on the shortest path between $v$ and $w$ (including the endpoints). 
By Definition~\ref{d:j.defective},
any clause neighboring to a non-defective variable must be nice, 
so the number of nice clauses
on the shortest path between $v$ and $w$
must be at least $d(v,w) - \mathfrak{B}(v,w)$.

	\[

	\le
	\sum_{w\in B_s(v)}
	\bigg( \frac{O(1)}{4^k}\bigg)^{d(v,w)-\mathfrak{B}(v,w) }
	\le \frac14\,,
	\]
where the last inequality holds 
by the definition 
\eqref{eq-def-rad} of the containment radius,
since we set $s=\textup{rad}(v)$.

We maintain a queue (a first-in first-out list) of variables, starting from $Q_0=(v)$. Then, at each time step $\ell\ge1$, we remove the first element $w_\ell$ of $Q_{\ell-1}$ to produce $(Q_{\ell-1})'$. We then explore the neighborhood of $w_\ell$ to
depth $s_\ell$ where $s_\ell=1$ if $w_\ell$ is non-defective, and $s_\ell=\textup{rad}(w_\ell)$ otherwise. Let $\mathfrak{F}(v)_\ell$ be the variables of $\mathfrak{F}(v)$ that are \emph{newly} discovered in this exploration. We then take the ones at the boundary of $B_{s_\ell}(w_\ell)$ and append them to the queue:
	\[
	Q_\ell 
	=\bigg( (Q_{\ell-1})'
	,\mathfrak{F}(v)_\ell \cap 
	\partial_\circ B_{s_\ell}(w_\ell)\bigg)\,.
	\]
The exploration continues until the first time $\tau(v)$ that $Q_{\tau(v)}=\varnothing$. Let $\zeta_\ell \equiv |Q_\ell|-|Q_{\ell-1}|$.
 Under the randomness of the matching $\mathfrak{M}$, 
 as long as $\ell/n = o_n(1)$
 and $Q_{\ell-1}\ne\varnothing$, 
 it follows from the preceding bounds
 on $f(\bm{T})$ that
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\zeta_\ell
	\le -1 + \frac14 \bigg( 1 + o_n(1)\bigg)\,.
	\]
Once some vertices have already been explored,
\eqref{e:conditional.law.of.clause.type} is no longer an exact expression for the conditional 
law of subsequent clause types in the exploration
--- however, since we assume that $\ell/n=o_n(1)$ 
and that $\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero,
there remains a linear number of unexplored vertices of each type, so 
\eqref{e:conditional.law.of.clause.type}
is correct up to a multiplicative factor
$1 + o_n(1)$.
Thus, as long as 
$\ell/n=o_n(1)$
 and $Q_{\ell-1}\ne\varnothing$, 
we have $\mathbb{E}\zeta_\ell\le -1/2$.
Since all variables in $\mathscr{G}$ must be fair 
(Definition~\ref{d:perfect.fair}),
we have $0 \le 1+\zeta_\ell \le \exp(k^2 R)$
with probability one. It follows by the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality that for a large enough constant $C=C(k,R)$,
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\Big(\tau(v) \ge C\ln n\Big)
	\le
	\mathbb{P}\bigg( |Q_{C\ln n}|
		-\mathbb{E} |Q_{C\ln n}| \ge \frac{C\ln n}{2} \bigg)
	\ll \frac1n\,.
	\]

$\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero,
we see that the chance for the exploration to close more than two cycles is at most $(\ln n)^{O(1)}/n^2 \ll 1/n$. Taking a union bound over all $v\in V$ gives
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}\bigg(
	\Big\{
	(\mathscr{G},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}) :
	\textup{any connected component of
	$\mathfrak{F}$
	contains a bicycle}
	\Big\}
	\bigg)
	= o_n(1)\,,
	\]

$v=v_0 a_1 v_1 \cdots a_\ell v_\ell$ emanating from $v$. If $a_j$ is a nice clause, then we have 
$g(v_{j-1},a_j,v_j) \le O(1/4^k)$
by a similar calculation as for \eqref{e:nice.free.branching}.
In any case we always have
$g(v_{j-1},a_j,v_j)\le1$. 
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:contained}
that $\mathfrak{B}(v,w)$ counts the number of defective variables on the shortest path between $v$ and $w$ (including the endpoints). 
By Definition~\ref{d:j.defective},
any clause neighboring to a non-defective variable must be nice, 
so the number of nice clauses
on the shortest path between $v$ and $w$
must be at least $d(v,w) - \mathfrak{B}(v,w)$.
It follows that
	\[
	f(\bm{T})
	\le
	\sum_{w\in B_s(v)}
	\bigg( \frac{O(1)}{4^k}\bigg)^{d(v,w)-\mathfrak{B}(v,w) }
	\le \frac14\,,
	\]
where the last inequality holds 
by the definition 
\eqref{eq-def-rad} of the containment radius,
since we set $s=\textup{rad}(v)$.

Now consider exploration of $\mathfrak{F}(v)$ by the following modified breadth-first search procedure.
We maintain a queue (a first-in first-out list) of variables, starting from $Q_0=(v)$. Then, at each time step $\ell\ge1$, we remove the first element $w_\ell$ of $Q_{\ell-1}$ to produce $(Q_{\ell-1})'$. We then explore the neighborhood of $w_\ell$ to
depth $s_\ell$ where $s_\ell=1$ if $w_\ell$ is non-defective, and $s_\ell=\textup{rad}(w_\ell)$ otherwise. Let $\mathfrak{F}(v)_\ell$ be the variables of $\mathfrak{F}(v)$ that are \emph{newly} discovered in this exploration. We then take the ones at the boundary of $B_{s_\ell}(w_\ell)$ and append them to the queue:
	\[
	Q_\ell 
	=\bigg( (Q_{\ell-1})'
	,\mathfrak{F}(v)_\ell \cap 
	\partial_\circ B_{s_\ell}(w_\ell)\bigg)\,.
	\]
The exploration continues until the first time $\tau(v)$ that $Q_{\tau(v)}=\varnothing$. Let $\zeta_\ell \equiv |Q_\ell|-|Q_{\ell-1}|$.
 Under the randomness of the matching $\mathfrak{M}$, 
 as long as $\ell/n = o_n(1)$
 and $Q_{\ell-1}\ne\varnothing$, 
 it follows from the preceding bounds
 on $f(\bm{T})$ that
	\[
	\mathbb{E}\zeta_\ell
	\le -1 + \frac14 \bigg( 1 + o_n(1)\bigg)\,.
	\]
Once some vertices have already been explored,
\eqref{e:conditional.law.of.clause.type} is no longer an exact expression for the conditional 
law of subsequent clause types in the exploration
--- however, since we assume that $\ell/n=o_n(1)$ 
and that $\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero,
there remains a linear number of unexplored vertices of each type, so 
\eqref{e:conditional.law.of.clause.type}
is correct up to a multiplicative factor
$1 + o_n(1)$.
Thus, as long as 
$\ell/n=o_n(1)$
 and $Q_{\ell-1}\ne\varnothing$, 
we have $\mathbb{E}\zeta_\ell\le -1/2$.
Since all variables in $\mathscr{G}$ must be fair 
(Definition~\ref{d:perfect.fair}),
we have $0 \le 1+\zeta_\ell \le \exp(k^2 R)$
with probability one. It follows by the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality that for a large enough constant $C=C(k,R)$,
	\[
	\mathbb{P}\Big(\tau(v) \ge C\ln n\Big)
	\le
	\mathbb{P}\bigg( |Q_{C\ln n}|
		-\mathbb{E} |Q_{C\ln n}| \ge \frac{C\ln n}{2} \bigg)
	\ll \frac1n\,.
	\]
On the other hand, again using that
$\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero,
we see that the chance for the exploration to close more than two cycles is at most $(\ln n)^{O(1)}/n^2 \ll 1/n$. Taking a union bound over all $v\in V$ gives
	\[
	\mathbb{Q}_\mathcal{D}\bigg(
	\Big\{
	(\mathscr{G},\smash{\vec{\sigma}}) :
	\textup{any connected component of
	$\mathfrak{F}$
	contains a bicycle}
	\Big\}
	\bigg)
	= o_n(1)\,,
	\]
as long as 
$\mathscr{D}$ is bounded away from zero
in the sense of \eqref{e:pos.frac}. The result follows by appealing to Proposition~\ref{p:posfrac}.

	\frac{(\ln n)^3}{n}
	\le \frac{|S|}{|V|} \le \frac{k^2}{2^k}\,,
	\end{equation}

$C(v)$ of directed paths

$|D| \le 2 \epsilon_*|S|$.

where $a$ is forcing to $v$ under $\smash{\vec{x}}^1$,
and $u\in S\setminus\set{v}$.

\item For each $v\in B$,
every clause $a$ that forces to $v$ under $\smash{\vec{x}}^1$ appears in exactly one element of $C(v)$.

	\leftarrow a_2 \leftarrow u_2

	\[

	\textup{number of variables in 
	$(\gamma\setminus \partial_\circ U)$}

	\le \frac{\epsilon_*}{1-2\epsilon_*}
	\le 2\epsilon_*\,.

	\[

	\ge\frac{|X'|}{|V|}
	\ge \frac{(\ln n)^4}{C(k,R) \cdot 2n}
	\ge \frac{(\ln n)^3}{n}\,,
	\]
