Consequently, if $d_H(\smash{\vec{x}}^1,\smash{\vec{x}}^2)
= |\set{v\in V : (x^1)_v \ne (x^2)_v}|$, the set
	\[
	X\equiv \bigg\{v\in V:
		(x^1)_v\ne (x^2)_v,
		(x^1)_v\ne\SPIN{f}\bigg\}
	\]
must have cardinality $|X| \ge d_H(\smash{\vec{x}}^1,\smash{\vec{x}}^2)/2$. The assumed overlap $z\in I_2$ then implies
	\begin{equation}\label{e:sep.bounds.on.X}
	\frac{(\ln n)^4}{2n}
	\le \frac{|X|}{|V|}
	\le \frac{k^2}{2^k}\,.
	\end{equation}
Since the $\smash{\vec{x}}^i$ differ on $X$
and $\smash{\vec{x}}^1$ is not $\SPIN{free}$ on $X$,
it must be that $X$ is \bemph{internally forced} with respect to $\smash{\vec{x}}^1$ --- that is to say, each $v\in X$ is forced, but only by clauses involving at least one other variable from $X$. This implies that for any $v\in X$ we can find a path
	\begin{equation}\label{e:forcing.path} 
	v=u_0 \leftarrow a_1 \leftarrow u_1
	\leftarrow a_2 \leftarrow u_2
	\leftarrow \ldots\end{equation}
where $a_i$ is forcing to $u_{i-1}$, and 
$u_i \in X$ with $u_i \ne u_{i-1}$. Since the graph is finite, any such path must eventually close on itself to form a directed cycle within $X$. It follows that every maximal connected component of $X$ must contain at least one cycle.\smallskip

\noindent
\bemph{Step 2. Extract $S\subseteq X$ 
which has a small fraction of defects, and 
is internally forced.} If $X$ does not intersect 
any compound enclosure
(Definition~\ref{d:enclosure})
in the processed graph $\mathscr{G}$,
then $X$ does not contain any defective variable, and we simply take $S=X$.

If $U = U^\circ \sqcup \partial_\circ U$ is a compound enclosure and
 $X \cap U\ne\varnothing$, then we must have $X \cap \partial_\circ U\ne\varnothing$ --- indeed, if it were not the case, then $X\cap U = X\cap U^\circ$ would be a collection of maximal connected components of $X$, and each of these components would be a tree (since $U$ itself must be a tree). This contradicts our earlier observation that every maximal connected component of $X$ must contain at least one cycle.

We shall define a subset $S_U\subseteq X\cap U$ as follows. As we just saw, each connected component of $X\cap U$ induces a tree $\mathscr{T}\subseteq\mathscr{G}$ that intersects $\partial_\circ U$. Since $X$ is internally forced, the tree $\mathscr{T}$ must be covered by forcing paths \eqref{e:forcing.path}; this makes $\mathscr{T}$ into a \textsc{dag} (directed acyclic graph). Consider the variables of the \textsc{dag} with out-degree zero (meaning that they do not participate in any clause that forces another variable): if these all lie in $\partial_\circ U$, then we simply put
 all the variables of $\mathscr{T}_U$ into $S_U$. 
Otherwise, suppose the \textsc{dag} contains a variable $v\notin \partial_\circ U$ with out-degree zero:
then we can replace $X$ by $X\setminus \set{v}$, which is also internally forced. We continue pruning variables in this way until we arrive at $X'\subseteq X$ such that in the \textsc{dag} corresponding to $X'\cap U$, all variables of out-degree zero lie in $\partial_\circ U$. We then set $S_U = X' \cap U$: by construction, $S_U$ contains $X \cap \partial_\circ U$. Moreover, if we take $S$ to be the union of 
all the perfect variables in $X$ together with $S_U$
for all compound enclosures $U$, then $S$ is internally forced.

Each variable in $S_U \cap U^\circ$ has positive out-degree (by the above construction) and positive in-degree (since $S$ is internally forced). This means that if we view $S_U$ as an undirected subgraph of $\mathscr{G}$, each of its connected components must be a tree all of whose leaves lie in $\partial_\circ U$. It follows that $S_U$ can be covered by a disjoint union of (undirected) paths $\gamma$ where each $\gamma$ has a variable in $\partial_\circ U$ at one (or both) of its endpoints. 
Each $\gamma$ has length at most $R'$, the maximum diameter of $U$. By the construction of compound enclosures (Definition~\ref{d:enclosure}), each variable in $v\in \partial_\circ U$ is perfect, hence orderly (Definition~\ref{d:orderly}), so each $\gamma$ has at most $\epsilon_*$ fraction defective variables.
This implies that $S_U$ has at most $\epsilon_*$ fraction of defective variables. Moreover, if $\gamma$ contains any defective variable, then it must contain at least $1/\epsilon_*$ variables. It follows that the fraction of defective variables in $\gamma\setminus\partial_\circ U$ is at most
	\[
	\frac{\epsilon_* \cdot (\textup{number of variables in $\gamma$})}{
	\textup{number of variables in 
	$(\gamma\setminus \partial_\circ U)$}
	}
	\le \frac{\epsilon_*}{1-2\epsilon_*}
	\le 2\epsilon_*\,.
	\]
It follows that $S_U \setminus \partial_\circ U$ has at most $2\epsilon_*$ fraction of defective variables. Since every defective variable in $S$ must be contained in some $S_U \setminus \partial_\circ U$,
and the sets $S_U \setminus \partial_\circ U$ are pairwise disjoint, we conclude that $S$ has 
at most $2\epsilon_*$ fraction of defective variables. 
\smallskip

\noindent\bemph{Step 3. Choose paths $C(v)$ for $v\in S$.} Recall that $S=B\sqcup D$ where $D$ is the subset of defective variables in $S$. For $v\in D$, choose a single path $u\to a\to v$ such that $a$ is forcing to $v$ and $u\in S$, and let $C(v)$ consist of this path alone. For $v\in B$, for every clause $a$ that is forcing to $v$, choose a path $u\to a\to v$ with $u\in S$, and add this path to $C(v)$. Thus, for $v\in B$, every clause forcing to $v$ is covered by exactly one path in $C(v)$. This finishes the construction. Finally, since $S\subseteq X$ and $X$ satisfies \eqref{e:sep.bounds.on.X}, it is clear that $S$ satisfies the upper bound 
in \eqref{e:sep.bounds.on.size.of.S}, so it remains only to verify the lower bound. To this end, partition $X=X'\sqcup X''$ where $X'$ is the subset of all perfect variables in $X$. We can define a mapping $f: X''\to X'$ where we map $u\in X''$
to $v\in X'$ such that $v$ is on the boundary of the compound enclosure containing $u$. Recall that the maximum size of a compound enclosure is bounded by a constant depending only on $k$ and $R$. Moreover, a perfect variable must be nice, so its degree is $O(k2^k)$. This implies that for any $v\in X'$, its preimage $f^{-1}(v)\subseteq X''$ has size at most $C(k,R)$. It follows that $|X''| \le C(k,R) |X|$. Since $S\supseteq X'$ by construction, we conclude using the lower bound in \eqref{e:sep.bounds.on.X} that (for large $n$) we have
	\[
	\frac{|S|}{|V|}
	\ge\frac{|X'|}{|V|}
	\ge \frac{(\ln n)^4}{C(k,R) \cdot 2n}
	\ge \frac{(\ln n)^3}{n}\,,
	\]
as claimed. This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: entropy maximization on rooted trees
nodes.statement: Let T be a finite tree rooted at a clause a_textuptextscrt with exactly one child, which we refer to as the root variable v_textuptextscrt. We use L T to denote the set of all leaf vertices of T other than a_textuptextscrt, and we assume L T consists of variables only. We use delta T to denote the edges incident to L T. From now on we will refer to L T and delta T respectively as the ``boundary variables'' and ``boundary edges'' of T. A small example appears in Figure~. In the applications of this definition in the analysis of Section~, we will take T to be a nice (Definition~) subtree of a compound enclosure U. As a result, the notations that follow are purposefully similar to those of Definition~. Let \[ bmDelta(T) equiv left\ hspace-3ptc textupprobability measures nu over\\ textuppair colorings (smashvecsigma^1,smashvecsigma^2) of T hspace-3ptright\\,. \] We say that nuinbmDelta(T) is bemphjudicious if all of its edge marginals match the canonical marginals of Definition~: that is, for all edges e in T and for both j=1,2, we have nu((sigma_e)^j=sigma)=_starhspace-1ptpi_e(sigma) for all sigmainsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb. Let omega_delta T denote a tuple (omega_e)_eindelta T where each omega_e is a judicious probability measure on setSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb^2. We then let \[ bmJ(T ; omega_delta T) equiv left\ hspace-3ptc nuinbmDelta(T): textupnu is judicious,\\ textupand nu_e=omega_e for all eindelta T hspace-3pt right\\,, \] where nu_e denotes the marginal of nu on edge e. Define the constrained optimizer nu^textupop(T;omega_delta T) equiv textuparg\,max_nu bigg\ H(nu) : nu in bmJ(T,omega_delta T)bigg\\,. Given weights Lambda on T, we also define the unconstrained optimizer nu[T;Lambda] equiv textuparg\,max_nu bigg\ H(nu) + langle lnLambda,nurangle : nu in bmDelta(T)bigg\\,, where langlelnLambda,nurangle denotes the expected value of lnLambda(smashvecsigma) with smashvecsigma distributed according to nu. Note that by elementary calculus, the solution nu=nu[T;Lambda] of is given explicitly by nu(smashvecsigma) = fracIndtextupsmashvecsigma is a valid coloring of T Lambda(smashvecsigma)bmz[T;Lambda] where bmz[T;Lambda] is the normalizing constant. Finally, we say that Lambda are bemphLagrangian weights (for the constrained optimization problem nu^textupop(T;omega_delta T in ) if langlelnLambda,nurangle is constant over nuinbmJ(T;omega_delta T). We will parametrize Lagrangian weights in a particular way, described in Definition~ below.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{d:clause.rel.error}
In the pair model, given any two functions $g,h:\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2\to(0,\infty)$, we write
	\[
	\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(g,h)
	=\begin{pmatrix}
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{h(\sigma)}{g(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=0\bigg\} \smallskip\\
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{h(\sigma)}{g(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=1\bigg\} \smallskip \\
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{h(\sigma)}{g(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=2\bigg\}
	\end{pmatrix}
	\in\mathbb{R}^3.
	\]
We write $\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(g,h) \le \vec{s}$
to mean that $\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(g,h)$ is coordinatewise upper bounded by $\vec{s}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
In most cases we use this notation when both $g$ and $h$ are clause-to-variable messages in the pair model.

\label{r:adjusted.bp.stability}Recall that in the single-copy model, if $U$ is a tree whose leaves are all variables and whose clauses are all strictly coherent, then Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights} guarantees the existence of weights ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$ such that
the ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_U$-weighted Gibbs measure on $U$ has edge marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$. If $U$ is moreover nice, then the weights are constructed explicitly by 
Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit}. Recall that the corresponding
 \textsc{bp} solution 
 is not given by ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}q$, but rather by ${}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q$
 as defined by \eqref{e:redistributed.bp.messages}.
It follows from Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit}
that 
	\[
	\bigg\|
	\frac{{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e}-1\bigg\|_\infty 
	+\bigg\|
	\frac{{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e}-1\bigg\|_\infty 
	\le \frac{O(1)}{k^{r/2}}\]
for all edges $e$ of $T$. If $R\ge k$ (as assumed in 
Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}), then this error is very small. In particular, 
on nice edges it implies that ${}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q$ will satisfy the same estimates as ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}q$ from Definition~\ref{d:nice}. For this reason, we assume $R\ge k$ in the rest of the section, even when not explicitly stated. From now on we denote
${}_{*}q\equiv{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q\otimes{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q$. In the setting of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange},
we have a tree $T$ as in Definition~\ref{d:nu.judicious} 
or Figure~\ref{f:nice.subtree.of.compound.enclosure}. Let $T\setminus a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ denote the tree $T$ with $a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ removed: then all the leaves of $T\setminus a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ are variables, so ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_{T\setminus a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$ is defined by
Corollaries~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights} and \ref{c:clause.bp.weights.explicit}. Then, for a single-copy coloring $\smash{\vec{\tau}}=\smash{\vec{\tau}}_T$ on $T$, we define
	\begin{equation}\label{e:Lmstar.T.short.defn}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T(\smash{\vec{\tau}})
	\equiv
	{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}(\tau_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}})
	\cdot
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_{T\setminus a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}(\smash{\vec{\tau}}_{T\setminus a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}})\,,
	\end{equation}
that is, we put an additional weight ${}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$ on the root clause $a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.
As a consequence, in the ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T$-weighted model on $T$, the \textsc{bp} message from $a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ to $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ will be precisely ${}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$.

Recall from Remark~ that _*q=_bullethspace-1ptqotimes_bullethspace-1ptq. We then take the weights to be of form \[ Lambda(smashvecsigma) = _*hatq_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt(sigma_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt)Bigg\ prod_vin V_Tsetminus L T Lambda_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) Bigg\ Bigg\prod_eindelta T lambda_e(sigma_e) Bigg\\,, \] where for each internal variable vin V_TsetminusL T the weight factorizes as Lambda_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) equiv overbraceBigg(prod_j=1,2 (lambda_v)^j((x_v)^j)Bigg)^lambda_v(x_v) prod_eindelta v overbraceBigg( prod_j=1,2 (lambda_e)^j((sigma_e)^j) Bigg)^lambda_e(sigma_e)\,. If Lambda is any weight on T of the functional form just described, then Lambda is a Lagrangian weight in the sense of Definition~, meaning that langlelnLambda,nurangle is constant over nuinbmJ(T;omega_delta T). Conversely, it is easy to see that any Lagrangian weight can be expressed in this form. Next, recalling the discussion of S, there is a unique solution q=q_textuptextscbp(T;Lambda) for the Lambda-weighted textscbp recursions on T, obtained by recursing inwards from the leaves. In particular, for eindelta T we have simply dotq_e=lambda_e, and at the root we have hatq_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt=_*hatq_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt. Likewise, the marginal law on any edge e of T is given by nu_e(sigma) cong dotq_e(sigma) hatq_e(sigma) for sigmainsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb^2.

nodes.statement: Continuing in the setting of Proposition~, we now define a sequence of weights Lambda_t (parametrized as in Definition~ for each tge0), which will be proved in this section to converge as ttoinfty to the Lagrangian weights Lambda_inftyequivLambda(T;omega_delta T) of Proposition~. At the same time we will define messages q_t which will converge as ttoinfty to the textscbp solution qequiv q_textuptextscbp(T;Lambda_infty) for the Lambda_infty-weighted model on T, as discussed above. We initialize our construction at t=0 with weights \[ Lambda_0(smashvecsigma) equiv Big(_starhspace-1ptLambda_Totimes_starhspace-1ptLambda_TBig)(smashvecsigma) equiv prod_j=1,2 _starhspace-1ptLambda_T(smashvecsigma^j) \] where _starhspace-1ptLambda_T are the single-copy weights defined by in Remark~. More explicitly, if smashvectau denotes a single-copy coloring of T, then its weight under _starhspace-1ptLambda_T is given by _starhspace-1ptLambda_T(smashvectau) =_bullethspace-1pthatq_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt(sigma_a_textuptextscrtv_textuptextscrt) Bigg\ prod_vin V_Tsetminus L T overbrace Bigg( _starhspace-1ptlambda_v(x_v) prod_eindelta v _starhspace-1ptlambda_e(tau_e) Bigg)^_starhspace-1ptLambda_v(smashvectau_delta v) Bigg\ Bigg\ prod_eindelta T _starhspace-1ptlambda_e(tau_e) Bigg\\,, where x_vinsetSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf denotes the frozen spin corresponding to smashvectau_delta v, and we recall from Corollary~ that for eindelta T we take _starhspace-1ptlambda_e = _bullethspace-1ptdotq_e as defined by . \label{d:nice.lagrange.defn.weights}
Continuing in the setting of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}, we now define a sequence of weights $\Lambda_t$ (parametrized as in Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda} for each $t\ge0$), which will be proved in this section to converge as $t\to\infty$ to the Lagrangian weights $\Lambda_\infty\equiv\Lambda(T;\omega_{\delta T})$ of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}. At the same time we will define messages $q_t$ which will converge as $t\to\infty$ to the \textsc{bp} solution $q\equiv q_\textup{\textsc{bp}}(T;\Lambda_\infty)$ for the
$\Lambda_\infty$-weighted model on $T$, as discussed above. We initialize our construction
at $t=0$ with weights
	\[
	\Lambda_0(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\equiv 
	\Big({}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T\otimes{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T\Big)(\smash{\vec{\sigma}})
	\equiv \prod_{j=1,2} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^j)
	\]
where ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T$ are the single-copy weights defined by
\eqref{e:Lmstar.T.short.defn} in Remark~\ref{r:adjusted.bp.stability}. More explicitly, if $\smash{\vec{\tau}}$ denotes a single-copy coloring of $T$, then its weight under ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T$ is given by
	\begin{equation}\label{e:explicit.Lmstar.T}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_T(\smash{\vec{\tau}})
	={}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}(\sigma_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}) 
	\Bigg\{
	\prod_{v\in V_T\setminus \mathcal{L} T}
	\overbrace{
	\Bigg(
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_v(x_v)
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e(\tau_e)
	\Bigg)}^{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\Lambda_v(\smash{\vec{\tau}}_{\delta v})}
	\Bigg\}
	\Bigg\{
	\prod_{e\in\delta T}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e(\tau_e)
	\Bigg\}\,,\end{equation}
where $x_v\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}$ denotes the frozen spin corresponding to $\smash{\vec{\tau}}_{\delta v}$,
and we recall from 
 Corollary~\ref{c:clause.bp.weights}
 that for $e\in\delta T$ we take
 ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\lambda_e = {}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e$ as defined by \eqref{e:redistributed.bp.messages}. Note that $\Lambda_0$ is indeed of the functional form specified in Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda}. 
Let $q_0\equiv q_\textup{\textsc{bp}}(T;\Lambda_0)$;
explicitly, we have
$q_0={}_{*}q\equiv {}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q\otimes{}_\bullet\hspace{-1pt}q$
 (see Remark~\ref{r:adjusted.bp.stability}). 
For $t\ge1$, given $\Lambda_{t-1}$ we define updated weights $\Lambda_t$ (also of the functional form 
from Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda}) by making the following series of updates, started from the boundary $\delta T$ and working up to the root, then working back down to the boundary:
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
\item \bemph{Boundary updates.}
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda} that for each boundary edge $e=(av)\in\delta T$, the weight $\lambda_e$ is equivalent to the variable-to-clause message $\dot{q}_e$. We update these weights by setting
	\[
	\lambda_{av,t}(\sigma)
	\equiv \dot{q}_{va,t}(\sigma)
	\equiv 
	\frac{\omega_{av}(\sigma)}
		{\hat{q}_{av,t-1}(\sigma)}
	\Bigg/\Bigg(
	\sum_\tau
	\frac{\omega_{av}(\tau)}{\hat{q}_{av,t-1}(\tau)}
	\Bigg)\,.
	\]


\item \bemph{Upward pass (from boundary to root).}
Having updated the boundary messages,
go up the tree,
alternating steps (a) and (b),
starting with step (a) at the clauses incident to $\delta T$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item At a clause $a\ne a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, suppose the upward messages $\dot{q}_{ua}$ from the child variables $u$ have just been updated to their $t$-versions, while the downward message $\hat{q}_{va}$ from the parent variable $v$ is still at its $(t-1)$-version. 
Then apply \textsc{bp} to update the upward message from the clause,
	\[
	\hat{q}_{av,t}
	=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{av}[\dot{q}_t].
	\]
(Note that we have not yet defined $\dot{q}_t$ on all edges of $T$, but the right-hand side is well-defined since it depends only on the $\dot{q}_t$ messages coming from the child variables $u$ of $a$.)


\item At an internal variable $v$,
suppose the upward messages
$\hat{q}_{bv}$ from the child clauses
$b$ have just been updated to their $t$-versions; while the downward message
$\hat{q}_{av}$ from the parent clause $a$,
as well as the variable weight $\Lambda_v$,
are still at their $(t-1)$-versions.
Let $\Lambda_{v,t}$ be the unique choice of weights,
 of the functional form
\eqref{e:factorize.internal.weights.in.cpd} from
Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda}, such that the measure 
	\begin{equation}\label{e:var.update.II.b}
	\nu_{\delta v, t}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v}) 
	\equiv
	\frac{1}{\bm{\dot{z}}_{v,t}}
	\varphi_v(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\Lambda_{v,t}(\smash{\vec{\sigma}}_{\delta v})
	\Bigg\{
	\hat{q}_{av,t-1}(\sigma_{av})
	\prod_{b \in \partial v\setminus a}
	\hat{q}_{bv,t}(\sigma_{bv})
	\Bigg\}
	\end{equation}
is judicious (in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:nu.judicious}).
For now we assume that the weights $\Lambda_{v,t}$ exist;
we will explicitly construct them in Proposition~\ref{p:var.update} below. After obtaining $\Lambda_{v,t}$, we apply \textsc{bp} to update the message upward from variable $v$, that is to say, we let
	\[
	\dot{q}_{va,t}
	=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{va}[\hat{q}_t;\Lambda_{v,t}]\,.
	\]
(Note again that we have not yet defined $\hat{q}_t$ on all edges of $T$, but the right-hand side is well-defined since it depends only on the $\hat{q}_t$ messages coming from the child clauses $b$ of $v$.)
\end{enumerate}
The upward pass is completed once we have applied step (2b) at the root $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$.

\item \bemph{Downward pass (from root to boundary).} Recall from Definition~\ref{d:param.weights.Lambda} that we always put weight ${}_{*}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}$ on the root clause $a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$, and this will also be the \textsc{bp} message from $a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$ to $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$. We therefore start the downward pass with the trivial update
	\begin{equation}\label{e:message.from.top.always.product}
	\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}},t}
	=\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}},t-1}
	=\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}},0}
	= {}_{*}\hat{q}_{a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}}\,.
	\end{equation}
Then continue down the tree,
alternating steps (a) and (b),
starting from step (a) at $v_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item At an internal variable $v$,
suppose that the downward message $\hat{q}_{bv}$
from the parent clause $b$ has just been updated to its $t$-version. This means the upward messages
$\hat{q}_{av}$ from the child clauses $a$,
as well as the variable weight $\Lambda_v$,
were already updated to their $t$-versions during the preceding upward pass. Now apply \textsc{bp} to update the downward messages from the variable,
	\[
	\dot{q}_{va,t}
	=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{va}\bigg[
		\Big( \hat{q}_{bv,t-1};
		(\hat{q}_{cv,t}
		:c\in\partial v\setminus\set{a,b})
		\Big) ;\Lambda_{v,t}
		\bigg]
	\]
where we have chosen to use the
$(t-1)$-version of the downward message $\hat{q}_{bv}$
rather than the $t$-version.
This is merely convenient for our analysis, but will have no effect on the limit since the messages all converge.

\item At a clause $a\ne a_\textup{\textsc{rt}}$,
suppose the downward message $\dot{q}_{ua}$
from the parent variable $u$
has just been updated to its $t$-version.
This means the upward messages
$\dot{q}_{va}$ from the child variables $v$
were already updated to their $t$-versions
during the preceding upward pass. 
Apply \textsc{bp} to update the downward messages from the clause, again using
for convenience the $(t-1)$-version
of the message from above: 
	\[
	\hat{q}_{av,t}
	=\textup{\footnotesize\textsf{BP}}_{av}\bigg[
		\Big(\dot{q}_{ua,t-1},
		(\dot{q}_{wa,t}:
		w\in\partial a\setminus\set{u,v})
		\Big)
		\bigg].
	\]
\end{enumerate}
The downward pass is completed once we have applied step (3b) at each of the clauses incident to the boundary edges $\delta T$. This completes the definition of $\Lambda_t$ and $q_t$.
\end{enumerate}
In summary, by iterating the above steps, we obtain
$(\Lambda_t,q_t)$ for all $t\ge0$ on $T$.
 The next few subsections (\S\ref{ss:clause.update}--\ref{ss:contraction.nondefect}) are devoted to analyzing this iteration under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}.

In the pair model, given two variable-to-clause messages $p$ and $q$ (both probability measures on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2$), let $P$ and $Q$ be their reweightings as defined by \eqref{e:reweighted.messages.v.to.c}.
For $j=1,2$ let $P^j$ and $Q^j$ be the marginals of $P$ and $Q$ on the $j$-th coordinate. We then write
	\[\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(p,q)
	=\begin{pmatrix}
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2,
			\SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=0\bigg\} \smallskip\\
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2,
			\SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=1\bigg\} \smallskip\\
	\displaystyle
	\max
	\bigg\{ \bigg|\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2,
			\SSPIN{r}[\sigma]=2\bigg\} \smallskip\\
	\displaystyle
	\max\bigg\{
	\sum_{j=1,2}\bigg|\frac{Q^j(\sigma)}
		{P^j(\sigma)}-1\bigg|
		: \sigma \in \set{\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}
	\bigg\}\smallskip\\
	\displaystyle
	\sum_{j=1,2}\bigg|\frac{Q^j(\SSPIN{r})}
		{P^j(\SSPIN{r})}-1\bigg|
	\end{pmatrix}
	\in\mathbb{R}^5\,.
	\]
We write $\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(p,q) \le \vec{s}$
to mean that $\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(p,q)$ is coordinatewise upper bounded by $\vec{s}\in\mathbb{R}^5$.

\label{l:transfer.error}
Let $v$ be a nice variable with incoming messages $\hat{q}$ (in the pair model) satisfying \eqref{e:condition.on.hat.messages}.
Consider two weight functions 
$\lambda=\lambda^1\otimes\lambda^2$ and $\theta=\theta^1\otimes\theta^2$ 
where $\lambda^j,\theta^j:\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}\to(0,\infty)$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{e:bound.on.frozen.weights}
	\adjustlimits
	\sum_{j=1,2}
	\sum_{x\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}} 
	\Bigg( \Big|\lambda^j(x)-1\Big|
	+\Big|\theta^j(x)-1\Big|\Bigg)
	\le \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\zeta}}\,.\end{equation}
Let $\nu$ be the law of the frozen spin $x_v\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}^2$ that results from the messages $\hat{q}$ and the weights $\lambda$,
and let $\mu$ be the law of $x_v$
that results from $\hat{q}$ and $\theta$. Then for the marginal on the first copy we have
	\[
	\nu^1(x^1)
	=	
	\Bigg\{1+
	O\bigg(
		\frac{k^{O(1)}\|\delta^2\|_\infty}{2^{k\zeta}}
		\bigg)\Bigg\}
	\bigg(\frac{\lambda^1\mu^1}{\theta^1}\bigg) (x^1)
	 \Bigg/
	 \Bigg(
	\sum_{y^1} \bigg(\frac{\lambda^1\mu^1}{\theta^1} \bigg)
			(y^1)\Bigg)
	\,,\quad
	\delta^j\equiv \frac{\lambda^j}{\theta^j}-1\,.
	\]
That is to say, $\nu^1$ is approximately equal to the reweighting of $\mu^1$ by $\lambda^1/\theta^1$, 
and does not depend much on $\lambda^2/\theta^2$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{\pi}$ be the law of the frozen spin $x=x_v\in\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}^2$ that results from
messages $\hat{q}$ and weights $\lambda^1\otimes\theta^2$. Then
	\[
	\bar{\pi}(x)
	\cong \frac{\lambda^1(x^1)}{\theta^1(x^1)}
		\mu(x)\,,
	\]
from which it follows that the marginal of $\bar{\pi}$ on the first copy is exactly
	\[
	\bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	= \bigg(\frac{\lambda^1\mu^1}{\theta^1}\bigg) (x^1)
	 \Bigg/
	 \Bigg(
	\sum_{y^1} \bigg(\frac{\lambda^1\mu^1}{\theta^1} \bigg)
			(y^1)\Bigg)\,.
	\]
It remains to compare $\nu^1$ with $\bar{\pi}^1$. To this end, note it follows from 
Lemma~\ref{l:variable.close.to.product}
together with the assumption \eqref{e:bound.on.frozen.weights} that $\bar{\pi}$ also satisfies the estimates
\eqref{e:frozen.product.approx}
or equivalently
\eqref{e:frozen.product.approx.pi}. We thus have $e:\set{\SPIN{-},\SPIN{+},\SPIN{f}}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{e:frozen.product.approx.err}
	\bar{\pi}(x)
	=\pi(x^1)\pi(x^2)
	\bigg( 1 + e(x)\bigg)\,,\quad
	|e(x)| \le 
		 \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\zeta}}\,.
	\end{equation}
Recall that we defined $\delta^j\equiv \lambda^j/\theta^j-1$. Then, with $z$ a normalizing constant, we have
	\[
	\nu(x)
	=\frac1z \frac{\lambda^2(x^2)}{\theta^2(x^2)}
	\bar{\pi}(x)
	=\frac1z
	\Big(1 + \delta^2(x^2) \Big) \bar{\pi}(x)\,.
	\]
We can use \eqref{e:frozen.product.approx.err} to estimate the normalizing constant as
	\begin{align*}
	z
	&= \sum_x
	\Big(1 + \delta^2(x^2) \Big)
	\bar{\pi}(x)
	= 1 + \sum_x\delta^2(x^2) 
	\bar{\pi}(x)
	= 1 + \sum_{x^1}
		\pi(x^1)
		\sum_{x^2} \pi(x^2) \delta^2(x^2) 
		\Big(1+ e(x)\Big)\\
	&= \Bigg\{1 + \sum_{x^2} \pi(x^2) \delta^2(x^2) \Bigg\}
	\Bigg\{1
	+ O\bigg(
		\frac{k^{O(1)}\|\delta^2\|_\infty}{2^{k\zeta}}
		\bigg)\Bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
Similarly, we can also use \eqref{e:frozen.product.approx.err} to estimate
	\begin{align*}
	\sum_{x^2}
	\Big(1 + \delta^2(x^2) \Big) \bar{\pi}(x)
	&=\bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	+ \sum_{x^2}\delta^2(x^2) \bar{\pi}(x) 
	=\bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	+ \pi(x^1)\sum_{x^2}\delta^2(x^2)
		\pi(x^2)\Big(1+e(x)\Big)\\
	&=\bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	+ \pi(x^1) \sum_{x^2} \pi(x^2) \delta^2(x^2) 
	+ O\bigg(
		\frac{k^{O(1)}\|\delta^2\|_\infty}{2^{k\zeta}}
		\bigg)\\
	&= \bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	\Bigg\{
	1+\sum_{x^2} \pi(x^2) \delta^2(x^2) 
	\Bigg\}
	\Bigg\{1+
	O\bigg(
		\frac{k^{O(1)}\|\delta^2\|_\infty}{2^{k\zeta}}
		\bigg)\Bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
Taking the ratio between the last two quantities gives
	\[
	\nu^1(x^1)
	=\bar{\pi}^1(x^1)
	\Bigg\{1+
	O\bigg(
		\frac{k^{O(1)}\|\delta^2\|_\infty}{2^{k\zeta}}
		\bigg)\Bigg\}\,.
	\]
This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{p:var.update}
nodes.statement: We first define a sequence of weights Lambda_t, then analyze the construction to show that they converge to the desired weights Lambda_infty=Lambda. We emphasize that this index t is bemphpurely local to the proof of this proposition, and is not the same as the t that indexes the up-and-down passes in Definition~. The proof below is divided into a few numbered parts. bemphPart~1. Iterative definition of weights. Initialize Lambda_0=Theta. For all tge0, given the weights Lambda_t, let nu_tequivnu_delta v[Lambda_t;hatq]. Then, for all eindelta v, update the edge weights by setting, for both j=1,2, (lambda_e,t+1)^j =(lambda_e,t)^j cdot frac _starhspace-1ptpi_e(SSPINr) / _starhspace-1ptpi_e(SSPINb) (nu_e,t)^j (SSPINr) / (nu_e,t)^j(SSPINb)\,. Let nu_t+1/2 be the measure that results from incoming messages hatq, frozen spin weights lambda_t, and edge weights lambda_e,t+1 for all eindelta v. Let pi_t+1/2 be the induced measure on the frozen spin xinsetSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf^2. Let pi be the measure on the single spin x^jinsetSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf that is induced by _starhspace-1ptpi. Then update the frozen spin weights by setting, for both j=1,2, (lambda_t+1)^j(x^j) =(lambda_t)^j(x^j) cdot fracpi(x^j) / pi(SPIN+) (pi_t+1/2)^j(x^j) / (pi_t+1/2)^j(SPIN+)\,. This concludes the definition of the weights Lambda_t+1. bemphPart~2. Definition of error quantities. Define the error quantities \[ (delta_t)^j equiv sum_xinsetSPIN-,SPINf Bigg| fracpi(x^j)/pi(SPIN+) (pi_t)^j(x^j)/(pi_t)^j(SPIN+) -1 Bigg|\,, (rho_e,t)^j equiv bigg| frac _starhspace-1ptpi_e(SSPINr) / _starhspace-1ptpi_e(SSPINb) (nu_e,t)^j (SSPINr) / (nu_e,t)^j(SSPINb) -1 bigg|\,. \] We will keep track of the aggregate errors \[ bmdelta_t equivsum_j=1,2 (delta_t)^j\,, rho_e,t equiv sum_j=1,2 (rho_e,t)^j\,, bmrho_t equiv sum_eindelta v rho_e,t\,. \] For the initial measure nu_0=nu_delta v[Lambda_0;hatq]=nu_delta v[Theta;hatq], it follows by straightforward calculations that (delta_0)^j &le OBigg(sum_e'indelta vbigg\ epsilon_e' +fracdotepsilon_e'2^k +fracminsetddotepsilon_e',1 2^k(1+zeta) bigg\ Bigg) = O(textuperr_v)\,,\\ (rho_e,0)^j &le OBigg( dotepsilon_e +fracminsetddotepsilon_e,12^kzeta +textuperr_v Bigg) for both j=1,2 --- this makes use of the assumptions~ and . bemphPart~3. Effect of update on edge weights (from t to t+1/2). Recall that for each integer tge0, the procedure described in Part~1 goes from t to t+1/2 by the update on all the edge weights, leaving the frozen spin weights unchanged. For this update, Lemma~ gives (rho_e,t+1/2)^1 le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\(rho_e,t)^2 + fracbmrho_t2^k Bigg\\,, with the analogous bound if we exchange j=1,2. Summing over j=1,2 and over all eindelta v gives bmrho_t+1/2 le frack^O(1)2^kzeta bmrho_t\,. Meanwhile, the error in the frozen spin marginals can change by at most bmdelta_t+1/2 le bmdelta_t +frack^O(1) 2^k(1+zeta) bmrho_t \,, by a very similar calculation. bemphPart~4. Effect of update on frozen spin weights (from t+1/2 to t+1. Next recall that for each integer tge0, the procedure of Part~1 goes from t+1/2 to t+1 by the update on the frozen spin weights, leaving the edge weights unchanged. As a result the SPINred-to-SPINblue ratios are unaffected, so (rho_e,t+1)^j=(rho_e,t)^j. As for the frozen spin marginals, the result of Lemma~ gives bmdelta_t+1 le frack^O(1)bmdelta_t+1/22^kzeta le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\ bmdelta_t + fracbmrho_t2^k(1+zeta) Bigg\ where the last step is by . bemphPart~5. Conclusion. For each integer tge0, when we go from t to t+1 in the procedure of Part~1, it follows by combining and that \[ bmdelta_t+1\\ bmrho_t+1 le frack^O(1)2^kzeta 1 & 2^-k(1+zeta) \\ 0 & 1 bmdelta_t \\ bmrho_t \] (having used also that bmrho_t+1/2=bmrho_t). This implies \[ Upsilon_t+1 equiv bmdelta_t+1 +fracbmrho_t+12^k le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\ bmdelta_t + fracbmrho_t2^k Bigg\ = frack^O(1)2^kzeta Upsilon_t\,. \] It follows that the iteration defined in Part~1 converges. The error on the frozen spin weights can be bounded as sum_j=1,2 sum_xinsetSPIN-,SPINf Bigg|fraclambda^j(x)theta^j(x)-1Bigg| &le OBigg( sum_t=0^infty sum_j=1,2 sum_xinsetSPIN-,SPINf bigg|frac(lambda_t+1)^j(x)(lambda_t)^j(x)-1bigg| Bigg)\\ &le OBigg( sum_t=0^infty bmdelta_tBigg) le OBigg( sum_t=0^inftyUpsilon_tBigg) le O(Upsilon_0) le O(textuperr_v)\,. To bound the error on the edge weights, let us first note that for any eindelta v, implies \[ sum_tge1 rho_e,t le frack^O(1)2^kzeta sum_tge0Bigg\ rho_e,t + fracbmrho_t2^k Bigg\ le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\ sum_tge1 rho_e,t +bigg( rho_e,0 +sum_tge0 Upsilon_tbigg)Bigg\\,, \] and rearranging the inequality gives \[ sum_tge1 rho_e,t le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\ rho_e,0 + sum_tge0 Upsilon_tBigg\ le frack^O(1)2^kzeta Bigg\ rho_e,0 + textuperr_vBigg\\,. \] It follows from this that the total error on the edge weights can be bounded as sum_j=1,2 Bigg|frac(lambda_e)^j (theta_e)^j-1Bigg| &le OBigg(sum_t=0^infty rho_e,tBigg) le OBigg( rho_e,0 + frack^O(1)2^kzeta textuperr_v Bigg) le OBigg( dotepsilon_e +fracminsetddotepsilon_e,12^kzeta +textuperr_v Bigg)\,. This concludes the proof.

\label{l:marginal.error}
Suppose at the edge $e=(av)$
we have variable-to-clause messages
$p$ and $q$
(both going from $v$ to $a$), and a clause-to-variable message $h$ (going from $a$ to $v$), all probability measures on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$. Let $P,Q$ be the reweightings of $p,q$ defined by \eqref{e:reweighted.messages.v.to.c}. Let $H$ be the reweighting of $h$, with non-normalized version $W$, as defined by \eqref{e:reweighted.messages.c.to.v}. Assume
	\begin{equation}\label{e:beta.one.eighth}
	\bigg\|W -\frac19
	\bigg\|_\infty \le \frac1{18}\,.
	\end{equation}
Define the corresponding edge marginals
(probability measures on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$)
	\[
	\pi_p(\sigma)
	\equiv
	\frac{P(\sigma) W(\sigma)}
	{z_p}\,,\quad
	\pi_q(\sigma)
	\equiv
	\frac{Q(\sigma) W(\sigma)}
	{z_q}\,,
	\]
where $z_p,z_q$ are the normalizing constants. If $\pi_p$ and $\pi_q$ have the same marginals on the first copy, $(\pi_p)^1=(\pi_q)^1$, then the first-copy marginals of $P$ and $Q$ satisfy
	\[\Bigg|\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
		-1\Bigg|
	\le
	\overbrace{
	O(1)
	\bigg\|W -\frac19\bigg\|_\infty
	\sum_\tau
	P(\tau)\Bigg(1 + 
	\frac{\Ind{\tau^1=\sigma^1}}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	\Bigg)
	\Bigg|\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\Bigg|
	}^{\textup{this tighter bound is
	used in the proof of 
	Lemma~\ref{l:first.update.at.boundary}}}
	\le O(1)
	\bigg\|W -\frac19\bigg\|_\infty
	\bigg\|\frac{P}{Q} -1\bigg\|_\infty\,.
	\]
The analogous statement holds if we instead have 
$(\pi_p)^2=(\pi_q)^2$.

\begin{proof}
For the purposes of the proof, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2$ denote
	\[
	\delta(\sigma)
	\equiv \frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\,,\quad
	\beta(\sigma)
	\equiv W(\sigma)-\frac19\,.
	\]
Note that, since $P$ is a probability measure over $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2$, we have
	\[
	z_p
	= \sum_\sigma P(\sigma) \bigg(W(\sigma)-\frac19\bigg)
		+ \frac19 \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
	= \sum_\sigma P(\sigma) \beta(\sigma) +\frac19
	\in \bigg[\frac1{18},\frac3{18}\bigg]\,,
	\]
where the last step uses the assumption 
\eqref{e:beta.one.eighth}. The same bound holds for $z_q$. Next we have
	\[
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	-1
	=
	\frac{z_q-z_p}{z_p}
	+\frac{z_q}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	\bigg(
		\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\bigg)\,;
	\]
we will bound separately the two terms on the right-hand side. For the first term we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:marginal.error.z.error}
	|z_q-z_p|
	=\Bigg| \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
		\bigg(
		\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1
		\bigg)
		\bigg(
		W(\sigma)-\frac19
		\bigg)\Bigg|
	=\Bigg| \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
		\delta(\sigma)\beta(\sigma)\Bigg|
	\le
	\|\beta\|_\infty
	\sum_\sigma P(\sigma) |\delta(\sigma)|\,,
	\end{equation}
which implies $|z_q-z_p| \le \|\beta\|_\infty\|\delta\|_\infty$. For the second term,
direct algebraic manipulations give
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{1}{9}\Bigg(
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\Bigg)
	&=
	\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\Bigg\{
	\frac1{z_q}
	Q(\sigma)
	\bigg(W(\sigma) - \beta(\sigma)\bigg)
	-\frac1{z_p}
	P(\sigma)
	\bigg(W(\sigma) - \beta(\sigma)\bigg)
	\Bigg\}\\
	&= 
	\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\beta(\sigma)
	\Bigg\{
	\frac{P(\sigma)}{z_p}
	- \frac{Q(\sigma)}{z_q}
	\Bigg\}
	+ \underbrace{
		 (\pi_q)^1(\sigma^1)- (\pi_q)^1(\sigma^1)
		 }_{\textup{zero}}\\
	&=\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\beta(\sigma)
	P(\sigma)\Bigg\{
	\frac{z_q-z_p}{z_pz_q}
	-
	\frac{1}{z_q}
	\bigg(
	\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1
	\bigg)
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\end{align*}
from which it follows (dividing through by $P^1(\sigma^1)$) that
	\[
	\frac{1}{P^1(\sigma^1)}\Bigg|
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\Bigg|
	\le \|\beta\|_\infty \cdot O
	\Bigg( |z_q-z_p|
	+ 
	\sum_\tau
	\frac{\Ind{\tau^1=\sigma^1}}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	P(\tau)\delta(\tau)
	\Bigg)\,,
	\]
having used that $z_p,z_q \in[1/18,3/18]$.
Combining with \eqref{e:marginal.error.z.error} proves the lemma.
\end{proof}

For the purposes of the proof, for $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2$ denote
	\[
	\delta(\sigma)
	\equiv \frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1\,,\quad
	\beta(\sigma)
	\equiv W(\sigma)-\frac19\,.
	\]
Note that, since $P$ is a probability measure over $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}^2$, we have
	\[
	z_p
	= \sum_\sigma P(\sigma) \bigg(W(\sigma)-\frac19\bigg)
		+ \frac19 \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
	= \sum_\sigma P(\sigma) \beta(\sigma) +\frac19
	\in \bigg[\frac1{18},\frac3{18}\bigg]\,,
	\]
where the last step uses the assumption 
\eqref{e:beta.one.eighth}. The same bound holds for $z_q$. Next we have
	\[
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	-1
	=
	\frac{z_q-z_p}{z_p}
	+\frac{z_q}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	\bigg(
		\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\bigg)\,;
	\]
we will bound separately the two terms on the right-hand side. For the first term we have
	\begin{equation}\label{e:marginal.error.z.error}
	|z_q-z_p|
	=\Bigg| \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
		\bigg(
		\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1
		\bigg)
		\bigg(
		W(\sigma)-\frac19
		\bigg)\Bigg|
	=\Bigg| \sum_\sigma P(\sigma)
		\delta(\sigma)\beta(\sigma)\Bigg|
	\le
	\|\beta\|_\infty
	\sum_\sigma P(\sigma) |\delta(\sigma)|\,,
	\end{equation}
which implies $|z_q-z_p| \le \|\beta\|_\infty\|\delta\|_\infty$. For the second term,
direct algebraic manipulations give
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{1}{9}\Bigg(
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\Bigg)
	&=
	\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\Bigg\{
	\frac1{z_q}
	Q(\sigma)
	\bigg(W(\sigma) - \beta(\sigma)\bigg)
	-\frac1{z_p}
	P(\sigma)
	\bigg(W(\sigma) - \beta(\sigma)\bigg)
	\Bigg\}\\
	&= 
	\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\beta(\sigma)
	\Bigg\{
	\frac{P(\sigma)}{z_p}
	- \frac{Q(\sigma)}{z_q}
	\Bigg\}
	+ \underbrace{
		 (\pi_q)^1(\sigma^1)- (\pi_q)^1(\sigma^1)
		 }_{\textup{zero}}\\
	&=\sum_{\sigma \in \set{\sigma^1}\times\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{c}}}
	\beta(\sigma)
	P(\sigma)\Bigg\{
	\frac{z_q-z_p}{z_pz_q}
	-
	\frac{1}{z_q}
	\bigg(
	\frac{Q(\sigma)}{P(\sigma)}-1
	\bigg)
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\end{align*}
from which it follows (dividing through by $P^1(\sigma^1)$) that
	\[
	\frac{1}{P^1(\sigma^1)}\Bigg|
	\frac{Q^1(\sigma^1)}{z_q}
	-\frac{P^1(\sigma^1)}{z_p}\Bigg|
	\le \|\beta\|_\infty \cdot O
	\Bigg( |z_q-z_p|
	+ 
	\sum_\tau
	\frac{\Ind{\tau^1=\sigma^1}}{P^1(\sigma^1)}
	P(\tau)\delta(\tau)
	\Bigg)\,,
	\]
having used that $z_p,z_q \in[1/18,3/18]$.
Combining with \eqref{e:marginal.error.z.error} proves the lemma.

nodes.statement: In this remark we give some explanation for the choice of the vectors vecdelta and vecepsilon in Proposition~. If we take the product of the 3times 5 matrix in with the 5times3 matrix in , the result can be (entrywise) upper bounded as \[ hattextupM dottextupM_textupint le k^O(1) 2^-kzeta & (vartheta_*)^1/4 2^-k & (vartheta_*)^1/4 2^-k(1+zeta)\\ 2^k(1-zeta) & 2^-kzeta & 2^-kzeta\\ 2^k & 1 & 2^-kzeta le k^O(1) 2^-k \\ vartheta_* \\ (vartheta_*)^-1 2^kvartheta_* & (vartheta_*)^1/4 & (vartheta_*)^5 \,. \] For the last bound on the right-hand side, the vector vecepsilon from from Proposition~ is a right eigenvector with eigenvalue O(vartheta_*). This explains why vecepsilon is a good choice for our purposes (although it is certainly not the unique choice that would give a sufficiently good bound). On the other hand, given vecepsilon, we chose the vector vecdelta to satisfy the bounds and . (Again, it is certainly not the unique one that suffices for our purposes.)

nodes.name: \hypertarget{p:nice.tree.lagrange.proof}{Proof of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}}
nodes.statement: It is clear from Proposition~ that the construction of Definition~ converges to the desired Lagrangian weights LambdaequivLambda(T;omega_delta T). The corresponding Gibbs measure nu=nu[T;Lambda] has then edge marginals nu_av cong dotq_va hatq_av where dotq_vaequivdotq_va,infty and hatq_avequivhatq_av,infty are the limiting textscbp messages. It remains only to verify the estimate . By Proposition~, on any edge (av) we have, abbreviating xi_aequivxi_a(T;omega_delta T), dddottextupfootnotesize ERR(_*dotq_va,dotq_va) le sum_tge1 dddottextupfootnotesize ERR(dotq_va,t-1,dotq_va,t) &le O(1) xi_a vecdelta\,,\\ widehattextupfootnotesize ERR(_*hatq_av,hatq_av) le sum_tge1 widehattextupfootnotesize ERR(hatq_av,t-1,hatq_av,t) &le O(1) xi_a (k^2c(vartheta_*)^1/3)^2 vecepsilon\,. This implies, for all edges (av) in T and all sigmainsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb^2, the bound \[Bigg|fracdotq_va(sigma)_*dotq_va(sigma) -1Bigg| +Bigg|frachatq_av(sigma)_*hatq_av(sigma) -1Bigg| le OBigg( fracxi_a(vartheta_*)^IndSSPINrinsetsigma^1,sigma^2 Bigg)\,. \] Since nu_av cong dotq_va hatq_av, it follows straightforwardly that \[Bigg| fracnu_av(sigma) _*omega_av(sigma)-1Bigg| le OBigg( fracxi_a(vartheta_*)^IndSSPINrinsetsigma^1,sigma^2 Bigg)\,. \] Recalling gives textupdisc_av(nu_av)le O(xi_a), as claimed.
nodes.raw_latex:
It is clear from
Proposition~\ref{p:induct}
that the construction of
Definition~\ref{d:nice.lagrange.defn.weights} converges to the desired Lagrangian weights
$\Lambda\equiv\Lambda(T;\omega_{\delta T})$.
The corresponding Gibbs measure $\nu=\nu[T;\Lambda]$
has then edge marginals $\nu_{av} \cong \dot{q}_{va} \hat{q}_{av}$ where $\dot{q}_{va}\equiv\dot{q}_{va,\infty}$
and $\hat{q}_{av}\equiv\hat{q}_{av,\infty}$
are the limiting \textsc{bp} messages. 
It remains only to verify the estimate
\eqref{e:clause.xi.prelim.defn}. By Proposition~\ref{p:induct}, on any edge $(av)$ we have, abbreviating
$\xi_a\equiv\xi_a(T;\omega_{\delta T})$,
	\begin{align*}
	\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}({}_{*}\dot{q}_{va},\dot{q}_{va})
	\le
	\sum_{t\ge1}
	\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(\dot{q}_{va,t-1},\dot{q}_{va,t})
	&\le O(1)
	\xi_a \vec{\delta}\,,\\
	\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}({}_{*}\hat{q}_{av},\hat{q}_{av})
	\le
	\sum_{t\ge1}
	\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(\hat{q}_{av,t-1},\hat{q}_{av,t})
	&\le O(1)
	\xi_a (k^{2c}(\vartheta_*)^{1/3})^2 \vec{\epsilon}\,.
	\end{align*}
This implies, for 
all edges $(av)$ in $T$ and all $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$, the bound
	\[\Bigg|\frac{\dot{q}_{va}(\sigma)}{{}_{*}\dot{q}_{va}(\sigma)}
	-1\Bigg| 
	+\Bigg|\frac{\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma)}{{}_{*}\hat{q}_{av}(\sigma)}
	-1\Bigg| 
	\le O\Bigg(
	\frac{\xi_a}{(\vartheta_*)^{\Ind{\SSPIN{r}\in\set{\sigma^1,\sigma^2}}}}
	\Bigg)\,.
	\]
Since $\nu_{av} \cong \dot{q}_{va} \hat{q}_{av}$, it follows straightforwardly that
	\[\Bigg|
	\frac{\nu_{av}(\sigma)}
	{{}_{*}\omega_{av}(\sigma)}-1\Bigg|
	\le
	O\Bigg(
	\frac{\xi_a}{(\vartheta_*)^{\Ind{\SSPIN{r}\in\set{\sigma^1,\sigma^2}}}}
	\Bigg)\,.
	\]
Recalling
\eqref{e:def.discrepancy.measure.e}
gives
$\textup{\textsf{disc}}_{av}(\nu_{av})\le O(\xi_a)$, as claimed.

nodes.name:
parametrization of Lagrangian weights $\Psi$
on a depth-one neighborhood of a non-compound variable
nodes.statement: Let U be the depth-one tree from Definition~, rooted at a variable v of (non-compound) total type bmT. For an augmented pair coloring (smashvecsigma,smashvecbmL) of U, we will define weight functions PsiequivPsi_U parametrized as \[ Psi(smashvecsigma,smashvecbmL) = Psi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) cdot Bigg\ prod_eindelta U psi_e(sigma_e,bmL_e) Bigg\\,,\] where the root variable weight Psi_v takes the form Psi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) equiv underbrace varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) Bigg\ prod_j=1,2 psi^j(x^j)Bigg\ Bigg\ prod_eindelta v prod_j=1,2 (psi_e)^j((sigma_e)^j) Bigg\ _textupdenote this psi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) Bigg\ prod_eindelta v underbraceBigg( psi_e(bmL_e) prod_j=1,2 (psi_e)^j((sigma_e)^j \,|\,bmL_e) Bigg)_ textupdenote this psi_e(sigma_e,bmL_e) Bigg\\,, --- in the above, varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) is the indicator of a valid pair coloring smashvecsigma_delta v (i.e., the pair version of ), and xinsetSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf^2 denotes the pair frozen spin corresponding to smashvecsigma_delta v. If Psi is any weight on U of the functional form just described, then Psi is a Lagrangian weight for the optimization problem from Proposition~, meaning that langle lnLambda,nurangle is constant over nuinbmJ_D(U;omega_delta U). Conversely, it is easy to see that any Lagrangian weight can be expressed in this form. Moreover, for our convenience we have chosen weights that are somewhat over-parametrized, since we have edge weights (psi_e)^j((sigma_e)^j) as well as (psi_e)^j((sigma_e)^j\,|\,bmL_e).

nodes.name:
iterative construction of weights
for a non-compound variable
nodes.statement: In the setting of Proposition~, we again let U be the depth-one tree from Definition~. We now define a sequence of weights Psi_t on U (parametrized as in Definition~ for each tge0), which will be shown to converge as ttoinfty to the Lagrangian weights Psi_inftyequiv Psi_D(U;omega_delta U) of Proposition~. At the same time we will define messages q_t which will converge as ttoinfty to the textscbp solution qequiv q_textuptextscbp(U;Psi_infty) for the Psi_infty-weighted model on U. (On each edge e of U, the textscbp messages dotq_e,t and hatq_e,t will now be probability measures on tuple (sigma,bmL) where sigmainsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb^2 while bmL ranges over all possible types for the clause incident to e.) To start the construction, let _starhspace-1ptLambda_U denote the single-copy weights on U given by Corollary~ (and explicitly constructed in Corollary~) --- similarly to , if smashvectauequivsmashvectau_U is a single-copy coloring of U, then \[ _starhspace-1ptLambda_U(smashvectau) =overbrace Bigg\_starhspace-1ptlambda_v(x_v) prod_eindelta v _starhspace-1ptlambda_e(tau_e) Bigg\ ^_starhspace-1ptLambda_v(smashvectau_delta v) Bigg\ prod_eindelta U _starhspace-1ptlambda_e(tau_e) Bigg\ \] where x_vinsetSPIN-,SPIN+,SPINf denotes the frozen spin corresponding to smashvectau_delta v, and for eindelta U we take _starhspace-1ptlambda_e=_bullethspace-1ptdotq_e as defined by . Next, recalling , we define _starhspace-1ptpsi_e(bmL)equiv pi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt_e). We initialize our construction at t=0 with \[ Psi_0(smashvecsigma,smashvecbmL) equiv Bigg\ prod_j=1,2 _starhspace-1ptLambda_U(smashvecsigma^j)Bigg\ Bigg\ prod_eindelta v _starhspace-1ptpsi_e(bmL_e)Bigg\\,,\] where (smashvecsigma,smashvecbmL)equiv(smashvecsigma_U,smashvecbmL_U) denotes an augmented pair coloring of U. This fits the functional form prescribed in Definition~ above, since we can rewrite Psi_0(smashvecsigma,smashvecbmL) &= Psi_v,0(smashvecsigma_delta v,bmL_delta v) cdotBigg\ prod_eindelta U overbraceBigg( prod_j=1,2 _starhspace-1ptlambda_e((sigma_e)^j) Bigg)^psi_e,0(sigma_e,bmL_e) Bigg\\,,\\ Psi_v,0(smashvecsigma_delta v,bmL_delta v) &=underbrace Bigg\prod_j=1,2 _starhspace-1ptLambda_v((smashvecsigma_delta v)^j) Bigg\_psi_v,0(smashvecsigma_delta v) Bigg\ prod_eindelta v _starhspace-1ptpsi_e(bmL_e) Bigg\\,, which is consistent with if for all eindelta v we take psi_e,0(sigma,bmL) equiv_starhspace-1ptpsi_e(sigma,bmL), where _starhspace-1ptpsi_e(sigma,bmL) equiv_starhspace-1ptpsi_e(bmL) Bigg\prod_j=1,2 (_starhspace-1ptpsi_e)^j(sigma^j\,|\,bmL) Bigg\ = _starhspace-1ptpsi_e(bmL) = pi(bmL\,|\,bmt_e)\,. Having defined Psi_0, we let q_0equiv q_textuptextscbp(U;Psi_0). Recall that omega_delta U is given, and abbreviate Omegaequivtextupaug(omega), as defined by . For tge1, given Psi_t-1 we define updated weights Psi_t by making the following series of updates, started from the boundary delta U and working up to the root v, then working back down to delta U: [I.] item bemphBoundary updates. For each leaf edge e=(au)in delta U, we update its weight by setting \[ psi_e,t(sigma,bmL) equiv dotq_e,t(sigma,bmL) equiv fracOmega_e(sigma,bmL)hatq_e,t(sigma,bmL) Bigg/ Bigg(sum_sigma',bmL' fracOmega_e(sigma',bmL') hatq_e,t(sigma',bmL') Bigg)\,. \] item bemphUpward pass through clauses. For each clause a in U, update hatq_av,tequivtextupfootnotesizeBP_av[dotq_t]. item bemphRoot variable update. Recall that varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) denotes the indicator of a valid augmented pair coloring of delta v. Suppose inductively that the measure Big(nu_delta v[Psi_v,t-1;hatq_t-1] Big) (smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) equiv frac1bmdotz_v,t-1 varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v;smashvecbmL_delta v) Psi_v,t-1 (smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) prod_eindelta v hatq_e,t-1(sigma_e,bmL_e) is fully judicious on delta v. We will show below, in Proposition~, how to define updated weights Psi_v,t such that nu_delta v[Psi_v,t;hatq_t] is also fully judicious on delta v. We then use this to update dotq_va,tequivtextupfootnotesizeBP_va[hatq_t;Psi_v,t] for all ainpartial v. item bemphDownward pass through clauses. For each clause a in U, update \[hatq_au,tequiv textupfootnotesizeBP_au bigg[Big( dotq_va,t-1, (dotq_wa,t)_winpartial asetminus setu,v Big) bigg] \] for each child variable uinpartial asetminus v. This completes the definition of Psi_t and q_t. In summary, by iterating the above steps, we obtain (Psi_t,q_t) for all tge0 on T. The remainder of this subsection is devoted to analyzing this iteration under the assumptions of Proposition~.

\label{d:judicious.with.types}
In the setting of Definition~\ref{d:judicious.augmented.alphabet}, let $\nu$ be a probability measure on augmented colorings $(\smash{\vec{\sigma}},\smash{\vec{\bm{L}}})$ of $U$. For any edge $e$ of $U$ we let $\nu_e$ be the marginal law of $(\sigma_e,\bm{L}_e)$ under $\nu$. We say $\nu_e$ is \bemph{judicious on average} if
	\[
	\bar{\nu}_e(\sigma_e)
	\equiv \sum_{\bm{L}_e}
	\bar{\nu}_e(\sigma_e,\bm{L}_e)
	\]
is a judicious measure on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$, in the sense of \eqref{e:margin.judicious}.
We say that $\nu_e$ is \bemph{conditionally judicious} if for all clause types $\bm{L}_e$ that can appear on edge $e$, the conditional measure $\nu_e(\sigma_e\,|\,\bm{L}_e)$ is a judicious measure on $\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$, 
again in the sense of \eqref{e:margin.judicious}.
Note that \bemph{fully judicious}
(Definition~\ref{d:judicious.augmented.alphabet}) implies conditionally judicious which implies judicious on average.

Let $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{q}$ be two nonnegative measures on pairs $(\sigma,\bm{L})$ where $\sigma\in\set{\SSPIN{r},\SSPIN{y},\SSPIN{g},\SSPIN{b}}^2$ and $\bm{L}$ ranges over clause types. In what follows we shall write
	\[
	\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{p},\hat{q})
	\le \vec{\epsilon} = \begin{pmatrix}
	\epsilon \\ \dot{\epsilon} \\ \ddot{\epsilon}
	\end{pmatrix}
	\]
to indicate that
$\widehat{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(\hat{p}(\cdot\,|\,\bm{L}),
	\hat{q}(\cdot\,|\,\bm{L})) \le\vec{\epsilon}$
for all $\bm{L}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:clause.rel.error}, and that
	\[
	\max_{\bm{L}}\Bigg\{
	\bigg|\frac{\hat{q}(\bm{L})}{\hat{p}(\bm{L})}-1
	\bigg|\Bigg\}\le \epsilon\,.
	\]
If $\dot{p}$ and $\dot{q}$
are two probability measures on pairs $(\sigma,\bm{L})$,

in an analogous fashion, extending the notation from Definition~\ref{d:var.rel.error}.

We again recall from that varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) denotes the indicator of a valid augmented pair coloring of delta v. It can be expressed as \[ varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) = varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) prod_eindelta v IndbmL_eni bmt_e\,, \] where varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) is the indicator of a valid pair coloring on delta v (not augmented with clause types) as defined in ; and we write bmLnibmt to indicate that bmL_j=bmt for j=j(bmt). bemphhypertargetp:ctypes.varupdate.ITERATIVE.CONSTRUCTIONPart~1. Iterative construction of Psi_v. We first give an iterative definition for a sequence of weights Psi_v,t (tge0), all of the functional form . We emphasize that this index t is bemphpurely local to the proof of this proposition, and is not the same as the t that indexes the up-and-down passes in Definition~. We will show in the remainder of the proof that this sequence converges as ttoinfty to the desired weights Psi_v=Psi_v,infty. Initialize Psi_v,0equivPhi_v. For each tge0, we will update from Psi_v,t to Psi_v,t+1 in three stages, summarized by the following table: c|ccc & psi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) & (psi_e)^j(sigma^j\,|\,bmL) & psi_e(bmL) \\ hline Psi_v,t & t & t & t \\ Psi_v,t+1/3 & t+1 & t & t \\ Psi_v,t+2/3 & t+1 & t+1 & t --- e.g., the last row of the table indicates that the weight Psi_v,t+2/3 is defined by with the (t+1)-versions of psi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) and (psi_e)^j(sigma^j\,|\,bmL) (for both j=1,2 and all eindelta v), but with the t-version of psi_e(bmL) (again for all eindelta v). For notational convenience, we also define Psi_tequiv Phi for all t<0, and hatq_e,t(sigma,bmL) equiv hatp_e(sigma,bmL) &textupif t<0\,,\\ hatq_e(sigma,bmL) &textupif tge0\,.\\ We then abbreviate nu_tequivnu_delta v[Psi_v,t;hatq_t], using the notation of ; in particular this means nu_t=nu_delta v[Phi;hatp] for all t<0, while nu_0=nu_delta v[Phi;hatq]. For t>0, the weights of are defined by the following procedure (with t denoting an integer time from now on): [A.] item From t to t+1/3: we will suppose inductively that the measure nu_t-2/3 is judicious on average (in the terminology of Definition~). (For t=0, recall that we defined nu_-2/3equivnu_delta v[Phi,hatp], which by hypothesis is fully judicious and therefore also judicious on average.) At time t (for tge0) we have \[ nu_t(smashvecsigma_delta v,smashvecbmL_delta v) = frac1bmdotz_v,t varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) psi_v,t(smashvecsigma_delta v) prod_eindelta v Bigg\ Ind bmL_enibmt_e psi_e,t(sigma_e,bmL_e) hatq_e(sigma_e,bmL_e) Bigg\\,. \] The marginal law of smashvecsigma_delta v under nu_t can then be expressed as barnu_t(smashvecsigma_delta v) cong varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) psi_v,t(smashvecsigma_delta v) prod_eindelta v barq_e,t(sigma_e)\,, where barq_e,t denotes the message at time t averaged over bmL: barq_e,t(sigma) equiv frac1barz_e,t sum_bmL IndbmLnibmt_e psi_e,t(sigma,bmL) hatq_e,t(sigma,bmL)\,, where hatq_e,t is defined by . Since we also defined psi_e,tequivphi_e for negative t, this means that barq_e,t(sigma_e) is also well-defined for negative t. For instance, the marginal law of smashvecsigma_delta v at time t-2/3 is barnu_t-2/3(smashvecsigma_delta v) cong varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) psi_v,t(smashvecsigma_delta v) prod_eindelta v barq_e,t-1(sigma_e)\,, including in the case t=0. Now, from the inductive assumption, nu_t-2/3 is judicious on average, which means that the measure barnu_t-2/3 in is judicious in the sense of Definition~. Comparing with , we see that we can apply Proposition~ --- with the variable weight function psi_v,t(smashvecsigma_delta v) and the two sets of incoming messages barq_e,t-1 and barq_e,t --- to define a new variable weight function psi_v,t+1(smashvecsigma_delta v) such that the measure \[ barnu_t+1/3(smashvecsigma_delta v) cong varphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v) psi_v,t+1(smashvecsigma_delta v) prod_eindelta v barq_e,t(sigma_e) \] is judicious in the sense of Definition~, i.e., such that nu_t+1/3 is judicious on average. Note that, since t+1/3=(t+1)-2/3, this verifies the inductive assumption that nu_t-2/3 is judicious on average. item From t+1/3 to t+2/3: for all eindelta v and both j=1,2, update frac(psi_e,t+1)^j (tau\,|\,bmL) (psi_e,t)^j( tau\,|\,bmL) = frac_starhspace-1ptpi_e(tau) (nu_e,t+1/3)^j(tau\,|\,bmL) for all tauinsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb. item From t+2/3 to t+1: for all eindelta v and both j=1,2, update fracpsi_e,t+1(bmL)psi_e,t(bmL) = fracpi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt_e) nu_e,t+2/3 (bmL_e) \,, using the notation from . nodes.statement: We must argue that the iterative construction of Definition~ converges to the desired weights PsiequivPsi_D(U;omega_delta U) asserted by the proposition. The argument closely follows the outline of the proofs of Propositions~ and . For each leaf edge e=(au)indelta U, it is easy to check that at the initial stage t=0 we have \[ hatq_e,0(sigma,bmL) cong pi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt_p(e)) _*hatq_e(sigma)\,, \] where p(e)=(av) (as in ). On the other hand, for each eindelta U we are given the edge marginal \[ Omega_e(sigma,bmL) =Omega_e(bmL) Omega_e(sigma\,|\,bmL) = pi_D(bmL\,|\,bmt_p(e)) omega_bmL,j(sigma)\,, \] with j=j(bmt_e). Applying Step~I in Definition~ gives \[ dotq_e,1(sigma,bmL) cong fracOmega_e(sigma,bmL) hatq_e,0(sigma,bmL) cong fracomega_bmL,j(sigma) _*hatq_e(sigma)\,. \] It follows that dddottextupERR(dotq_e,0,dotq_e,1) (in the notation of Definition~) can be bounded in the same way as dddottextupfootnotesize ERR(dotq_e,0,dotq_e,1) is bounded by Lemma~, using assumption~ in place of assumption~. We can then repeat the argument from the hyperlinkp:induct.proofproof of Proposition~, with the following modifications: [--] item The base case is the bound on dddottextupERR(dotq_e,0,dotq_e,1), (as opposed to dddottextupfootnotesize ERR(dotq_e,0,dotq_e,1) in the original argument); item We apply Proposition~ conditional on the clause type bmL; and item We apply Proposition~ in place of Proposition~ and Corollary~. This modification gives that for any edge e in U, the variable-to-clause message error dddottextupERR(dotq_e,t-1,dotq_e,t) satisfies the bound , while the clause-to-variable message error widehattextupERR(hatq_e,t-1,hatq_e,t) satisfies the bound . Substituting these bounds into the hyperlinkp:nice.tree.lagrange.proofproof of Proposition~ gives the result.
nodes.raw_latex:
We must argue that the iterative construction of Definition~\ref{d:lagrange.defn.Augmented} converges to the desired weights $\Psi\equiv\Psi_{\mathscr{D}}(U;\omega_{\delta U})$ asserted by the proposition. The argument closely follows the outline of the proofs of
Propositions~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange} and \ref{p:induct}. For each leaf edge $e=(au)\in\delta U$, it is easy to check that at the initial stage $t=0$ we have
	\[
	\hat{q}_{e,0}(\sigma,\bm{L})
	\cong \pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_{p(e)})
	{}_{*}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)\,,
	\]
where $p(e)=(av)$ (as in \eqref{e:pi.DD.first.appearance}). On the other hand, for each $e\in\delta U$ we are given the edge marginal
	\[
	\Omega_e(\sigma,\bm{L})
	=\Omega_e(\bm{L})
	\Omega_e(\sigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	= \pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_{p(e)})
	\omega_{\bm{L},j}(\sigma)\,,
	\]
with $j=j(\bm{t}_e)$. Applying Step~I in Definition~\ref{d:lagrange.defn.Augmented} gives
	\[
	\dot{q}_{e,1}(\sigma,\bm{L})
	\cong \frac{\Omega_e(\sigma,\bm{L})}
		{\hat{q}_{e,0}(\sigma,\bm{L})}
	\cong \frac{\omega_{\bm{L},j}(\sigma)}
		{{}_{*}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)}\,.
	\]
It follows that $\dddot{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\dot{q}_{e,0},\dot{q}_{e,1})$
(in the notation of Definition~\ref{d:rel.error.notation.w.types})
can be bounded in the same way as
$\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(\dot{q}_{e,0},\dot{q}_{e,1})$
is bounded by Lemma~\ref{l:first.update.at.boundary}, using assumption~\eqref{e:apriori.assump.omega.Augmented} in place of assumption~\eqref{e:apriori.assump.omega}. We can then repeat the argument from the 
\hyperlink{p:induct.proof}{proof of Proposition~\ref{p:induct}}, with the following modifications:
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item The base case is the bound on
$\dddot{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\dot{q}_{e,0},\dot{q}_{e,1})$,
(as opposed to
$\dddot{\textup{\textsf{\footnotesize ERR}}}(\dot{q}_{e,0},\dot{q}_{e,1})$ in the original argument);
\item We apply 
Proposition~\ref{p:clause.update} conditional on the clause type $\bm{L}$; and
\item We apply Proposition~\ref{p:ctypes.varupdate}
in place of Proposition~\ref{p:var.update}
and Corollary~\ref{c:var.update}.
\end{enumerate}
This modification gives that for any edge $e$ in $U$, 
the variable-to-clause message error 
$\dddot{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\dot{q}_{e,t-1},\dot{q}_{e,t})$ satisfies the bound \eqref{e:induction.variable.error},
while the clause-to-variable message error 
$\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,t-1},\hat{q}_{e,t})$
 satisfies the bound \eqref{e:induction.clause.error}. Substituting these bounds into the 
\hyperlink{p:nice.tree.lagrange.proof}{proof of Proposition~\ref{p:nice.tree.lagrange}}
gives the result.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{l:relative.entropy}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be any finite set, and suppose
 $\nu(a)=\Lambda(a)/z$ is a probability measure over $a\in\mathcal{A}$. We then have
	\[
	\mathcal{H}(\mu\,|\,\nu)
	=\Bigg\{\mathcal{H}(\nu)- \mathcal{H}(\mu)\Bigg\}
	+\Big\langle \nu-\mu,\ln\Lambda\Big\rangle
	\]
for any probability measure $\mu$ over $\mathcal{A}$.

\begin{proof}
The relative entropy of $\mu$ with respect to $\nu$ is
	\[
	\mathcal{H}(\mu\,|\,\nu)
	= \bigg\langle \mu, \ln\frac{\mu}{\nu}\bigg\rangle
	= -\mathcal{H}(\mu) - \Big\langle\mu,\ln\nu\Big\rangle
	= -\mathcal{H}(\mu) - \bigg\langle\mu,\ln
		\frac{\Lambda}{z}\bigg\rangle
	= -\mathcal{H}(\mu) - \Big\langle\mu,\ln\Lambda\Big\rangle
		 + \ln z\,.
	\]
Applying this identity with $\mu=\nu$ gives
	\[
	0 = \mathcal{H}(\nu\,|\,\nu)
	= -\mathcal{H}(\nu) - \Big\langle\nu,\ln\Lambda\Big\rangle
		 + \ln z\,.
	\]
Subtracting the two expressions gives the conclusion.
\end{proof}

We also assume that the profile D expands on type-subsets, which by Lemma~ occurs with high probability. Now take any maximizer omega=omega(D) from --- we have not yet argued that it is unique. By the expansion condition and the a~priori estimate Proposition~ (and recalling from Definition~ that zeta=zeta_*/4), we know that omega satisfies the estimate on all (bmL,j) such that bmL(j) is a strongly non-defective edge type in the sense of Remark~. bemphProof that omega(D)=_*omega uniquely maximizes bmPsi=bmPsi_D,2 on bmI_0. Therefore the right-hand side of also vanishes: \[ max_nu' Bigg\ H(nu') : nu' in bmJ(U,omega_delta U) Bigg\ =max_mu' Bigg\ H(mu') : mu' in bmDelta(U;omega_U)Bigg\ \] Since the entropy function H is strictly concave on bmJ(U,omega_delta U)supseteq bmDelta(U;omega_U), this implies mu=nu where nonumber nu &=nu^textupop(U;omega_delta U) = textuparg\,max_nu' Bigg\ H(nu') : nu' in bmJ(U,omega_delta U)Bigg\\,,\\ mu &= mu(U;omega) =textuparg\,max_mu' Bigg\ H(mu') : mu' in bmDelta(U;omega_U)Bigg\\,. (Note that mu,nu are uniquely defined by the strict concavity of H.) Likewise, by Proposition~, if U is the depth-one neighborhood of any non-compound variable, then we must have mu=nu where nu=nu^textupop(U;omega_delta U) and mu=mu(U;omega_U) (the only difference being that these are now in the augmented pair coloring model). Indeed, let D(omega) = max_e Bigg\ textupdisc_e(omega) : textupe is niceBigg\\,, and let e_star be any nice edge that attains the maximum. \label{d:joins}
Let $U$ be a compound enclosure: recall that this means $U=U^\circ\cup\partial_\circ U$ where $\partial_\circ U$ is the boundary of perfect variables. Suppose that an internal variable $v_\star\in U^\circ$ is designated as the ``root.'' Let $\kappa_*$ be the defect buffer depth from Definition~\ref{d:j.defective}, and let $\mathcal{M} \equiv (\kappa_*)^{1/4}$. If a variable $u\in U^\circ$ lies at distance $\ell\mathcal{M}^2$ from $v_\star$ for some positive integer $\ell$, and moreover does not lie within distance $5\mathcal{M}^2$ of any non-nice variable, then we call $u$ a \bemph{terminal}. Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the set of all terminals in $U$. Let $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X})$ denote the set of all clauses $a$ in $U$ such that $a$ is the parent of a terminal variable (again, regarding $U$ as being rooted at $v_\star$). 
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item If $J=J^\circ\cup\partial J^\circ$ where $J^\circ$ is the maximal connected component of $U\setminus\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X})$ containing $v_\star$, and $\partial J^\circ\equiv\partial_\circ J$ is the set of variables in $U\setminus J^\circ$ at unit distance from $J^\circ$, then we call $J$ 
the \bemph{root join}.
\item If instead $J=J^\circ \cup(av) \cup (\partial(J^\circ\setminus v))$ where $J^\circ$ is a maximal connected component of $U\setminus\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X})$ not containing $v_\star$, $v$ is the terminal variable in $J^\circ$ that lies closest to $v_\star$, and $a\in\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X})$ is the parent clause of $v$, then we call $J$ a \bemph{non-root join}. We call $(av)$ the root edge of $J$.
\end{enumerate}
With a mild abuse of notation, we use $J$ to denote both the subset of variables and the induced subgraph of $U$. The join $J$ is termed \bemph{non-defective} if it does not intersect any defect. Otherwise we say that the join $J$ is \bemph{defective}. For any choice of $v_\star\in U^\circ$, this definition decomposes $U$ into joins. The joins naturally have a tree structure, where the root of the tree is the root join.

The subset partial_circ Usubseteq L U is the boundary of perfect variables, so these variables are not leaves in the full graph G. \label{r:boundaries.of.joins}
Let $\mathcal{L} U$ denote the set of all leaf variables of the compound enclosure $U$. The subset $\partial_\circ U\subseteq \mathcal{L} U$ is the boundary of perfect variables, so these variables are not leaves in the full graph $\mathscr{G}$. The variables in the complement $\mathcal{L} U\setminus U$ are leaves in the full graph $\mathscr{G}$ --- in particular, this means they are not nice (Definition~\ref{d:nice}), hence they are defective. 
We thus have two cases:
\begin{enumerate}[--]
\item If $J$ is a non-defective join, then all its leaf variables must belong either to $\partial_\circ U$ or to the terminal set $\mathcal{X}$. In this case we let $\delta J$ denote the set of edges incident to all leaf variables of $J$.
\item If $J$ is a defective join, then it cannot intersect $\partial_\circ U$: this is because any defect has at its boundary a buffer of nice variables of depth at least $\kappa_*$ (Definition~\ref{d:j.defective}), so the $\kappa_*$-neighborhood of any variable in $\partial_\circ U$ is nice.
In this case we let $\delta J\equiv \delta' J$.
\end{enumerate}
These two cases will be treated separately in the analysis below.

Given smashvecsigma, let smashvecvarsigmainS^E be defined by setting \[varsigma_eequiv SSPINwequivSPINwhite &if sigma_einsetSSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb and smashvecsigma_delta asetminus e contains at least two SPINcyan edges,\\ SSPINy&textupif sigma_e=SSPINy,\\ SSPINc&textupif sigma_einsetSSPINg,SSPINb.\\ \] Let smashvecupsiloninT^E be defined by setting \[upsilon_e = SPINvequivSPINviolet &textupif sigma_e=SSPINr and smashvecsigma_delta vsetminus e contains at least one SPINred edge,\\ sigma_einsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb &textupotherwise. \] Finally, let vecSigmainA^E be defined by setting \[ Sigma_e equiv SSPINwequivSPINwhite &if sigma_einsetSSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb and smashvecsigma_delta asetminus e contains at least two SPINcyan edges,\\ SPINvequivSPINviolet &if sigma_e=SSPINr and smashvecsigma_delta vsetminus e contains at least one SPINred edge,\\ sigma_einsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINg,SSPINb &otherwise. \] The new colors setSSPINw,SPINv indicate edges that are ``flexible'' in some sense: from a clause's perspective, SPINwhite indicates an edge that can be SPINyellow, SPINgreen, or SPINblue without violating the clause constraint. nodes.name: pair empirical measure in expanded alphabet
nodes.statement: Throughout the remainder of this section, on a (processed) textupk-textscsat instance G=(V,F,E), we denote pair colorings in the expanded alphabets as setlengthjot0pt smashvecsigma &equiv (smashvecsigma^1,smashvecsigma^2) inX^EtimesX^E\,,\\ smashvecvarsigma &equiv (smashvecvarsigma^1, smashvecvarsigma^2) in S^EtimesS^E\,,\\ smashvecupsilon &equiv (smashvecupsilon^1,smashvecupsilon^2) in T^EtimesT^E\,,\\ smashvecSigma &equiv (vecSigma^1,vecSigma^2) inA^EtimesA^E\,. As before, we use omegaequiv(omega_bmL,j)_bmL,j to denote the pair empirical measure, which we assume to be judicious in the sense of Definition~. We let bmvarpiequiv(bmvarpi_bmL,j)_bmL,j denote the pair empirical measure of (smashvecsigma,smashvecSigma), so that each entry bmvarpi_bmL,j is a probability measure over elements (sigma,Sigma)inX^2timesA^2. The marginal of bmvarpi on the X^2-coordinate is given by omega. Clearly, by the mappings of Definition~, each bmvarpi_bmL,j also induces a probability measure over (sigma,varsigma)inX^2timesS^2 and (sigma,upsilon)inX^2timesT^2. We let zeta_bmL,j denote the marginal law of varsigma under bmvarpi_bmL,j.
nodes.raw_latex:
Throughout the remainder of this section, on a (processed) $\textup{$k$-\textsc{sat}}$ instance $\mathscr{G}=(V,F,E)$,
we denote pair colorings in the expanded alphabets as
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	\smash{\vec{\sigma}} &\equiv (\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^1,\smash{\vec{\sigma}}^2)
	\in\mathscr{X}^E\times\mathscr{X}^E\,,\\
	\smash{\vec{\varsigma}}
	&\equiv (\smash{\vec{\varsigma}}^1,
		\smash{\vec{\varsigma}}^2)
	\in \mathscr{S}^E\times\mathscr{S}^E\,,\\
	\smash{\vec{\upsilon}}
	&\equiv
	(\smash{\vec{\upsilon}}^1,\smash{\vec{\upsilon}}^2)

Note that since omega is judicious and bmL is nice, \[ hatnu_bmL(SPINA^c) lesum_j=1^K omega_bmL,j(SSPINrSSPINr) lesum_i=1,2 sum_j=1^K (omega_bmL,j)^i(SSPINr) = 2sum_j=1^K _starhspace-1ptpi_bmL(j)(SSPINr) le Obigg( frack2^kbigg)\,. \] Let mu(smashvecsigma)equiv hatnu_bmL(smashvecsigma\,|\, SPINA) for smashvecsigmainsetSSPINr,SSPINy,SSPINc^2K. Let Omega be the maximizer of that is consistent with omega, and let bmvarpi_bmL,j be the resulting joint distribution of (sigma,upsilon). Then there exists an absolute constant epsilon_3 (depending only on epsilon_2) such that for every edge eindelta v(x) we have \[left. r bmvarpi_bmL,j( upsilon=SPINvSPINv \,|\, sigma=SSPINrSSPINr)\\ bmvarpi_bmL,j( upsilon^1=SPINv \,|\, sigma=SSPINrSSPINb )\\ bmvarpi_bmL,j( upsilon^2=SPINv \,|\,sigma=SSPINbSSPINr )\\ hspace-4pt right\ ge 1-frac12^kepsilon_3 \] for j=j(bmt) and all clause types bmL such that bmL(j)=bmt. Throughout the proof, epsilon_3 denotes a small positive number, whose value may change from one occurrence to the next, but ultimately is taken as an absolute constant that depends only on epsilon_2. bemphStep 1. Reduction to entropy maximization for a conditional measure. Note from that if we fix Omega_bmt, then we obtain separate entropy maximization problems over Omega_bmT and Omega_bmL. Let us therefore fix Omega_bmt=(textupaug_D(omega))_bmt, and consider the optimization over Omega_bmT. Let v denote a variable of type bmT, and write Omega_vequivOmega_bmT. By the method of Lagrange multipliers, the optimal Omega_v must take the form \[ Omega_vBig( (smashvecsigma,bmL)_delta vBig) = fracvarphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v)bmdotz prod_eindelta v hatq_e(sigma_e,bmL_e)\,,\] where each hatq_e is a probability measure over elements (sigma,bmL), chosen such that Omega_v has marginals Omega_eequivOmega_bmt for eindelta v and bmtequivbmt_e. The marginal of Omega_v on (smashvecsigma_delta v,bmL_e) is \[ Omega_v(smashvecsigma_delta v,bmL_e) = fracvarphi_v(smashvecsigma_delta v)bmdotz hatq_e(sigma_e,bmL_e) prod_e'indelta vsetminus e barq_e'(sigma_e')\,, \] where barq_e' denotes the marginal of hatq_e' on sigma_e' alone. Thus, for the purposes of this lemma, it suffices to estimate only dotnu_bmT(cdot\,|\,sigma_e). To this end, assume without loss x=SPIN+, and consider the event x_v=SPIN+SPIN+.
